----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Abñozfhw adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ubozçyq and fgyqðozçyq, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ç, oz, s, g, yq, l, m, è and some occurrences of w, e.g. yqf ubozçyq ynçñàksf (a beautiful garden), yqf ubozàn wgàdàdoz (a handsome man), yqfoz ubozànànoz abozàdàdoz (a beautiful woman), ànozàb ubozçyqi ozfabçfàxàb (the beautiful children), ànozàb ubozànànozàb àdçsàbgfàb (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -oz to the masculine form, e.g., ajñçfàk > ajñçfàkoz, ànozfàx > ànozfàxoz, àzozñàbçf > àzozñàbçfoz. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ozàn, -sàn, -gf, -ozf, -gàb or -çàb double their final consonant before adding -oz (e.g., hñyqozàn > hñyqozànànoz, ajozfàxsàn > ajozfàxsànànoz, ubgf > ubgffoz, çfhsozf > çfhsozffoz, ajñgàb > ajñgàbàboz, and ubçàb > ubçàbàboz).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -h change to -hwoz (e.g., ubànçfh > ubànçfhwoz); those ending in -ozyqñ or -ozyqi change to -ozyqàboz (e.g., àzñgàdozàxàxozyqñ > àzñgàdozàxàxozyqàboz, abyqñsozyqi > abyqñsozyqàboz), with the exception of the irregular ðsozyqi (old) whose feminine form is ðsozsànànoz; -aj changes to -ajyqoz (e.g., àngfaj > àngfajyqoz); -sab changes to -sðoz (e.g., çhàxsab > çhàxsðoz); -ozab changes to -èðoz (e.g., ubñozab > ubñèðoz); -ozñ changes to -èñoz (e.g., màxñçfajozñ > màxñçfajèñoz); -ozàx changes to -èàxoz (e.g., sfcyqsozàx > sfcyqsèàxoz); and adjectives ending in -gyq have a special form -gàn (becoming -gànànoz in feminine) that appears before ç, oz, s, g, yq, l, m, è and some occurrences of w, (e.g., abgyq/abgàn > abgànànoz, àdgyq/àdgàn > àdgànànoz).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -oz, it does not change in the feminine (cf. yqf wgàdàdoz ñshwoz 'a rich man' > yqfoz abozàdàdoz ñshwoz 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -àb to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., yngàns > yngànsàb, yngànsoz > yngànsozàb). If the basic form ends in -àb, -i, or -þ, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ubçàb > ubçàb, ajmfmñozyqi > ajmfmñozyqi, àkgyqi > àkgyqi), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Abñozfhw adjectives ending in -ozçyq take the ending -i in the masculine plural (e.g., fgyqðozçyq > fgyqðozçyqi). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -çàn, which normally change to -çyqi in the masculine plural (e.g., wsðozñfçàn > wsðozñfçyqi, hozfàxñçàn > hozfàxñçyqi), with only two exceptions: abçàxçàn > abçàxçànàb and fçðçàn > fçðçànàb which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: hozfàxñçànoz > hozfàxñçànozàb.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in ànoz ñgyqajoz ðsf (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are ubozçyq (beautiful), ubgf (good), ubñozab (brief), ajñçfàk (big/tall), ajñgàb (fat/large), abçyqi (false), wçyqàx (high), àngfaj (long), ubñozab (brief), ynozyqfoz (young), yngàns (pretty), àdçyqðçsàb (bad), àdozsànànozyqñ (best), fgyqðozçyq (new), àzozàxsàx (small), ðsozyqi (old); e.g., yqfoz abozàdàdoz ubozànànoz ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Abñozfhw, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Abñozfhw personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

------------------------

------------------------

         | 2nd (informal)   | àxyq
         | 2nd (formal)     | ðgyqàb
         | 3rd (masculine)  | sàn
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ozànànoz
         | 3rd (neutral)    | gf
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | fgyqàb
         | 2nd              | ðgyqàb
         | 3rd (masculine)  | sànàb
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ozànànozàb
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun ynoz occurs before ç, oz, s, g, yq, l, m, è, ê and some occurrences of w, it becomes yn'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Abñozfhw are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Abñozfhw is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) çðgsñ ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êàxñoz ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êàxñoz, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is çðgsñ. Forms of êàxñoz are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Abñozfhw, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Abñozfhw verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Abñozfhw verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -sàbàb- between the stem and the ending.

    In àzçñànçsozfàx, the stem àzçñàn- indicates that the verb is àzçñànozñ (to speak) and the ending -çsozfàx marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In absfsàbàbgfàb, the stem absf- indicates that the verb is absfsñ (to finish), the suffix -sàbàb- follows it, and the inflection -gfàb marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Abñozfhw they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    àzçñànozñ: ynoz àzçñànozñçsàb, àxyq àzçñànçàb, cyq'sànàb àzçñànçàbàbozfàx, cyqoz fgyqàb àzçñànsgfàb, àzçñànozþ...
    absfsñ: ynoz absfsñçsàb, ðgyqàb absfîàxozàb, cyq'sànàb absfsàbàbozfàx, absfsàb, cyqoz fgyqàb absfsàbàbsgfàb...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ðgyqàngsñ: ynoz ðozyqi, àxyq ðozyqi, sàn ðozyqàx, fgyqàb ðgyqàngfàb, ðgyqàb ðgyqànozþ, sànàb ðozyqànozfàx.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly çðgsñ, êàxñoz, çànànozñ and abçsñoz), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ozñ (with the exception of çànànozñ, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    çsàdozñ, ubçànçlozñ, hwçfàxozñ, ozfðglozñ, abozñàdozñ, àdçfajozñ, àzçàbàbozñ, àzçlozñ, àzñgàdozfozñ, ñozajçñàkozñ, etc.

        For example, for the verb àzçñànozñ, the stem is àzçñàn- and the ending is -ozñ.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -sñ whose present participle ends in -sàbàbçfàx:

    ubmfsñ, hgàdàzçàxsñ, àkmajyqozñàzsñ, abànozyqñsñ, ajñçfàksñ, wçïñ, sfðozàbàxsñ, àzgànsñ, ñgyqajsñ, ñyqajsñ, àbçànsñ, etc.

        For example, for the verb absfsñ, the stem is absf- and the ending is -sñ.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êàxñoz and çðgsñ, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. ynoz ñozajçñàkoz means "I watch".

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -oz and -àb, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "yqf abñyqsàx hgfabsàx", "yqfoz àzgsñoz hgfabsàxoz", "àkozàb abñyqsàxàb hgfabsàxàb", and "àkozàb àzgsñozàb hgfabsàxozàb."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -m for the 1st group verbs, or in -s for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -yq (ozfàxozfàkñoz ozfàxozfàkyq, ubgsñoz ubyq, ànsñoz ànyq, etc. and àbçðgsñ àbyq, ðgsñ ðyq, àzgyqðgsñ àzyq), -sàb (àdozàxàxñoz àdsàb, àzñozfàkñoz àzñsàb, etc.), -yqàb (sfhànyqñoz sfhànyqàb and ñozhànyqñoz ñozhànyqàb and only these verbs), -sàx (àdçyqàksñoz àdçyqàksàx, àksñoz àksàx, etc.), -àx (verbs in -sfàkñoz : àzozsfàkñoz àzozsfàx), -ozñàx (gyqðñsñ gyqðozñàx, hgyqðñsñ hgyqðozñàx, gababñsñ gababozñàx and àbgyqababñsñ àbgyqababozñàx), or ozyq (çðgsñ ozyq). 

*Compound Tenses

Abñozfhw compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either çðgsñ or êàxñoz) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Abñozfhw, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Abñozfhw. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either çðgsñ or êàxñoz in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "yn'çs àdçfajm" (I ate) or "sàn ozàbàx çññsðm" (He arrived). çðgsñ is used with most verbs, while êàxñoz is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, çðgsñ should be used by default.

WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Zotlàiñuj is subject-verb-object (SVO).

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Zotlàiñuj, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Zotlàiñuj has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Zotlàiñuj, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Zotlàiñuj article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is ràlà. For example, in the phrase "ràlà ñujfam" (the cat), ràlà shows that the noun ñujfam (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is ràfa. An example is "ràfa gàfaþðpyi" (the house), where ràfa shows that gàfaþðpyi (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ràlàð for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "ràlàð ñujfamð", the cats; "ràlàð gàfaþðpyið", the houses.)

In summary, ràlà is used with masculine singular nouns, ràfa with feminine singular nouns, and ràlàð with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Zotlàiñuj.

Before fa, là, þ, py, w, e, ñà, n and some occurrences of j, the singular masculine article ràlà becomes rà'.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -ð (e.g., gàfaþðpyi > gàfaþðpyið 'houses').

Øñuañæœbx has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Øñuañæœbx, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Øñuañæœbx article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is èañ. For example, in the phrase "èañ œbxén" (the cat), èañ shows that the noun œbxén (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is èé. An example is "èé péyœmfæ" (the house), where èé shows that péyœmfæ (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is èañœm for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "èañœm œbxénœm", the cats; "èañœm péyœmfæœm", the houses.)

In summary, èañ is used with masculine singular nouns, èé with feminine singular nouns, and èañœm with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Øñuañæœbx.

Before é, añ, y, f, er, em, àç, o and some occurrences of x, the singular masculine article èañ becomes è'.

NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Øñuañæœbx noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Øñuañæœbx nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -œm (e.g., péyœmfæ > péyœmfæœm 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -éer and -añer take the ending -àd instead of -œm (e.g., nereméer > nereméeràd 'pipes', œçañer > œçañeràd 'games'), except for the nouns èéækéer, œméuuéer, êæañer, and vèañer which form their plural by adding -œm (e.g., êæañer > êæañerœm 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -fer form their plural with -àd. These are þañæfer, œbéyèèfer, xyvfer, vyœçfer, êfer, œbxfer, and œçferœçfer (e.g., þañæfer > þañæferàd 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -fer, such as vyœmfer or nufer, follow the regular plural pattern and take -œm (e.g., nufer > nuferœm 'holes').

Nouns that end in -œm, -àd or -àr in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., èé œbufyàd 'the cross' > èañœm œbufyàd 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -éè typically change to -éeràd in the plural (e.g., œçferuæéè > œçferuæéeràd 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -éè are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -œm instead. These are véè, œbéè, œbéuæéôéè, œbxéœbéè, øñañœmnyôéè, uàçœbynéè, œmañuôéè and uàçþéè (e.g., èañ øñañœmnyôéè > èañœm øñañœmnyôéèœm).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -éyè change to -éeràd in the plural. Examples of this pattern include véyè, œbfuéyè, àçpéyè, œmferêyuéyè, nuéôéyè, and ôynuéyè (e.g., ôynuéyè > ôynuéeràd 'stained glass windows'). However, some -éyè nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -œm, notably uéyè, énnyuéyè, œbxéækéyè, kàçnéyè, þferôañuæéyè and êfunéyè (e.g., eræ uéyè > kañœm uéyèœm 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Øñuañæœbx are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Øñuañæœbx adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like vañéer and æferôañéer, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with é, añ, y, f, er, em, àç, o and some occurrences of x, e.g. eræ vañéer œçéukyæ (a beautiful garden), eræ vañè xfppañ (a handsome man), eræañ vañèèañ øñañppañ (a beautiful woman), èañœm vañéeràd añæøñéænœm (the beautiful children), èañœm vañèèañœm péyœmfæœm (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -añ to the masculine form, e.g., þuéæk > þuéækañ, èañæn > èañænañ, êañuœméæ > êañuœméæañ. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. If an adjective's basic form ends in -añ, it does not change in the feminine (cf. eræ xfppañ uyœbxañ 'a rich man' > eræañ øñañppañ uyœbxañ 'a rich woman').

In Øñuañæœbx, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents.

-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Øñuañæœbx are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Øñuañæœbx is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) éôfyu ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of ednuañ ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is ednuañ, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is éôfyu. Forms of ednuañ are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Øñuañæœbx, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Øñuañæœbx verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Øñuañæœbx verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -yœmœm- between the stem and the ending.

    In êéuèéyañæn, the stem êéuè- indicates that the verb is êéuèañu (to speak) and the ending -éyañæn marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In øñyæyœmœmfæœm, the stem øñyæ- indicates that the verb is øñyæyu (to finish), the suffix -yœmœm- follows it, and the inflection -fæœm marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Øñuañæœbx they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    êéuèañu: œçañ êéuèañuéyœm, ner êéuèéœm, ader'yèœm êéuèéœmœmañæn, aderañ æferœm êéuèyfæœm, êéuèañàr...
    øñyæyu: œçañ øñyæyuéyœm, ôferœm øñyæînañœm, ader'yèœm øñyæyœmœmañæn, øñyæyœm, aderañ æferœm øñyæyœmœmyfæœm...

    ôferèfyu: œçañ ôañeràd, ner ôañeràd, yè ôañern, æferœm ôferèfæœm, ôferœm ôferèañàr, yèœm ôañerèañæn.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly éôfyu, ednuañ, éèèañu and øñéyuañ), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -añu (with the exception of éèèañu, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

* Number
As in English, Ekenygéwàryv nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -ub (e.g., çécàwubybéw > çécàwubybéwub 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -écs and -ygs take the ending -f instead of -ub (e.g., ukspécs > ukspécsf 'pipes', qygs > qygsf 'games'), except for the nouns èécéwébécs, ubécenenécs, ejéwygs, and éjèygs which form their plural by adding -ub (e.g., ejéwygs > ejéwygsub 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -ybs form their plural with -f. These are zygéwybs, àrécàwèèybs, yvàwéjybs, éjàwqybs, ejybs, àryvybs, and qybsqybs (e.g., zygéwybs > zygéwybsf 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -ybs, such as éjàwubybs or ukenybs, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ub (e.g., ukenybs > ukenybsub 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ub, -f or -uw in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., èéc àrenybàwf 'the cross' > èygub àrenybàwf 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -écè typically change to -écsf in the plural (e.g., qybsenéwécè > qybsenéwécsf 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -écè are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ub instead. These are éjécè, àrécè, àrécenéwécxécè, àryvécàrécè, mygubukàwxécè, endàràwukécè, ubygenxécè and endzécè (e.g., èyg mygubukàwxécè > èygub mygubukàwxécèub).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -écàwè change to -écsf in the plural. Examples of this pattern include éjécàwè, àrybenécàwè, dçécàwè, ubybsejàwenécàwè, ukenécxécàwè, and xàwukenécàwè (e.g., xàwukenécàwè > xàwukenécsf 'stained glass windows'). However, some -écàwè nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ub, notably enécàwè, écukukàwenécàwè, àryvécéwébécàwè, ébdukécàwè, zybsxygenéwécàwè and ejybenukécàwè (e.g., séw enécàwè > ébygub enécàwèub 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ekenygéwàryv are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ekenygéwàryv adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like éjygécs and éwybsxygécs, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with éc, yg, àw, yb, s, p, d, àv and some occurrences of yv, e.g. séw éjygécs qécenébàwéw (a beautiful garden), séw éjygè yvybççyg (a handsome man), séwyg éjygèèyg mygççyg (a beautiful woman), èygub éjygécsf ygéwmécéwukub (the beautiful children), èygub éjygèèygub çécàwubybéwub (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -yg to the masculine form, e.g., zenécéwéb > zenécéwébyg, èygéwuk > èygéwukyg, ejygenubécéw > ejygenubécéwyg. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ygè, -àwè, -ybéw, -ygéw, -ybub or -écub double their final consonant before adding -yg (e.g., àrensygè > àrensygèèyg, zygéwukàwè > zygéwukàwèèyg, éjybéw > éjybéwéwyg, écéwàràwygéw > écéwàràwygéwéwyg, zenybub > zenybububyg, and éjécub > éjécububyg).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -àr change to -àryvyg (e.g., éjèécéwàr > éjèécéwàryvyg); those ending in -ygsen or -ygsf change to -ygsubyg (e.g., ejenybçygukukygsen > ejenybçygukukygsubyg, msenàwygsf > msenàwygsubyg), with the exception of the irregular xàwygsf (old) whose feminine form is xàwygàwèèyg; -z changes to -zsyg (e.g., èybéwz > èybéwzsyg); -àwm changes to -àwxyg (e.g., écàrukàwm > écàrukàwxyg); -ygm changes to -àvxyg (e.g., éjenygm > éjenàvxyg); -ygen changes to -àvenyg (e.g., dukenécéwzygen > dukenécéwzàvenyg); -yguk changes to -àvukyg (e.g., àwéwhsàwyguk > àwéwhsàwàvukyg); and adjectives ending in -ybs have a special form -ybè (becoming -ybèèyg in feminine) that appears before éc, yg, àw, yb, s, p, d, àv and some occurrences of yv, (e.g., mybs/mybè > mybèèyg, çybs/çybè > çybèèyg).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -yg, it does not change in the feminine (cf. séw yvybççyg enàwàryvyg 'a rich man' > séwyg mygççyg enàwàryvyg 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ub to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., qybèàw > qybèàwub, qybèàwyg > qybèàwygub). If the basic form ends in -ub, -f, or -uw, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., éjécub > éjécub, zdéwdenygsf > zdéwdenygsf, ébybsf > ébybsf), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ekenygéwàryv adjectives ending in -ygécs take the ending -f in the masculine plural (e.g., éwybsxygécs > éwybsxygécsf). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -écè, which normally change to -écsf in the masculine plural (e.g., yvàwxygenéwécè > yvàwxygenéwécsf, àrygéwukenécè > àrygéwukenécsf), with only two exceptions: mécukécè > mécukécèub and éwécxécè > éwécxécèub which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: àrygéwukenécèyg > àrygéwukenécèygub.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in èyg enybszyg xàwéw (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are éjygécs (beautiful), éjybéw (good), éjenygm (brief), zenécéwéb (big/tall), zenybub (fat/large), mécsf (false), yvécsuk (high), èybéwz (long), éjenygm (brief), qygséwyg (young), qybèàw (pretty), çécsxécàwub (bad), çygàwèèygsen (best), éwybsxygécs (new), ejygukàwuk (small), xàwygsf (old); e.g., séwyg mygççyg éjygèèyg ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ekenygéwàryv, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ekenygéwàryv personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | qyg
         | 2nd (informal)   | uks
         | 2nd (formal)     | xybsub
         | 3rd (masculine)  | àwè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ygèèyg
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ybéw
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | éwybsub
         | 2nd              | xybsub
         | 3rd (masculine)  | àwèub
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ygèèygub
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun qyg occurs before éc, yg, àw, yb, s, p, d, àv, ê and some occurrences of yv, it becomes q'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ekenygéwàryv are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ekenygéwàryv is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) écxybàwen ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êukenyg ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êukenyg, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is écxybàwen. Forms of êukenyg are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ekenygéwàryv, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ekenygéwàryv verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ekenygéwàryv verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -àwubub- between the stem and the ending.

    In ejécenèécàwygéwuk, the stem ejécenè- indicates that the verb is ejécenèygen (to speak) and the ending -écàwygéwuk marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In màwéwàwububybéwub, the stem màwéw- indicates that the verb is màwéwàwen (to finish), the suffix -àwubub- follows it, and the inflection -ybéwub marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ekenygéwàryv they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ejécenèygen: qyg ejécenèygenécàwub, uks ejécenèécub, hs'àwèub ejécenèécububygéwuk, hsyg éwybsub ejécenèàwybéwub, ejécenèyguw...
    màwéwàwen: qyg màwéwàwenécàwub, xybsub màwéwîukygub, hs'àwèub màwéwàwububygéwuk, màwéwàwub, hsyg éwybsub màwéwàwububàwybéwub...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    xybsèybàwen: qyg xygsf, uks xygsf, àwè xygsuk, éwybsub xybsèybéwub, xybsub xybsèyguw, àwèub xygsèygéwuk.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly écxybàwen, êukenyg, écèèygen and mécàwenyg), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ygen (with the exception of écèèygen, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    écàwçygen, éjécèécpygen, àryvécéwukygen, ygéwxybpygen, mygençygen, çécéwzygen, ejécububygen, ejécpygen, ejenybçygéwygen, enygzécenébygen, etc.

        For example, for the verb ejécenèygen, the stem is ejécenè- and the ending is -ygen.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -àwen whose present participle ends in -àwububécéwuk:

    éjdéwàwen, àrybçejécukàwen, ébdzsygenejàwen, mèygsenàwen, zenécéwébàwen, yvécïen, àwéwxygubukàwen, ejybèàwen, enybszàwen, enszàwen, ubécèàwen, etc.

        For example, for the verb màwéwàwen, the stem is màwéw- and the ending is -àwen.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êukenyg and écxybàwen, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. qyg enygzécenébyg means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

**Imperfect indicative

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -yg and -ub, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "séw mensàwuk àrybéwmàwuk", "séwyg ejybàwenyg àrybéwmàwukyg", "ébygub mensàwukub àrybéwmàwukub", and "ébygub ejybàwenygub àrybéwmàwukygub."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -d for the 1st group verbs, or in -àw for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -s (ygéwukygéwébenyg ygéwukygéwébs, éjybàwenyg éjs, èàwenyg ès, etc. and ubécxybàwen ubs, xybàwen xs, ejybsxybàwen ejs), -àwub (çygukukenyg çàwub, ejenygéwébenyg ejenàwub, etc.), -sub (àwéwàrèsenyg àwéwàrèsub and enygàrèsenyg enygàrèsub and only these verbs), -àwuk (çécsébàwenyg çécsébàwuk, ébàwenyg ébàwuk, etc.), -uk (verbs in -àwéwébenyg : ejygàwéwébenyg ejygàwéwuk), -ygenuk (ybsxenàwen ybsxygenuk, àrybsxenàwen àrybsxygenuk, ybmmenàwen ybmmygenuk and ubybsmmenàwen ubybsmmygenuk), or ygs (écxybàwen ygs). 

*Compound Tenses

WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Cyplàgrao is subject-verb-object (SVO).

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Cyplàgrao, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
Cyplàgrao has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Cyplàgrao, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Cyplàgrao article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is rilà. For example, in the phrase "rilà raoruw" (the cat), rilà shows that the noun raoruw (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is riru. An example is "riru qyrurànynug" (the house), where riru shows that qyrurànynug (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is rilàny for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "rilàny raoruwny", the cats; "rilàny qyrurànynugny", the houses.)

In summary, rilà is used with masculine singular nouns, riru with feminine singular nouns, and rilàny with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Cyplàgrao.

Before ru, là, rà, nu, su, b, f, qà and some occurrences of o, the singular masculine article rilà becomes ri'.

* Gender
Every Cyplàgrao noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Cyplàgrao nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -ny (e.g., qyrurànynug > qyrurànynugny 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -rusu and -làsu take the ending -è instead of -ny (e.g., wsubrusu > wsubrusuè 'pipes', sàlàsu > sàlàsuè 'games'), except for the nouns rirugçrusu, nyrupprusu, laglàsu, and vrilàsu which form their plural by adding -ny (e.g., laglàsu > laglàsuny 'tires').

----------

The most common word order in Unixbàfagw is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    s’vekixb uxb agwkagkuxvè (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Unixbàfagw, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Unixbàfagw has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Unixbàfagw, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Unixbàfagw article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is uxb. For example, in the phrase "uxb agwvè" (the cat), uxb shows that the noun agwvè (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is uxv. An example is "uxv àxvoékàf" (the house), where uxv shows that àxvoékàf (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is uxbé for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "uxbé agwvèé", the cats; "uxbé àxvoékàfé", the houses.)

In summary, uxb is used with masculine singular nouns, uxv with feminine singular nouns, and uxbé with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Unixbàfagw.

Before v, b, o, k, ax, ç, àn, ug and some occurrences of w, the singular masculine article uxb becomes ux'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Unixbàfagw noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Unixbàfagw nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -é (e.g., àxvoékàf > àxvoékàfé 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -vax and -bax take the ending -af instead of -é (e.g., èaxçvax > èaxçvaxaf 'pipes', sbax > sbaxaf 'games'), except for the nouns uxvàfevax, évixixvax, ulàfbax, and cuxbax which form their plural by adding -é (e.g., ulàfbax > ulàfbaxé 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -kax form their plural with -af. These are ihbàfkax, agvouxuxkax, wockax, coskax, ulkax, agwkax, and skaxskax (e.g., ihbàfkax > ihbàfkaxaf 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -kax, such as coékax or èixkax, follow the regular plural pattern and take -é (e.g., èixkax > èixkaxé 'holes').

Nouns that end in -é, -af or -uq in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., uxv agixkoaf 'the cross' > uxbé agixkoaf 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -vux typically change to -vaxaf in the plural (e.g., skaxixàfvux > skaxixàfvaxaf 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -vux are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -é instead. These are cvux, agvux, agvixàfvtvux, agwvagvux, mbéèotvux, ixànagoèvux, ébixtvux and ixànihvux (e.g., uxb mbéèotvux > uxbé mbéèotvuxé).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -voux change to -vaxaf in the plural. Examples of this pattern include cvoux, agkixvoux, ànàxvoux, ékaxuloixvoux, èixvtvoux, and toèixvoux (e.g., toèixvoux > toèixvaxaf 'stained glass windows'). However, some -voux nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -é, notably ixvoux, vèèoixvoux, agwvàfevoux, eànèvoux, ihkaxtbixàfvoux and ulkixèvoux (e.g., axàf ixvoux > ebé ixvouxé 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Unixbàfagw are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Unixbàfagw adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like cbvax and àfkaxtbvax, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with v, b, o, k, ax, ç, àn, ug and some occurrences of w, e.g. axàf cbvax svixeoàf (a beautiful garden), axàf cbux wkàxàxb (a handsome man), axàfb cbuxuxb mbàxàxb (a beautiful woman), uxbé cbvaxaf bàfmvàfèé (the beautiful children), uxbé cbuxuxbé àxvoékàfé (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -b to the masculine form, e.g., ihixvàfe > ihixvàfeb, uxbàfè > uxbàfèb, ulbixévàf > ulbixévàfb. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -bux, -oux, -kàf, -bàf, -ké or -vé double their final consonant before adding -b (e.g., agixaxbux > agixaxbuxuxb, ihbàfèoux > ihbàfèouxuxb, ckàf > ckàfàfb, vàfagobàf > vàfagobàfàfb, ihixké > ihixkééb, and cvé > cvééb).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -ag change to -agwb (e.g., cuxvàfag > cuxvàfagwb); those ending in -baxix or -baxaf change to -baxéb (e.g., ulixkàxbèèbaxix > ulixkàxbèèbaxéb, maxixobaxaf > maxixobaxéb), with the exception of the irregular tobaxaf (old) whose feminine form is tobouxuxb; -ih changes to -ihaxb (e.g., uxkàfih > uxkàfihaxb); -om changes to -otb (e.g., vagèom > vagèotb); -bm changes to -ugtb (e.g., cixbm > cixugtb); -bix changes to -ugixb (e.g., ànèixvàfihbix > ànèixvàfihugixb); -bè changes to -ugèb (e.g., oàfpaxobè > oàfpaxougèb); and adjectives ending in -kax have a special form -kux (becoming -kuxuxb in feminine) that appears before v, b, o, k, ax, ç, àn, ug and some occurrences of w, (e.g., mkax/mkux > mkuxuxb, àxkax/àxkux > àxkuxuxb).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -b, it does not change in the feminine (cf. axàf wkàxàxb ixoagwb 'a rich man' > axàfb mbàxàxb ixoagwb 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -é to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., skuxo > skuxoé, skuxob > skuxobé). If the basic form ends in -é, -af, or -uq, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., cvé > cvé, ihànàfànixbaxaf > ihànàfànixbaxaf, ekaxaf > ekaxaf), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Unixbàfagw adjectives ending in -bvax take the ending -af in the masculine plural (e.g., àfkaxtbvax > àfkaxtbvaxaf). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -vux, which normally change to -vaxaf in the masculine plural (e.g., wotbixàfvux > wotbixàfvaxaf, agbàfèixvux > agbàfèixvaxaf), with only two exceptions: mvèvux > mvèvuxé and àfvtvux > àfvtvuxé which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: agbàfèixvuxb > agbàfèixvuxbé.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in uxb ixkaxihb toàf (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are cbvax (beautiful), ckàf (good), cixbm (brief), ihixvàfe (big/tall), ihixké (fat/large), mvaxaf (false), wvaxè (high), uxkàfih (long), cixbm (brief), sbaxàfb (young), skuxo (pretty), àxvaxtvoé (bad), àxbouxuxbaxix (best), àfkaxtbvax (new), ulbèoè (small), tobaxaf (old); e.g., axàfb mbàxàxb cbuxuxb ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Unixbàfagw, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Unixbàfagw personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | sb
         | 2nd (informal)   | èax
         | 2nd (formal)     | tkaxé
         | 3rd (masculine)  | oux
         | 3rd (feminine)   | buxuxb
         | 3rd (neutral)    | kàf
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | àfkaxé
         | 2nd              | tkaxé
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ouxé
         | 3rd (feminine)   | buxuxbé
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun sb occurs before v, b, o, k, ax, ç, àn, ug, ê and some occurrences of w, it becomes s'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Unixbàfagw are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Unixbàfagw is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) vtkoix ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êèixb ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êèixb, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is vtkoix. Forms of êèixb are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Unixbàfagw, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Unixbàfagw verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Unixbàfagw verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -oéé- between the stem and the ending.

    In ulvixuxvobàfè, the stem ulvixux- indicates that the verb is ulvixuxbix (to speak) and the ending -vobàfè marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In moàfoéékàfé, the stem moàf- indicates that the verb is moàfoix (to finish), the suffix -oéé- follows it, and the inflection -kàfé marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Unixbàfagw they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ulvixuxbix: sb ulvixuxbixvoé, èax ulvixuxvé, pax'ouxé ulvixuxvéébàfè, paxb àfkaxé ulvixuxokàfé, ulvixuxbuq...
    moàfoix: sb moàfoixvoé, tkaxé moàfîèbé, pax'ouxé moàfoéébàfè, moàfoé, paxb àfkaxé moàfoééokàfé...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    tkaxuxkoix: sb tbaxaf, èax tbaxaf, oux tbaxè, àfkaxé tkaxuxkàfé, tkaxé tkaxuxbuq, ouxé tbaxuxbàfè.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly vtkoix, êèixb, vuxuxbix and mvoixb), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -bix (with the exception of vuxuxbix, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    voàxbix, cvuxvçbix, agwvàfèbix, bàftkçbix, mbixàxbix, àxvàfihbix, ulvéébix, ulvçbix, ulixkàxbàfbix, ixbihvixebix, etc.

        For example, for the verb ulvixuxbix, the stem is ulvixux- and the ending is -bix.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -oix whose present participle ends in -oéévàfè:

    cànàfoix, agkàxulvèoix, eànihaxbixuloix, muxbaxixoix, ihixvàfeoix, wvïix, oàftbéèoix, ulkuxoix, ixkaxihoix, ixaxihoix, évuxoix, etc.

        For example, for the verb moàfoix, the stem is moàf- and the ending is -oix.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êèixb and vtkoix, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. sb ixbihvixeb means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -bix (all verbs of the first group): -b, -bé, -b, -kàfé, -buq, -bàfè.
    Verbs ending in -oix (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -oé, -oé, -oè, -oéékàfé, -oéébuq, -oéébàfè. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -ixb (part of the third group): -é, -é, - , -kàfé, -buq, -bàfè.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "sb ixbihvixevoé" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -bix suffix, e.g., ixbihvixebix -> ixbihvixe-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -oix suffix plus the -oéé suffix, e.g., agwkoéoix -> agwkoéoéé-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -voé, -voé, -voè, -okàfé, -obuq, -vobàfè.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb vtkoix. They are always regular: -vo, -vé, -v, -kàfé, -buq, -kàfè.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -b and -é, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "axàf mixaxoè agkàfmoè", "axàfb ulkoixb agkàfmoèb", "ebé mixaxoèé agkàfmoèé", and "ebé ulkoixbé agkàfmoèbé."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -àn for the 1st group verbs, or in -o for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -ax (bàfèbàfeixb bàfèbàfeax, ckoixb cax, uxoixb uxax, etc. and évtkoix éax, tkoix tax, ulkaxtkoix ulax), -oé (àxbèèixb àxoé, ulixbàfeixb ulixoé, etc.), -axé (oàfaguxaxixb oàfaguxaxé and ixbaguxaxixb ixbaguxaxé and only these verbs), -oè (àxvaxeoixb àxvaxeoè, eoixb eoè, etc.), -è (verbs in -oàfeixb : ulboàfeixb ulboàfè), -bixè (kaxtixoix kaxtbixè, agkaxtixoix agkaxtbixè, kmmixoix kmmbixè and ékaxmmixoix ékaxmmbixè), or bax (vtkoix bax). 

*Compound Tenses

Unixbàfagw compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either vtkoix or êèixb) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Unixbàfagw, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Unixbàfagw. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either vtkoix or êèixb in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "s'vo àxvàfihàn" (I ate) or "oux béè vixixotàn" (He arrived). vtkoix is used with most verbs, while êèixb is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, vtkoix should be used by default.

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is ej. For example, in the phrase "ej rnélifà" (the cat), ej shows that the noun rnélifà (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is eli. An example is "eli vlioydèlé" (the house), where eli shows that vlioydèlé (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ejy for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "ejy rnélifày", the cats; "ejy vlioydèléy", the houses.)

In summary, ej is used with masculine singular nouns, eli with feminine singular nouns, and ejy with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Fuçèjlérné.

Before li, j, o, dè, dà, xé, q, nè and some occurrences of né, the singular masculine article ej becomes e'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Fuçèjlérné noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Fuçèjlérné nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -y (e.g., vlioydèlé > vlioydèléy 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -lidà and -jdà take the ending -k instead of -y (e.g., fàdàxélidà > fàdàxélidàk 'pipes', sjdà > sjdàk 'games'), except for the nouns elilétlidà, yliçèçèlidà, làléjdà, and pejdà which form their plural by adding -y (e.g., làléjdà > làléjdày 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -dèdà form their plural with -k. These are hjlédèdà, rlioeedèdà, néopdèdà, posdèdà, làdèdà, rnédèdà, and sdèdàsdèdà (e.g., hjlédèdà > hjlédèdàk 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -dèdà, such as poydèdà or fàçèdèdà, follow the regular plural pattern and take -y (e.g., fàçèdèdà > fàçèdèdày 'holes').

Nouns that end in -y, -k or -z in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., eli rçèdèok 'the cross' > ejy rçèdèok 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -lie typically change to -lidàk in the plural (e.g., sdèdàçèlélie > sdèdàçèlélidàk 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -lie are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -y instead. These are plie, rlie, rliçèlélialie, rnélirlie, fujyfàoalie, çèqrofàlie, yjçèalie and çèqhlie (e.g., ej fujyfàoalie > ejy fujyfàoaliey).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -lioe change to -lidàk in the plural. Examples of this pattern include plioe, rdèçèlioe, qvlioe, ydèdàlàoçèlioe, fàçèlialioe, and aofàçèlioe (e.g., aofàçèlioe > aofàçèlidàk 'stained glass windows'). However, some -lioe nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -y, notably çèlioe, lifàfàoçèlioe, rnélilétlioe, tqfàlioe, hdèdàajçèlélioe and làdèçèfàlioe (e.g., dàlé çèlioe > tjy çèlioey 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Fuçèjlérné are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Fuçèjlérné adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like pjlidà and lédèdàajlidà, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with li, j, o, dè, dà, xé, q, nè and some occurrences of né, e.g. dàlé pjlidà sliçètolé (a beautiful garden), dàlé pje nédèvvj (a handsome man), dàléj pjeej fujvvj (a beautiful woman), ejy pjlidàk jléfuliléfày (the beautiful children), ejy pjeejy vlioydèléy (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -j to the masculine form, e.g., hçèlilét > hçèlilétj, ejléfà > ejléfàj, làjçèylilé > làjçèyliléj. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -je, -oe, -dèlé, -jlé, -dèy or -liy double their final consonant before adding -j (e.g., rçèdàje > rçèdàjeej, hjléfàoe > hjléfàoeej, pdèlé > pdèléléj, lilérojlé > lilérojléléj, hçèdèy > hçèdèyyj, and pliy > pliyyj).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -r change to -rnéj (e.g., pelilér > pelilérnéj); those ending in -jdàçè or -jdàk change to -jdàyj (e.g., làçèdèvjfàfàjdàçè > làçèdèvjfàfàjdàyj, fudàçèojdàk > fudàçèojdàyj), with the exception of the irregular aojdàk (old) whose feminine form is aojoeej; -h changes to -hdàj (e.g., edèléh > edèléhdàj); -ofu changes to -oaj (e.g., lirfàofu > lirfàoaj); -jfu changes to -nèaj (e.g., pçèjfu > pçènèaj); -jçè changes to -nèçèj (e.g., qfàçèliléhjçè > qfàçèliléhnèçèj); -jfà changes to -nèfàj (e.g., olécédàojfà > olécédàonèfàj); and adjectives ending in -dèdà have a special form -dèe (becoming -dèeej in feminine) that appears before li, j, o, dè, dà, xé, q, nè and some occurrences of né, (e.g., fudèdà/fudèe > fudèeej, vdèdà/vdèe > vdèeej).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -j, it does not change in the feminine (cf. dàlé nédèvvj çèornéj 'a rich man' > dàléj fujvvj çèornéj 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -y to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., sdèeo > sdèeoy, sdèeoj > sdèeojy). If the basic form ends in -y, -k, or -z, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., pliy > pliy, hqléqçèjdàk > hqléqçèjdàk, tdèdàk > tdèdàk), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Fuçèjlérné adjectives ending in -jlidà take the ending -k in the masculine plural (e.g., lédèdàajlidà > lédèdàajlidàk). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -lie, which normally change to -lidàk in the masculine plural (e.g., néoajçèlélie > néoajçèlélidàk, rjléfàçèlie > rjléfàçèlidàk), with only two exceptions: fulifàlie > fulifàliey and lélialie > lélialiey which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: rjléfàçèliej > rjléfàçèliejy.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in ej çèdèdàhj aolé (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are pjlidà (beautiful), pdèlé (good), pçèjfu (brief), hçèlilét (big/tall), hçèdèy (fat/large), fulidàk (false), nélidàfà (high), edèléh (long), pçèjfu (brief), sjdàléj (young), sdèeo (pretty), vlidàalioy (bad), vjoeejdàçè (best), lédèdàajlidà (new), làjfàofà (small), aojdàk (old); e.g., dàléj fujvvj pjeej ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Fuçèjlérné, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Fuçèjlérné personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | sj
         | 2nd (informal)   | fàdà
         | 2nd (formal)     | adèdày
         | 3rd (masculine)  | oe
         | 3rd (feminine)   | jeej
         | 3rd (neutral)    | dèlé
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | lédèdày
         | 2nd              | adèdày
         | 3rd (masculine)  | oey
         | 3rd (feminine)   | jeejy
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun sj occurs before li, j, o, dè, dà, xé, q, nè, ê and some occurrences of né, it becomes s'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Fuçèjlérné are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Fuçèjlérné is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) liadèoçè ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êfàçèj ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êfàçèj, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is liadèoçè. Forms of êfàçèj are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Fuçèjlérné, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Fuçèjlérné verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Fuçèjlérné verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -oyy- between the stem and the ending.

    In làliçèeliojléfà, the stem làliçèe- indicates that the verb is làliçèejçè (to speak) and the ending -liojléfà marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In fuoléoyydèléy, the stem fuolé- indicates that the verb is fuoléoçè (to finish), the suffix -oyy- follows it, and the inflection -dèléy marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Fuçèjlérné they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    làliçèejçè: sj làliçèejçèlioy, fàdà làliçèeliy, cédà'oey làliçèeliyyjléfà, cédàj lédèdày làliçèeodèléy, làliçèejz...
    fuoléoçè: sj fuoléoçèlioy, adèdày fuoléîfàjy, cédà'oey fuoléoyyjléfà, fuoléoy, cédàj lédèdày fuoléoyyodèléy...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    adèdàedèoçè: sj ajdàk, fàdà ajdàk, oe ajdàfà, lédèdày adèdàedèléy, adèdày adèdàejz, oey ajdàejléfà.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly liadèoçè, êfàçèj, lieejçè and fulioçèj), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -jçè (with the exception of lieejçè, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    liovjçè, plielixéjçè, rnéliléfàjçè, jléadèxéjçè, fujçèvjçè, vliléhjçè, làliyyjçè, làlixéjçè, làçèdèvjléjçè, çèjhliçètjçè, etc.

        For example, for the verb làliçèejçè, the stem is làliçèe- and the ending is -jçè.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -oçè whose present participle ends in -oyyliléfà:

    pqléoçè, rdèvlàlifàoçè, tqhdàjçèlàoçè, fuejdàçèoçè, hçèlilétoçè, néliïçè, oléajyfàoçè, làdèeoçè, çèdèdàhoçè, çèdàhoçè, ylieoçè, etc.

        For example, for the verb fuoléoçè, the stem is fuolé- and the ending is -oçè.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êfàçèj and liadèoçè, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. sj çèjhliçètj means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -jçè (all verbs of the first group): -j, -jy, -j, -dèléy, -jz, -jléfà.
    Verbs ending in -oçè (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -oy, -oy, -ofà, -oyydèléy, -oyyjz, -oyyjléfà. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -çèj (part of the third group): -y, -y, - , -dèléy, -jz, -jléfà.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "sj çèjhliçètlioy" means "I was watching".

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -j and -y, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "dàlé fuçèdàofà rdèléfuofà", "dàléj làdèoçèj rdèléfuofàj", "tjy fuçèdàofày rdèléfuofày", and "tjy làdèoçèjy rdèléfuofàjy."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -q for the 1st group verbs, or in -o for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -dà (jléfàjlétçèj jléfàjlétdà, pdèoçèj pdà, eoçèj edà, etc. and yliadèoçè ydà, adèoçè adà, làdèdàadèoçè làdà), -oy (vjfàfàçèj voy, làçèjlétçèj làçèoy, etc.), -dày (oléredàçèj oléredày and çèjredàçèj çèjredày and only these verbs), -ofà (vlidàtoçèj vlidàtofà, toçèj tofà, etc.), -fà (verbs in -olétçèj : làjolétçèj làjoléfà), -jçèfà (dèdàaçèoçè dèdàajçèfà, rdèdàaçèoçè rdèdàajçèfà, dèfufuçèoçè dèfufujçèfà and ydèdàfufuçèoçè ydèdàfufujçèfà), or jdà (liadèoçè jdà). 

*Compound Tenses

Fuçèjlérné compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either liadèoçè or êfàçèj) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Fuçèjlérné, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past
