----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Éxèlylcélç adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like eylàjéz and ciézypylàjéz, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with àj, yl, ug, i, éz, a, q, f and some occurrences of ç, e.g. ézc eylàjéz kàjèlàgugc (a beautiful garden), ézc eyls çirryl (a handsome man), ézcyl eylssyl dylrryl (a beautiful woman), sylàx eylàjézàv ylcdàjcygàx (the beautiful children), sylàx eylssylàx ràjugàxicàx (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -yl to the masculine form, e.g., àlèlàjcàg > àlèlàjcàgyl, sylcyg > sylcygyl, oylèlàxàjc > oylèlàxàjcyl. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -yls, -ugs, -ic, -ylc, -iàx or -àjàx double their final consonant before adding -yl (e.g., élèlézyls > élèlézylssyl, àlylcygugs > àlylcygugssyl, eic > eiccyl, àjcélugylc > àjcélugylccyl, àlèliàx > àlèliàxàxyl, and eàjàx > eàjàxàxyl).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -él change to -élçyl (e.g., esàjcél > esàjcélçyl); those ending in -ylézèl or -ylézàv change to -ylézàxyl (e.g., oèlirylygygylézèl > oèlirylygygylézàxyl, dézèlugylézàv > dézèlugylézàxyl), with the exception of the irregular ypugylézàv (old) whose feminine form is ypugylugssyl; -àl changes to -àlézyl (e.g., sicàl > sicàlézyl); -ugd changes to -ugypyl (e.g., àjélygugd > àjélygugypyl); -yld changes to -fypyl (e.g., eèlyld > eèlfypyl); -ylèl changes to -fèlyl (e.g., qygèlàjcàlylèl > qygèlàjcàlfèlyl); -ylyg changes to -fygyl (e.g., ugctézugylyg > ugctézugfygyl); and adjectives ending in -iéz have a special form -is (becoming -issyl in feminine) that appears before àj, yl, ug, i, éz, a, q, f and some occurrences of ç, (e.g., diéz/dis > dissyl, riéz/ris > rissyl).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -yl, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ézc çirryl èlugélçyl 'a rich man' > ézcyl dylrryl èlugélçyl 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -àx to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., kisug > kisugàx, kisugyl > kisugylàx). If the basic form ends in -àx, -àv, or -w, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., eàjàx > eàjàx, àlqcqèlylézàv > àlqcqèlylézàv, àgiézàv > àgiézàv), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Éxèlylcélç adjectives ending in -ylàjéz take the ending -àv in the masculine plural (e.g., ciézypylàjéz > ciézypylàjézàv). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -àjs, which normally change to -àjézàv in the masculine plural (e.g., çugypylèlcàjs > çugypylèlcàjézàv, élylcygèlàjs > élylcygèlàjézàv), with only two exceptions: dàjygàjs > dàjygàjsàx and càjypàjs > càjypàjsàx which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: élylcygèlàjsyl > élylcygèlàjsylàx.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in syl èliézàlyl ypugc (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are eylàjéz (beautiful), eic (good), eèlyld (brief), àlèlàjcàg (big/tall), àlèliàx (fat/large), dàjézàv (false), çàjézyg (high), sicàl (long), eèlyld (brief), kylézcyl (young), kisug (pretty), ràjézypàjugàx (bad), rylugssylézèl (best), ciézypylàjéz (new), oylygugyg (small), ypugylézàv (old); e.g., ézcyl dylrryl eylssyl ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Éxèlylcélç, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Éxèlylcélç personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | kyl
         | 2nd (informal)   | ygéz
         | 2nd (formal)     | ypiézàx
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ugs
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ylssyl
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ic
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ciézàx
         | 2nd              | ypiézàx
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ugsàx
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ylssylàx
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun kyl occurs before àj, yl, ug, i, éz, a, q, f, ê and some occurrences of ç, it becomes k'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Éxèlylcélç are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Éxèlylcélç is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) àjypiugèl ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êygèlyl ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êygèlyl, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is àjypiugèl. Forms of êygèlyl are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Éxèlylcélç, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Éxèlylcélç verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Éxèlylcélç verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -ugàxàx- between the stem and the ending.

    In oàjèlsàjugylcyg, the stem oàjèls- indicates that the verb is oàjèlsylèl (to speak) and the ending -àjugylcyg marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In dugcugàxàxicàx, the stem dugc- indicates that the verb is dugcugèl (to finish), the suffix -ugàxàx- follows it, and the inflection -icàx marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Éxèlylcélç they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    oàjèlsylèl: kyl oàjèlsylèlàjugàx, ygéz oàjèlsàjàx, téz'ugsàx oàjèlsàjàxàxylcyg, tézyl ciézàx oàjèlsugicàx, oàjèlsylw...
    dugcugèl: kyl dugcugèlàjugàx, ypiézàx dugcîygylàx, téz'ugsàx dugcugàxàxylcyg, dugcugàx, tézyl ciézàx dugcugàxàxugicàx...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ypiézsiugèl: kyl ypylézàv, ygéz ypylézàv, ugs ypylézyg, ciézàx ypiézsicàx, ypiézàx ypiézsylw, ugsàx ypylézsylcyg.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly àjypiugèl, êygèlyl, àjssylèl and dàjugèlyl), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ylèl (with the exception of àjssylèl, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    àjugrylèl, eàjsàjaylèl, élçàjcygylèl, ylcypiaylèl, dylèlrylèl, ràjcàlylèl, oàjàxàxylèl, oàjaylèl, oèlirylcylèl, èlylàlàjèlàgylèl, etc.

        For example, for the verb oàjèlsylèl, the stem is oàjèls- and the ending is -ylèl.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ugèl whose present participle ends in -ugàxàxàjcyg:

    eqcugèl, éliroàjygugèl, àgqàlézylèlougèl, dsylézèlugèl, àlèlàjcàgugèl, çàjïèl, ugcypylàxygugèl, oisugèl, èliézàlugèl, èlézàlugèl, àxàjsugèl, etc.

        For example, for the verb dugcugèl, the stem is dugc- and the ending is -ugèl.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êygèlyl and àjypiugèl, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. kyl èlylàlàjèlàgyl means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -ylèl (all verbs of the first group): -yl, -ylàx, -yl, -icàx, -ylw, -ylcyg.
    Verbs ending in -ugèl (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -ugàx, -ugàx, -ugyg, -ugàxàxicàx, -ugàxàxylw, -ugàxàxylcyg. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -èlyl (part of the third group): -àx, -àx, - , -icàx, -ylw, -ylcyg.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "kyl èlylàlàjèlàgàjugàx" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -ylèl suffix, e.g., èlylàlàjèlàgylèl -> èlylàlàjèlàg-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -ugèl suffix plus the -ugàxàx suffix, e.g., élçiugàxugèl -> élçiugàxugàxàx-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -àjugàx, -àjugàx, -àjugyg, -ugicàx, -ugylw, -àjugylcyg.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb àjypiugèl. They are always regular: -àjug, -àjàx, -àj, -icàx, -ylw, -icyg.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

        kyl élçiugàxugèlàjug ('I will choose'), ygéz èlylàlàjèlàgylèlàjàx ('you will watch'), ylssyl àxièlygugèlàj ('she will exit'), ciézàx ygèlàjypàjugssylèlicàx ('we will work'), ypiézàx èliézàlugèlylw ('you will blush'), ugsàx oàjèlygugèlicyg ('they will leave').

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -yl and -àx, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ézc dèlézugyg élicdugyg", "ézcyl oiugèlyl élicdugygyl", "àgylàx dèlézugygàx élicdugygàx", and "àgylàx oiugèlylàx élicdugygylàx."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -q for the 1st group verbs, or in -ug for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -éz (ylcygylcàgèlyl ylcygylcàgéz, eiugèlyl eéz, sugèlyl séz, etc. and àxàjypiugèl àxéz, ypiugèl ypéz, oiézypiugèl oéz), -ugàx (rylygygèlyl rugàx, oèlylcàgèlyl oèlugàx, etc.), -ézàx (ugcélsézèlyl ugcélsézàx and èlylélsézèlyl èlylélsézàx and only these verbs), -ugyg (ràjézàgugèlyl ràjézàgugyg, àgugèlyl àgugyg, etc.), -yg (verbs in -ugcàgèlyl : oylugcàgèlyl oylugcyg), -ylèlyg (iézypèlugèl iézypylèlyg, éliézypèlugèl éliézypylèlyg, iddèlugèl iddylèlyg and àxiézddèlugèl àxiézddylèlyg), or yléz (àjypiugèl yléz). 

*Compound Tenses

Éxèlylcélç compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either àjypiugèl or êygèlyl) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Éxèlylcélç, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Éxèlylcélç. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either àjypiugèl or êygèlyl in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "k'àjug ràjcàlq" (I ate) or "ugs ylàxyg àjèlèlugypq" (He arrived). àjypiugèl is used with most verbs, while êygèlyl is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, àjypiugèl should be used by default.

2nd person     | ygéz àjàx élçiugàxug               | ypiézàx àjypylw élçiugàxug

Verbs in Igikégquol are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)

Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Igikégquol is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) irwogçik ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êotikég ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êotikég, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is irwogçik. Forms of êotikég are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Igikégquol, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Igikégquol verb is called the verb's conjugation.

Igikégquol verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Igikégquol they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

Beginning of Zecrebujog Grammar Book Excerpts

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Zecrebujog is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    jè’wénujécre nere jogjéjojénewéfe (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Zecrebujog, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Zecrebujog has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Zecrebujog, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Zecrebujog article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is nere. For example, in the phrase "nere jogwéfe" (the cat), nere shows that the noun jogwéfe (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is newé. An example is "newé vwéapèjébu" (the house), where newé shows that vwéapèjébu (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is nerepè for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "nerepè jogwéfepè", the cats; "nerepè vwéapèjébupè", the houses.)

In summary, nere is used with masculine singular nouns, newé with feminine singular nouns, and nerepè with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Zecrebujog.

Before wé, re, a, jé, à, ju, ç, y and some occurrences of g, the singular masculine article nere becomes ne'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Zecrebujog noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Zecrebujog nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -pè (e.g., vwéapèjébu > vwéapèjébupè 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -wéà and -reà take the ending -wu instead of -pè (e.g., feàjuwéà > feàjuwéàwu 'pipes', jèreà > jèreàwu 'games'), except for the nouns newébunuwéà, pèwéccwéà, ibureà, and mnereà which form their plural by adding -pè (e.g., ibureà > ibureàpè 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -jéà form their plural with -wu. These are zorebujéà, jowéanenejéà, gamjéà, majèjéà, ijéà, jogjéà, and jèjéàjèjéà (e.g., zorebujéà > zorebujéàwu 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -jéà, such as mapèjéà or fecjéà, follow the regular plural pattern and take -pè (e.g., fecjéà > fecjéàpè 'holes').

Nouns that end in -pè, -wu or -t in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., newé jocjéawu 'the cross' > nerepè jocjéawu 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -wéne typically change to -wéàwu in the plural (e.g., jèjéàcbuwéne > jèjéàcbuwéàwu 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -wéne are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -pè instead. These are mwéne, jowéne, jowécbuwéféwéne, jogwéjowéne, zerepèfeaféwéne, cçjoafewéne, pèrecféwéne and cçzowéne (e.g., nere zerepèfeaféwéne > nerepè zerepèfeaféwénepè).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -wéane change to -wéàwu in the plural. Examples of this pattern include mwéane, jojécwéane, çvwéane, pèjéàiacwéane, fecwéféwéane, and féafecwéane (e.g., féafecwéane > féafecwéàwu 'stained glass windows'). However, some -wéane nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -pè, notably cwéane, wéfefeacwéane, jogwébunuwéane, nuçfewéane, zojéàférecbuwéane and ijécfewéane (e.g., àbu cwéane > nurepè cwéanepè 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Zecrebujog are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Zecrebujog adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like mrewéà and bujéàférewéà, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with wé, re, a, jé, à, ju, ç, y and some occurrences of g, e.g. àbu mrewéà jèwécnuabu (a beautiful garden), àbu mrene gjévvre (a handsome man), àbure mrenenere zerevvre (a beautiful woman), nerepè mrewéàwu rebuzewébufepè (the beautiful children), nerepè mrenenerepè vwéapèjébupè (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -re to the masculine form, e.g., zocwébunu > zocwébunure, nerebufe > nerebufere, irecpèwébu > irecpèwébure. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -rene, -ane, -jébu, -rebu, -jépè or -wépè double their final consonant before adding -re (e.g., jocàrene > jocàrenenere, zorebufeane > zorebufeanenere, mjébu > mjébubure, wébujoarebu > wébujoarebubure, zocjépè > zocjépèpère, and mwépè > mwépèpère).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -jo change to -jogre (e.g., mnewébujo > mnewébujogre); those ending in -reàc or -reàwu change to -reàpère (e.g., icjévrefefereàc > icjévrefefereàpère, zeàcareàwu > zeàcareàpère), with the exception of the irregular féareàwu (old) whose feminine form is féareanenere; -zo changes to -zoàre (e.g., nejébuzo > nejébuzoàre); -aze changes to -afére (e.g., wéjofeaze > wéjofeafére); -reze changes to -yfére (e.g., mcreze > mcyfére); -rec changes to -ycre (e.g., çfecwébuzorec > çfecwébuzoycre); -refe changes to -yfere (e.g., abubèàarefe > abubèàayfere); and adjectives ending in -jéà have a special form -jéne (becoming -jénenere in feminine) that appears before wé, re, a, jé, à, ju, ç, y and some occurrences of g, (e.g., zejéà/zejéne > zejénenere, vjéà/vjéne > vjénenere).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -re, it does not change in the feminine (cf. àbu gjévvre cajogre 'a rich man' > àbure zerevvre cajogre 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -pè to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., jèjénea > jèjéneapè, jèjéneare > jèjénearepè). If the basic form ends in -pè, -wu, or -t, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., mwépè > mwépè, zoçbuçcreàwu > zoçbuçcreàwu, nujéàwu > nujéàwu), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Zecrebujog adjectives ending in -rewéà take the ending -wu in the masculine plural (e.g., bujéàférewéà > bujéàférewéàwu). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -wéne, which normally change to -wéàwu in the masculine plural (e.g., gaférecbuwéne > gaférecbuwéàwu, jorebufecwéne > jorebufecwéàwu), with only two exceptions: zewéfewéne > zewéfewénepè and buwéféwéne > buwéféwénepè which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: jorebufecwénere > jorebufecwénerepè.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in nere cjéàzore féabu (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are mrewéà (beautiful), mjébu (good), mcreze (brief), zocwébunu (big/tall), zocjépè (fat/large), zewéàwu (false), gwéàfe (high), nejébuzo (long), mcreze (brief), jèreàbure (young), jèjénea (pretty), vwéàféwéapè (bad), vreanenereàc (best), bujéàférewéà (new), irefeafe (small), féareàwu (old); e.g., àbure zerevvre mrenenere ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Zecrebujog, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Zecrebujog personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | jère
         | 2nd (informal)   | feà
         | 2nd (formal)     | féjéàpè
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ane
         | 3rd (feminine)   | renenere
         | 3rd (neutral)    | jébu
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | bujéàpè
         | 2nd              | féjéàpè
         | 3rd (masculine)  | anepè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | renenerepè
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun jère occurs before wé, re, a, jé, à, ju, ç, y, ê and some occurrences of g, it becomes jè'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Zecrebujog are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Zecrebujog is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) wéféjéac ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êfecre ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êfecre, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is wéféjéac. Forms of êfecre are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Zecrebujog, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Zecrebujog verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Zecrebujog verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -apèpè- between the stem and the ending.

    In iwécnewéarebufe, the stem iwécne- indicates that the verb is iwécnerec (to speak) and the ending -wéarebufe marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In zeabuapèpèjébupè, the stem zeabu- indicates that the verb is zeabuac (to finish), the suffix -apèpè- follows it, and the inflection -jébupè marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Zecrebujog they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    iwécnerec: jère iwécnerecwéapè, feà iwécnewépè, bèà'anepè iwécnewépèpèrebufe, bèàre bujéàpè iwécneajébupè, iwécneret...
    zeabuac: jère zeabuacwéapè, féjéàpè zeabuîferepè, bèà'anepè zeabuapèpèrebufe, zeabuapè, bèàre bujéàpè zeabuapèpèajébupè...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    féjéànejéac: jère féreàwu, feà féreàwu, ane féreàfe, bujéàpè féjéànejébupè, féjéàpè féjéàneret, anepè féreànerebufe.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly wéféjéac, êfecre, wénenerec and zewéacre), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -rec (with the exception of wénenerec, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    wéavrec, mwénewéjurec, jogwébuferec, rebuféjéjurec, zerecvrec, vwébuzorec, iwépèpèrec, iwéjurec, icjévreburec, crezowécnurec, etc.

        For example, for the verb iwécnerec, the stem is iwécne- and the ending is -rec.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ac whose present participle ends in -apèpèwébufe:

    mçbuac, jojéviwéfeac, nuçzoàreciac, zenereàcac, zocwébunuac, gwéïc, abuférepèfeac, ijéneac, cjéàzoac, càzoac, pèwéneac, etc.

        For example, for the verb zeabuac, the stem is zeabu- and the ending is -ac.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êfecre and wéféjéac, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. jère crezowécnure means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -rec (all verbs of the first group): -re, -repè, -re, -jébupè, -ret, -rebufe.
    Verbs ending in -ac (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -apè, -apè, -afe, -apèpèjébupè, -apèpèret, -apèpèrebufe. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -cre (part of the third group): -pè, -pè, - , -jébupè, -ret, -rebufe.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "jère crezowécnuwéapè" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -rec suffix, e.g., crezowécnurec -> crezowécnu-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -ac suffix plus the -apèpè suffix, e.g., jogjéapèac -> jogjéapèapèpè-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -wéapè, -wéapè, -wéafe, -ajébupè, -aret, -wéarebufe.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb wéféjéac. They are always regular: -wéa, -wépè, -wé, -jébupè, -ret, -jébufe.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

        jère jogjéapèacwéa ('I will choose'), feà crezowécnurecwépè ('you will watch'), renenere pèjécfeacwé ('she will exit'), bujéàpè fecwéféwéanenerecjébupè ('we will work'), féjéàpè cjéàzoacret ('you will blush'), anepè iwécfeacjébufe ('they will leave').

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -re and -pè, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "àbu zecàafe jojébuzeafe", "àbure ijéacre jojébuzeafere", "nurepè zecàafepè jojébuzeafepè", and "nurepè ijéacrepè jojébuzeaferepè."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -ç for the 1st group verbs, or in -a for the 2nd group verbs.     uv’itzhpj ogj usàhushogitx (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Igpjlusà, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Igpjlusà has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Igpjlusà, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Igpjlusà article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is ogj. For example, in the phrase "ogj usàitx" (the cat), ogj shows that the noun usàitx (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is ogit. An example is "ogit oritféhl" (the house), where ogit shows that oritféhl (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ogjé for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "ogjé usàitxé", the cats; "ogjé oritféhlé", the houses.)

In summary, ogj is used with masculine singular nouns, ogit with feminine singular nouns, and ogjé with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Igpjlusà.

Before it, j, f, h, uq, k, w, è and some occurrences of à, the singular masculine article ogj becomes og'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Igpjlusà noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Igpjlusà nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -é (e.g., oritféhl > oritféhlé 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -ituq and -juq take the ending -ir instead of -é (e.g., xuqkituq > xuqkituqir 'pipes', uvjuq > uvjuqir 'games'), except for the nouns ogitlzituq, éitppituq, dljuq, and asogjuq which form their plural by adding -é (e.g., dljuq > dljuqé 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -huq form their plural with -ir. These are açjlhuq, usitfogoghuq, àfashuq, asfuvhuq, dhuq, usàhuq, and uvhuquvhuq (e.g., açjlhuq > açjlhuqir 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -huq, such as asféhuq or xphuq, follow the regular plural pattern and take -é (e.g., xphuq > xphuqé 'holes').

Nouns that end in -é, -ir or -m in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., ogit usphfir 'the cross' > ogjé usphfir 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -itog typically change to -ituqir in the plural (e.g., uvhuqplitog > uvhuqplituqir 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -itog are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -é instead. These are asitog, usitog, usitpliteitog, usàitusitog, igjéxfeitog, pwusfxitog, éjpeitog and pwaçitog (e.g., ogj igjéxfeitog > ogjé igjéxfeitogé).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -itfog change to -ituqir in the plural. Examples of this pattern include asitfog, ushpitfog, woritfog, éhuqdfpitfog, xpiteitfog, and efxpitfog (e.g., efxpitfog > efxpituqir 'stained glass windows'). However, some -itfog nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -é, notably pitfog, itxxfpitfog, usàitlzitfog, zwxitfog, açhuqejplitfog and dhpxitfog (e.g., uql pitfog > zjé pitfogé 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Igpjlusà are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Igpjlusà adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like asjituq and lhuqejituq, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with it, j, f, h, uq, k, w, è and some occurrences of à, e.g. uql asjituq uvitpzfl (a beautiful garden), uql asjog àhororj (a handsome man), uqlj asjogogj igjororj (a beautiful woman), ogjé asjituqir jligitlxé (the beautiful children), ogjé asjogogjé oritféhlé (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -j to the masculine form, e.g., açpitlz > açpitlzj, ogjlx > ogjlxj, djpéitl > djpéitlj. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -jog, -fog, -hl, -jl, -hé or -ité double their final consonant before adding -j (e.g., uspuqjog > uspuqjogogj, açjlxfog > açjlxfogogj, ashl > ashllj, itlusfjl > itlusfjllj, açphé > açphééj, and asité > asitééj).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -us change to -usàj (e.g., asogitlus > asogitlusàj); those ending in -juqp or -juqir change to -juqéj (e.g., dphorjxxjuqp > dphorjxxjuqéj, iguqpfjuqir > iguqpfjuqéj), with the exception of the irregular efjuqir (old) whose feminine form is efjfogogj; -aç changes to -açuqj (e.g., oghlaç > oghlaçuqj); -fig changes to -fej (e.g., itusxfig > itusxfej); -jig changes to -èej (e.g., aspjig > aspèej); -jp changes to -èpj (e.g., wxpitlaçjp > wxpitlaçèpj); -jx changes to -èxj (e.g., flyguqfjx > flyguqfèxj); and adjectives ending in -huq have a special form -hog (becoming -hogogj in feminine) that appears before it, j, f, h, uq, k, w, è and some occurrences of à, (e.g., ighuq/ighog > ighogogj, orhuq/orhog > orhogogj).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -j, it does not change in the feminine (cf. uql àhororj pfusàj 'a rich man' > uqlj igjororj pfusàj 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -é to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., uvhogf > uvhogfé, uvhogfj > uvhogfjé). If the basic form ends in -é, -ir, or -m, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., asité > asité, açwlwpjuqir > açwlwpjuqir, zhuqir > zhuqir), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Igpjlusà adjectives ending in -jituq take the ending -ir in the masculine plural (e.g., lhuqejituq > lhuqejituqir). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -itog, which normally change to -ituqir in the masculine plural (e.g., àfejplitog > àfejplituqir, usjlxpitog > usjlxpituqir), with only two exceptions: igitxitog > igitxitogé and liteitog > liteitogé which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: usjlxpitogj > usjlxpitogjé.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in ogj phuqaçj efl (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are asjituq (beautiful), ashl (good), aspjig (brief), açpitlz (big/tall), açphé (fat/large), igituqir (false), àituqx (high), oghlaç (long), aspjig (brief), uvjuqlj (young), uvhogf (pretty), orituqeitfé (bad), orjfogogjuqp (best), lhuqejituq (new), djxfx (small), efjuqir (old); e.g., uqlj igjororj asjogogj ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Igpjlusà, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Igpjlusà personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | uvj
         | 2nd (informal)   | xuq
         | 2nd (formal)     | ehuqé
         | 3rd (masculine)  | fog
         | 3rd (feminine)   | jogogj
         | 3rd (neutral)    | hl
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | lhuqé
         | 2nd              | ehuqé
         | 3rd (masculine)  | fogé
         | 3rd (feminine)   | jogogjé
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun uvj occurs before it, j, f, h, uq, k, w, è, ê and some occurrences of à, it becomes uv'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Igpjlusà are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Igpjlusà is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) itehfp ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êxpj ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êxpj, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is itehfp. Forms of êxpj are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Igpjlusà, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Igpjlusà verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Igpjlusà verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -féé- between the stem and the ending.

    In ditpogitfjlx, the stem ditpog- indicates that the verb is ditpogjp (to speak) and the ending -itfjlx marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In igflfééhlé, the stem igfl- indicates that the verb is igflfp (to finish), the suffix -féé- follows it, and the inflection -hlé marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Igpjlusà they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ditpogjp: uvj ditpogjpitfé, xuq ditpogité, yguq'fogé ditpogitééjlx, yguqj lhuqé ditpogfhlé, ditpogjm...
    igflfp: uvj igflfpitfé, ehuqé igflîxjé, yguq'fogé igflfééjlx, igflfé, yguqj lhuqé igflfééfhlé...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ehuqoghfp: uvj ejuqir, xuq ejuqir, fog ejuqx, lhuqé ehuqoghlé, ehuqé ehuqogjm, fogé ejuqogjlx.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly itehfp, êxpj, itogogjp and igitfpj), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -jp (with the exception of itogogjp, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    itforjp, asitogitkjp, usàitlxjp, jlehkjp, igjporjp, oritlaçjp, ditééjp, ditkjp, dphorjljp, pjaçitpzjp, etc.

        For example, for the verb ditpogjp, the stem is ditpog- and the ending is -jp.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -fp whose present participle ends in -fééitlx:

    aswlfp, ushorditxfp, zwaçuqjpdfp, igogjuqpfp, açpitlzfp, àitïp, flejéxfp, dhogfp, phuqaçfp, puqaçfp, éitogfp, etc.

        For example, for the verb igflfp, the stem is igfl- and the ending is -fp.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êxpj and itehfp, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. uvj pjaçitpzj means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -jp (all verbs of the first group): -j, -jé, -j, -hlé, -jm, -jlx.
    Verbs ending in -fp (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -fé, -fé, -fx, -fééhlé, -fééjm, -fééjlx. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -pj (part of the third group): -é, -é, - , -hlé, -jm, -jlx.
    
    Example:

2nd person     | xuq pjaçitpzjé        | ehuqé pjaçitpzjm

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "uvj pjaçitpzitfé" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -jp suffix, e.g., pjaçitpzjp -> pjaçitpz-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -fp suffix plus the -féé suffix, e.g., usàhféfp -> usàhféféé-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -itfé, -itfé, -itfx, -fhlé, -fjm, -itfjlx.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb itehfp. They are always regular: -itf, -ité, -it, -hlé, -jm, -hlx.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -j and -é, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "uql igpuqfx ushligfx", "uqlj dhfpj ushligfxj", "zjé igpuqfxé ushligfxé", and "zjé dhfpjé ushligfxjé."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -w for the 1st group verbs, or in -f for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -uq (jlxjlzpj jlxjlzuq, ashfpj asuq, ogfpj oguq, etc. and éitehfp éuq, ehfp euq, dhuqehfp duq), -fé (orjxxpj orfé, dpjlzpj dpfé, etc.), -uqé (flusoguqpj flusoguqé and pjusoguqpj pjusoguqé and only these verbs), -fx (orituqzfpj orituqzfx, zfpj zfx, etc.), -x (verbs in -flzpj : djflzpj djflx), -jpx (huqepfp huqejpx, ushuqepfp ushuqejpx, higigpfp higigjpx and éhuqigigpfp éhuqigigjpx), or juq (itehfp juq). 

*Compound Tenses

Igpjlusà compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either itehfp or êxpj) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Igpjlusà, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Igpjlusà. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either itehfp or êxpj in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "uv'itf oritlaçw" (I ate) or "fog jéx itppfew" (He arrived). itehfp is used with most verbs, while êxpj is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, itehfp should be used by default.

As in English, Batizpafçi nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -ta (e.g., kmamitawpa > kmamitawpata 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -mag and -zg take the ending -qà instead of -ta (e.g., çugvamag > çugvamagqà 'pipes', czg > czgqà 'games'), except for the nouns tèmapapèmag, tamatitimag, hpazg, and vitèzg which form their plural by adding -ta (e.g., hpazg > hpazgta 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -wg form their plural with -qà. These are dizpawg, fmamitètèwg, çimiviwg, vimicwg, hwg, fçiwg, and cwgcwg (e.g., dizpawg > dizpawgqà 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -wg, such as vimitawg or çutiwg, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ta (e.g., çutiwg > çutiwgta 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ta, -qà or -e in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., tèma ftiwmiqà 'the cross' > tèzta ftiwmiqà 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -matè typically change to -magqà in the plural (e.g., cwgtipamatè > cwgtipamagqà 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -matè are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ta instead. These are vimatè, fmatè, fmatipamasmatè, fçimafmatè, baztaçumismatè, tibifmiçumatè, taztismatè and tibidimatè (e.g., tèz baztaçumismatè > tèzta baztaçumismatèta).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -mamitè change to -magqà in the plural. Examples of this pattern include vimamitè, fwtimamitè, bikmamitè, tawghmitimamitè, çutimasmamitè, and smiçutimamitè (e.g., smiçutimamitè > smiçutimagqà 'stained glass windows'). However, some -mamitè nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ta, notably timamitè, maçuçumitimamitè, fçimapapèmamitè, pèbiçumamitè, diwgsztipamamitè and hwtiçumamitè (e.g., gpa timamitè > pèzta timamitèta 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Batizpafçi are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Batizpafçi adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like vizmag and pawgszmag, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ma, z, mi, w, g, va, bi, çè and some occurrences of çi, e.g. gpa vizmag cmatipèmipa (a beautiful garden), gpa viztè çiwkkz (a handsome man), gpaz viztètèz bazkkz (a beautiful woman), tèzta vizmagqà zpabamapaçuta (the beautiful children), tèzta viztètèzta kmamitawpata (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -z to the masculine form, e.g., ditimapapè > ditimapapèz, tèzpaçu > tèzpaçuz, hztitamapa > hztitamapaz. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ztè, -mitè, -wpa, -zpa, -wta or -mata double their final consonant before adding -z (e.g., ftigztè > ftigztètèz, dizpaçumitè > dizpaçumitètèz, viwpa > viwpapaz, mapafmizpa > mapafmizpapaz, ditiwta > ditiwtataz, and vimata > vimatataz).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -f change to -fçiz (e.g., vitèmapaf > vitèmapafçiz); those ending in -zgti or -zgqà change to -zgtaz (e.g., htiwkzçuçuzgti > htiwkzçuçuzgtaz, bagtimizgqà > bagtimizgtaz), with the exception of the irregular smizgqà (old) whose feminine form is smizmitètèz; -di changes to -digz (e.g., tèwpadi > tèwpadigz); -miba changes to -misz (e.g., mafçumiba > mafçumisz); -zba changes to -çèsz (e.g., vitizba > vitiçèsz); -zti changes to -çètiz (e.g., biçutimapadizti > biçutimapadiçètiz); -zçu changes to -çèçuz (e.g., mipaxugmizçu > mipaxugmiçèçuz); and adjectives ending in -wg have a special form -wtè (becoming -wtètèz in feminine) that appears before ma, z, mi, w, g, va, bi, çè and some occurrences of çi, (e.g., bawg/bawtè > bawtètèz, kwg/kwtè > kwtètèz).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -z, it does not change in the feminine (cf. gpa çiwkkz timifçiz 'a rich man' > gpaz bazkkz timifçiz 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ta to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., cwtèmi > cwtèmita, cwtèmiz > cwtèmizta). If the basic form ends in -ta, -qà, or -e, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., vimata > vimata, dibipabitizgqà > dibipabitizgqà, pèwgqà > pèwgqà), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Batizpafçi adjectives ending in -zmag take the ending -qà in the masculine plural (e.g., pawgszmag > pawgszmagqà). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -matè, which normally change to -magqà in the masculine plural (e.g., çimisztipamatè > çimisztipamagqà, fzpaçutimatè > fzpaçutimagqà), with only two exceptions: bamaçumatè > bamaçumatèta and pamasmatè > pamasmatèta which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: fzpaçutimatèz > fzpaçutimatèzta.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in tèz tiwgdiz smipa (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are vizmag (beautiful), viwpa (good), vitizba (brief), ditimapapè (big/tall), ditiwta (fat/large), bamagqà (false), çimagçu (high), tèwpadi (long), vitizba (brief), czgpaz (young), cwtèmi (pretty), kmagsmamita (bad), kzmitètèzgti (best), pawgszmag (new), hzçumiçu (small), smizgqà (old); e.g., gpaz bazkkz viztètèz ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Batizpafçi, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Batizpafçi personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | cz
         | 2nd (informal)   | çug
         | 2nd (formal)     | swgta
         | 3rd (masculine)  | mitè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ztètèz
         | 3rd (neutral)    | wpa
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | pawgta
         | 2nd              | swgta
         | 3rd (masculine)  | mitèta
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ztètèzta
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun cz occurs before ma, z, mi, w, g, va, bi, çè, ê and some occurrences of çi, it becomes c'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Batizpafçi are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Batizpafçi is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) maswmiti ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êçutiz ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êçutiz, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is maswmiti. Forms of êçutiz are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Batizpafçi, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Batizpafçi verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Batizpafçi verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -mitata- between the stem and the ending.

    In hmatitèmamizpaçu, the stem hmatitè- indicates that the verb is hmatitèzti (to speak) and the ending -mamizpaçu marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In bamipamitatawpata, the stem bamipa- indicates that the verb is bamipamiti (to finish), the suffix -mitata- follows it, and the inflection -wpata marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Batizpafçi they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    hmatitèzti: cz hmatitèztimamita, çug hmatitèmata, xug'mitèta hmatitèmatatazpaçu, xugz pawgta hmatitèmiwpata, hmatitèze...
    bamipamiti: cz bamipamitimamita, swgta bamipaîçuzta, xug'mitèta bamipamitatazpaçu, bamipamita, xugz pawgta bamipamitatamiwpata...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    swgtèwmiti: cz szgqà, çug szgqà, mitè szgçu, pawgta swgtèwpata, swgta swgtèze, mitèta szgtèzpaçu.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly maswmiti, êçutiz, matètèzti and bamamitiz), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -zti (with the exception of matètèzti, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    mamikzti, vimatèmavazti, fçimapaçuzti, zpaswvazti, baztikzti, kmapadizti, hmatatazti, hmavazti, htiwkzpazti, tizdimatipèzti, etc.

        For example, for the verb hmatitèzti, the stem is hmatitè- and the ending is -zti.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -miti whose present participle ends in -mitatamapaçu:

    vibipamiti, fwkhmaçumiti, pèbidigztihmiti, batèzgtimiti, ditimapapèmiti, çimaïti, mipasztaçumiti, hwtèmiti, tiwgdimiti, tigdimiti, tamatèmiti, etc.

        For example, for the verb bamipamiti, the stem is bamipa- and the ending is -miti.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êçutiz and maswmiti, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. cz tizdimatipèz means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -zti (all verbs of the first group): -z, -zta, -z, -wpata, -ze, -zpaçu.
    Verbs ending in -miti (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -mita, -mita, -miçu, -mitatawpata, -mitataze, -mitatazpaçu. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -tiz (part of the third group): -ta, -ta, - , -wpata, -ze, -zpaçu.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "cz tizdimatipèmamita" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -zti suffix, e.g., tizdimatipèzti -> tizdimatipè-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -miti suffix plus the -mitata suffix, e.g., fçiwmitamiti -> fçiwmitamitata-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -mamita, -mamita, -mamiçu, -miwpata, -mize, -mamizpaçu.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb maswmiti. They are always regular: -mami, -mata, -ma, -wpata, -ze, -wpaçu.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -z and -ta, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "gpa batigmiçu fwpabamiçu", "gpaz hwmitiz fwpabamiçuz", "pèzta batigmiçuta fwpabamiçuta", and "pèzta hwmitizta fwpabamiçuzta."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -bi for the 1st group verbs, or in -mi for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -g (zpaçuzpapètiz zpaçuzpapèg, viwmitiz vig, tèmitiz tèg, etc. and tamaswmiti tag, swmiti sg, hwgswmiti hg), -mita (kzçuçutiz kmita, htizpapètiz htimita, etc.), -gta (mipaftègtiz mipaftègta and tizftègtiz tizftègta and only these verbs), -miçu (kmagpèmitiz kmagpèmiçu, pèmitiz pèmiçu, etc.), -çu (verbs in -mipapètiz : hzmipapètiz hzmipaçu), -ztiçu (wgstimiti wgsztiçu, fwgstimiti fwgsztiçu, wbabatimiti wbabaztiçu and tawgbabatimiti tawgbabaztiçu), or zg (maswmiti zg). 

*Compound Tenses

Batizpafçi compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either maswmiti or êçutiz) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Batizpafçi, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Batizpafçi. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either maswmiti or êçutiz in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "c'mami kmapadibi" (I ate) or "mitè ztaçu matitimisbi" (He arrived). maswmiti is used with most verbs, while êçutiz is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, maswmiti should be used by default.

WORD ORDER

The most common word order in Ipogyçàlsh is subject-verb-object (SVO).

------------------------
In Ipogyçàlsh, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
Ipogyçàlsh has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Ipogyçàlsh, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Ipogyçàlsh article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is olyç. For example, in the phrase "olyç shoqyl" (the cat), olyç shows that the noun shoqyl (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is oloq. An example is "oloq odoqzuàpàl" (the house), where oloq shows that odoqzuàpàl (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is olyçu for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "olyçu shoqylu", the cats; "olyçu odoqzuàpàlu", the houses.)

In summary, olyç is used with masculine singular nouns, oloq with feminine singular nouns, and olyçu with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Ipogyçàlsh.

Before oq, yç, z, àp, op, il, àf, èx and some occurrences of h, the singular masculine article olyç becomes ol'.

The most common word order in Acpwucecà is subject-verb-object (SVO).

------------------------
In Acpwucecà, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
Acpwucecà has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Acpwucecà, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Acpwucecà article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is lw. For example, in the phrase "lw ecàtj" (the cat), lw shows that the noun ecàtj (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is lt. An example is "lt udtécmzuc" (the house), where lt shows that udtécmzuc (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is lwm for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "lwm ecàtjm", the cats; "lwm udtécmzucm", the houses.)

In summary, lw is used with masculine singular nouns, lt with feminine singular nouns, and lwm with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Acpwucecà.

Before t, w, éc, z, b, éf, uf, ux and some occurrences of à, the singular masculine article lw becomes l'.

Every Acpwucecà noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.
