Additionally, adjectives ending in -ôc change to -ôcfûd (e.g., abacôjôbôc > abacôjôbôcfûd); those ending in -ûduûç or -ûduà change to -ûduûlûd (e.g., ûcûçrôpûdvvûduûç > ûcûçrôpûdvvûduûlûd, ûhuûçæcûduà > ûhuûçæcûduûlûd), with the exception of the irregular øæcûduà (old) whose feminine form is øæcûdæcacacûd; -x changes to -xuûd (e.g., acrôbx > acrôbxuûd); -æcûh changes to -æcøûd (e.g., ôjôcvæcûh > ôjôcvæcøûd); -ûdûh changes to -âbøûd (e.g., abûçûdûh > abûçâbøûd); -ûdûç changes to -âbûçûd (e.g., èvûçôjôbxûdûç > èvûçôjôbxâbûçûd); -ûdv changes to -âbvûd (e.g., æcôbâkuæcûdv > æcôbâkuæcâbvûd); and adjectives ending in -ru have a special form -rac (becoming -racacûd in feminine) that appears before ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb and some occurrences of f, (e.g., ûhru/ûhrac > ûhracacûd, ôpru/ôprac > ôpracacûd).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -ûd, it does not change in the feminine (cf. uôb frôpôpûd ûçæcôcfûd 'a rich man' > uôbûd ûhûdôpôpûd ûçæcôcfûd 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ûl to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., âlracæc > âlracæcûl, âlracæcûd > âlracæcûdûl). If the basic form ends in -ûl, -à, or -ûb, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., abôjûl > abôjûl, xèôbèûçûduà > xèôbèûçûduà, ûkruà > ûkruà), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ûhûçûdôbôcf adjectives ending in -ûdôju take the ending -à in the masculine plural (e.g., ôbruøûdôju > ôbruøûdôjuà). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -ôjac, which normally change to -ôjuà in the masculine plural (e.g., fæcøûdûçôbôjac > fæcøûdûçôbôjuà, ôcûdôbvûçôjac > ôcûdôbvûçôjuà), with only two exceptions: ûhôjvôjac > ûhôjvôjacûl and ôbôjøôjac > ôbôjøôjacûl which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ôcûdôbvûçôjacûd > ôcûdôbvûçôjacûdûl.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in acûd ûçruxûd øæcôb (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are abûdôju (beautiful), abrôb (good), abûçûdûh (brief), xûçôjôbûk (big/tall), xûçrûl (fat/large), ûhôjuà (false), fôjuv (high), acrôbx (long), abûçûdûh (brief), âlûduôbûd (young), âlracæc (pretty), ôpôjuøôjæcûl (bad), ôpûdæcacacûduûç (best), ôbruøûdôju (new), ûcûdvæcv (small), øæcûduà (old); e.g., uôbûd ûhûdôpôpûd abûdacacûd ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ûhûçûdôbôcf, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ûhûçûdôbôcf personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | âlûd
         | 2nd (informal)   | vu
         | 2nd (formal)     | øruûl
         | 3rd (masculine)  | æcac
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ûdacacûd
         | 3rd (neutral)    | rôb
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ôbruûl
         | 2nd              | øruûl
         | 3rd (masculine)  | æcacûl
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ûdacacûdûl
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun âlûd occurs before ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb, œ and some occurrences of f, it becomes âl'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ûhûçûdôbôcf are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ûhûçûdôbôcf is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ôjøræcûç ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of œvûçûd ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is œvûçûd, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ôjøræcûç. Forms of œvûçûd are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ûhûçûdôbôcf, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ûhûçûdôbôcf verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ûhûçûdôbôcf verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -æcûlûl- between the stem and the ending.

    In ûcôjûçacôjæcûdôbv, the stem ûcôjûçac- indicates that the verb is ûcôjûçacûdûç (to speak) and the ending -ôjæcûdôbv marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ûhæcôbæcûlûlrôbûl, the stem ûhæcôb- indicates that the verb is ûhæcôbæcûç (to finish), the suffix -æcûlûl- follows it, and the inflection -rôbûl marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ûhûçûdôbôcf they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ûcôjûçacûdûç: âlûd ûcôjûçacûdûçôjæcûl, vu ûcôjûçacôjûl, âku'æcacûl ûcôjûçacôjûlûlûdôbv, âkuûd ôbruûl ûcôjûçacæcrôbûl, ûcôjûçacûdûb...
    ûhæcôbæcûç: âlûd ûhæcôbæcûçôjæcûl, øruûl ûhæcôbâcvûdûl, âku'æcacûl ûhæcôbæcûlûlûdôbv, ûhæcôbæcûl, âkuûd ôbruûl ûhæcôbæcûlûlæcrôbûl...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    øruacræcûç: âlûd øûduà, vu øûduà, æcac øûduv, ôbruûl øruacrôbûl, øruûl øruacûdûb, æcacûl øûduacûdôbv.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ôjøræcûç, œvûçûd, ôjacacûdûç and ûhôjæcûçûd), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ûdûç (with the exception of ôjacacûdûç, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ôjæcôpûdûç, abôjacôjoûdûç, ôcfôjôbvûdûç, ûdôbøroûdûç, ûhûdûçôpûdûç, ôpôjôbxûdûç, ûcôjûlûlûdûç, ûcôjoûdûç, ûcûçrôpûdôbûdûç, ûçûdxôjûçûkûdûç, etc.

        For example, for the verb ûcôjûçacûdûç, the stem is ûcôjûçac- and the ending is -ûdûç.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -æcûç whose present participle ends in -æcûlûlôjôbv:

    abèôbæcûç, ôcrôpûcôjvæcûç, ûkèxuûdûçûcæcûç, ûhacûduûçæcûç, xûçôjôbûkæcûç, fôjïûç, æcôbøûdûlvæcûç, ûcracæcûç, ûçruxæcûç, ûçuxæcûç, ûlôjacæcûç, etc.

        For example, for the verb ûhæcôbæcûç, the stem is ûhæcôb- and the ending is -æcûç.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries œvûçûd and ôjøræcûç, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

**Past participle

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Radylatcse has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Radylatcse, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Radylatcse article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is bla. For example, in the phrase "bla csekq" (the cat), bla shows that the noun csekq (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is bk. An example is "bk mkdàryjt" (the house), where bk shows that mkdàryjt (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is blary for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "blary csekqry", the cats; "blary mkdàryjtry", the houses.)

In summary, bla is used with masculine singular nouns, bk with feminine singular nouns, and blary with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Radylatcse.

Before k, la, dà, j, w, fa, ge, u and some occurrences of se, the singular masculine article bla becomes b'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Radylatcse noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Radylatcse nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -ry (e.g., mkdàryjt > mkdàryjtry 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -kw and -law take the ending -ly instead of -ry (e.g., qwfakw > qwfakwly 'pipes', plaw > plawly 'games'), except for the nouns bktvkw, rykdydykw, sytlaw, and çablaw which form their plural by adding -ry (e.g., sytlaw > sytlawry 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -jw form their plural with -ly. These are zylatjw, ckdàbbjw, sedàçajw, çadàpjw, syjw, csejw, and pjwpjw (e.g., zylatjw > zylatjwly 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -jw, such as çadàryjw or qdyjw, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ry (e.g., qdyjw > qdyjwry 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ry, -ly or -zo in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., bk cdyjdàly 'the cross' > blary cdyjdàly 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -kb typically change to -kwly in the plural (e.g., pjwdytkb > pjwdytkwly 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -kb are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ry instead. These are çakb, ckb, ckdytkikb, csekckb, èlaryqdàikb, dygecdàqkb, ryladyikb and dygezykb (e.g., bla èlaryqdàikb > blary èlaryqdàikbry).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -kdàb change to -kwly in the plural. Examples of this pattern include çakdàb, cjdykdàb, gemkdàb, ryjwsydàdykdàb, qdykikdàb, and idàqdykdàb (e.g., idàqdykdàb > idàqdykwly 'stained glass windows'). However, some -kdàb nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ry, notably dykdàb, kqqdàdykdàb, csektvkdàb, vgeqkdàb, zyjwiladytkdàb and syjdyqkdàb (e.g., wt dykdàb > vlary dykdàbry 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Radylatcse are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Radylatcse adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like çalakw and tjwilakw, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with k, la, dà, j, w, fa, ge, u and some occurrences of se, e.g. wt çalakw pkdyvdàt (a beautiful garden), wt çalab sejmmla (a handsome man), wtla çalabbla èlammla (a beautiful woman), blary çalakwly latèktqry (the beautiful children), blary çalabblary mkdàryjtry (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -la to the masculine form, e.g., zydyktv > zydyktvla, blatq > blatqla, syladyrykt > syladyryktla. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -lab, -dàb, -jt, -lat, -jry or -kry double their final consonant before adding -la (e.g., cdywlab > cdywlabbla, zylatqdàb > zylatqdàbbla, çajt > çajttla, ktcdàlat > ktcdàlattla, zydyjry > zydyjryryla, and çakry > çakryryla).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -c change to -csela (e.g., çabktc > çabktcsela); those ending in -lawdy or -lawly change to -lawryla (e.g., sydyjmlaqqlawdy > sydyjmlaqqlawryla, èwdydàlawly > èwdydàlawryla), with the exception of the irregular idàlawly (old) whose feminine form is idàladàbbla; -zy changes to -zywla (e.g., bjtzy > bjtzywla); -dàè changes to -dàila (e.g., kcqdàè > kcqdàila); -laè changes to -uila (e.g., çadylaè > çadyuila); -lady changes to -udyla (e.g., geqdyktzylady > geqdyktzyudyla); -laq changes to -uqla (e.g., dàtéwdàlaq > dàtéwdàuqla); and adjectives ending in -jw have a special form -jb (becoming -jbbla in feminine) that appears before k, la, dà, j, w, fa, ge, u and some occurrences of se, (e.g., èjw/èjb > èjbbla, mjw/mjb > mjbbla).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -la, it does not change in the feminine (cf. wt sejmmla dydàcsela 'a rich man' > wtla èlammla dydàcsela 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ry to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., pjbdà > pjbdàry, pjbdàla > pjbdàlary). If the basic form ends in -ry, -ly, or -zo, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., çakry > çakry, zygetgedylawly > zygetgedylawly, vjwly > vjwly), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Radylatcse adjectives ending in -lakw take the ending -ly in the masculine plural (e.g., tjwilakw > tjwilakwly). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -kb, which normally change to -kwly in the masculine plural (e.g., sedàiladytkb > sedàiladytkwly, clatqdykb > clatqdykwly), with only two exceptions: èkqkb > èkqkbry and tkikb > tkikbry which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: clatqdykbla > clatqdykblary.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in bla dyjwzyla idàt (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are çalakw (beautiful), çajt (good), çadylaè (brief), zydyktv (big/tall), zydyjry (fat/large), èkwly (false), sekwq (high), bjtzy (long), çadylaè (brief), plawtla (young), pjbdà (pretty), mkwikdàry (bad), mladàbblawdy (best), tjwilakw (new), sylaqdàq (small), idàlawly (old); e.g., wtla èlammla çalabbla ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Radylatcse, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Radylatcse personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | pla
         | 2nd (informal)   | qw
         | 2nd (formal)     | ijwry
         | 3rd (masculine)  | dàb
         | 3rd (feminine)   | labbla
         | 3rd (neutral)    | jt
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | tjwry
         | 2nd              | ijwry
         | 3rd (masculine)  | dàbry
         | 3rd (feminine)   | labblary
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun pla occurs before k, la, dà, j, w, fa, ge, u, ê and some occurrences of se, it becomes p'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Radylatcse are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Radylatcse is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) kijdàdy ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êqdyla ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êqdyla, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is kijdàdy. Forms of êqdyla are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Radylatcse, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Radylatcse verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Radylatcse verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -dàryry- between the stem and the ending.

    In sykdybkdàlatq, the stem sykdyb- indicates that the verb is sykdyblady (to speak) and the ending -kdàlatq marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In èdàtdàryryjtry, the stem èdàt- indicates that the verb is èdàtdàdy (to finish), the suffix -dàryry- follows it, and the inflection -jtry marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Radylatcse they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    sykdyblady: pla sykdybladykdàry, qw sykdybkry, éw'dàbry sykdybkryrylatq, éwla tjwry sykdybdàjtry, sykdyblazo...
    èdàtdàdy: pla èdàtdàdykdàry, ijwry èdàtîqlary, éw'dàbry èdàtdàryrylatq, èdàtdàry, éwla tjwry èdàtdàryrydàjtry...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ijwbjdàdy: pla ilawly, qw ilawly, dàb ilawq, tjwry ijwbjtry, ijwry ijwblazo, dàbry ilawblatq.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly kijdàdy, êqdyla, kbblady and èkdàdyla), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -lady (with the exception of kbblady, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    kdàmlady, çakbkfalady, csektqlady, latijfalady, èladymlady, mktzylady, sykryrylady, sykfalady, sydyjmlatlady, dylazykdyvlady, etc.

        For example, for the verb sykdyblady, the stem is sykdyb- and the ending is -lady.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -dàdy whose present participle ends in -dàryryktq:

    çagetdàdy, cjmsykqdàdy, vgezywladysydàdy, èblawdydàdy, zydyktvdàdy, sekïdy, dàtilaryqdàdy, syjbdàdy, dyjwzydàdy, dywzydàdy, rykbdàdy, etc.

        For example, for the verb èdàtdàdy, the stem is èdàt- and the ending is -dàdy.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êqdyla and kijdàdy, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. pla dylazykdyvla means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -lady (all verbs of the first group): -la, -lary, -la, -jtry, -lazo, -latq.
    Verbs ending in -dàdy (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -dàry, -dàry, -dàq, -dàryryjtry, -dàryrylazo, -dàryrylatq. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -dyla (part of the third group): -ry, -ry, - , -jtry, -lazo, -latq.
    
    Example:

-------------------------------
1st person     | pla dylazykdyvla         | tjwry dylazykdyvjtry
2nd person     | qw dylazykdyvlary        | ijwry dylazykdyvlazo

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "pla dylazykdyvkdàry" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -lady suffix, e.g., dylazykdyvlady -> dylazykdyv-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -dàdy suffix plus the -dàryry suffix, e.g., csejdàrydàdy -> csejdàrydàryry-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -kdàry, -kdàry, -kdàq, -dàjtry, -dàlazo, -kdàlatq.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb kijdàdy. They are always regular: -kdà, -kry, -k, -jtry, -lazo, -jtq.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -la and -ry, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "wt èdywdàq cjtèdàq", "wtla syjdàdyla cjtèdàqla", "vlary èdywdàqry cjtèdàqry", and "vlary syjdàdylary cjtèdàqlary."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -ge for the 1st group verbs, or in -dà for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -w (latqlatvdyla latqlatvw, çajdàdyla çaw, bdàdyla bw, etc. and rykijdàdy ryw, ijdàdy iw, syjwijdàdy syw), -dàry (mlaqqdyla mdàry, sydylatvdyla sydydàry, etc.), -wry (dàtcbwdyla dàtcbwry and dylacbwdyla dylacbwry and only these verbs), -dàq (mkwvdàdyla mkwvdàq, vdàdyla vdàq, etc.), -q (verbs in -dàtvdyla : syladàtvdyla syladàtq), -ladyq (jwidydàdy jwiladyq, cjwidydàdy cjwiladyq, jèèdydàdy jèèladyq and ryjwèèdydàdy ryjwèèladyq), or law (kijdàdy law). 

*Compound Tenses

Radylatcse compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either kijdàdy or êqdyla) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Radylatcse, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Radylatcse. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either kijdàdy or êqdyla in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "p'kdà mktzyge" (I ate) or "dàb laryq kdydydàige" (He arrived). kijdàdy is used with most verbs, while êqdyla is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, kijdàdy should be used by default.

Example:

Person         | Singular                     | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | p'kdà dylazykdyvge               | tjwry kijtry dylazykdyvge
2nd person     | qw kry dylazykdyvge              | ijwry kilazo dylazykdyvge
3rd person     | dàb/labbla/jt k dylazykdyvge       | dàbry/labblary jtq dylazykdyvge
-------------------------------

2nd Group: csejdàrydàdy (to choose)
-------------------------------

Verbs in Voéjudocb are conjugated to reflect the following information:

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Nèérèpzgy is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    a’wytyqérè lrè zgyqzqlwym (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Nèérèpzgy, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Nèérèpzgy has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Nèérèpzgy, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Nèérèpzgy article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is lrè. For example, in the phrase "lrè zgywym" (the cat), lrè shows that the noun zgywym (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is lwy. An example is "lwy wèwyroreqp" (the house), where lwy shows that wèwyroreqp (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is lrère for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "lrère zgywymre", the cats; "lrère wèwyroreqpre", the houses.)

In summary, lrè is used with masculine singular nouns, lwy with feminine singular nouns, and lrère with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Nèérèpzgy.

Before wy, rè, ro, q, çe, f, s, bo and some occurrences of gy, the singular masculine article lrè becomes l'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Nèérèpzgy noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Nèérèpzgy nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -re (e.g., wèwyroreqp > wèwyroreqpre 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -wyçe and -rèçe take the ending -d instead of -re (e.g., mçefwyçe > mçefwyçed 'pipes', arèçe > arèçed 'games'), except for the nouns lwyptywyçe, rewyééwyçe, xprèçe, and nolrèçe which form their plural by adding -re (e.g., xprèçe > xprèçere 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -qçe form their plural with -d. These are kirèpqçe, zwyrollqçe, gyronoqçe, noroaqçe, xqçe, zgyqçe, and aqçeaqçe (e.g., kirèpqçe > kirèpqçed 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -qçe, such as nororeqçe or méqçe, follow the regular plural pattern and take -re (e.g., méqçe > méqçere 'holes').

Nouns that end in -re, -d or -j in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., lwy zéqrod 'the cross' > lrère zéqrod 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -wyl typically change to -wyçed in the plural (e.g., aqçeépwyl > aqçeépwyçed 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -wyl are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -re instead. These are nowyl, zwyl, zwyépwyàwyl, zgywyzwyl, nèrèremroàwyl, észromwyl, rerèéàwyl and éskiwyl (e.g., lrè nèrèremroàwyl > lrère nèrèremroàwylre).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -wyrol change to -wyçed in the plural. Examples of this pattern include nowyrol, zqéwyrol, swèwyrol, reqçexroéwyrol, méwyàwyrol, and àroméwyrol (e.g., àroméwyrol > àroméwyçed 'stained glass windows'). However, some -wyrol nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -re, notably éwyrol, wymmroéwyrol, zgywyptywyrol, tysmwyrol, kiqçeàrèépwyrol and xqémwyrol (e.g., çep éwyrol > tyrère éwyrolre 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Nèérèpzgy are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Nèérèpzgy adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like norèwyçe and pqçeàrèwyçe, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with wy, rè, ro, q, çe, f, s, bo and some occurrences of gy, e.g. çep norèwyçe awyétyrop (a beautiful garden), çep norèl gyqwèwèrè (a handsome man), çeprè norèllrè nèrèwèwèrè (a beautiful woman), lrère norèwyçed rèpnèwypmre (the beautiful children), lrère norèllrère wèwyroreqpre (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -rè to the masculine form, e.g., kiéwypty > kiéwyptyrè, lrèpm > lrèpmrè, xrèérewyp > xrèérewyprè. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -rèl, -rol, -qp, -rèp, -qre or -wyre double their final consonant before adding -rè (e.g., zéçerèl > zéçerèllrè, kirèpmrol > kirèpmrollrè, noqp > noqpprè, wypzrorèp > wypzrorèpprè, kiéqre > kiéqrererè, and nowyre > nowyrererè).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -z change to -zgyrè (e.g., nolwypz > nolwypzgyrè); those ending in -rèçeé or -rèçed change to -rèçererè (e.g., xéqwèrèmmrèçeé > xéqwèrèmmrèçererè, nèçeérorèçed > nèçeérorèçererè), with the exception of the irregular àrorèçed (old) whose feminine form is àrorèrollrè; -ki changes to -kiçerè (e.g., lqpki > lqpkiçerè); -ronè changes to -roàrè (e.g., wyzmronè > wyzmroàrè); -rènè changes to -boàrè (e.g., noérènè > noéboàrè); -rèé changes to -boérè (e.g., sméwypkirèé > sméwypkiboérè); -rèm changes to -bomrè (e.g., ropnyçerorèm > ropnyçerobomrè); and adjectives ending in -qçe have a special form -ql (becoming -qllrè in feminine) that appears before wy, rè, ro, q, çe, f, s, bo and some occurrences of gy, (e.g., nèqçe/nèql > nèqllrè, wèqçe/wèql > wèqllrè).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -rè, it does not change in the feminine (cf. çep gyqwèwèrè érozgyrè 'a rich man' > çeprè nèrèwèwèrè érozgyrè 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -re to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., aqlro > aqlrore, aqlrorè > aqlrorère). If the basic form ends in -re, -d, or -j, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., nowyre > nowyre, kispsérèçed > kispsérèçed, tyqçed > tyqçed), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Nèérèpzgy adjectives ending in -rèwyçe take the ending -d in the masculine plural (e.g., pqçeàrèwyçe > pqçeàrèwyçed). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -wyl, which normally change to -wyçed in the masculine plural (e.g., gyroàrèépwyl > gyroàrèépwyçed, zrèpméwyl > zrèpméwyçed), with only two exceptions: nèwymwyl > nèwymwylre and pwyàwyl > pwyàwylre which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: zrèpméwylrè > zrèpméwylrère.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in lrè éqçekirè àrop (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are norèwyçe (beautiful), noqp (good), noérènè (brief), kiéwypty (big/tall), kiéqre (fat/large), nèwyçed (false), gywyçem (high), lqpki (long), noérènè (brief), arèçeprè (young), aqlro (pretty), wèwyçeàwyrore (bad), wèrèrollrèçeé (best), pqçeàrèwyçe (new), xrèmrom (small), àrorèçed (old); e.g., çeprè nèrèwèwèrè norèllrè ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Nèérèpzgy, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Nèérèpzgy personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------

------------------------
Singular | 1st              | arè
         | 2nd (informal)   | mçe
         | 2nd (formal)     | àqçere
         | 3rd (masculine)  | rol
         | 3rd (feminine)   | rèllrè
         | 3rd (neutral)    | qp
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | pqçere
         | 2nd              | àqçere
         | 3rd (masculine)  | rolre
         | 3rd (feminine)   | rèllrère
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun arè occurs before wy, rè, ro, q, çe, f, s, bo, ê and some occurrences of gy, it becomes a'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Nèérèpzgy are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Nèérèpzgy is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) wyàqroé ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êmérè ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êmérè, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is wyàqroé. Forms of êmérè are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Nèérèpzgy, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Nèérèpzgy verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Nèérèpzgy verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -rorere- between the stem and the ending.

    In xwyélwyrorèpm, the stem xwyél- indicates that the verb is xwyélrèé (to speak) and the ending -wyrorèpm marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In nèroprorereqpre, the stem nèrop- indicates that the verb is nèroproé (to finish), the suffix -rorere- follows it, and the inflection -qpre marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Nèérèpzgy they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    xwyélrèé: arè xwyélrèéwyrore, mçe xwyélwyre, nyçe'rolre xwyélwyrererèpm, nyçerè pqçere xwyélroqpre, xwyélrèj...
    nèroproé: arè nèroproéwyrore, àqçere nèropîmrère, nyçe'rolre nèroprorererèpm, nèroprore, nyçerè pqçere nèroprorereroqpre...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    àqçelqroé: arè àrèçed, mçe àrèçed, rol àrèçem, pqçere àqçelqpre, àqçere àqçelrèj, rolre àrèçelrèpm.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly wyàqroé, êmérè, wyllrèé and nèwyroérè), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -rèé (with the exception of wyllrèé, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    wyrowèrèé, nowylwyfrèé, zgywypmrèé, rèpàqfrèé, nèrèéwèrèé, wèwypkirèé, xwyrererèé, xwyfrèé, xéqwèrèprèé, érèkiwyétyrèé, etc.

        For example, for the verb xwyélrèé, the stem is xwyél- and the ending is -rèé.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -roé whose present participle ends in -rorerewypm:

    nosproé, zqwèxwymroé, tyskiçerèéxroé, nèlrèçeéroé, kiéwyptyroé, gywyïé, ropàrèremroé, xqlroé, éqçekiroé, éçekiroé, rewylroé, etc.

        For example, for the verb nèroproé, the stem is nèrop- and the ending is -roé.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êmérè and wyàqroé, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. arè érèkiwyétyrè means "I watch".

    Verbs ending in -roé (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -rore, -rore, -rom, -rorereqpre, -rorererèj, -rorererèpm. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -érè (part of the third group): -re, -re, - , -qpre, -rèj, -rèpm.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "arè érèkiwyétywyrore" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -rèé suffix, e.g., érèkiwyétyrèé -> érèkiwyéty-.

    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -wyrore, -wyrore, -wyrom, -roqpre, -rorèj, -wyrorèpm.

**Past participle

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Haikbodf is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    mè’zxoéik buk dfédébuzça (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Haikbodf, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Haikbodf has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Haikbodf, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Haikbodf article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is buk. For example, in the phrase "buk dfzça" (the cat), buk shows that the noun dfzça (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is buz. An example is "buz gèzynébo" (the house), where buz shows that gèzynébo (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is bukn for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "bukn dfzçan", the cats; "bukn gèzynébon", the houses.)

In summary, buk is used with masculine singular nouns, buz with feminine singular nouns, and bukn with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Haikbodf.

Before z, k, y, é, ma, j, à, wu and some occurrences of f, the singular masculine article buk becomes bu'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Haikbodf noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Haikbodf nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -n (e.g., gèzynébo > gèzynébon 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -zma and -kma take the ending -t instead of -n (e.g., çamajzma > çamajzmat 'pipes', mèkma > mèkmat 'games'), except for the nouns buzboxozma, nziizma, vabokma, and rbukma which form their plural by adding -n (e.g., vabokma > vabokman 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -éma form their plural with -t. These are pkboéma, dzybubuéma, fyréma, rymèéma, vaéma, dféma, and mèémamèéma (e.g., pkboéma > pkboémat 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -éma, such as rynéma or çaiéma, follow the regular plural pattern and take -n (e.g., çaiéma > çaiéman 'holes').

Nouns that end in -n, -t or -çe in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., buz diéyt 'the cross' > bukn diéyt 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -zbu typically change to -zmat in the plural (e.g., mèémaibozbu > mèémaibozmat 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -zbu are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -n instead. These are rzbu, dzbu, dzibozþzbu, dfzdzbu, haknçayþzbu, iàdyçazbu, nkiþzbu and iàpzbu (e.g., buk haknçayþzbu > bukn haknçayþzbun).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -zybu change to -zmat in the plural. Examples of this pattern include rzybu, déizybu, àgèzybu, némavayizybu, çaizþzybu, and þyçaizybu (e.g., þyçaizybu > þyçaizmat 'stained glass windows'). However, some -zybu nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -n, notably izybu, zçaçayizybu, dfzboxozybu, xoàçazybu, pémaþkibozybu and vaéiçazybu (e.g., mabo izybu > xokn izybun 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Haikbodf are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Haikbodf adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like rkzma and boémaþkzma, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with z, k, y, é, ma, j, à, wu and some occurrences of f, e.g. mabo rkzma mèzixoybo (a beautiful garden), mabo rkbu fégègèk (a handsome man), mabok rkbubuk hakgègèk (a beautiful woman), bukn rkzmat kbohazboçan (the beautiful children), bukn rkbubukn gèzynébon (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -k to the masculine form, e.g., pizboxo > pizboxok, bukboça > bukboçak, vakinzbo > vakinzbok.

If an adjective's basic form ends in -k, it does not change in the feminine (cf. mabo fégègèk iydfk 'a rich man' > mabok hakgègèk iydfk 'a rich woman').

If the basic form ends in -n, -t, or -çe, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., rzn > rzn, pàboàikmat > pàboàikmat, xoémat > xoémat), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in buk iémapk þybo (the red wine). --------
In Haikbodf, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Haikbodf personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

VERBS
-----
Verbs in Haikbodf are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Haikbodf is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) zþéyi ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êçaik ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êçaik, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is zþéyi. As in English, Ykeéjègujès nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -ut (e.g., vobutçèg > vobutçègut 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -oà and -éjà take the ending -yw instead of -ut (e.g., ràhoà > ràhoàyw 'pipes', céjà > céjàyw 'games'), except for the nouns éxoègloà, utoeeoà, zègéjà, and ytéxéjà which form their plural by adding -ut (e.g., zègéjà > zègéjàut 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -çà form their plural with -yw. These are ixéjègçà, ujobéxéxçà, èsbytçà, ytbcçà, zçà, ujèsçà, and cçàcçà (e.g., ixéjègçà > ixéjègçàyw 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -çà, such as ytbutçà or reçà, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ut (e.g., reçà > reçàut 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ut, -yw or -ud in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., éxo ujeçbyw 'the cross' > éxéjut ujeçbyw 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -oéx typically change to -oàyw in the plural (e.g., cçàeègoéx > cçàeègoàyw 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -oéx are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ut instead. These are ytoéx, ujoéx, ujoeègofoéx, ujèsoujoéx, ykéjutrbfoéx, emujbroéx, utéjefoéx and emixoéx (e.g., éxéj ykéjutrbfoéx > éxéjut ykéjutrbfoéxut).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -obéx change to -oàyw in the plural. Examples of this pattern include ytobéx, ujçeobéx, mvobéx, utçàzbeobéx, reofobéx, and fbreobéx (e.g., fbreobéx > fbreoàyw 'stained glass windows'). However, some -obéx nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ut, notably eobéx, orrbeobéx, ujèsoèglobéx, lmrobéx, ixçàféjeègobéx and zçerobéx (e.g., àèg eobéx > léjut eobéxut 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ykeéjègujès are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ykeéjègujès adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ytéjoà and ègçàféjoà, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with o, éj, b, ç, à, h, m, q and some occurrences of ès, e.g. àèg ytéjoà coelbèg (a beautiful garden), àèg ytéjéx èsçvvéj (a handsome man), àègéj ytéjéxéxéj ykéjvvéj (a beautiful woman), éxéjut ytéjoàyw éjègykoègrut (the beautiful children), éxéjut ytéjéxéxéjut vobutçègut (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -éj to the masculine form, e.g., ixeoègl > ixeoègléj, éxéjègr > éxéjègréj, zéjeutoèg > zéjeutoègéj. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -éjéx, -béx, -çèg, -éjèg, -çut or -out double their final consonant before adding -éj (e.g., ujeàéjéx > ujeàéjéxéxéj, ixéjègrbéx > ixéjègrbéxéxéj, ytçèg > ytçègègéj, oègujbéjèg > oègujbéjègègéj, ixeçut > ixeçututéj, and ytout > ytoututéj).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -uj change to -ujèséj (e.g., ytéxoèguj > ytéxoègujèséj); those ending in -éjàe or -éjàyw change to -éjàutéj (e.g., zeçvéjrréjàe > zeçvéjrréjàutéj, ykàebéjàyw > ykàebéjàutéj), with the exception of the irregular fbéjàyw (old) whose feminine form is fbéjbéxéxéj; -ix changes to -ixàéj (e.g., éxçègix > éxçègixàéj); -byk changes to -bféj (e.g., oujrbyk > oujrbféj); -éjyk changes to -qféj (e.g., yteéjyk > yteqféj); -éje changes to -qeéj (e.g., mreoègixéje > mreoègixqeéj); -éjr changes to -qréj (e.g., bègugàbéjr > bègugàbqréj); and adjectives ending in -çà have a special form -çéx (becoming -çéxéxéj in feminine) that appears before o, éj, b, ç, à, h, m, q and some occurrences of ès, (e.g., ykçà/ykçéx > ykçéxéxéj, vçà/vçéx > vçéxéxéj).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -éj, it does not change in the feminine (cf. àèg èsçvvéj ebujèséj 'a rich man' > àègéj ykéjvvéj ebujèséj 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ut to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., cçéxb > cçéxbut, cçéxbéj > cçéxbéjut). If the basic form ends in -ut, -yw, or -ud, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ytout > ytout, ixmègmeéjàyw > ixmègmeéjàyw, lçàyw > lçàyw), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ykeéjègujès adjectives ending in -éjoà take the ending -yw in the masculine plural (e.g., ègçàféjoà > ègçàféjoàyw). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -oéx, which normally change to -oàyw in the masculine plural (e.g., èsbféjeègoéx > èsbféjeègoàyw, ujéjègreoéx > ujéjègreoàyw), with only two exceptions: ykoroéx > ykoroéxut and ègofoéx > ègofoéxut which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ujéjègreoéxéj > ujéjègreoéxéjut.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in éxéj eçàixéj fbèg (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are ytéjoà (beautiful), ytçèg (good), yteéjyk (brief), ixeoègl (big/tall), ixeçut (fat/large), ykoàyw (false), èsoàr (high), éxçègix (long), yteéjyk (brief), céjàègéj (young), cçéxb (pretty), voàfobut (bad), véjbéxéxéjàe (best), ègçàféjoà (new), zéjrbr (small), fbéjàyw (old); e.g., àègéj ykéjvvéj ytéjéxéxéj ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ykeéjègujès, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ykeéjègujès personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | céj
         | 2nd (informal)   | rà
         | 2nd (formal)     | fçàut
         | 3rd (masculine)  | béx
         | 3rd (feminine)   | éjéxéxéj
         | 3rd (neutral)    | çèg
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ègçàut
         | 2nd              | fçàut
         | 3rd (masculine)  | béxut
         | 3rd (feminine)   | éjéxéxéjut
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun céj occurs before o, éj, b, ç, à, h, m, q, ê and some occurrences of ès, it becomes c'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ykeéjègujès are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ykeéjègujès is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ofçbe ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êreéj ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êreéj, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ofçbe. Forms of êreéj are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ykeéjègujès, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ykeéjègujès verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ykeéjègujès verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -butut- between the stem and the ending.

    In zoeéxobéjègr, the stem zoeéx- indicates that the verb is zoeéxéje (to speak) and the ending -obéjègr marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ykbègbututçègut, the stem ykbèg- indicates that the verb is ykbègbe (to finish), the suffix -butut- follows it, and the inflection -çègut marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ykeéjègujès they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    zoeéxéje: céj zoeéxéjeobut, rà zoeéxout, ugà'béxut zoeéxoututéjègr, ugàéj ègçàut zoeéxbçègut, zoeéxéjud...
    ykbègbe: céj ykbègbeobut, fçàut ykbègîréjut, ugà'béxut ykbègbututéjègr, ykbègbut, ugàéj ègçàut ykbègbututbçègut...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    fçàéxçbe: céj féjàyw, rà féjàyw, béx féjàr, ègçàut fçàéxçègut, fçàut fçàéxéjud, béxut féjàéxéjègr.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ofçbe, êreéj, oéxéxéje and ykobeéj), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -éje (with the exception of oéxéxéje, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    obvéje, ytoéxohéje, ujèsoègréje, éjègfçhéje, ykéjevéje, voègixéje, zoututéje, zohéje, zeçvéjègéje, eéjixoeléje, etc.

        For example, for the verb zoeéxéje, the stem is zoeéx- and the ending is -éje.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -be whose present participle ends in -bututoègr:

    ytmègbe, ujçvzorbe, lmixàéjezbe, ykéxéjàebe, ixeoèglbe, èsoïe, bègféjutrbe, zçéxbe, eçàixbe, eàixbe, utoéxbe, etc.

        For example, for the verb ykbègbe, the stem is ykbèg- and the ending is -be.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êreéj and ofçbe, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. céj eéjixoeléj means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -éje (all verbs of the first group): -éj, -éjut, -éj, -çègut, -éjud, -éjègr.
    Verbs ending in -be (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -but, -but, -br, -bututçègut, -bututéjud, -bututéjègr. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -eéj (part of the third group): -ut, -ut, - , -çègut, -éjud, -éjègr.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "céj eéjixoelobut" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -éje suffix, e.g., eéjixoeléje -> eéjixoel-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -be suffix plus the -butut suffix, e.g., ujèsçbutbe -> ujèsçbutbutut-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -obut, -obut, -obr, -bçègut, -béjud, -obéjègr.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -éj and -ut, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "àèg ykeàbr ujçègykbr", "àègéj zçbeéj ujçègykbréj", "léjut ykeàbrut ujçègykbrut", and "léjut zçbeéjut ujçègykbréjut."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -m for the 1st group verbs, or in -b for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -à (éjègréjègleéj éjègréjèglà, ytçbeéj ytà, éxbeéj éxà, etc. and utofçbe utà, fçbe fà, zçàfçbe zà), -but (véjrreéj vbut, zeéjègleéj zebut, etc.), -àut (bègujéxàeéj bègujéxàut and eéjujéxàeéj eéjujéxàut and only these verbs), -br (voàlbeéj voàlbr, lbeéj lbr, etc.), -r (verbs in -bègleéj : zéjbègleéj zéjbègr), -éjer (çàfebe çàféjer, ujçàfebe ujçàféjer, çykykebe çykykéjer and utçàykykebe utçàykykéjer), or éjà (ofçbe éjà). 

*Compound Tenses

Ykeéjègujès compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either ofçbe or êreéj) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Ykeéjègujès, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Ykeéjègujès. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either ofçbe or êreéj in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "c'ob voègixm" (I ate) or "béx éjutr oeebfm" (He arrived). ofçbe is used with most verbs, while êreéj is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, ofçbe should be used by default.

Example:

1st Group: eéjixoeléje (to watch)
-------------------------------
Person         | Singular                     | Plural
-------------------------------

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Hohèqdésèà has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Hohèqdésèà, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Hohèqdésèà article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is siq. For example, in the phrase "siq sèàjidè" (the cat), siq shows that the noun sèàjidè (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is siji. An example is "siji zjirçèxèdé" (the house), where siji shows that zjirçèxèdé (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is siqçè for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "siqçè sèàjidèçè", the cats; "siqçè zjirçèxèdéçè", the houses.)

In summary, siq is used with masculine singular nouns, siji with feminine singular nouns, and siqçè with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Hohèqdésèà.

Before ji, q, r, xè, xy, e, pi, t and some occurrences of à, the singular masculine article siq becomes si'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Hohèqdésèà noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Hohèqdésèà nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -çè (e.g., zjirçèxèdé > zjirçèxèdéçè 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -jixy and -qxy take the ending -sé instead of -çè (e.g., dèxyejixy > dèxyejixysé 'pipes', léqxy > léqxysé 'games'), except for the nouns sijidégéjixy, çèjihèhèjixy, adéqxy, and ksiqxy which form their plural by adding -çè (e.g., adéqxy > adéqxyçè 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -xèxy form their plural with -sé. These are pèqdéxèxy, sèjirsisixèxy, àrkxèxy, krléxèxy, axèxy, sèàxèxy, and léxèxyléxèxy (e.g., pèqdéxèxy > pèqdéxèxysé 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -xèxy, such as krçèxèxy or dèhèxèxy, follow the regular plural pattern and take -çè (e.g., dèhèxèxy > dèhèxèxyçè 'holes').

Nouns that end in -çè, -sé or -jo in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., siji sèhèxèrsé 'the cross' > siqçè sèhèxèrsé 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -jisi typically change to -jixysé in the plural (e.g., léxèxyhèdéjisi > léxèxyhèdéjixysé 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -jisi are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -çè instead. These are kjisi, sèjisi, sèjihèdéjiþjisi, sèàjisèjisi, nqçèdèrþjisi, hèpisèrdèjisi, çèqhèþjisi and hèpipèjisi (e.g., siq nqçèdèrþjisi > siqçè nqçèdèrþjisiçè).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -jirsi change to -jixysé in the plural. Examples of this pattern include kjirsi, sèxèhèjirsi, pizjirsi, çèxèxyarhèjirsi, dèhèjiþjirsi, and þrdèhèjirsi (e.g., þrdèhèjirsi > þrdèhèjixysé 'stained glass windows'). However, some -jirsi nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -çè, notably hèjirsi, jidèdèrhèjirsi, sèàjidégéjirsi, gépidèjirsi, pèxèxyþqhèdéjirsi and axèhèdèjirsi (e.g., xydé hèjirsi > géqçè hèjirsiçè 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Hohèqdésèà are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Hohèqdésèà adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like kqjixy and déxèxyþqjixy, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ji, q, r, xè, xy, e, pi, t and some occurrences of à, e.g. xydé kqjixy léjihègérdé (a beautiful garden), xydé kqsi àxèzzq (a handsome man), xydéq kqsisiq nqzzq (a beautiful woman), siqçè kqjixysé qdénjidédèçè (the beautiful children), siqçè kqsisiqçè zjirçèxèdéçè (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -q to the masculine form, e.g., pèhèjidégé > pèhèjidégéq, siqdédè > siqdédèq, aqhèçèjidé > aqhèçèjidéq. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -qsi, -rsi, -xèdé, -qdé, -xèçè or -jiçè double their final consonant before adding -q (e.g., sèhèxyqsi > sèhèxyqsisiq, pèqdédèrsi > pèqdédèrsisiq, kxèdé > kxèdédéq, jidésèrqdé > jidésèrqdédéq, pèhèxèçè > pèhèxèçèçèq, and kjiçè > kjiçèçèq).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -sè change to -sèàq (e.g., ksijidésè > ksijidésèàq); those ending in -qxyhè or -qxysé change to -qxyçèq (e.g., ahèxèzqdèdèqxyhè > ahèxèzqdèdèqxyçèq, nxyhèrqxysé > nxyhèrqxyçèq), with the exception of the irregular þrqxysé (old) whose feminine form is þrqrsisiq; -pè changes to -pèxyq (e.g., sixèdépè > sixèdépèxyq); -rn changes to -rþq (e.g., jisèdèrn > jisèdèrþq); -qn changes to -tþq (e.g., khèqn > khètþq); -qhè changes to -thèq (e.g., pidèhèjidépèqhè > pidèhèjidépèthèq); -qdè changes to -tdèq (e.g., rdégyxyrqdè > rdégyxyrtdèq); and adjectives ending in -xèxy have a special form -xèsi (becoming -xèsisiq in feminine) that appears before ji, q, r, xè, xy, e, pi, t and some occurrences of à, (e.g., nxèxy/nxèsi > nxèsisiq, zxèxy/zxèsi > zxèsisiq).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -q, it does not change in the feminine (cf. xydé àxèzzq hèrsèàq 'a rich man' > xydéq nqzzq hèrsèàq 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -çè to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., léxèsir > léxèsirçè, léxèsirq > léxèsirqçè). If the basic form ends in -çè, -sé, or -jo, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., kjiçè > kjiçè, pèpidépihèqxysé > pèpidépihèqxysé, géxèxysé > géxèxysé), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Hohèqdésèà adjectives ending in -qjixy take the ending -sé in the masculine plural (e.g., déxèxyþqjixy > déxèxyþqjixysé). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -jisi, which normally change to -jixysé in the masculine plural (e.g., àrþqhèdéjisi > àrþqhèdéjixysé, sèqdédèhèjisi > sèqdédèhèjixysé), with only two exceptions: njidèjisi > njidèjisiçè and déjiþjisi > déjiþjisiçè which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: sèqdédèhèjisiq > sèqdédèhèjisiqçè.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in siq hèxèxypèq þrdé (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are kqjixy (beautiful), kxèdé (good), khèqn (brief), pèhèjidégé (big/tall), pèhèxèçè (fat/large), njixysé (false), àjixydè (high), sixèdépè (long), khèqn (brief), léqxydéq (young), léxèsir (pretty), zjixyþjirçè (bad), zqrsisiqxyhè (best), déxèxyþqjixy (new), aqdèrdè (small), þrqxysé (old); e.g., xydéq nqzzq kqsisiq ("a beautiful woman").
