**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -jy and -jè, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "écè ntoétàu vèkycèntàu", "écèjy bkytàtojy vèkycèntàujy", "ljyjè ntoétàujè vèkycèntàujè", and "ljyjè bkytàtojyjè vèkycèntàujyjè."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -z for the 1st group verbs, or in -tà for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -é (jycèujycèltojy jycèujycèlé, pkytàtojy pé, cytàtojy cyé, etc. and jèxçkytàto jèé, çkytàto çé, bkyéçkytàto bé), -tàjè (ajyuutojy atàjè, btojycèltojy btotàjè, etc.), -éjè (tàcèvècyétojy tàcèvècyéjè and tojyvècyétojy tojyvècyéjè and only these verbs), -tàu (axéltàtojy axéltàu, ltàtojy ltàu, etc.), -u (verbs in -tàcèltojy : bjytàcèltojy bjytàcèu), -jytou (kyéçtotàto kyéçjytou, vèkyéçtotàto vèkyéçjytou, kynntotàto kynnjytou and jèkyénntotàto jèkyénnjytou), or jyé (xçkytàto jyé). 

*Compound Tenses

Vitojycèvèjà compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either xçkytàto or êutojy) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Vitojycèvèjà, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Vitojycèvèjà. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either xçkytàto or êutojy in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "s'xtà axcèhz" (I ate) or "tàcy jyjèu xtototàçz" (He arrived). xçkytàto is used with most verbs, while êutojy is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, xçkytàto should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Vitojycèvèjà: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is xçkytàto.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) jycycyjyjè kycèu lkytoatà. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) vècyxtàtojy x çé ljyée pxcyjytàcèjyjè. ("vècyxtàtojy saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) tàcy r xçxtàu ljyée pxcyjytàcèjyjè. vècyxtàtojy cyjyjè x çéjyjè. ("There were two whales. vècyxtàtojy saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) gyéjycycyjyjè pxcyjytàcèjyjè vècyxtàtojy x-u-jycycyjy çéjyjè ? ("Which whales did vècyxtàtojy see?")
        (relative clause introduced by gyéjy) cyjyjè ljyée pxcyjytàcèjyjè gyéjy vècyxtàtojy x çéjyjè ("the two whales that vècyxtàtojy saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Vitojycèvèjà.

B. The auxiliary is êutojy, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        jycycyjyjè jèkycèu xtototàçzjyjè. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is êutojy and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with xçkytàto in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears after the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) jycycyjyjè jèjy jèkycèu jèévèvèzlz. cèkyéjè cèkyéjè jèkyaajyjè bxtocyz. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object after verb) jycycyjyjè jèjy jèkycèu bkyjèz ljyjè gyéjyjèutàkycèjè. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears before the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) s'xtà nxtàu écèjy uxtoujy. cyjyjè jycènxcèujè jèjy cyx jèkycèu bxtouxhzjy. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")
        (wh-question) gyéjycycyjy uxtoujy jèjy jèkycèu-tàcyjè bxtouxhzjy ? ("Which pie did they share?")
        (gyéjy relative) cyx uxtoujy gyéjy cyjyjè jycènxcèujè jèjy jèkycèu bxtouxhzjy ("the pie that the children shared")

    The reflexive pronoun can itself be the direct object, in which case the participle agrees with it (and therefore with the subject). This also includes "inherently reflexive" verbs, for which the reflexive pronoun cannot be interpreted semantically as an object (direct or indirect) of the verb.

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -jaki, -koki, -zs, -jas, -zdi or -ydi double their final consonant before adding -ja (e.g., qwnéjaki > qwnéjakikija, jijaslékoki > jijaslékokikija, mèzs > mèzssja, ysqkojas > ysqkojassja, jiwzdi > jiwzdidija, and mèydi > mèydidija).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -q change to -qdaja (e.g., mèkiysq > mèkiysqdaja); those ending in -janéw or -janéç change to -janédija (e.g., àwzbjaléléjanéw > àwzbjaléléjanédija, lanéwkojanéç > lanéwkojanédija), with the exception of the irregular jékojanéç (old) whose feminine form is jékojakokikija; -ji changes to -jinéja (e.g., kizsji > kizsjinéja); -kola changes to -kojéja (e.g., yqlékola > yqlékojéja); -jala changes to -vjéja (e.g., mèwjala > mèwvjéja); -jaw changes to -vwja (e.g., uléwysjijaw > uléwysjivwja); -jalé changes to -vléja (e.g., kostonékojalé > kostonékovléja); and adjectives ending in -zné have a special form -zki (becoming -zkikija in feminine) that appears before y, ja, ko, z, né, g, u, v and some occurrences of da, (e.g., lazné/lazki > lazkikija, bzné/bzki > bzkikija).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -ja, it does not change in the feminine (cf. nés dazbbja wkoqdaja 'a rich man' > nésja lajabbja wkoqdaja 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -di to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., ezkiko > ezkikodi, ezkikoja > ezkikojadi). If the basic form ends in -di, -ç, or -jo, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., mèydi > mèydi, jiusuwjanéç > jiusuwjanéç, déznéç > déznéç), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Lawjasqda adjectives ending in -jayné take the ending -ç in the masculine plural (e.g., sznéjéjayné > sznéjéjaynéç). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -yki, which normally change to -ynéç in the masculine plural (e.g., dakojéjawsyki > dakojéjawsynéç, qjasléwyki > qjasléwynéç), with only two exceptions: layléyki > layléykidi and syjéyki > syjéykidi which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: qjasléwykija > qjasléwykijadi.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in kija wznéjija jékos (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are mèjayné (beautiful), mèzs (good), mèwjala (brief), jiwysdé (big/tall), jiwzdi (fat/large), laynéç (false), daynélé (high), kizsji (long), mèwjala (brief), ejanésja (young), ezkiko (pretty), bynéjéykodi (bad), bjakokikijanéw (best), sznéjéjayné (new), àjalékolé (small), jékojanéç (old); e.g., nésja lajabbja mèjakikija ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Lawjasqda, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Lawjasqda personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | eja
         | 2nd (informal)   | léné
         | 2nd (formal)     | jéznédi
         | 3rd (masculine)  | koki
         | 3rd (feminine)   | jakikija
         | 3rd (neutral)    | zs
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | sznédi
         | 2nd              | jéznédi
         | 3rd (masculine)  | kokidi
         | 3rd (feminine)   | jakikijadi
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun eja occurs before y, ja, ko, z, né, g, u, v, ê and some occurrences of da, it becomes e'.

*Relative pronouns

Lawjasqda, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, tonéko is ordinarily used: ki'dazbbja tonéko y jézkiu by mèkoqgqkijaléléja ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that tonéko in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: kijadi mèkoqgqkijaléléjadi tonéko zslé uléu jézkiujadi ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, tonéja (or toné' before y, ja, ko, z, né, g, u, v and some occurrences of da) is ordinarily used: kiy mèkoqgqkijaléléja toné'koki y jézkiuja ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like tonéko, tonéja does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Lawjasqda are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Lawjasqda is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) yjézkow ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êléwja ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êléwja, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is yjézkow. Forms of êléwja are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Lawjasqda, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Lawjasqda verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Lawjasqda verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -kodidi- between the stem and the ending.

    In àywkiykojaslé, the stem àywki- indicates that the verb is àywkijaw (to speak) and the ending -ykojaslé marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In lakoskodidizsdi, the stem lakos- indicates that the verb is lakoskow (to finish), the suffix -kodidi- follows it, and the inflection -zsdi marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Lawjasqda they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    àywkijaw: eja àywkijawykodi, léné àywkiydi, toné'kokidi àywkiydidijaslé, tonéja sznédi àywkikozsdi, àywkijajo...
    lakoskow: eja lakoskowykodi, jéznédi lakosîléjadi, toné'kokidi lakoskodidijaslé, lakoskodi, tonéja sznédi lakoskodidikozsdi...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    jéznékizkow: eja jéjanéç, léné jéjanéç, koki jéjanélé, sznédi jéznékizsdi, jéznédi jéznékijajo, kokidi jéjanékijaslé.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly yjézkow, êléwja, ykikijaw and laykowja), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -jaw (with the exception of ykikijaw, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ykobjaw, mèykiygjaw, qdaysléjaw, jasjézgjaw, lajawbjaw, bysjijaw, àydidijaw, àygjaw, àwzbjasjaw, wjajiywdéjaw, etc.

        For example, for the verb àywkijaw, the stem is àywki- and the ending is -jaw.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -kow whose present participle ends in -kodidiyslé:

    mèuskow, qzbàylékow, déujinéjawàkow, lakijanéwkow, jiwysdékow, dayïw, kosjéjadilékow, àzkikow, wznéjikow, wnéjikow, diykikow, etc.

        For example, for the verb lakoskow, the stem is lakos- and the ending is -kow.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êléwja and yjézkow, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. eja wjajiywdéja means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -jaw (all verbs of the first group): -ja, -jadi, -ja, -zsdi, -jajo, -jaslé.
    Verbs ending in -kow (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -kodi, -kodi, -kolé, -kodidizsdi, -kodidijajo, -kodidijaslé. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -wja (part of the third group): -di, -di, - , -zsdi, -jajo, -jaslé.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "eja wjajiywdéykodi" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -jaw suffix, e.g., wjajiywdéjaw -> wjajiywdé-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -kow suffix plus the -kodidi suffix, e.g., qdazkodikow -> qdazkodikodidi-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -ykodi, -ykodi, -ykolé, -kozsdi, -kojajo, -ykojaslé.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -ja and -di, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "nés lawnékolé qzslakolé", "nésja àzkowja qzslakoléja", "déjadi lawnékolédi qzslakolédi", and "déjadi àzkowjadi qzslakoléjadi."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -u for the 1st group verbs, or in -ko for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -né (jasléjasdéwja jasléjasdéné, mèzkowja mèné, kikowja kiné, etc. and diyjézkow diné, jézkow jéné, àznéjézkow àné), -kodi (bjaléléwja bkodi, àwjasdéwja àwkodi, etc.), -nédi (kosqkinéwja kosqkinédi and wjaqkinéwja wjaqkinédi and only these verbs), -kolé (bynédékowja bynédékolé, dékowja dékolé, etc.), -lé (verbs in -kosdéwja : àjakosdéwja àjakoslé), -jawlé (znéjéwkow znéjéjawlé, qznéjéwkow qznéjéjawlé, zlalawkow zlalajawlé and diznélalawkow diznélalajawlé), or jané (yjézkow jané). 

*Compound Tenses

Lawjasqda compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either yjézkow or êléwja) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Lawjasqda, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Lawjasqda. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either yjézkow or êléwja in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "e'yko bysjiu" (I ate) or "koki jadilé ywwkojéu" (He arrived). yjézkow is used with most verbs, while êléwja is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, yjézkow should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Lawjasqda: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is yjézkow.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) jakikijadi zslé dézwbko. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) qkiykowja y jéné déjanéç mèykijakosjadi. ("qkiykowja saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) koki g yjéykolé déjanéç mèykijakosjadi. qkiykowja kijadi y jénéjadi. ("There were two whales. qkiykowja saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) tonéjakikijadi mèykijakosjadi qkiykowja y-lé-jakikija jénéjadi ? ("Which whales did qkiykowja see?")
        (relative clause introduced by tonéja) kijadi déjanéç mèykijakosjadi tonéja qkiykowja y jénéjadi ("the two whales that qkiykowja saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Lawjasqda.

B. The auxiliary is êléwja, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        jakikijadi dizslé ywwkojéujadi. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is êléwja and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with yjézkow in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears after the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) jakikijadi dija dizslé dinéqqudéu. sznédi sznédi dizbbjadi àywkiu. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object after verb) jakikijadi dija dizslé àzdiu déjadi tonéjadilékozsdi. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears before the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) e'yko laykolé nésja léywléja. kijadi jaslayslédi dija kiy dizslé àywléyjiuja. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")

Nouns ending in -loy and -qy take the ending -ç instead of -ho (e.g., nytuloy > nytuloyç 'pipes', kqy > kqyç 'games'), except for the nouns èlogoliloy, holoziziloy, dogoqy, and vèqy which form their plural by adding -ho (e.g., dogoqy > dogoqyho 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -wy form their plural with -ç. These are baqgowy, colomèèwy, hàmvwy, vmkwy, dowy, cohàwy, and kwykwy (e.g., baqgowy > baqgowyç 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -wy, such as vmhowy or nziwy, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ho (e.g., nziwy > nziwyho 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ho, -ç or -é in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., èlo coziwmç 'the cross' > èqho coziwmç 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -loè typically change to -loyç in the plural (e.g., kwyzigoloè > kwyzigoloyç 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -loè are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ho instead. These are vloè, coloè, colozigolojloè, cohàlocoloè, taqhonmjloè, zixcomnloè, hoqzijloè and zixbaloè (e.g., èq taqhonmjloè > èqho taqhonmjloèho).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -lomè change to -loyç in the plural. Examples of this pattern include vlomè, cowzilomè, xdulomè, howydomzilomè, nzilojlomè, and jmnzilomè (e.g., jmnzilomè > jmnziloyç 'stained glass windows'). However, some -lomè nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ho, notably zilomè, lonnmzilomè, cohàlogolilomè, lixnlomè, bawyjqzigolomè and dowzinlomè (e.g., ygo zilomè > liqho zilomèho 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Taziqgocohà are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Taziqgocohà adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like vqloy and gowyjqloy, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with lo, q, m, w, y, tu, x, to and some occurrences of hà, e.g. ygo vqloy klozilimgo (a beautiful garden), ygo vqè hàwduduq (a handsome man), ygoq vqèèq taqduduq (a beautiful woman), èqho vqloyç qgotalogonho (the beautiful children), èqho vqèèqho dulomhowgoho (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -q to the masculine form, e.g., bazilogoli > bazilogoliq, èqgon > èqgonq, doqzihologo > doqzihologoq. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -qè, -mè, -wgo, -qgo, -who or -loho double their final consonant before adding -q (e.g., coziyqè > coziyqèèq, baqgonmè > baqgonmèèq, vwgo > vwgogoq, logocomqgo > logocomqgogoq, baziwho > baziwhohoq, and vloho > vlohohoq).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -co change to -cohàq (e.g., vèlogoco > vèlogocohàq); those ending in -qyzi or -qyç change to -qyhoq (e.g., doziwduqnnqyzi > doziwduqnnqyhoq, tayzimqyç > tayzimqyhoq), with the exception of the irregular jmqyç (old) whose feminine form is jmqmèèq; -ba changes to -bayq (e.g., èwgoba > èwgobayq); -mta changes to -mjq (e.g., loconmta > loconmjq); -qta changes to -tojq (e.g., vziqta > vzitojq); -qzi changes to -toziq (e.g., xnzilogobaqzi > xnzilogobatoziq); -qn changes to -tonq (e.g., mgociymqn > mgociymtonq); and adjectives ending in -wy have a special form -wè (becoming -wèèq in feminine) that appears before lo, q, m, w, y, tu, x, to and some occurrences of hà, (e.g., tawy/tawè > tawèèq, duwy/duwè > duwèèq).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -q, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ygo hàwduduq zimcohàq 'a rich man' > ygoq taqduduq zimcohàq 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ho to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., kwèm > kwèmho, kwèmq > kwèmqho). If the basic form ends in -ho, -ç, or -é, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., vloho > vloho, baxgoxziqyç > baxgoxziqyç, liwyç > liwyç), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Taziqgocohà adjectives ending in -qloy take the ending -ç in the masculine plural (e.g., gowyjqloy > gowyjqloyç). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -loè, which normally change to -loyç in the masculine plural (e.g., hàmjqzigoloè > hàmjqzigoloyç, coqgonziloè > coqgonziloyç), with only two exceptions: talonloè > talonloèho and golojloè > golojloèho which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: coqgonziloèq > coqgonziloèqho.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in èq ziwybaq jmgo (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are vqloy (beautiful), vwgo (good), vziqta (brief), bazilogoli (big/tall), baziwho (fat/large), taloyç (false), hàloyn (high), èwgoba (long), vziqta (brief), kqygoq (young), kwèm (pretty), duloyjlomho (bad), duqmèèqyzi (best), gowyjqloy (new), doqnmn (small), jmqyç (old); e.g., ygoq taqduduq vqèèq ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Taziqgocohà, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Taziqgocohà personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | kq
         | 2nd (informal)   | ny
         | 2nd (formal)     | jwyho
         | 3rd (masculine)  | mè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | qèèq
         | 3rd (neutral)    | wgo
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | gowyho
         | 2nd              | jwyho
         | 3rd (masculine)  | mèho
         | 3rd (feminine)   | qèèqho
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun kq occurs before lo, q, m, w, y, tu, x, to, ê and some occurrences of hà, it becomes k'.

*Relative pronouns

Taziqgocohà, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ciym is ordinarily used: è'hàwduduq ciym lo jwèx dulo vmcotucoèqnnq ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ciym in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: èqho vmcotucoèqnnqho ciym wgon xnx jwèxqho ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, ciyq (or ciy' before lo, q, m, w, y, tu, x, to and some occurrences of hà) is ordinarily used: èlo vmcotucoèqnnq ciy'mè lo jwèxq ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ciym, ciyq does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Taziqgocohà are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Taziqgocohà is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) lojwmzi ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of ênziq ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is ênziq, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is lojwmzi. Forms of ênziq are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Taziqgocohà, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Taziqgocohà verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Taziqgocohà verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -mhoho- between the stem and the ending.

    In dolozièlomqgon, the stem doloziè- indicates that the verb is dolozièqzi (to speak) and the ending -lomqgon marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In tamgomhohowgoho, the stem tamgo- indicates that the verb is tamgomzi (to finish), the suffix -mhoho- follows it, and the inflection -wgoho marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Taziqgocohà they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    dolozièqzi: kq dolozièqzilomho, ny dolozièloho, ciy'mèho dolozièlohohoqgon, ciyq gowyho dolozièmwgoho, dolozièqé...
    tamgomzi: kq tamgomzilomho, jwyho tamgoînqho, ciy'mèho tamgomhohoqgon, tamgomho, ciyq gowyho tamgomhohomwgoho...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    jwyèwmzi: kq jqyç, ny jqyç, mè jqyn, gowyho jwyèwgoho, jwyho jwyèqé, mèho jqyèqgon.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly lojwmzi, ênziq, loèèqzi and talomziq), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -qzi (with the exception of loèèqzi, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    lomduqzi, vloèlotuqzi, cohàlogonqzi, qgojwtuqzi, taqziduqzi, dulogobaqzi, dolohohoqzi, dolotuqzi, doziwduqgoqzi, ziqbaloziliqzi, etc.

        For example, for the verb dolozièqzi, the stem is doloziè- and the ending is -qzi.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -mzi whose present participle ends in -mhohologon:

    vxgomzi, cowdudolonmzi, lixbayqzidomzi, taèqyzimzi, bazilogolimzi, hàloïzi, mgojqhonmzi, dowèmzi, ziwybamzi, ziybamzi, holoèmzi, etc.

        For example, for the verb tamgomzi, the stem is tamgo- and the ending is -mzi.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries ênziq and lojwmzi, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. kq ziqbaloziliq means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -qzi (all verbs of the first group): -q, -qho, -q, -wgoho, -qé, -qgon.
    Verbs ending in -mzi (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -mho, -mho, -mn, -mhohowgoho, -mhohoqé, -mhohoqgon. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -ziq (part of the third group): -ho, -ho, - , -wgoho, -qé, -qgon.
    
    Example:

Person         | Singular             | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | kq ziqbaloziliq         | gowyho ziqbaloziliwgoho
2nd person     | ny ziqbaloziliqho        | jwyho ziqbaloziliqé
3rd person     | mè/qèèq/wgo ziqbaloziliq | mèho/qèèqho ziqbaloziliqgon
-------------------------------

-------------------------------

2nd person     | ny cohàwmhomho         | jwyho cohàwmhomhohoqé
3rd person     | mè/qèèq/wgo cohàwmhomn | mèho/qèèqho cohàwmhomhohoqgon

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "kq ziqbalozililomho" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -qzi suffix, e.g., ziqbaloziliqzi -> ziqbalozili-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -mzi suffix plus the -mhoho suffix, e.g., cohàwmhomzi -> cohàwmhomhoho-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -lomho, -lomho, -lomn, -mwgoho, -mqé, -lomqgon.

-------------------------------

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb lojwmzi. They are always regular: -lom, -loho, -lo, -wgoho, -qé, -wgon.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -q and -ho, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ygo taziymn cowgotamn", "ygoq dowmziq cowgotamnq", "liqho taziymnho cowgotamnho", and "liqho dowmziqho cowgotamnqho."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -x for the 1st group verbs, or in -m for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -y (qgonqgoliziq qgonqgoliy, vwmziq vy, èmziq èy, etc. and holojwmzi hoy, jwmzi jy, dowyjwmzi doy), -mho (duqnnziq dumho, doziqgoliziq dozimho, etc.), -yho (mgocoèyziq mgocoèyho and ziqcoèyziq ziqcoèyho and only these verbs), -mn (duloylimziq duloylimn, limziq limn, etc.), -n (verbs in -mgoliziq : doqmgoliziq doqmgon), -qzin (wyjzimzi wyjqzin, cowyjzimzi cowyjqzin, wtatazimzi wtataqzin and howytatazimzi howytataqzin), or qy (lojwmzi qy). 

*Compound Tenses

Taziqgocohà compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either lojwmzi or ênziq) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Taziqgocohà, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Taziqgocohà. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either lojwmzi or ênziq in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "k'lom dulogobax" (I ate) or "mè qhon lozizimjx" (He arrived). lojwmzi is used with most verbs, while ênziq is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, lojwmzi should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Taziqgocohà: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is lojwmzi.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) qèèqho wgon liwzidum. ("They (fem.) slept.")

Additionally, adjectives ending in -me change to -mesw (e.g., çéfcàdme > çéfcàdmesw); those ending in -wrx or -wrq change to -wrpew (e.g., cextcéwñeñewrx > cextcéwñeñewrpew, corxnwrq > corxnwrpew), with the exception of the irregular ðonwrq (old) whose feminine form is ðonwnffw; -ñé changes to -ñérw (e.g., ftdñé > ftdñérw); -nco changes to -nðow (e.g., càmeñenco > càmeñenðow); -wco changes to -ñaðow (e.g., çéxwco > çéxñaðow); -wx changes to -ñaxw (e.g., cañexcàdñéwx > cañexcàdñéñaxw); -wñe changes to -ñañew (e.g., ndurnwñe > ndurnñañew); and adjectives ending in -tr have a special form -tf (becoming -tffw in feminine) that appears before cà, w, n, t, r, ho, ca, ña and some occurrences of s, (e.g., cotr/cotf > cotffw, cétr/cétf > cétffw).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -w, it does not change in the feminine (cf. rd stcécéw xnmesw 'a rich man' > rdw cowcécéw xnmesw 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -pe to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., botfn > botfnpe, botfnw > botfnwpe). If the basic form ends in -pe, -q, or -þà, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., çécàpe > çécàpe, ñécadcaxwrq > ñécadcaxwrq, matrq > matrq), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Coxwdmes adjectives ending in -wcàr take the ending -q in the masculine plural (e.g., dtrðowcàr > dtrðowcàrq). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -càf, which normally change to -càrq in the masculine plural (e.g., snðowxdcàf > snðowxdcàrq, mewdñexcàf > mewdñexcàrq), with only two exceptions: cocàñecàf > cocàñecàfpe and dcàðocàf > dcàðocàfpe which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: mewdñexcàfw > mewdñexcàfwpe.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in fw xtrñéw ðond (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are çéwcàr (beautiful), çétd (good), çéxwco (brief), ñéxcàdma (big/tall), ñéxtpe (fat/large), cocàrq (false), scàrñe (high), ftdñé (long), çéxwco (brief), bowrdw (young), botfn (pretty), cécàrðocànpe (bad), céwnffwrx (best), dtrðowcàr (new), cewñenñe (small), ðonwrq (old); e.g., rdw cowcécéw çéwffw ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Coxwdmes, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Coxwdmes personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | bow
         | 2nd (informal)   | ñer
         | 2nd (formal)     | ðotrpe
         | 3rd (masculine)  | nf
         | 3rd (feminine)   | wffw
         | 3rd (neutral)    | td
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | dtrpe
         | 2nd              | ðotrpe
         | 3rd (masculine)  | nfpe
         | 3rd (feminine)   | wffwpe
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun bow occurs before cà, w, n, t, r, ho, ca, ña, ê and some occurrences of s, it becomes bo'.

*Relative pronouns

Coxwdmes, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, urn is ordinarily used: f'stcécéw urn cà ðotfca cécà çénmehomefwñeñew ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that urn in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: fwpe çénmehomefwñeñewpe urn tdñe cañeca ðotfcawpe ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, urw (or ur' before cà, w, n, t, r, ho, ca, ña and some occurrences of s) is ordinarily used: fcà çénmehomefwñeñew ur'nf cà ðotfcaw ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like urn, urw does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Coxwdmes are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Coxwdmes is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) càðotnx ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êñexw ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êñexw, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is càðotnx. Forms of êñexw are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Coxwdmes, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Coxwdmes verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Coxwdmes verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -npepe- between the stem and the ending.

    In cecàxfcànwdñe, the stem cecàxf- indicates that the verb is cecàxfwx (to speak) and the ending -cànwdñe marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In condnpepetdpe, the stem cond- indicates that the verb is condnx (to finish), the suffix -npepe- follows it, and the inflection -tdpe marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Coxwdmes they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    cecàxfwx: bow cecàxfwxcànpe, ñer cecàxfcàpe, ur'nfpe cecàxfcàpepewdñe, urw dtrpe cecàxfntdpe, cecàxfwþà...
    condnx: bow condnxcànpe, ðotrpe condîñewpe, ur'nfpe condnpepewdñe, condnpe, urw dtrpe condnpepentdpe...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ðotrftnx: bow ðowrq, ñer ðowrq, nf ðowrñe, dtrpe ðotrftdpe, ðotrpe ðotrfwþà, nfpe ðowrfwdñe.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly càðotnx, êñexw, càffwx and cocànxw), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -wx (with the exception of càffwx, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    càncéwx, çécàfcàhowx, mescàdñewx, wdðothowx, cowxcéwx, cécàdñéwx, cecàpepewx, cecàhowx, cextcéwdwx, xwñécàxmawx, etc.

        For example, for the verb cecàxfwx, the stem is cecàxf- and the ending is -wx.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -nx whose present participle ends in -npepecàdñe:

    çécadnx, metcécecàñenx, macañérwxcenx, cofwrxnx, ñéxcàdmanx, scàïx, ndðowpeñenx, cetfnx, xtrñénx, xrñénx, pecàfnx, etc.

        For example, for the verb condnx, the stem is cond- and the ending is -nx.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êñexw and càðotnx, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. bow xwñécàxmaw means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -wx (all verbs of the first group): -w, -wpe, -w, -tdpe, -wþà, -wdñe.
    Verbs ending in -nx (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -npe, -npe, -nñe, -npepetdpe, -npepewþà, -npepewdñe. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -xw (part of the third group): -pe, -pe, - , -tdpe, -wþà, -wdñe.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "bow xwñécàxmacànpe" means "I was watching".

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -w and -pe, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "rd coxrnñe metdconñe", "rdw cetnxw metdconñew", "mawpe coxrnñepe metdconñepe", and "mawpe cetnxwpe metdconñewpe."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -ca for the 1st group verbs, or in -n for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -r (wdñewdmaxw wdñewdmar, çétnxw çér, fnxw fr, etc. and pecàðotnx per, ðotnx ðor, cetrðotnx cer), -npe (céwñeñexw cénpe, cexwdmaxw cexnpe, etc.), -rpe (ndmefrxw ndmefrpe and xwmefrxw xwmefrpe and only these verbs), -nñe (cécàrmanxw cécàrmanñe, manxw manñe, etc.), -ñe (verbs in -ndmaxw : cewndmaxw cewndñe), -wxñe (trðoxnx trðowxñe, metrðoxnx metrðowxñe, tcocoxnx tcocowxñe and petrcocoxnx petrcocowxñe), or wr (càðotnx wr). 

*Compound Tenses

Coxwdmes compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either càðotnx or êñexw) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Coxwdmes, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Coxwdmes. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either càðotnx or êñexw in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "bo'càn cécàdñéca" (I ate) or "nf wpeñe càxxnðoca" (He arrived). càðotnx is used with most verbs, while êñexw is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, càðotnx should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Coxwdmes: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is càðotnx.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) wffwpe tdñe matxcén. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) mefcànxw cà ðor mawrq çécàfwndwpe. ("mefcànxw saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) nf ho càðocànñe mawrq çécàfwndwpe. mefcànxw fwpe cà ðorwpe. ("There were two whales. mefcànxw saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) urwffwpe çécàfwndwpe mefcànxw cà-ñe-wffw ðorwpe ? ("Which whales did mefcànxw see?")
        (relative clause introduced by urw) fwpe mawrq çécàfwndwpe urw mefcànxw cà ðorwpe ("the two whales that mefcànxw saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Coxwdmes.

B. The auxiliary is êñexw, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        wffwpe petdñe càxxnðocawpe. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is êñexw and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with càðotnx in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears after the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) wffwpe pew petdñe permemecamaca. dtrpe dtrpe petcécéwpe cecàxfca. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object after verb) wffwpe pew petdñe cetpeca mawpe urwpeñentdpe. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears before the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) bo'càn cocànñe rdw ñecàxñew. fwpe wdcocàdñepe pew fcà petdñe cecàxñecàñécaw. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")

Beginning of Kêtelâæx Grammar Book Excerpts

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Kêtelâæx is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    kû’bûøbâte he æxbâæbâhbûmo (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Kêtelâæx, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Kêtelâæx has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Kêtelâæx, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Kêtelâæx article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is he. For example, in the phrase "he æxbûmo" (the cat), he shows that the noun æxbûmo (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is hbû. An example is "hbû zbûnmêbâlâ" (the house), where hbû shows that zbûnmêbâlâ (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is hemê for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "hemê æxbûmomê", the cats; "hemê zbûnmêbâlâmê", the houses.)

In summary, he is used with masculine singular nouns, hbû with feminine singular nouns, and hemê with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Kêtelâæx.

Before bû, e, n, bâ, j, è, u, sî and some occurrences of x, the singular masculine article he becomes h'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Kêtelâæx noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Kêtelâæx nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -mê (e.g., zbûnmêbâlâ > zbûnmêbâlâmê 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -bûj and -ej take the ending -qâ instead of -mê (e.g., mojèbûj > mojèbûjqâ 'pipes', kûej > kûejqâ 'games'), except for the nouns hbûlâøbûj, mêbûttbûj, qîlâej, and fîhej which form their plural by adding -mê (e.g., qîlâej > qîlâejmê 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -bâj form their plural with -qâ. These are ielâbâj, æbûnhhbâj, xnfîbâj, fînkûbâj, qîbâj, æxbâj, and kûbâjkûbâj (e.g., ielâbâj > ielâbâjqâ 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -bâj, such as fînmêbâj or motbâj, follow the regular plural pattern and take -mê (e.g., motbâj > motbâjmê 'holes').

Nouns that end in -mê, -qâ or -kî in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., hbû ætbânqâ 'the cross' > hemê ætbânqâ 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -bûh typically change to -bûjqâ in the plural (e.g., kûbâjtlâbûh > kûbâjtlâbûjqâ 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -bûh are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -mê instead. These are fîbûh, æbûh, æbûtlâbûvâbûh, æxbûæbûh, wemêmonvâbûh, tuænmobûh, mêetvâbûh and tuibûh (e.g., he wemêmonvâbûh > hemê wemêmonvâbûhmê).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -bûnh change to -bûjqâ in the plural. Examples of this pattern include fîbûnh, æbâtbûnh, uzbûnh, mêbâjqîntbûnh, motbûvâbûnh, and vânmotbûnh (e.g., vânmotbûnh > vânmotbûjqâ 'stained glass windows'). However, some -bûnh nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -mê, notably tbûnh, bûmomontbûnh, æxbûlâøbûnh, øumobûnh, ibâjvâetlâbûnh and qîbâtmobûnh (e.g., jlâ tbûnh > øemê tbûnhmê 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Kêtelâæx are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Kêtelâæx adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like fîebûj and lâbâjvâebûj, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with bû, e, n, bâ, j, è, u, sî and some occurrences of x, e.g. jlâ fîebûj kûbûtønlâ (a beautiful garden), jlâ fîeh xbâzze (a handsome man), jlâe fîehhe wezze (a beautiful woman), hemê fîebûjqâ elâwbûlâmomê (the beautiful children), hemê fîehhemê zbûnmêbâlâmê (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -e to the masculine form, e.g., itbûlâø > itbûlâøe, helâmo > helâmoe, qîetmêbûlâ > qîetmêbûlâe. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -eh, -nh, -bâlâ, -elâ, -bâmê or -bûmê double their final consonant before adding -e (e.g., ætjeh > ætjehhe, ielâmonh > ielâmonhhe, fîbâlâ > fîbâlâlâe, bûlâænelâ > bûlâænelâlâe, itbâmê > itbâmêmêe, and fîbûmê > fîbûmêmêe).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -æ change to -æxe (e.g., fîhbûlâæ > fîhbûlâæxe); those ending in -ejt or -ejqâ change to -ejmêe (e.g., qîtbâzemomoejt > qîtbâzemomoejmêe, wjtnejqâ > wjtnejmêe), with the exception of the irregular vânejqâ (old) whose feminine form is vânenhhe; -i changes to -ije (e.g., hbâlâi > hbâlâije); -nw changes to -nvâe (e.g., bûæmonw > bûæmonvâe); -ew changes to -sîvâe (e.g., fîtew > fîtsîvâe); -et changes to -sîte (e.g., umotbûlâiet > umotbûlâisîte); -emo changes to -sîmoe (e.g., nlâôjnemo > nlâôjnsîmoe); and adjectives ending in -bâj have a special form -bâh (becoming -bâhhe in feminine) that appears before bû, e, n, bâ, j, è, u, sî and some occurrences of x, (e.g., wbâj/wbâh > wbâhhe, zbâj/zbâh > zbâhhe).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -e, it does not change in the feminine (cf. jlâ xbâzze tnæxe 'a rich man' > jlâe wezze tnæxe 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -mê to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., kûbâhn > kûbâhnmê, kûbâhne > kûbâhnemê). If the basic form ends in -mê, -qâ, or -kî, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., fîbûmê > fîbûmê, iulâutejqâ > iulâutejqâ, øbâjqâ > øbâjqâ), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Kêtelâæx adjectives ending in -ebûj take the ending -qâ in the masculine plural (e.g., lâbâjvâebûj > lâbâjvâebûjqâ). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -bûh, which normally change to -bûjqâ in the masculine plural (e.g., xnvâetlâbûh > xnvâetlâbûjqâ, æelâmotbûh > æelâmotbûjqâ), with only two exceptions: wbûmobûh > wbûmobûhmê and lâbûvâbûh > lâbûvâbûhmê which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: æelâmotbûhe > æelâmotbûhemê.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in he tbâjie vânlâ (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are fîebûj (beautiful), fîbâlâ (good), fîtew (brief), itbûlâø (big/tall), itbâmê (fat/large), wbûjqâ (false), xbûjmo (high), hbâlâi (long), fîtew (brief), kûejlâe (young), kûbâhn (pretty), zbûjvâbûnmê (bad), zenhhejt (best), lâbâjvâebûj (new), qîemonmo (small), vânejqâ (old); e.g., jlâe wezze fîehhe ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Kêtelâæx, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Kêtelâæx personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | kûe
         | 2nd (informal)   | moj
         | 2nd (formal)     | vâbâjmê
         | 3rd (masculine)  | nh
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ehhe
         | 3rd (neutral)    | bâlâ
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | lâbâjmê
         | 2nd              | vâbâjmê
         | 3rd (masculine)  | nhmê
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ehhemê
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun kûe occurs before bû, e, n, bâ, j, è, u, sî, r and some occurrences of x, it becomes kû'.

*Relative pronouns

Kêtelâæx, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ôjn is ordinarily used: h'xbâzze ôjn bû vâbâhu zbû fînæèæhemomoe ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ôjn in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: hemê fînæèæhemomoemê ôjn bâlâmo umou vâbâhuemê ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, ôje (or ôj' before bû, e, n, bâ, j, è, u, sî and some occurrences of x) is ordinarily used: hbû fînæèæhemomoe ôj'nh bû vâbâhue ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ôjn, ôje does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Kêtelâæx are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Kêtelâæx is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) bûvâbânt ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of rmote ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is rmote, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is bûvâbânt. Forms of rmote are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Kêtelâæx, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Kêtelâæx verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Kêtelâæx verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -nmêmê- between the stem and the ending.

    In qîbûthbûnelâmo, the stem qîbûth- indicates that the verb is qîbûthet (to speak) and the ending -bûnelâmo marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In wnlânmêmêbâlâmê, the stem wnlâ- indicates that the verb is wnlânt (to finish), the suffix -nmêmê- follows it, and the inflection -bâlâmê marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Kêtelâæx they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    qîbûthet: kûe qîbûthetbûnmê, moj qîbûthbûmê, ôj'nhmê qîbûthbûmêmêelâmo, ôje lâbâjmê qîbûthnbâlâmê, qîbûthekî...
    wnlânt: kûe wnlântbûnmê, vâbâjmê wnlâkâmoemê, ôj'nhmê wnlânmêmêelâmo, wnlânmê, ôje lâbâjmê wnlânmêmênbâlâmê...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    vâbâjhbânt: kûe vâejqâ, moj vâejqâ, nh vâejmo, lâbâjmê vâbâjhbâlâmê, vâbâjmê vâbâjhekî, nhmê vâejhelâmo.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly bûvâbânt, rmote, bûhhet and wbûnte), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -et (with the exception of bûhhet, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    bûnzet, fîbûhbûèet, æxbûlâmoet, elâvâbâèet, wetzet, zbûlâiet, qîbûmêmêet, qîbûèet, qîtbâzelâet, teibûtøet, etc.

        For example, for the verb qîbûthet, the stem is qîbûth- and the ending is -et.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -nt whose present participle ends in -nmêmêbûlâmo:

    fîulânt, æbâzqîbûmont, øuijetqînt, whejtnt, itbûlâønt, xbûït, nlâvâemêmont, qîbâhnt, tbâjint, tjint, mêbûhnt, etc.

        For example, for the verb wnlânt, the stem is wnlâ- and the ending is -nt.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries rmote and bûvâbânt, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. kûe teibûtøe means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -et (all verbs of the first group): -e, -emê, -e, -bâlâmê, -ekî, -elâmo.
    Verbs ending in -nt (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -nmê, -nmê, -nmo, -nmêmêbâlâmê, -nmêmêekî, -nmêmêelâmo. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -te (part of the third group): -mê, -mê, - , -bâlâmê, -ekî, -elâmo.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "kûe teibûtøbûnmê" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -et suffix, e.g., teibûtøet -> teibûtø-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -nt suffix plus the -nmêmê suffix, e.g., æxbânmênt -> æxbânmênmêmê-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -bûnmê, -bûnmê, -bûnmo, -nbâlâmê, -nekî, -bûnelâmo.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb bûvâbânt. They are always regular: -bûn, -bûmê, -bû, -bâlâmê, -ekî, -bâlâmo.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.
