However, some -xuwh nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -og, notably ûpxuwh, xululuwûpxuwh, odmxèægxuwh, ægiulxuwh, îyvâbéûpèxuwh and ayvûpulxuwh (e.g., âè ûpxuwh > ægéog ûpxuwhog 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ovûpéèodm are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ovûpéèodm adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like qéxâ and èyvâbéxâ, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with x, é, uw, yv, â, j, i, t and some occurrences of m, e.g. âè qéxâ ænxûpæguwè (a beautiful garden), âè qéh myvààé (a handsome man), âèé qéhhé ovéààé (a beautiful woman), héog qéxâr éèovxèulog (the beautiful children), héog qéhhéog àxuwogyvèog (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -é to the masculine form, e.g., îûpxèæg > îûpxèægé, héèul > héèulé, aéûpogxè > aéûpogxèé. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -éh, -uwh, -yvè, -éè, -yvog or -xog double their final consonant before adding -é (e.g., odûpâéh > odûpâéhhé, îéèuluwh > îéèuluwhhé, qyvè > qyvèèé, xèoduwéè > xèoduwéèèé, îûpyvog > îûpyvogogé, and qxog > qxogogé).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -od change to -odmé (e.g., qhxèod > qhxèodmé); those ending in -éâûp or -éâr change to -éâogé (e.g., aûpyvàéululéâûp > aûpyvàéululéâogé, ovâûpuwéâr > ovâûpuwéâogé), with the exception of the irregular buwéâr (old) whose feminine form is buwéuwhhé; -î changes to -îâé (e.g., hyvèî > hyvèîâé); -uwov changes to -uwbé (e.g., xoduluwov > xoduluwbé); -éov changes to -tbé (e.g., qûpéov > qûptbé); -éûp changes to -tûpé (e.g., iulûpxèîéûp > iulûpxèîtûpé); -éul changes to -tulé (e.g., uwèôâuwéul > uwèôâuwtulé); and adjectives ending in -yvâ have a special form -yvh (becoming -yvhhé in feminine) that appears before x, é, uw, yv, â, j, i, t and some occurrences of m, (e.g., ovyvâ/ovyvh > ovyvhhé, àyvâ/àyvh > àyvhhé).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -é, it does not change in the feminine (cf. âè myvààé ûpuwodmé 'a rich man' > âèé ovéààé ûpuwodmé 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -og to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., ænyvhuw > ænyvhuwog, ænyvhuwé > ænyvhuwéog). If the basic form ends in -og, -r, or -ud, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., qxog > qxog, îièiûpéâr > îièiûpéâr, ægyvâr > ægyvâr), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ovûpéèodm adjectives ending in -éxâ take the ending -r in the masculine plural (e.g., èyvâbéxâ > èyvâbéxâr). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -xh, which normally change to -xâr in the masculine plural (e.g., muwbéûpèxh > muwbéûpèxâr, odéèulûpxh > odéèulûpxâr), with only two exceptions: ovxulxh > ovxulxhog and èxbxh > èxbxhog which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: odéèulûpxhé > odéèulûpxhéog.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in hé ûpyvâîé buwè (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are qéxâ (beautiful), qyvè (good), qûpéov (brief), îûpxèæg (big/tall), îûpyvog (fat/large), ovxâr (false), mxâul (high), hyvèî (long), qûpéov (brief), ænéâèé (young), ænyvhuw (pretty), àxâbxuwog (bad), àéuwhhéâûp (best), èyvâbéxâ (new), aéuluwul (small), buwéâr (old); e.g., âèé ovéààé qéhhé ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ovûpéèodm, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ovûpéèodm personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | æné
         | 2nd (informal)   | ulâ
         | 2nd (formal)     | byvâog
         | 3rd (masculine)  | uwh
         | 3rd (feminine)   | éhhé
         | 3rd (neutral)    | yvè
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | èyvâog
         | 2nd              | byvâog
         | 3rd (masculine)  | uwhog
         | 3rd (feminine)   | éhhéog
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun æné occurs before x, é, uw, yv, â, j, i, t, e and some occurrences of m, it becomes æn'.

*Relative pronouns

Ovûpéèodm, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ôâuw is ordinarily used: h'myvààé ôâuw x byvhi àx quwodjodhéululé ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ôâuw in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: héog quwodjodhéululéog ôâuw yvèul iuli byvhiéog ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, ôâé (or ôâ' before x, é, uw, yv, â, j, i, t and some occurrences of m) is ordinarily used: hx quwodjodhéululé ôâ'uwh x byvhié ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ôâuw, ôâé does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ovûpéèodm are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ovûpéèodm is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) xbyvuwûp ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of eulûpé ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is eulûpé, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is xbyvuwûp. Forms of eulûpé are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ovûpéèodm, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ovûpéèodm verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ovûpéèodm verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -uwogog- between the stem and the ending.

    In axûphxuwéèul, the stem axûph- indicates that the verb is axûphéûp (to speak) and the ending -xuwéèul marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ovuwèuwogogyvèog, the stem ovuwè- indicates that the verb is ovuwèuwûp (to finish), the suffix -uwogog- follows it, and the inflection -yvèog marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ovûpéèodm they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    axûphéûp: æné axûphéûpxuwog, ulâ axûphxog, ôâ'uwhog axûphxogogéèul, ôâé èyvâog axûphuwyvèog, axûphéud...
    ovuwèuwûp: æné ovuwèuwûpxuwog, byvâog ovuwèæluléog, ôâ'uwhog ovuwèuwogogéèul, ovuwèuwog, ôâé èyvâog ovuwèuwogoguwyvèog...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    byvâhyvuwûp: æné béâr, ulâ béâr, uwh béâul, èyvâog byvâhyvèog, byvâog byvâhéud, uwhog béâhéèul.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly xbyvuwûp, eulûpé, xhhéûp and ovxuwûpé), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -éûp (with the exception of xhhéûp, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    xuwàéûp, qxhxjéûp, odmxèuléûp, éèbyvjéûp, ovéûpàéûp, àxèîéûp, axogogéûp, axjéûp, aûpyvàéèéûp, ûpéîxûpægéûp, etc.

        For example, for the verb axûphéûp, the stem is axûph- and the ending is -éûp.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -uwûp whose present participle ends in -uwogogxèul:

    qièuwûp, odyvàaxuluwûp, ægiîâéûpauwûp, ovhéâûpuwûp, îûpxèæguwûp, mxïûp, uwèbéoguluwûp, ayvhuwûp, ûpyvâîuwûp, ûpâîuwûp, ogxhuwûp, etc.

        For example, for the verb ovuwèuwûp, the stem is ovuwè- and the ending is -uwûp.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries eulûpé and xbyvuwûp, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. æné ûpéîxûpægé means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -éûp (all verbs of the first group): -é, -éog, -é, -yvèog, -éud, -éèul.
    Verbs ending in -uwûp (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -uwog, -uwog, -uwul, -uwogogyvèog, -uwogogéud, -uwogogéèul. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -ûpé (part of the third group): -og, -og, - , -yvèog, -éud, -éèul.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "æné ûpéîxûpægxuwog" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -éûp suffix, e.g., ûpéîxûpægéûp -> ûpéîxûpæg-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -uwûp suffix plus the -uwogog suffix, e.g., odmyvuwoguwûp -> odmyvuwoguwogog-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -xuwog, -xuwog, -xuwul, -uwyvèog, -uwéud, -xuwéèul.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -é and -og, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "âè ovûpâuwul odyvèovuwul", "âèé ayvuwûpé odyvèovuwulé", "ægéog ovûpâuwulog odyvèovuwulog", and "ægéog ayvuwûpéog odyvèovuwuléog."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -i for the 1st group verbs, or in -uw for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -â (éèuléèægûpé éèuléèægâ, qyvuwûpé qâ, huwûpé hâ, etc. and ogxbyvuwûp ogâ, byvuwûp bâ, ayvâbyvuwûp aâ), -uwog (àéululûpé àuwog, aûpéèægûpé aûpuwog, etc.), -âog (uwèodhâûpé uwèodhâog and ûpéodhâûpé ûpéodhâog and only these verbs), -uwul (àxâæguwûpé àxâæguwul, æguwûpé æguwul, etc.), -ul (verbs in -uwèægûpé : aéuwèægûpé aéuwèul), -éûpul (yvâbûpuwûp yvâbéûpul, odyvâbûpuwûp odyvâbéûpul, yvovovûpuwûp yvovovéûpul and ogyvâovovûpuwûp ogyvâovovéûpul), or éâ (xbyvuwûp éâ). 

*Compound Tenses

Ovûpéèodm compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either xbyvuwûp or eulûpé) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Ovûpéèodm, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Ovûpéèodm. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either xbyvuwûp or eulûpé in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "æn'xuw àxèîi" (I ate) or "uwh éogul xûpûpuwbi" (He arrived). xbyvuwûp is used with most verbs, while eulûpé is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, xbyvuwûp should be used by default.

3rd person     | uwh/éhhé/yvè x ûpéîxûpægi       | uwhog/éhhéog yvèul ûpéîxûpægi

In Àjhykzeiþ, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Àjhykzeiþ has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Àjhykzeiþ, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Àjhykzeiþ article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is ðyk. For example, in the phrase "ðyk eiþàþx" (the cat), ðyk shows that the noun eiþàþx (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is ðàþ. An example is "ðàþ évàþéñyþimz" (the house), where ðàþ shows that évàþéñyþimz (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ðykyþ for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "ðykyþ eiþàþxyþ", the cats; "ðykyþ évàþéñyþimzyþ", the houses.)

In summary, ðyk is used with masculine singular nouns, ðàþ with feminine singular nouns, and ðykyþ with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Àjhykzeiþ.

Before àþ, yk, éñ, im, él, àk, o, añ and some occurrences of iþ, the singular masculine article ðyk becomes ð'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Àjhykzeiþ noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Àjhykzeiþ nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -yþ (e.g., évàþéñyþimz > évàþéñyþimzyþ 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -àþél and -ykél take the ending -éd instead of -yþ (e.g., xélàkàþél > xélàkàþéléd 'pipes', gykél > gykéléd 'games'), except for the nouns ðàþzaþàþél, yþàþhhàþél, ylzykél, and fðykél which form their plural by adding -yþ (e.g., ylzykél > ylzykélyþ 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -imél form their plural with -éd. These are açykzimél, eàþéñððimél, iþéñfimél, féñgimél, ylimél, eiþimél, and gimélgimél (e.g., açykzimél > açykziméléd 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -imél, such as féñyþimél or xhimél, follow the regular plural pattern and take -yþ (e.g., xhimél > xhimélyþ 'holes').

Nouns that end in -yþ, -éd or -è in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., ðàþ ehiméñéd 'the cross' > ðykyþ ehiméñéd 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -àþð typically change to -àþéléd in the plural (e.g., gimélhzàþð > gimélhzàþéléd 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -àþð are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -yþ instead. These are fàþð, eàþð, eàþhzàþijàþð, eiþàþeàþð, sykyþxéñijàþð, hoeéñxàþð, yþykhijàþð and hoaçàþð (e.g., ðyk sykyþxéñijàþð > ðykyþ sykyþxéñijàþðyþ).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -àþéñð change to -àþéléd in the plural. Examples of this pattern include fàþéñð, eimhàþéñð, oévàþéñð, yþimélyléñhàþéñð, xhàþijàþéñð, and ijéñxhàþéñð (e.g., ijéñxhàþéñð > ijéñxhàþéléd 'stained glass windows'). However, some -àþéñð nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -yþ, notably hàþéñð, àþxxéñhàþéñð, eiþàþzaþàþéñð, aþoxàþéñð, açimélijykhzàþéñð and ylimhxàþéñð (e.g., élz hàþéñð > aþykyþ hàþéñðyþ 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Àjhykzeiþ are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Àjhykzeiþ adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like fykàþél and zimélijykàþél, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with àþ, yk, éñ, im, él, àk, o, añ and some occurrences of iþ, e.g. élz fykàþél gàþhaþéñz (a beautiful garden), élz fykð iþimévévyk (a handsome man), élzyk fykððyk sykévévyk (a beautiful woman), ðykyþ fykàþéléd ykzsàþzxyþ (the beautiful children), ðykyþ fykððykyþ évàþéñyþimzyþ (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -yk to the masculine form, e.g., açhàþzaþ > açhàþzaþyk, ðykzx > ðykzxyk, ylykhyþàþz > ylykhyþàþzyk. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ykð, -éñð, -imz, -ykz, -imyþ or -àþyþ double their final consonant before adding -yk (e.g., ehélykð > ehélykððyk, açykzxéñð > açykzxéñððyk, fimz > fimzzyk, àþzeéñykz > àþzeéñykzzyk, açhimyþ > açhimyþyþyk, and fàþyþ > fàþyþyþyk).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -e change to -eiþyk (e.g., fðàþze > fðàþzeiþyk); those ending in -ykélh or -ykéléd change to -ykélyþyk (e.g., ylhimévykxxykélh > ylhimévykxxykélyþyk, sélhéñykéléd > sélhéñykélyþyk), with the exception of the irregular ijéñykéléd (old) whose feminine form is ijéñykéñððyk; -aç changes to -açélyk (e.g., ðimzaç > ðimzaçélyk); -éñs changes to -éñijyk (e.g., àþexéñs > àþexéñijyk); -yks changes to -añijyk (e.g., fhyks > fhañijyk); -ykh changes to -añhyk (e.g., oxhàþzaçykh > oxhàþzaçañhyk); -ykx changes to -añxyk (e.g., éñzwéléñykx > éñzwéléñañxyk); and adjectives ending in -imél have a special form -imð (becoming -imððyk in feminine) that appears before àþ, yk, éñ, im, él, àk, o, añ and some occurrences of iþ, (e.g., simél/simð > simððyk, évimél/évimð > évimððyk).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -yk, it does not change in the feminine (cf. élz iþimévévyk héñeiþyk 'a rich man' > élzyk sykévévyk héñeiþyk 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -yþ to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., gimðéñ > gimðéñyþ, gimðéñyk > gimðéñykyþ). If the basic form ends in -yþ, -éd, or -è, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., fàþyþ > fàþyþ, açozohykéléd > açozohykéléd, aþiméléd > aþiméléd), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Àjhykzeiþ adjectives ending in -ykàþél take the ending -éd in the masculine plural (e.g., zimélijykàþél > zimélijykàþéléd). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -àþð, which normally change to -àþéléd in the masculine plural (e.g., iþéñijykhzàþð > iþéñijykhzàþéléd, eykzxhàþð > eykzxhàþéléd), with only two exceptions: sàþxàþð > sàþxàþðyþ and zàþijàþð > zàþijàþðyþ which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: eykzxhàþðyk > eykzxhàþðykyþ.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in ðyk himélaçyk ijéñz (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are fykàþél (beautiful), fimz (good), fhyks (brief), açhàþzaþ (big/tall), açhimyþ (fat/large), sàþéléd (false), iþàþélx (high), ðimzaç (long), fhyks (brief), gykélzyk (young), gimðéñ (pretty), évàþélijàþéñyþ (bad), évykéñððykélh (best), zimélijykàþél (new), ylykxéñx (small), ijéñykéléd (old); e.g., élzyk sykévévyk fykððyk ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Àjhykzeiþ, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Àjhykzeiþ personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | gyk
         | 2nd (informal)   | xél
         | 2nd (formal)     | ijimélyþ
         | 3rd (masculine)  | éñð
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ykððyk
         | 3rd (neutral)    | imz
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | zimélyþ
         | 2nd              | ijimélyþ
         | 3rd (masculine)  | éñðyþ
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ykððykyþ
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun gyk occurs before àþ, yk, éñ, im, él, àk, o, añ, ê and some occurrences of iþ, it becomes g'.

*Relative pronouns

Àjhykzeiþ, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, wéléñ is ordinarily used: ð'iþimévévyk wéléñ àþ ijimðo évàþ féñeàkeðykxxyk ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that wéléñ in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: ðykyþ féñeàkeðykxxykyþ wéléñ imzx oxo ijimðoykyþ ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, wélyk (or wél' before àþ, yk, éñ, im, él, àk, o, añ and some occurrences of iþ) is ordinarily used: ðàþ féñeàkeðykxxyk wél'éñð àþ ijimðoyk ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like wéléñ, wélyk does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Àjhykzeiþ are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Àjhykzeiþ is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) àþijiméñh ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êxhyk ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êxhyk, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is àþijiméñh. Forms of êxhyk are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Àjhykzeiþ, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Àjhykzeiþ verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Àjhykzeiþ verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -éñyþyþ- between the stem and the ending.

    In ylàþhðàþéñykzx, the stem ylàþhð- indicates that the verb is ylàþhðykh (to speak) and the ending -àþéñykzx marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In séñzéñyþyþimzyþ, the stem séñz- indicates that the verb is séñzéñh (to finish), the suffix -éñyþyþ- follows it, and the inflection -imzyþ marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Àjhykzeiþ they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ylàþhðykh: gyk ylàþhðykhàþéñyþ, xél ylàþhðàþyþ, wél'éñðyþ ylàþhðàþyþyþykzx, wélyk zimélyþ ylàþhðéñimzyþ, ylàþhðykè...
    séñzéñh: gyk séñzéñhàþéñyþ, ijimélyþ séñzîxykyþ, wél'éñðyþ séñzéñyþyþykzx, séñzéñyþ, wélyk zimélyþ séñzéñyþyþéñimzyþ...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ijimélðiméñh: gyk ijykéléd, xél ijykéléd, éñð ijykélx, zimélyþ ijimélðimzyþ, ijimélyþ ijimélðykè, éñðyþ ijykélðykzx.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly àþijiméñh, êxhyk, àþððykh and sàþéñhyk), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ykh (with the exception of àþððykh, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    àþéñévykh, fàþðàþàkykh, eiþàþzxykh, ykzijimàkykh, sykhévykh, évàþzaçykh, ylàþyþyþykh, ylàþàkykh, ylhimévykzykh, hykaçàþhaþykh, etc.

        For example, for the verb ylàþhðykh, the stem is ylàþhð- and the ending is -ykh.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -éñh whose present participle ends in -éñyþyþàþzx:

    fozéñh, eimévylàþxéñh, aþoaçélykhyléñh, sðykélhéñh, açhàþzaþéñh, iþàþïh, éñzijykyþxéñh, ylimðéñh, himélaçéñh, hélaçéñh, yþàþðéñh, etc.

        For example, for the verb séñzéñh, the stem is séñz- and the ending is -éñh.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êxhyk and àþijiméñh, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. gyk hykaçàþhaþyk means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -ykh (all verbs of the first group): -yk, -ykyþ, -yk, -imzyþ, -ykè, -ykzx.
    Verbs ending in -éñh (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -éñyþ, -éñyþ, -éñx, -éñyþyþimzyþ, -éñyþyþykè, -éñyþyþykzx. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -hyk (part of the third group): -yþ, -yþ, - , -imzyþ, -ykè, -ykzx.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "gyk hykaçàþhaþàþéñyþ" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -ykh suffix, e.g., hykaçàþhaþykh -> hykaçàþhaþ-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -éñh suffix plus the -éñyþyþ suffix, e.g., eiþiméñyþéñh -> eiþiméñyþéñyþyþ-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -àþéñyþ, -àþéñyþ, -àþéñx, -éñimzyþ, -éñykè, -àþéñykzx.



    Example:

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb àþijiméñh. They are always regular: -àþéñ, -àþyþ, -àþ, -imzyþ, -ykè, -imzx.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

        gyk eiþiméñyþéñhàþéñ ('I will choose'), xél hykaçàþhaþykhàþyþ ('you will watch'), ykððyk yþimhxéñhàþ ('she will exit'), zimélyþ xhàþijàþéñððykhimzyþ ('we will work'), ijimélyþ himélaçéñhykè ('you will blush'), éñðyþ ylàþhxéñhimzx ('they will leave').

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

Midacègeméhé has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Midacègeméhé, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Midacègeméhé article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is ncè. For example, in the phrase "ncè méhéliz" (the cat), ncè shows that the noun méhéliz (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is nli. An example is "nli qlirsitge" (the house), where nli shows that qlirsitge (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ncèsi for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "ncèsi méhélizsi", the cats; "ncèsi qlirsitgesi", the houses.)

In summary, ncè is used with masculine singular nouns, nli with feminine singular nouns, and ncèsi with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Midacègeméhé.

Before li, cè, r, t, va, à, x, vé and some occurrences of hé, the singular masculine article ncè becomes n'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Midacègeméhé noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Midacègeméhé nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -si (e.g., qlirsitge > qlirsitgesi 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -liva and -cèva take the ending -y instead of -si (e.g., zvaàliva > zvaàlivay 'pipes', dècèva > dècèvay 'games'), except for the nouns nligekliva, silidadaliva, bgecèva, and oncèva which form their plural by adding -si (e.g., bgecèva > bgecèvasi 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -tva form their plural with -y. These are cacègetva, mélirnntva, hérotva, ordètva, btva, méhétva, and dètvadètva (e.g., cacègetva > cacègetvay 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -tva, such as orsitva or zdatva, follow the regular plural pattern and take -si (e.g., zdatva > zdatvasi 'holes').

Nouns that end in -si, -y or -f in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., nli médatry 'the cross' > ncèsi médatry 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -lin typically change to -livay in the plural (e.g., dètvadagelin > dètvadagelivay 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -lin are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -si instead. These are olin, mélin, mélidagelihilin, méhélimélin, micèsizrhilin, daxmérzlin, sicèdahilin and daxcalin (e.g., ncè micèsizrhilin > ncèsi micèsizrhilinsi).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -lirn change to -livay in the plural. Examples of this pattern include olirn, métdalirn, xqlirn, sitvabrdalirn, zdalihilirn, and hirzdalirn (e.g., hirzdalirn > hirzdalivay 'stained glass windows'). However, some -lirn nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -si, notably dalirn, lizzrdalirn, méhéligeklirn, kxzlirn, catvahicèdagelirn and btdazlirn (e.g., vage dalirn > kcèsi dalirnsi 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Midacègeméhé are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Midacègeméhé adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ocèliva and getvahicèliva, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with li, cè, r, t, va, à, x, vé and some occurrences of hé, e.g. vage ocèliva dèlidakrge (a beautiful garden), vage ocèn hétqqcè (a handsome man), vagecè ocènncè micèqqcè (a beautiful woman), ncèsi ocèlivay cègemiligezsi (the beautiful children), ncèsi ocènncèsi qlirsitgesi (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -cè to the masculine form, e.g., cadaligek > cadaligekcè, ncègez > ncègezcè, bcèdasilige > bcèdasiligecè. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -cèn, -rn, -tge, -cège, -tsi or -lisi double their final consonant before adding -cè (e.g., médavacèn > médavacènncè, cacègezrn > cacègezrnncè, otge > otgegecè, ligemércège > ligemércègegecè, cadatsi > cadatsisicè, and olisi > olisisicè).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -mé change to -méhécè (e.g., onligemé > onligeméhécè); those ending in -cèvada or -cèvay change to -cèvasicè (e.g., bdatqcèzzcèvada > bdatqcèzzcèvasicè, mivadarcèvay > mivadarcèvasicè), with the exception of the irregular hircèvay (old) whose feminine form is hircèrnncè; -ca changes to -cavacè (e.g., ntgeca > ntgecavacè); -rmi changes to -rhicè (e.g., limézrmi > limézrhicè); -cèmi changes to -véhicè (e.g., odacèmi > odavéhicè); -cèda changes to -védacè (e.g., xzdaligecacèda > xzdaligecavédacè); -cèz changes to -vézcè (e.g., rgejvarcèz > rgejvarvézcè); and adjectives ending in -tva have a special form -tn (becoming -tnncè in feminine) that appears before li, cè, r, t, va, à, x, vé and some occurrences of hé, (e.g., mitva/mitn > mitnncè, qtva/qtn > qtnncè).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -cè, it does not change in the feminine (cf. vage hétqqcè darméhécè 'a rich man' > vagecè micèqqcè darméhécè 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -si to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., dètnr > dètnrsi, dètnrcè > dètnrcèsi). If the basic form ends in -si, -y, or -f, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., olisi > olisi, caxgexdacèvay > caxgexdacèvay, ktvay > ktvay), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Midacègeméhé adjectives ending in -cèliva take the ending -y in the masculine plural (e.g., getvahicèliva > getvahicèlivay). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -lin, which normally change to -livay in the masculine plural (e.g., hérhicèdagelin > hérhicèdagelivay, mécègezdalin > mécègezdalivay), with only two exceptions: milizlin > milizlinsi and gelihilin > gelihilinsi which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: mécègezdalincè > mécègezdalincèsi.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in ncè datvacacè hirge (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are ocèliva (beautiful), otge (good), odacèmi (brief), cadaligek (big/tall), cadatsi (fat/large), milivay (false), hélivaz (high), ntgeca (long), odacèmi (brief), dècèvagecè (young), dètnr (pretty), qlivahilirsi (bad), qcèrnncèvada (best), getvahicèliva (new), bcèzrz (small), hircèvay (old); e.g., vagecè micèqqcè ocènncè ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Midacègeméhé, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Midacègeméhé personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | dècè
         | 2nd (informal)   | zva
         | 2nd (formal)     | hitvasi
         | 3rd (masculine)  | rn
         | 3rd (feminine)   | cènncè
         | 3rd (neutral)    | tge
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | getvasi
         | 2nd              | hitvasi
         | 3rd (masculine)  | rnsi
         | 3rd (feminine)   | cènncèsi
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun dècè occurs before li, cè, r, t, va, à, x, vé, ê and some occurrences of hé, it becomes dè'.

*Relative pronouns

Midacègeméhé, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, jvar is ordinarily used: n'hétqqcè jvar li hitnx qli orméàméncèzzcè ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that jvar in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: ncèsi orméàméncèzzcèsi jvar tgez xzx hitnxcèsi ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, jvacè (or jva' before li, cè, r, t, va, à, x, vé and some occurrences of hé) is ordinarily used: nli orméàméncèzzcè jva'rn li hitnxcè ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like jvar, jvacè does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Midacègeméhé are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Midacègeméhé is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) lihitrda ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êzdacè ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êzdacè, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is lihitrda. Forms of êzdacè are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Midacègeméhé, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Midacègeméhé verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Midacègeméhé verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -rsisi- between the stem and the ending.

    In blidanlircègez, the stem blidan- indicates that the verb is blidancèda (to speak) and the ending -lircègez marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In mirgersisitgesi, the stem mirge- indicates that the verb is mirgerda (to finish), the suffix -rsisi- follows it, and the inflection -tgesi marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Midacègeméhé they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    blidancèda: dècè blidancèdalirsi, zva blidanlisi, jva'rnsi blidanlisisicègez, jvacè getvasi blidanrtgesi, blidancèf...
    mirgerda: dècè mirgerdalirsi, hitvasi mirgeîzcèsi, jva'rnsi mirgersisicègez, mirgersi, jvacè getvasi mirgersisirtgesi...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    hitvantrda: dècè hicèvay, zva hicèvay, rn hicèvaz, getvasi hitvantgesi, hitvasi hitvancèf, rnsi hicèvancègez.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly lihitrda, êzdacè, linncèda and milirdacè), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -cèda (with the exception of linncèda, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    lirqcèda, olinliàcèda, méhéligezcèda, cègehitàcèda, micèdaqcèda, qligecacèda, blisisicèda, bliàcèda, bdatqcègecèda, dacècalidakcèda, etc.

        For example, for the verb blidancèda, the stem is blidan- and the ending is -cèda.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -rda whose present participle ends in -rsisiligez:

    oxgerda, métqblizrda, kxcavacèdabrda, mincèvadarda, cadaligekrda, héliïda, rgehicèsizrda, btnrda, datvacarda, davacarda, silinrda, etc.

        For example, for the verb mirgerda, the stem is mirge- and the ending is -rda.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êzdacè and lihitrda, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. dècè dacècalidakcè means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -cèda (all verbs of the first group): -cè, -cèsi, -cè, -tgesi, -cèf, -cègez.
    Verbs ending in -rda (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -rsi, -rsi, -rz, -rsisitgesi, -rsisicèf, -rsisicègez. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -dacè (part of the third group): -si, -si, - , -tgesi, -cèf, -cègez.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "dècè dacècalidaklirsi" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -cèda suffix, e.g., dacècalidakcèda -> dacècalidak-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -rda suffix plus the -rsisi suffix, e.g., méhétrsirda -> méhétrsirsisi-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -lirsi, -lirsi, -lirz, -rtgesi, -rcèf, -lircègez.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb lihitrda. They are always regular: -lir, -lisi, -li, -tgesi, -cèf, -tgez.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -cè and -si, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "vage midavarz métgemirz", "vagecè btrdacè métgemirzcè", "kcèsi midavarzsi métgemirzsi", and "kcèsi btrdacèsi métgemirzcèsi."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -x for the 1st group verbs, or in -r for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -va (cègezcègekdacè cègezcègekva, otrdacè ova, nrdacè nva, etc. and silihitrda siva, hitrda hiva, btvahitrda bva), -rsi (qcèzzdacè qrsi, bdacègekdacè bdarsi, etc.), -vasi (rgeménvadacè rgeménvasi and dacèménvadacè dacèménvasi and only these verbs), -rz (qlivakrdacè qlivakrz, krdacè krz, etc.), -z (verbs in -rgekdacè : bcèrgekdacè bcèrgez), -cèdaz (tvahidarda tvahicèdaz, métvahidarda métvahicèdaz, tmimidarda tmimicèdaz and sitvamimidarda sitvamimicèdaz), or cèva (lihitrda cèva). 

*Compound Tenses

Midacègeméhé compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either lihitrda or êzdacè) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Midacègeméhé, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -bô, -éô, -âxh, -bh, -âxn or -an double their final consonant before adding -b (e.g., lpçbô > lpçbôôb, âñbhûéô > âñbhûéôôb, îfâxh > îfâxhhb, ahlébh > ahlébhhb, âñpâxn > âñpâxnnb, and îfan > îfannb).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -l change to -lytb (e.g., îfôahl > îfôahlytb); those ending in -bçp or -bçâr change to -bçnb (e.g., þpâxørbûûbçp > þpâxørbûûbçnb, eçpébçâr > eçpébçnb), with the exception of the irregular îtébçâr (old) whose feminine form is îtébéôôb; -âñ changes to -âñçb (e.g., ôâxhâñ > ôâxhâñçb); -ée changes to -éîtb (e.g., alûée > alûéîtb); -be changes to -wîtb (e.g., îfpbe > îfpwîtb); -bp changes to -wpb (e.g., yfûpahâñbp > yfûpahâñwpb); -bû changes to -wûb (e.g., éhgçébû > éhgçéwûb); and adjectives ending in -âxç have a special form -âxô (becoming -âxôôb in feminine) that appears before a, b, é, âx, ç, à, yf, w and some occurrences of yt, (e.g., eâxç/eâxô > eâxôôb, ørâxç/ørâxô > ørâxôôb).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -b, it does not change in the feminine (cf. çh ytâxørørb pélytb 'a rich man' > çhb ebørørb pélytb 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -n to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., zâxôé > zâxôén, zâxôéb > zâxôébn). If the basic form ends in -n, -âr, or -øñ, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., îfan > îfan, âñyfhyfpbçâr > âñyfhyfpbçâr, câxçâr > câxçâr), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Øspbhlyt adjectives ending in -baç take the ending -âr in the masculine plural (e.g., hâxçîtbaç > hâxçîtbaçâr). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -aô, which normally change to -açâr in the masculine plural (e.g., ytéîtbphaô > ytéîtbphaçâr, lbhûpaô > lbhûpaçâr), with only two exceptions: eaûaô > eaûaôn and haîtaô > haîtaôn which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: lbhûpaôb > lbhûpaôbn.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in ôb pâxçâñb îtéh (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are îfbaç (beautiful), îfâxh (good), îfpbe (brief), âñpahc (big/tall), âñpâxn (fat/large), eaçâr (false), ytaçû (high), ôâxhâñ (long), îfpbe (brief), zbçhb (young), zâxôé (pretty), øraçîtaén (bad), ørbéôôbçp (best), hâxçîtbaç (new), þbûéû (small), îtébçâr (old); e.g., çhb ebørørb îfbôôb ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Øspbhlyt, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Øspbhlyt personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | zb
         | 2nd (informal)   | ûç
         | 2nd (formal)     | îtâxçn
         | 3rd (masculine)  | éô
         | 3rd (feminine)   | bôôb
         | 3rd (neutral)    | âxh
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | hâxçn
         | 2nd              | îtâxçn
         | 3rd (masculine)  | éôn
         | 3rd (feminine)   | bôôbn
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun zb occurs before a, b, é, âx, ç, à, yf, w, øv and some occurrences of yt, it becomes z'.

*Relative pronouns

Øspbhlyt, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, gçé is ordinarily used: ô'ytâxørørb gçé a îtâxôyf øra îfélàlôbûûb ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that gçé in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: ôbn îfélàlôbûûbn gçé âxhû yfûyf îtâxôyfbn ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, gçb (or gç' before a, b, é, âx, ç, à, yf, w and some occurrences of yt) is ordinarily used: ôa îfélàlôbûûb gç'éô a îtâxôyfb ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like gçé, gçb does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Øspbhlyt are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Øspbhlyt is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) aîtâxép ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of øvûpb ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is øvûpb, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is aîtâxép. Forms of øvûpb are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Øspbhlyt, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Øspbhlyt verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Øspbhlyt verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -énn- between the stem and the ending.

    In þapôaébhû, the stem þapô- indicates that the verb is þapôbp (to speak) and the ending -aébhû marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In eéhénnâxhn, the stem eéh- indicates that the verb is eéhép (to finish), the suffix -énn- follows it, and the inflection -âxhn marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Øspbhlyt they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    þapôbp: zb þapôbpaén, ûç þapôan, gç'éôn þapôannbhû, gçb hâxçn þapôéâxhn, þapôbøñ...
    eéhép: zb eéhépaén, îtâxçn eéhmûbn, gç'éôn eéhénnbhû, eéhén, gçb hâxçn eéhénnéâxhn...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    îtâxçôâxép: zb îtbçâr, ûç îtbçâr, éô îtbçû, hâxçn îtâxçôâxhn, îtâxçn îtâxçôbøñ, éôn îtbçôbhû.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly aîtâxép, øvûpb, aôôbp and eaépb), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -bp (with the exception of aôôbp, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    aéørbp, îfaôaàbp, lytahûbp, bhîtâxàbp, ebpørbp, ørahâñbp, þannbp, þaàbp, þpâxørbhbp, pbâñapcbp, etc.

        For example, for the verb þapôbp, the stem is þapô- and the ending is -bp.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ép whose present participle ends in -énnahû:

    îfyfhép, lâxørþaûép, cyfâñçbpþép, eôbçpép, âñpahcép, ytaïp, éhîtbnûép, þâxôép, pâxçâñép, pçâñép, naôép, etc.

        For example, for the verb eéhép, the stem is eéh- and the ending is -ép.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries øvûpb and aîtâxép, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. zb pbâñapcb means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -bp (all verbs of the first group): -b, -bn, -b, -âxhn, -bøñ, -bhû.
    Verbs ending in -ép (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -én, -én, -éû, -énnâxhn, -énnbøñ, -énnbhû. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -pb (part of the third group): -n, -n, - , -âxhn, -bøñ, -bhû.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "zb pbâñapcaén" means "I was watching".

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -b and -n, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "çh epçéû lâxheéû", "çhb þâxépb lâxheéûb", "cbn epçéûn lâxheéûn", and "cbn þâxépbn lâxheéûbn."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -yf for the 1st group verbs, or in -é for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -ç (bhûbhcpb bhûbhcç, îfâxépb îfç, ôépb ôç, etc. and naîtâxép nç, îtâxép îtç, þâxçîtâxép þç), -én (ørbûûpb ørén, þpbhcpb þpén, etc.), -çn (éhlôçpb éhlôçn and pblôçpb pblôçn and only these verbs), -éû (øraçcépb øraçcéû, cépb céû, etc.), -û (verbs in -éhcpb : þbéhcpb þbéhû), -bpû (âxçîtpép âxçîtbpû, lâxçîtpép lâxçîtbpû, âxeepép âxeebpû and nâxçeepép nâxçeebpû), or bç (aîtâxép bç). 

*Compound Tenses

Øspbhlyt compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either aîtâxép or øvûpb) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Øspbhlyt, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Øspbhlyt. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either aîtâxép or øvûpb in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "z'aé ørahâñyf" (I ate) or "éô bnû appéîtyf" (He arrived). aîtâxép is used with most verbs, while øvûpb is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, aîtâxép should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Øspbhlyt: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is aîtâxép.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) bôôbn âxhû câxpøré. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) lôaépb a îtç cbçâr îfaôbéhbn. ("lôaépb saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) éô à aîtaéû cbçâr îfaôbéhbn. lôaépb ôbn a îtçbn. ("There were two whales. lôaépb saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) gçbôôbn îfaôbéhbn lôaépb a-û-bôôb îtçbn ? ("Which whales did lôaépb see?")
        (relative clause introduced by gçb) ôbn cbçâr îfaôbéhbn gçb lôaépb a îtçbn ("the two whales that lôaépb saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Øspbhlyt.

B. The auxiliary is øvûpb, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        bôôbn nâxhû appéîtyfbn. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is øvûpb and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with aîtâxép in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears after the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) bôôbn nb nâxhû nçllyfcyf. hâxçn hâxçn nâxørørbn þapôyf. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object after verb) bôôbn nb nâxhû þâxnyf cbn gçbnûéâxhn. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears before the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

However, some -ofk nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -às, notably itofk, onnfitofk, ecxoàguvofk, uvbnofk, icèvàrèguhitàgofk and àlèvitnofk (e.g., àràg itofk > uvuhàs itofkàs 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ihituhàgecx are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ihituhàgecx adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like þuhoàr and àgèvàrèguhoàr, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with o, uh, f, èv, àr, ig, b, é and some occurrences of x, e.g. àràg þuhoàr ècoituvfàg (a beautiful garden), àràg þuhk xèvehehuh (a handsome man), àràguh þuhkkuh ihuhehehuh (a beautiful woman), kuhàs þuhoàres uhàgihoàgnàs (the beautiful children), kuhàs þuhkkuhàs ehofàsèvàgàs (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -uh to the masculine form, e.g., icitoàguv > icitoàguvuh, kuhàgn > kuhàgnuh, àluhitàsoàg > àluhitàsoàguh. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -uhk, -fk, -èvàg, -uhàg, -èvàs or -oàs double their final consonant before adding -uh (e.g., ecitàruhk > ecitàruhkkuh, icuhàgnfk > icuhàgnfkkuh, þèvàg > þèvàgàguh, oàgecfuhàg > oàgecfuhàgàguh, icitèvàs > icitèvàsàsuh, and þoàs > þoàsàsuh).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -ec change to -ecxuh (e.g., þkoàgec > þkoàgecxuh); those ending in -uhàrit or -uhàres change to -uhàràsuh (e.g., àlitèvehuhnnuhàrit > àlitèvehuhnnuhàràsuh, ihàritfuhàres > ihàritfuhàràsuh), with the exception of the irregular ègfuhàres (old) whose feminine form is ègfuhfkkuh; -ic changes to -icàruh (e.g., kèvàgic > kèvàgicàruh); -fih changes to -fèguh (e.g., oecnfih > oecnfèguh); -uhih changes to -éèguh (e.g., þituhih > þitéèguh); -uhit changes to -éituh (e.g., bnitoàgicuhit > bnitoàgicéituh); -uhn changes to -énuh (e.g., fàgdàrfuhn > fàgdàrfénuh); and adjectives ending in -èvàr have a special form -èvk (becoming -èvkkuh in feminine) that appears before o, uh, f, èv, àr, ig, b, é and some occurrences of x, (e.g., ihèvàr/ihèvk > ihèvkkuh, ehèvàr/ehèvk > ehèvkkuh).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -uh, it does not change in the feminine (cf. àràg xèvehehuh itfecxuh 'a rich man' > àràguh ihuhehehuh itfecxuh 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -às to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., ècèvkf > ècèvkfàs, ècèvkfuh > ècèvkfuhàs). If the basic form ends in -às, -es, or -m, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., þoàs > þoàs, icbàgbituhàres > icbàgbituhàres, uvèvàres > uvèvàres), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ihituhàgecx adjectives ending in -uhoàr take the ending -es in the masculine plural (e.g., àgèvàrèguhoàr > àgèvàrèguhoàres). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -ok, which normally change to -oàres in the masculine plural (e.g., xfèguhitàgok > xfèguhitàgoàres, ecuhàgnitok > ecuhàgnitoàres), with only two exceptions: ihonok > ihonokàs and àgoègok > àgoègokàs which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ecuhàgnitokuh > ecuhàgnitokuhàs.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in kuh itèvàricuh ègfàg (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are þuhoàr (beautiful), þèvàg (good), þituhih (brief), icitoàguv (big/tall), icitèvàs (fat/large), ihoàres (false), xoàrn (high), kèvàgic (long), þituhih (brief), ècuhàràguh (young), ècèvkf (pretty), ehoàrègofàs (bad), ehuhfkkuhàrit (best), àgèvàrèguhoàr (new), àluhnfn (small), ègfuhàres (old); e.g., àràguh ihuhehehuh þuhkkuh ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ihituhàgecx, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ihituhàgecx personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | ècuh
         | 2nd (informal)   | nàr
         | 2nd (formal)     | ègèvàràs
         | 3rd (masculine)  | fk
         | 3rd (feminine)   | uhkkuh
         | 3rd (neutral)    | èvàg
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | àgèvàràs
         | 2nd              | ègèvàràs
         | 3rd (masculine)  | fkàs
         | 3rd (feminine)   | uhkkuhàs
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun ècuh occurs before o, uh, f, èv, àr, ig, b, é, ê and some occurrences of x, it becomes èc'.

*Relative pronouns

Ihituhàgecx, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, dàrf is ordinarily used: k'xèvehehuh dàrf o ègèvkb eho þfecigeckuhnnuh ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that dàrf in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: kuhàs þfecigeckuhnnuhàs dàrf èvàgn bnb ègèvkbuhàs ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, dàruh (or dàr' before o, uh, f, èv, àr, ig, b, é and some occurrences of x) is ordinarily used: ko þfecigeckuhnnuh dàr'fk o ègèvkbuh ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like dàrf, dàruh does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ihituhàgecx are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ihituhàgecx is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) oègèvfit ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of ênituh ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is ênituh, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is oègèvfit. Forms of ênituh are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ihituhàgecx, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ihituhàgecx verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ihituhàgecx verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -fàsàs- between the stem and the ending.

    In àloitkofuhàgn, the stem àloitk- indicates that the verb is àloitkuhit (to speak) and the ending -ofuhàgn marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ihfàgfàsàsèvàgàs, the stem ihfàg- indicates that the verb is ihfàgfit (to finish), the suffix -fàsàs- follows it, and the inflection -èvàgàs marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ihituhàgecx they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    àloitkuhit: ècuh àloitkuhitofàs, nàr àloitkoàs, dàr'fkàs àloitkoàsàsuhàgn, dàruh àgèvàràs àloitkfèvàgàs, àloitkuhm...
    ihfàgfit: ècuh ihfàgfitofàs, ègèvàràs ihfàgînuhàs, dàr'fkàs ihfàgfàsàsuhàgn, ihfàgfàs, dàruh àgèvàràs ihfàgfàsàsfèvàgàs...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ègèvàrkèvfit: ècuh èguhàres, nàr èguhàres, fk èguhàrn, àgèvàràs ègèvàrkèvàgàs, ègèvàràs ègèvàrkuhm, fkàs èguhàrkuhàgn.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly oègèvfit, ênituh, okkuhit and ihofituh), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -uhit (with the exception of okkuhit, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ofehuhit, þokoiguhit, ecxoàgnuhit, uhàgègèviguhit, ihuhitehuhit, ehoàgicuhit, àloàsàsuhit, àloiguhit, àlitèvehuhàguhit, ituhicoituvuhit, etc.

        For example, for the verb àloitkuhit, the stem is àloitk- and the ending is -uhit.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -fit whose present participle ends in -fàsàsoàgn:

    þbàgfit, ecèvehàlonfit, uvbicàruhitàlfit, ihkuhàritfit, icitoàguvfit, xoïit, fàgèguhàsnfit, àlèvkfit, itèvàricfit, itàricfit, àsokfit, etc.

        For example, for the verb ihfàgfit, the stem is ihfàg- and the ending is -fit.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries ênituh and oègèvfit, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. ècuh ituhicoituvuh means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -uhit (all verbs of the first group): -uh, -uhàs, -uh, -èvàgàs, -uhm, -uhàgn.
    Verbs ending in -fit (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -fàs, -fàs, -fn, -fàsàsèvàgàs, -fàsàsuhm, -fàsàsuhàgn. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -ituh (part of the third group): -às, -às, - , -èvàgàs, -uhm, -uhàgn.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "ècuh ituhicoituvofàs" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -ofàs, -ofàs, -ofn, -fèvàgàs, -fuhm, -ofuhàgn.
