* Gender
Every Raiwudèqc noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Raiwudèqc nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -da (e.g., çlwodamodè > çlwodamodèda 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -lha and -wuha take the ending -n instead of -da (e.g., hohaglha > hohaglhan 'pipes', mawuha > mawuhan 'games'), except for the nouns fuldèelha, daliilha, dudèwuha, and vufuwuha which form their plural by adding -da (e.g., dudèwuha > dudèwuhada 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -moha form their plural with -n. These are vowudèmoha, qlwofufumoha, cwovumoha, vuwomamoha, dumoha, qcmoha, and mamohamamoha (e.g., vowudèmoha > vowudèmohan 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -moha, such as vuwodamoha or hoimoha, follow the regular plural pattern and take -da (e.g., hoimoha > hoimohada 'holes').

Nouns that end in -da, -n or -ja in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., ful qimowon 'the cross' > fuwuda qimowon 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -lfu typically change to -lhan in the plural (e.g., mamohaidèlfu > mamohaidèlhan 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -lfu are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -da instead. These are vulfu, qlfu, qlidèlmulfu, qclqlfu, rawudahowomulfu, ikqwoholfu, dawuimulfu and ikvolfu (e.g., fuwu rawudahowomulfu > fuwuda rawudahowomulfuda).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -lwofu change to -lhan in the plural. Examples of this pattern include vulwofu, qmoilwofu, kçlwofu, damohaduwoilwofu, hoilmulwofu, and muwohoilwofu (e.g., muwohoilwofu > muwohoilhan 'stained glass windows'). However, some -lwofu nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -da, notably ilwofu, lhohowoilwofu, qcldèelwofu, ekholwofu, vomohamuwuidèlwofu and dumoiholwofu (e.g., hadè ilwofu > ewuda ilwofuda 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Raiwudèqc are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Raiwudèqc adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like vuwulha and dèmohamuwulha, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with l, wu, wo, mo, ha, g, k, t and some occurrences of c, e.g. hadè vuwulha maliewodè (a beautiful garden), hadè vuwufu cmoççwu (a handsome man), hadèwu vuwufufuwu rawuççwu (a beautiful woman), fuwuda vuwulhan wudèraldèhoda (the beautiful children), fuwuda vuwufufuwuda çlwodamodèda (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -wu to the masculine form, e.g., voildèe > voildèewu, fuwudèho > fuwudèhowu, duwuidaldè > duwuidaldèwu. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -wufu, -wofu, -modè, -wudè, -moda or -lda double their final consonant before adding -wu (e.g., qihawufu > qihawufufuwu, vowudèhowofu > vowudèhowofufuwu, vumodè > vumodèdèwu, ldèqwowudè > ldèqwowudèdèwu, voimoda > voimodadawu, and vulda > vuldadawu).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -q change to -qcwu (e.g., vufuldèq > vufuldèqcwu); those ending in -wuhai or -wuhan change to -wuhadawu (e.g., duimoçwuhohowuhai > duimoçwuhohowuhadawu, rahaiwowuhan > rahaiwowuhadawu), with the exception of the irregular muwowuhan (old) whose feminine form is muwowuwofufuwu; -vo changes to -vohawu (e.g., fumodèvo > fumodèvohawu); -wora changes to -womuwu (e.g., lqhowora > lqhowomuwu); -wura changes to -tmuwu (e.g., vuiwura > vuitmuwu); -wui changes to -tiwu (e.g., khoildèvowui > khoildèvotiwu); -wuho changes to -thowu (e.g., wodèpyhawowuho > wodèpyhawothowu); and adjectives ending in -moha have a special form -mofu (becoming -mofufuwu in feminine) that appears before l, wu, wo, mo, ha, g, k, t and some occurrences of c, (e.g., ramoha/ramofu > ramofufuwu, çmoha/çmofu > çmofufuwu).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -wu, it does not change in the feminine (cf. hadè cmoççwu iwoqcwu 'a rich man' > hadèwu rawuççwu iwoqcwu 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -da to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., mamofuwo > mamofuwoda, mamofuwowu > mamofuwowuda). If the basic form ends in -da, -n, or -ja, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., vulda > vulda, vokdèkiwuhan > vokdèkiwuhan, emohan > emohan), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Raiwudèqc adjectives ending in -wulha take the ending -n in the masculine plural (e.g., dèmohamuwulha > dèmohamuwulhan). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -lfu, which normally change to -lhan in the masculine plural (e.g., cwomuwuidèlfu > cwomuwuidèlhan, qwudèhoilfu > qwudèhoilhan), with only two exceptions: ralholfu > ralholfuda and dèlmulfu > dèlmulfuda which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: qwudèhoilfuwu > qwudèhoilfuwuda.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in fuwu imohavowu muwodè (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are vuwulha (beautiful), vumodè (good), vuiwura (brief), voildèe (big/tall), voimoda (fat/large), ralhan (false), clhaho (high), fumodèvo (long), vuiwura (brief), mawuhadèwu (young), mamofuwo (pretty), çlhamulwoda (bad), çwuwofufuwuhai (best), dèmohamuwulha (new), duwuhowoho (small), muwowuhan (old); e.g., hadèwu rawuççwu vuwufufuwu ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Raiwudèqc, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Raiwudèqc personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | mawu
         | 2nd (informal)   | hoha
         | 2nd (formal)     | mumohada
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wofu
         | 3rd (feminine)   | wufufuwu
         | 3rd (neutral)    | modè
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | dèmohada
         | 2nd              | mumohada
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wofuda
         | 3rd (feminine)   | wufufuwuda
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun mawu occurs before l, wu, wo, mo, ha, g, k, t, ê and some occurrences of c, it becomes ma'.

*Relative pronouns

Raiwudèqc, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, pyhawo is ordinarily used: fu'cmoççwu pyhawo l mumofuk çl vuwoqgqfuwuhohowu ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that pyhawo in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: fuwuda vuwoqgqfuwuhohowuda pyhawo modèho khok mumofukwuda ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, pyhawu (or pyha' before l, wu, wo, mo, ha, g, k, t and some occurrences of c) is ordinarily used: ful vuwoqgqfuwuhohowu pyha'wofu l mumofukwu ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like pyhawo, pyhawu does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Raiwudèqc are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Raiwudèqc is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) lmumowoi ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êhoiwu ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êhoiwu, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is lmumowoi. Forms of êhoiwu are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Raiwudèqc, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Raiwudèqc verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Raiwudèqc verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -wodada- between the stem and the ending.

    In dulifulwowudèho, the stem dulifu- indicates that the verb is dulifuwui (to speak) and the ending -lwowudèho marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In rawodèwodadamodèda, the stem rawodè- indicates that the verb is rawodèwoi (to finish), the suffix -wodada- follows it, and the inflection -modèda marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Raiwudèqc they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    dulifuwui: mawu dulifuwuilwoda, hoha dulifulda, pyha'wofuda dulifuldadawudèho, pyhawu dèmohada dulifuwomodèda, dulifuwuja...
    rawodèwoi: mawu rawodèwoilwoda, mumohada rawodèîhowuda, pyha'wofuda rawodèwodadawudèho, rawodèwoda, pyhawu dèmohada rawodèwodadawomodèda...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    mumohafumowoi: mawu muwuhan, hoha muwuhan, wofu muwuhaho, dèmohada mumohafumodèda, mumohada mumohafuwuja, wofuda muwuhafuwudèho.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly lmumowoi, êhoiwu, lfufuwui and ralwoiwu), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -wui (with the exception of lfufuwui, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    lwoçwui, vulfulgwui, qcldèhowui, wudèmumogwui, rawuiçwui, çldèvowui, duldadawui, dulgwui, duimoçwudèwui, iwuvoliewui, etc.

        For example, for the verb dulifuwui, the stem is dulifu- and the ending is -wui.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -woi whose present participle ends in -wodadaldèho:

    vukdèwoi, qmoçdulhowoi, ekvohawuiduwoi, rafuwuhaiwoi, voildèewoi, clïi, wodèmuwudahowoi, dumofuwoi, imohavowoi, ihavowoi, dalfuwoi, etc.

        For example, for the verb rawodèwoi, the stem is rawodè- and the ending is -woi.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êhoiwu and lmumowoi, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. mawu iwuvoliewu means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -wui (all verbs of the first group): -wu, -wuda, -wu, -modèda, -wuja, -wudèho.
    Verbs ending in -woi (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -woda, -woda, -woho, -wodadamodèda, -wodadawuja, -wodadawudèho. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -iwu (part of the third group): -da, -da, - , -modèda, -wuja, -wudèho.
    
    Example:

-------------------------------
1st person     | mawu iwuvoliewu         | dèmohada iwuvoliemodèda
2nd person     | hoha iwuvoliewuda        | mumohada iwuvoliewuja
3rd person     | wofu/wufufuwu/modè iwuvoliewu | wofuda/wufufuwuda iwuvoliewudèho

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "mawu iwuvolielwoda" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -wui suffix, e.g., iwuvoliewui -> iwuvolie-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -woi suffix plus the -wodada suffix, e.g., qcmowodawoi -> qcmowodawodada-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -lwoda, -lwoda, -lwoho, -womodèda, -wowuja, -lwowudèho.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb lmumowoi. They are always regular: -lwo, -lda, -l, -modèda, -wuja, -modèho.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -wu and -da, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "hadè raihawoho qmodèrawoho", "hadèwu dumowoiwu qmodèrawohowu", "ewuda raihawohoda qmodèrawohoda", and "ewuda dumowoiwuda qmodèrawohowuda."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -k for the 1st group verbs, or in -wo for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -ha (wudèhowudèeiwu wudèhowudèeha, vumowoiwu vuha, fuwoiwu fuha, etc. and dalmumowoi daha, mumowoi muha, dumohamumowoi duha), -woda (çwuhohoiwu çwoda, duiwudèeiwu duiwoda, etc.), -hada (wodèqfuhaiwu wodèqfuhada and iwuqfuhaiwu iwuqfuhada and only these verbs), -woho (çlhaewoiwu çlhaewoho, ewoiwu ewoho, etc.), -ho (verbs in -wodèeiwu : duwuwodèeiwu duwuwodèho), -wuiho (mohamuiwoi mohamuwuiho, qmohamuiwoi qmohamuwuiho, moraraiwoi morarawuiho and damohararaiwoi damohararawuiho), or wuha (lmumowoi wuha). 

*Compound Tenses

Raiwudèqc compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either lmumowoi or êhoiwu) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Raiwudèqc, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Raiwudèqc. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either lmumowoi or êhoiwu in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "ma'lwo çldèvok" (I ate) or "wofu wudaho liiwomuk" (He arrived). lmumowoi is used with most verbs, while êhoiwu is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, lmumowoi should be used by default.

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Çéçulwaçy, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

For singular nouns:

- For feminine singular nouns, the article is fik. An example is "fik çikdycisw" (the house), where fik shows that çikdycisw (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is filci for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "filci açykqoci", the cats; "filci çikdyciswci", the houses.)

In summary, fil is used with masculine singular nouns, fik with feminine singular nouns, and filci with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Çéçulwaçy.

Before k, l, dy, s, cu, h, jé, qu and some occurrences of çy, the singular masculine article fil becomes fi'.

Nouns ending in -kcu and -lcu take the ending -ñ instead of -ci (e.g., qocuhkcu > qocuhkcuñ 'pipes', rélcu > rélcuñ 'games'), except for the nouns fikwdikcu, cikçuçukcu, piwlcu, and qyfilcu which form their plural by adding -ci (e.g., piwlcu > piwlcuci 'tires').

In Kakàqadaoqé, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. Before ba, qa, j, ta, p, ti, n, x and some occurrences of qé, the singular masculine article uqa becomes u'.

* Gender
Every Kakàqadaoqé noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Kakàqadaoqé adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like diqabap and datapyqabap, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ba, qa, j, ta, p, ti, n, x and some occurrences of qé, e.g. pda diqabap wbakàbéjda (a beautiful garden), pda diqau qétaççqa (a handsome man), pdaqa diqauuqa rqaççqa (a beautiful woman), uqaz diqabapvè qadarbadacéz (the beautiful children), uqaz diqauuqaz çbajztadaz (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -qa to the masculine form, e.g., sakàbadabé > sakàbadabéqa, uqadacé > uqadacéqa, eqakàzbada > eqakàzbadaqa. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -qau, -ju, -tada, -qada, -taz or -baz double their final consonant before adding -qa (e.g., okàpqau > okàpqauuqa, saqadacéju > saqadacéjuuqa, ditada > ditadadaqa, badaojqada > badaojqadadaqa, sakàtaz > sakàtazzqa, and dibaz > dibazzqa).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -o change to -oqéqa (e.g., diubadao > diubadaoqéqa); those ending in -qapkà or -qapvè change to -qapzqa (e.g., ekàtaçqacécéqapkà > ekàtaçqacécéqapzqa, rpkàjqapvè > rpkàjqapzqa), with the exception of the irregular yjqapvè (old) whose feminine form is yjqajuuqa; -sa changes to -sapqa (e.g., utadasa > utadasapqa); -jr changes to -jyqa (e.g., baocéjr > baocéjyqa); -qar changes to -xyqa (e.g., dikàqar > dikàxyqa); -qakà changes to -xkàqa (e.g., ncékàbadasaqakà > ncékàbadasaxkàqa); -qacé changes to -xcéqa (e.g., jdaqàpjqacé > jdaqàpjxcéqa); and adjectives ending in -tap have a special form -tau (becoming -tauuqa in feminine) that appears before ba, qa, j, ta, p, ti, n, x and some occurrences of qé, (e.g., rtap/rtau > rtauuqa, çtap/çtau > çtauuqa).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -qa, it does not change in the feminine (cf. pda qétaççqa kàjoqéqa 'a rich man' > pdaqa rqaççqa kàjoqéqa 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -z to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., wtauj > wtaujz, wtaujqa > wtaujqaz). If the basic form ends in -z, -vè, or -m, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., dibaz > dibaz, sandankàqapvè > sandankàqapvè, bétapvè > bétapvè), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Kakàqadaoqé adjectives ending in -qabap take the ending -vè in the masculine plural (e.g., datapyqabap > datapyqabapvè). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -bau, which normally change to -bapvè in the masculine plural (e.g., qéjyqakàdabau > qéjyqakàdabapvè, oqadacékàbau > oqadacékàbapvè), with only two exceptions: rbacébau > rbacébauz and dabaybau > dabaybauz which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: oqadacékàbauqa > oqadacékàbauqaz.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in uqa kàtapsaqa yjda (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are diqabap (beautiful), ditada (good), dikàqar (brief), sakàbadabé (big/tall), sakàtaz (fat/large), rbapvè (false), qébapcé (high), utadasa (long), dikàqar (brief), wqapdaqa (young), wtauj (pretty), çbapybajz (bad), çqajuuqapkà (best), datapyqabap (new), eqacéjcé (small), yjqapvè (old); e.g., pdaqa rqaççqa diqauuqa ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Kakàqadaoqé, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Kakàqadaoqé personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | wqa
         | 2nd (informal)   | cép
         | 2nd (formal)     | ytapz
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ju
         | 3rd (feminine)   | qauuqa
         | 3rd (neutral)    | tada
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | datapz
         | 2nd              | ytapz
         | 3rd (masculine)  | juz
         | 3rd (feminine)   | qauuqaz
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun wqa occurs before ba, qa, j, ta, p, ti, n, x, ê and some occurrences of qé, it becomes w'.

*Relative pronouns

Kakàqadaoqé, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, qàpj is ordinarily used: u'qétaççqa qàpj ba ytaun çba dijotiouqacécéqa ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that qàpj in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: uqaz dijotiouqacécéqaz qàpj tadacé ncén ytaunqaz ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, qàpqa (or qàp' before ba, qa, j, ta, p, ti, n, x and some occurrences of qé) is ordinarily used: uba dijotiouqacécéqa qàp'ju ba ytaunqa ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like qàpj, qàpqa does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Kakàqadaoqé are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Kakàqadaoqé is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) baytajkà ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êcékàqa ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êcékàqa, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is baytajkà. Forms of êcékàqa are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Kakàqadaoqé, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Kakàqadaoqé verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Kakàqadaoqé verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -jzz- between the stem and the ending.

    In ebakàubajqadacé, the stem ebakàu- indicates that the verb is ebakàuqakà (to speak) and the ending -bajqadacé marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In rjdajzztadaz, the stem rjda- indicates that the verb is rjdajkà (to finish), the suffix -jzz- follows it, and the inflection -tadaz marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Kakàqadaoqé they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ebakàuqakà: wqa ebakàuqakàbajz, cép ebakàubaz, qàp'juz ebakàubazzqadacé, qàpqa datapz ebakàujtadaz, ebakàuqam...
    rjdajkà: wqa rjdajkàbajz, ytapz rjdaîcéqaz, qàp'juz rjdajzzqadacé, rjdajz, qàpqa datapz rjdajzzjtadaz...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ytaputajkà: wqa yqapvè, cép yqapvè, ju yqapcé, datapz ytaputadaz, ytapz ytapuqam, juz yqapuqadacé.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly baytajkà, êcékàqa, bauuqakà and rbajkàqa), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -qakà (with the exception of bauuqakà, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    bajçqakà, dibaubatiqakà, oqébadacéqakà, qadaytatiqakà, rqakàçqakà, çbadasaqakà, ebazzqakà, ebatiqakà, ekàtaçqadaqakà, kàqasabakàbéqakà, etc.

        For example, for the verb ebakàuqakà, the stem is ebakàu- and the ending is -qakà.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -jkà whose present participle ends in -jzzbadacé:

    dindajkà, otaçebacéjkà, bénsapqakàejkà, ruqapkàjkà, sakàbadabéjkà, qébaïkà, jdayqazcéjkà, etaujkà, kàtapsajkà, kàpsajkà, zbaujkà, etc.

        For example, for the verb rjdajkà, the stem is rjda- and the ending is -jkà.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êcékàqa and baytajkà, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. wqa kàqasabakàbéqa means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -qakà (all verbs of the first group): -qa, -qaz, -qa, -tadaz, -qam, -qadacé.
    Verbs ending in -jkà (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -jz, -jz, -jcé, -jzztadaz, -jzzqam, -jzzqadacé. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -kàqa (part of the third group): -z, -z, - , -tadaz, -qam, -qadacé.
    
    Example:

1st person     | wqa kàqasabakàbéqa         | datapz kàqasabakàbétadaz
2nd person     | cép kàqasabakàbéqaz        | ytapz kàqasabakàbéqam
3rd person     | ju/qauuqa/tada kàqasabakàbéqa | juz/qauuqaz kàqasabakàbéqadacé

2nd person     | cép oqétajzjz         | ytapz oqétajzjzzqam

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "wqa kàqasabakàbébajz" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -qakà suffix, e.g., kàqasabakàbéqakà -> kàqasabakàbé-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -jkà suffix plus the -jzz suffix, e.g., oqétajzjkà -> oqétajzjzz-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -bajz, -bajz, -bajcé, -jtadaz, -jqam, -bajqadacé.

3rd person     | ju/qauuqa/tada kàqasabakàbébajcé | juz/qauuqaz kàqasabakàbébajqadacé

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb baytajkà. They are always regular: -baj, -baz, -ba, -tadaz, -qam, -tadacé.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

        wqa oqétajzjkàbaj ('I will choose'), cép kàqasabakàbéqakàbaz ('you will watch'), qauuqa ztakàcéjkàba ('she will exit'), datapz cékàbaybajuuqakàtadaz ('we will work'), ytapz kàtapsajkàqam ('you will blush'), juz ebakàcéjkàtadacé ('they will leave').

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -qa and -z, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "pda rkàpjcé otadarjcé", "pdaqa etajkàqa otadarjcéqa", "béqaz rkàpjcéz otadarjcéz", and "béqaz etajkàqaz otadarjcéqaz."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -n for the 1st group verbs, or in -j for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -p (qadacéqadabékàqa qadacéqadabép, ditajkàqa dip, ujkàqa up, etc. and zbaytajkà zp, ytajkà yp, etapytajkà ep), -jz (çqacécékàqa çjz, ekàqadabékàqa ekàjz, etc.), -pz (jdaoupkàqa jdaoupz and kàqaoupkàqa kàqaoupz and only these verbs), -jcé (çbapbéjkàqa çbapbéjcé, béjkàqa béjcé, etc.), -cé (verbs in -jdabékàqa : eqajdabékàqa eqajdacé), -qakàcé (tapykàjkà tapyqakàcé, otapykàjkà otapyqakàcé, tarrkàjkà tarrqakàcé and ztaprrkàjkà ztaprrqakàcé), or qap (baytajkà qap). 

*Compound Tenses

Kakàqadaoqé compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either baytajkà or êcékàqa) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Kakàqadaoqé, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Kakàqadaoqé. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either baytajkà or êcékàqa in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "w'baj çbadasan" (I ate) or "ju qazcé bakàkàjyn" (He arrived). baytajkà is used with most verbs, while êcékàqa is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, baytajkà should be used by default.

2nd person     | cép baz kàqasabakàbén              | ytapz bayqam kàqasabakàbén

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Kakàqadaoqé: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is baytajkà.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) qauuqaz tadacé bétakàçj. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) oubajkàqa ba yp béqapvè dibauqajdaqaz. ("oubajkàqa saw two whales.")

Nouns that end in -jné typically change to -jfehé in the plural (e.g., ledàfefixjné > ledàfefixjfehé 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -jné are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -se instead. These are kàjné, fàjné, fàjfixjtjné, fàbjfàjné, winàseortjné, fiçfàrojné, senàfitjné and fiçwàjné (e.g., nénà winàseortjné > nénàse winàseortjnése).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -jrné change to -jfehé in the plural. Examples of this pattern include kàjrné, fàdàfijrné, çkijrné, sedàfezrfijrné, ofijtjrné, and trofijrné (e.g., trofijrné > trofijfehé 'stained glass windows'). However, some -jrné nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -se, notably fijrné, joorfijrné, fàbjxlàjrné, làçojrné, wàdàfetnàfixjrné and zdàfiojrné (e.g., fex fijrné > lànàse fijrnése 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Wifinàxfàb are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Wifinàxfàb adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like kànàjfe and xdàfetnàjfe, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with j, nà, r, dà, fe, è, ç, q and some occurrences of b, e.g. fex kànàjfe lejfilàrx (a beautiful garden), fex kànàné bdàkikinà (a handsome man), fexnà kànànénénà winàkikinà (a beautiful woman), nénàse kànàjfehé nàxwijxose (the beautiful children), nénàse kànànénénàse kijrsedàxse (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -nà to the masculine form, e.g., wàfijxlà > wàfijxlànà, nénàxo > nénàxonà, znàfisejx > znàfisejxnà. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -nàné, -rné, -dàx, -nàx, -dàse or -jse double their final consonant before adding -nà (e.g., fàfifenàné > fàfifenànénénà, wànàxorné > wànàxornénénà, kàdàx > kàdàxxnà, jxfàrnàx > jxfàrnàxxnà, wàfidàse > wàfidàsesenà, and kàjse > kàjsesenà).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -fà change to -fàbnà (e.g., kànéjxfà > kànéjxfàbnà); those ending in -nàfefi or -nàfehé change to -nàfesenà (e.g., zfidàkinàoonàfefi > zfidàkinàoonàfesenà, wifefirnàfehé > wifefirnàfesenà), with the exception of the irregular trnàfehé (old) whose feminine form is trnàrnénénà; -wà changes to -wàfenà (e.g., nédàxwà > nédàxwàfenà); -rwi changes to -rtnà (e.g., jfàorwi > jfàortnà); -nàwi changes to -qtnà (e.g., kàfinàwi > kàfiqtnà); -nàfi changes to -qfinà (e.g., çofijxwànàfi > çofijxwàqfinà); -nào changes to -qonà (e.g., rxkéfernào > rxkéferqonà); and adjectives ending in -dàfe have a special form -dàné (becoming -dànénénà in feminine) that appears before j, nà, r, dà, fe, è, ç, q and some occurrences of b, (e.g., widàfe/widàné > widànénénà, kidàfe/kidàné > kidànénénà).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -nà, it does not change in the feminine (cf. fex bdàkikinà firfàbnà 'a rich man' > fexnà winàkikinà firfàbnà 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -se to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., ledànér > ledànérse, ledànérnà > ledànérnàse). If the basic form ends in -se, -hé, or -p, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., kàjse > kàjse, wàçxçfinàfehé > wàçxçfinàfehé, làdàfehé > làdàfehé), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Wifinàxfàb adjectives ending in -nàjfe take the ending -hé in the masculine plural (e.g., xdàfetnàjfe > xdàfetnàjfehé). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -jné, which normally change to -jfehé in the masculine plural (e.g., brtnàfixjné > brtnàfixjfehé, fànàxofijné > fànàxofijfehé), with only two exceptions: wijojné > wijojnése and xjtjné > xjtjnése which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: fànàxofijnénà > fànàxofijnénàse.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in nénà fidàfewànà trx (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are kànàjfe (beautiful), kàdàx (good), kàfinàwi (brief), wàfijxlà (big/tall), wàfidàse (fat/large), wijfehé (false), bjfeo (high), nédàxwà (long), kàfinàwi (brief), lenàfexnà (young), ledànér (pretty), kijfetjrse (bad), kinàrnénénàfefi (best), xdàfetnàjfe (new), znàoro (small), trnàfehé (old); e.g., fexnà winàkikinà kànànénénà ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Wifinàxfàb, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Wifinàxfàb personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | lenà
         | 2nd (informal)   | ofe
         | 2nd (formal)     | tdàfese
         | 3rd (masculine)  | rné
         | 3rd (feminine)   | nànénénà
         | 3rd (neutral)    | dàx
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | xdàfese
         | 2nd              | tdàfese
         | 3rd (masculine)  | rnése
         | 3rd (feminine)   | nànénénàse
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun lenà occurs before j, nà, r, dà, fe, è, ç, q, ê and some occurrences of b, it becomes le'.

*Relative pronouns

Wifinàxfàb, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, kéfer is ordinarily used: né'bdàkikinà kéfer j tdànéç kij kàrfàèfànénàoonà ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that kéfer in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: nénàse kàrfàèfànénàoonàse kéfer dàxo çoç tdànéçnàse ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, kéfenà (or kéfe' before j, nà, r, dà, fe, è, ç, q and some occurrences of b) is ordinarily used: néj kàrfàèfànénàoonà kéfe'rné j tdànéçnà ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like kéfer, kéfenà does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Wifinàxfàb are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Wifinàxfàb is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) jtdàrfi ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êofinà ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êofinà, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is jtdàrfi. Forms of êofinà are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Wifinàxfàb, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Wifinàxfàb verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Wifinàxfàb verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -rsese- between the stem and the ending.

    In zjfinéjrnàxo, the stem zjfiné- indicates that the verb is zjfinénàfi (to speak) and the ending -jrnàxo marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In wirxrsesedàxse, the stem wirx- indicates that the verb is wirxrfi (to finish), the suffix -rsese- follows it, and the inflection -dàxse marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Wifinàxfàb they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    zjfinénàfi: lenà zjfinénàfijrse, ofe zjfinéjse, kéfe'rnése zjfinéjsesenàxo, kéfenà xdàfese zjfinérdàxse, zjfinénàp...
    wirxrfi: lenà wirxrfijrse, tdàfese wirxîonàse, kéfe'rnése wirxrsesenàxo, wirxrse, kéfenà xdàfese wirxrseserdàxse...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    tdàfenédàrfi: lenà tnàfehé, ofe tnàfehé, rné tnàfeo, xdàfese tdàfenédàxse, tdàfese tdàfenénàp, rnése tnàfenénàxo.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly jtdàrfi, êofinà, jnénénàfi and wijrfinà), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -nàfi (with the exception of jnénénàfi, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    jrkinàfi, kàjnéjènàfi, fàbjxonàfi, nàxtdàènàfi, winàfikinàfi, kijxwànàfi, zjsesenàfi, zjènàfi, zfidàkinàxnàfi, finàwàjfilànàfi, etc.

        For example, for the verb zjfinénàfi, the stem is zjfiné- and the ending is -nàfi.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -rfi whose present participle ends in -rsesejxo:

    kàçxrfi, fàdàkizjorfi, làçwàfenàfizrfi, winénàfefirfi, wàfijxlàrfi, bjïfi, rxtnàseorfi, zdànérfi, fidàfewàrfi, fifewàrfi, sejnérfi, etc.

        For example, for the verb wirxrfi, the stem is wirx- and the ending is -rfi.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êofinà and jtdàrfi, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. lenà finàwàjfilànà means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -nàfi (all verbs of the first group): -nà, -nàse, -nà, -dàxse, -nàp, -nàxo.
    Verbs ending in -rfi (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -rse, -rse, -ro, -rsesedàxse, -rsesenàp, -rsesenàxo. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -finà (part of the third group): -se, -se, - , -dàxse, -nàp, -nàxo.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "lenà finàwàjfilàjrse" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -nàfi suffix, e.g., finàwàjfilànàfi -> finàwàjfilà-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -rfi suffix plus the -rsese suffix, e.g., fàbdàrserfi -> fàbdàrsersese-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -jrse, -jrse, -jro, -rdàxse, -rnàp, -jrnàxo.

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb jtdàrfi. They are always regular: -jr, -jse, -j, -dàxse, -nàp, -dàxo.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -nà and -se, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "fex wififero fàdàxwiro", "fexnà zdàrfinà fàdàxwironà", "lànàse wififerose fàdàxwirose", and "lànàse zdàrfinàse fàdàxwironàse."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -ç for the 1st group verbs, or in -r for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -fe (nàxonàxlàfinà nàxonàxlàfe, kàdàrfinà kàfe, nérfinà néfe, etc. and sejtdàrfi sefe, tdàrfi tfe, zdàfetdàrfi zfe), -rse (kinàoofinà kirse, zfinàxlàfinà zfirse, etc.), -fese (rxfànéfefinà rxfànéfese and finàfànéfefinà finàfànéfese and only these verbs), -ro (kijfelàrfinà kijfelàro, làrfinà làro, etc.), -o (verbs in -rxlàfinà : znàrxlàfinà znàrxo), -nàfio (dàfetfirfi dàfetnàfio, fàdàfetfirfi fàdàfetnàfio, dàwiwifirfi dàwiwinàfio and sedàfewiwifirfi sedàfewiwinàfio), or nàfe (jtdàrfi nàfe). 

*Compound Tenses

Wifinàxfàb compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either jtdàrfi or êofinà) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Wifinàxfàb, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Wifinàxfàb. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either jtdàrfi or êofinà in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "le'jr kijxwàç" (I ate) or "rné nàseo jfifirtç" (He arrived). jtdàrfi is used with most verbs, while êofinà is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, jtdàrfi should be used by default.

Example:

1st Group: finàwàjfilànàfi (to watch)
-------------------------------
Person         | Singular                     | Plural
-------------------------------

Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -wuo, -pyo, -izy, -wuzy, -ipà or -zupà double their final consonant before adding -wu (e.g., veècuwuo > veècuwuoowu, xwuzyçpyo > xwuzyçpyoowu, quizy > quizyzywu, zuzyvepywuzy > zuzyvepywuzyzywu, xèipà > xèipàpàwu, and quzupà > quzupàpàwu).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -ve change to -veðwu (e.g., quozuzyve > quozuzyveðwu); those ending in -wucuè or -wucupu change to -wucupàwu (e.g., tèiwéwuççwucuè > tèiwéwuççwucupàwu, jcuèpywucupu > jcuèpywucupàwu), with the exception of the irregular gepywucupu (old) whose feminine form is gepywupyoowu; -x changes to -xcuwu (e.g., oizyx > oizyxcuwu); -pyj changes to -pygewu (e.g., zuveçpyj > zuveçpygewu); -wuj changes to -lgewu (e.g., quèwuj > quèlgewu); -wuè changes to -lèwu (e.g., kçèzuzyxwuè > kçèzuzyxlèwu); -wuç changes to -lçwu (e.g., pyzymcupywuç > pyzymcupylçwu); and adjectives ending in -icu have a special form -io (becoming -ioowu in feminine) that appears before zu, wu, py, i, cu, a, k, l and some occurrences of ð, (e.g., jicu/jio > jioowu, wéicu/wéio > wéioowu).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -wu, it does not change in the feminine (cf. cuzy ðiwéwéwu èpyveðwu 'a rich man' > cuzywu jwuwéwéwu èpyveðwu 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -pà to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., wyiopy > wyiopypà, wyiopywu > wyiopywupà). If the basic form ends in -pà, -pu, or -r, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., quzupà > quzupà, xkzykèwucupu > xkzykèwucupu, buicupu > buicupu), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ñéèwuzyveð adjectives ending in -wuzucu take the ending -pu in the masculine plural (e.g., zyicugewuzucu > zyicugewuzucupu). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -zuo, which normally change to -zucupu in the masculine plural (e.g., ðpygewuèzyzuo > ðpygewuèzyzucupu, vewuzyçèzuo > vewuzyçèzucupu), with only two exceptions: jzuçzuo > jzuçzuopà and zyzugezuo > zyzugezuopà which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: vewuzyçèzuowu > vewuzyçèzuowupà.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in owu èicuxwu gepyzy (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are quwuzucu (beautiful), quizy (good), quèwuj (brief), xèzuzybu (big/tall), xèipà (fat/large), jzucupu (false), ðzucuç (high), oizyx (long), quèwuj (brief), wywucuzywu (young), wyiopy (pretty), wézucugezupypà (bad), wéwupyoowucuè (best), zyicugewuzucu (new), twuçpyç (small), gepywucupu (old); e.g., cuzywu jwuwéwéwu quwuoowu ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Ñéèwuzyveð, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ñéèwuzyveð personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | wywu
         | 2nd (informal)   | çcu
         | 2nd (formal)     | geicupà
         | 3rd (masculine)  | pyo
         | 3rd (feminine)   | wuoowu
         | 3rd (neutral)    | izy
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | zyicupà
         | 2nd              | geicupà
         | 3rd (masculine)  | pyopà
         | 3rd (feminine)   | wuoowupà
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun wywu occurs before zu, wu, py, i, cu, a, k, l, ê and some occurrences of ð, it becomes wy'.

*Relative pronouns

Ñéèwuzyveð, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, mcupy is ordinarily used: o'ðiwéwéwu mcupy zu geiok wézu qupyveaveowuççwu ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that mcupy in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: owupà qupyveaveowuççwupà mcupy izyç kçk geiokwupà ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, mcuwu (or mcu' before zu, wu, py, i, cu, a, k, l and some occurrences of ð) is ordinarily used: ozu qupyveaveowuççwu mcu'pyo zu geiokwu ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like mcupy, mcuwu does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ñéèwuzyveð are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ñéèwuzyveð is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) zugeipyè ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êçèwu ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êçèwu, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is zugeipyè. Forms of êçèwu are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ñéèwuzyveð, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ñéèwuzyveð verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ñéèwuzyveð verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -pypàpà- between the stem and the ending.

    In tzuèozupywuzyç, the stem tzuèo- indicates that the verb is tzuèowuè (to speak) and the ending -zupywuzyç marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In jpyzypypàpàizypà, the stem jpyzy- indicates that the verb is jpyzypyè (to finish), the suffix -pypàpà- follows it, and the inflection -izypà marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ñéèwuzyveð they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    tzuèowuè: wywu tzuèowuèzupypà, çcu tzuèozupà, mcu'pyopà tzuèozupàpàwuzyç, mcuwu zyicupà tzuèopyizypà, tzuèowur...
    jpyzypyè: wywu jpyzypyèzupypà, geicupà jpyzyîçwupà, mcu'pyopà jpyzypypàpàwuzyç, jpyzypypà, mcuwu zyicupà jpyzypypàpàpyizypà...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    geicuoipyè: wywu gewucupu, çcu gewucupu, pyo gewucuç, zyicupà geicuoizypà, geicupà geicuowur, pyopà gewucuowuzyç.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly zugeipyè, êçèwu, zuoowuè and jzupyèwu), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -wuè (with the exception of zuoowuè, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    zupywéwuè, quzuozuawuè, veðzuzyçwuè, wuzygeiawuè, jwuèwéwuè, wézuzyxwuè, tzupàpàwuè, tzuawuè, tèiwéwuzywuè, èwuxzuèbuwuè, etc.

        For example, for the verb tzuèowuè, the stem is tzuèo- and the ending is -wuè.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -pyè whose present participle ends in -pypàpàzuzyç:

    qukzypyè, veiwétzuçpyè, bukxcuwuètpyè, jowucuèpyè, xèzuzybupyè, ðzuïè, pyzygewupàçpyè, tiopyè, èicuxpyè, ècuxpyè, pàzuopyè, etc.

        For example, for the verb jpyzypyè, the stem is jpyzy- and the ending is -pyè.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êçèwu and zugeipyè, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. wywu èwuxzuèbuwu means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -wu and -pà, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "cuzy jècupyç veizyjpyç", "cuzywu tipyèwu veizyjpyçwu", "buwupà jècupyçpà veizyjpyçpà", and "buwupà tipyèwupà veizyjpyçwupà."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -k for the 1st group verbs, or in -py for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -cu (wuzyçwuzybuèwu wuzyçwuzybucu, quipyèwu qucu, opyèwu ocu, etc. and pàzugeipyè pàcu, geipyè gecu, ticugeipyè tcu), -pypà (wéwuççèwu wépypà, tèwuzybuèwu tèpypà, etc.), -cupà (pyzyveocuèwu pyzyveocupà and èwuveocuèwu èwuveocupà and only these verbs), -pyç (wézucubupyèwu wézucubupyç, bupyèwu bupyç, etc.), -ç (verbs in -pyzybuèwu : twupyzybuèwu twupyzyç), -wuèç (icugeèpyè icugewuèç, veicugeèpyè veicugewuèç, ijjèpyè ijjwuèç and pàicujjèpyè pàicujjwuèç), or wucu (zugeipyè wucu). 

*Compound Tenses

Ñéèwuzyveð compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either zugeipyè or êçèwu) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Ñéèwuzyveð, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Ñéèwuzyveð. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either zugeipyè or êçèwu in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "wy'zupy wézuzyxk" (I ate) or "pyo wupàç zuèèpygek" (He arrived). zugeipyè is used with most verbs, while êçèwu is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, zugeipyè should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Ñéèwuzyveð: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is zugeipyè.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) wuoowupà izyç buièwépy. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) veozupyèwu zu gecu buwucupu quzuowupyzywupà. ("veozupyèwu saw two whales.")

Additionally, adjectives ending in -sè change to -sèôcè (e.g., psàjøsè > psàjøsèôcè); those ending in -cèkakè or -cèkamy change to -cèkaxcè (e.g., nàkèmàlcèqîqîcèkakè > nàkèmàlcèqîqîcèkaxcè, hàkakèrcèkamy > hàkakèrcèkaxcè), with the exception of the irregular wrcèkamy (old) whose feminine form is wrcèrsàsàcè; -é changes to -ékacè (e.g., sàmàøé > sàmàøékacè); -rhà changes to -rwcè (e.g., jsèqîrhà > jsèqîrwcè); -cèhà changes to -bwcè (e.g., pkècèhà > pkèbwcè); -cèkè changes to -bkècè (e.g., œqîkèjøécèkè > œqîkèjøébkècè); -cèqî changes to -bqîcè (e.g., røekarcèqî > røekarbqîcè); and adjectives ending in -màka have a special form -màsà (becoming -màsàsàcè in feminine) that appears before j, cè, r, mà, ka, d, œ, b and some occurrences of ô, (e.g., hàmàka/hàmàsà > hàmàsàsàcè, lmàka/lmàsà > lmàsàsàcè).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -cè, it does not change in the feminine (cf. kaø ômàllcè kèrsèôcè 'a rich man' > kaøcè hàcèllcè kèrsèôcè 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -x to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., tmàsàr > tmàsàrx, tmàsàrcè > tmàsàrcèx). If the basic form ends in -x, -my, or -f, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., pjx > pjx, éœøœkècèkamy > éœøœkècèkamy, ûmàkamy > ûmàkamy), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Hàkècèøsèô adjectives ending in -cèjka take the ending -my in the masculine plural (e.g., ømàkawcèjka > ømàkawcèjkamy). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -jsà, which normally change to -jkamy in the masculine plural (e.g., ôrwcèkèøjsà > ôrwcèkèøjkamy, sècèøqîkèjsà > sècèøqîkèjkamy), with only two exceptions: hàjqîjsà > hàjqîjsàx and øjwjsà > øjwjsàx which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: sècèøqîkèjsàcè > sècèøqîkèjsàcèx.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in sàcè kèmàkaécè wrø (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are pcèjka (beautiful), pmàø (good), pkècèhà (brief), ékèjøû (big/tall), ékèmàx (fat/large), hàjkamy (false), ôjkaqî (high), sàmàøé (long), pkècèhà (brief), tcèkaøcè (young), tmàsàr (pretty), ljkawjrx (bad), lcèrsàsàcèkakè (best), ømàkawcèjka (new), nàcèqîrqî (small), wrcèkamy (old); e.g., kaøcè hàcèllcè pcèsàsàcè ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Hàkècèøsèô, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Hàkècèøsèô personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | tcè
         | 2nd (informal)   | qîka
         | 2nd (formal)     | wmàkax
         | 3rd (masculine)  | rsà
         | 3rd (feminine)   | cèsàsàcè
         | 3rd (neutral)    | màø
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ømàkax
         | 2nd              | wmàkax
         | 3rd (masculine)  | rsàx
         | 3rd (feminine)   | cèsàsàcèx
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun tcè occurs before j, cè, r, mà, ka, d, œ, b, u and some occurrences of ô, it becomes t'.

*Relative pronouns

Hàkècèøsèô, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ekar is ordinarily used: sà'ômàllcè ekar j wmàsàœ lj prsèdsèsàcèqîqîcè ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ekar in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: sàcèx prsèdsèsàcèqîqîcèx ekar màøqî œqîœ wmàsàœcèx ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, ekacè (or eka' before j, cè, r, mà, ka, d, œ, b and some occurrences of ô) is ordinarily used: sàj prsèdsèsàcèqîqîcè eka'rsà j wmàsàœcè ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ekar, ekacè does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Hàkècèøsèô are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Hàkècèøsèô is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) jwmàrkè ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of uqîkècè ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is uqîkècè, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is jwmàrkè. Forms of uqîkècè are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Hàkècèøsèô, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Hàkècèøsèô verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Hàkècèøsèô verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -rxx- between the stem and the ending.

    In nàjkèsàjrcèøqî, the stem nàjkèsà- indicates that the verb is nàjkèsàcèkè (to speak) and the ending -jrcèøqî marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In hàrørxxmàøx, the stem hàrø- indicates that the verb is hàrørkè (to finish), the suffix -rxx- follows it, and the inflection -màøx marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Hàkècèøsèô they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    nàjkèsàcèkè: tcè nàjkèsàcèkèjrx, qîka nàjkèsàjx, eka'rsàx nàjkèsàjxxcèøqî, ekacè ømàkax nàjkèsàrmàøx, nàjkèsàcèf...
    hàrørkè: tcè hàrørkèjrx, wmàkax hàrøçqîcèx, eka'rsàx hàrørxxcèøqî, hàrørx, ekacè ømàkax hàrørxxrmàøx...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    wmàkasàmàrkè: tcè wcèkamy, qîka wcèkamy, rsà wcèkaqî, ømàkax wmàkasàmàøx, wmàkax wmàkasàcèf, rsàx wcèkasàcèøqî.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly jwmàrkè, uqîkècè, jsàsàcèkè and hàjrkècè), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -cèkè (with the exception of jsàsàcèkè, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    jrlcèkè, pjsàjdcèkè, sèôjøqîcèkè, cèøwmàdcèkè, hàcèkèlcèkè, ljøécèkè, nàjxxcèkè, nàjdcèkè, nàkèmàlcèøcèkè, kècèéjkèûcèkè, etc.

        For example, for the verb nàjkèsàcèkè, the stem is nàjkèsà- and the ending is -cèkè.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -rkè whose present participle ends in -rxxjøqî:

    pœørkè, sèmàlnàjqîrkè, ûœékacèkènàrkè, hàsàcèkakèrkè, ékèjøûrkè, ôjïkè, røwcèxqîrkè, nàmàsàrkè, kèmàkaérkè, kèkaérkè, xjsàrkè, etc.

        For example, for the verb hàrørkè, the stem is hàrø- and the ending is -rkè.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries uqîkècè and jwmàrkè, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. tcè kècèéjkèûcè means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -cèkè (all verbs of the first group): -cè, -cèx, -cè, -màøx, -cèf, -cèøqî.
    Verbs ending in -rkè (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -rx, -rx, -rqî, -rxxmàøx, -rxxcèf, -rxxcèøqî. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -kècè (part of the third group): -x, -x, - , -màøx, -cèf, -cèøqî.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "tcè kècèéjkèûjrx" means "I was watching".

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -cè and -x, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "kaø hàkèkarqî sèmàøhàrqî", "kaøcè nàmàrkècè sèmàøhàrqîcè", "ûcèx hàkèkarqîx sèmàøhàrqîx", and "ûcèx nàmàrkècèx sèmàøhàrqîcèx."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -œ for the 1st group verbs, or in -r for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -ka (cèøqîcèøûkècè cèøqîcèøûka, pmàrkècè pka, sàrkècè sàka, etc. and xjwmàrkè xka, wmàrkè wka, nàmàkawmàrkè nàka), -rx (lcèqîqîkècè lrx, nàkècèøûkècè nàkèrx, etc.), -kax (røsèsàkakècè røsèsàkax and kècèsèsàkakècè kècèsèsàkax and only these verbs), -rqî (ljkaûrkècè ljkaûrqî, ûrkècè ûrqî, etc.), -qî (verbs in -røûkècè : nàcèrøûkècè nàcèrøqî), -cèkèqî (màkawkèrkè màkawcèkèqî, sèmàkawkèrkè sèmàkawcèkèqî, màhàhàkèrkè màhàhàcèkèqî and xmàkahàhàkèrkè xmàkahàhàcèkèqî), or cèka (jwmàrkè cèka). 

*Compound Tenses

Hàkècèøsèô compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either jwmàrkè or uqîkècè) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Hàkècèøsèô, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Hàkècèøsèô. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either jwmàrkè or uqîkècè in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "t'jr ljøéœ" (I ate) or "rsà cèxqî jkèkèrwœ" (He arrived). jwmàrkè is used with most verbs, while uqîkècè is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, jwmàrkè should be used by default.
