Additionally, adjectives ending in -yç change to -yçexyq (e.g., pifswyç > pifswyçexyq); those ending in -yqevé or -yqevèv change to -yqevayq (e.g., déoçèryqèçèçyqevé > déoçèryqèçèçyqevayq, jevéeqyqevèv > jevéeqyqevayq), with the exception of the irregular ceqyqevèv (old) whose feminine form is ceqyqeqififyq; -ik changes to -ikevyq (e.g., ifoçwik > ifoçwikevyq); -eqj changes to -eqcyq (e.g., syçèçeqj > syçèçeqcyq); -yqj changes to -gcyq (e.g., péyqj > pégcyq); -yqé changes to -géyq (e.g., yxèçéswikyqé > yxèçéswikgéyq); -yqèç changes to -gèçyq (e.g., eqwheveqyqèç > eqwheveqgèçyq); and adjectives ending in -oçev have a special form -oçif (becoming -oçififyq in feminine) that appears before s, yq, eq, oç, ev, eç, yx, g and some occurrences of ex, (e.g., joçev/joçif > joçififyq, èroçev/èroçif > èroçififyq).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -yq, it does not change in the feminine (cf. evw exoçèrèryq éeqyçexyq 'a rich man' > evwyq jyqèrèryq éeqyçexyq 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -a to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., noçifeq > noçifeqa, noçifeqyq > noçifeqyqa). If the basic form ends in -a, -èv, or -à, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., psa > psa, ikyxwyxéyqevèv > ikyxwyxéyqevèv, zoçevèv > zoçevèv), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Oqéyqwyçex adjectives ending in -yqsev take the ending -èv in the masculine plural (e.g., woçevcyqsev > woçevcyqsevèv). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -sif, which normally change to -sevèv in the masculine plural (e.g., exeqcyqéwsif > exeqcyqéwsevèv, yçyqwèçésif > yçyqwèçésevèv), with only two exceptions: jsèçsif > jsèçsifa and wscsif > wscsifa which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: yçyqwèçésifyq > yçyqwèçésifyqa.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in ifyq éoçevikyq ceqw (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are pyqsev (beautiful), poçw (good), péyqj (brief), ikéswz (big/tall), ikéoça (fat/large), jsevèv (false), exsevèç (high), ifoçwik (long), péyqj (brief), nyqevwyq (young), noçifeq (pretty), èrsevcseqa (bad), èryqeqififyqevé (best), woçevcyqsev (new), dyqèçeqèç (small), ceqyqevèv (old); e.g., evwyq jyqèrèryq pyqififyq ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Oqéyqwyçex, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Oqéyqwyçex personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | nyq
         | 2nd (informal)   | èçev
         | 2nd (formal)     | coçeva
         | 3rd (masculine)  | eqif
         | 3rd (feminine)   | yqififyq
         | 3rd (neutral)    | oçw
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | woçeva
         | 2nd              | coçeva
         | 3rd (masculine)  | eqifa
         | 3rd (feminine)   | yqififyqa
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun nyq occurs before s, yq, eq, oç, ev, eç, yx, g, ê and some occurrences of ex, it becomes n'.

*Relative pronouns

Oqéyqwyçex, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, heveq is ordinarily used: if'exoçèrèryq heveq s coçifyx èrs peqyçeçyçifyqèçèçyq ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that heveq in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: ifyqa peqyçeçyçifyqèçèçyqa heveq oçwèç yxèçyx coçifyxyqa ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, hevyq (or hev' before s, yq, eq, oç, ev, eç, yx, g and some occurrences of ex) is ordinarily used: ifs peqyçeçyçifyqèçèçyq hev'eqif s coçifyxyq ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like heveq, hevyq does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Oqéyqwyçex are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Oqéyqwyçex is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) scoçeqé ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êèçéyq ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êèçéyq, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is scoçeqé. Forms of êèçéyq are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Oqéyqwyçex, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Oqéyqwyçex verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Oqéyqwyçex verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -eqaa- between the stem and the ending.

    In dséifseqyqwèç, the stem dséif- indicates that the verb is dséifyqé (to speak) and the ending -seqyqwèç marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In jeqweqaaoçwa, the stem jeqw- indicates that the verb is jeqweqé (to finish), the suffix -eqaa- follows it, and the inflection -oçwa marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Oqéyqwyçex they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    dséifyqé: nyq dséifyqéseqa, èçev dséifsa, hev'eqifa dséifsaayqwèç, hevyq woçeva dséifeqoçwa, dséifyqà...
    jeqweqé: nyq jeqweqéseqa, coçeva jeqwîèçyqa, hev'eqifa jeqweqaayqwèç, jeqweqa, hevyq woçeva jeqweqaaeqoçwa...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    coçevifoçeqé: nyq cyqevèv, èçev cyqevèv, eqif cyqevèç, woçeva coçevifoçwa, coçeva coçevifyqà, eqifa cyqevifyqwèç.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly scoçeqé, êèçéyq, sififyqé and jseqéyq), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -yqé (with the exception of sififyqé, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    seqèryqé, psifseçyqé, yçexswèçyqé, yqwcoçeçyqé, jyqéèryqé, èrswikyqé, dsaayqé, dseçyqé, déoçèryqwyqé, éyqiksézyqé, etc.

        For example, for the verb dséifyqé, the stem is dséif- and the ending is -yqé.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -eqé whose present participle ends in -eqaaswèç:

    pyxweqé, yçoçèrdsèçeqé, zyxikevyqédeqé, jifyqevéeqé, ikéswzeqé, exsïé, eqwcyqaèçeqé, doçifeqé, éoçevikeqé, éevikeqé, asifeqé, etc.

        For example, for the verb jeqweqé, the stem is jeqw- and the ending is -eqé.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êèçéyq and scoçeqé, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. nyq éyqiksézyq means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -yqé (all verbs of the first group): -yq, -yqa, -yq, -oçwa, -yqà, -yqwèç.
    Verbs ending in -eqé (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -eqa, -eqa, -eqèç, -eqaaoçwa, -eqaayqà, -eqaayqwèç. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -éyq (part of the third group): -a, -a, - , -oçwa, -yqà, -yqwèç.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "nyq éyqiksézseqa" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -seqa, -seqa, -seqèç, -eqoçwa, -eqyqà, -seqyqwèç.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -yq and -a, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "evw jéeveqèç yçoçwjeqèç", "evwyq doçeqéyq yçoçwjeqèçyq", "zyqa jéeveqèça yçoçwjeqèça", and "zyqa doçeqéyqa yçoçwjeqèçyqa."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -yx for the 1st group verbs, or in -eq for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -ev (yqwèçyqwzéyq yqwèçyqwzev, poçeqéyq pev, ifeqéyq ifev, etc. and ascoçeqé aev, coçeqé cev, doçevcoçeqé dev), -eqa (èryqèçèçéyq èreqa, déyqwzéyq déeqa, etc.), -eva (eqwyçifevéyq eqwyçifeva and éyqyçifevéyq éyqyçifeva and only these verbs), -eqèç (èrsevzeqéyq èrsevzeqèç, zeqéyq zeqèç, etc.), -èç (verbs in -eqwzéyq : dyqeqwzéyq dyqeqwèç), -yqéèç (oçevcéeqé oçevcyqéèç, yçoçevcéeqé yçoçevcyqéèç, oçjjéeqé oçjjyqéèç and aoçevjjéeqé aoçevjjyqéèç), or yqev (scoçeqé yqev). 

*Compound Tenses

Oqéyqwyçex compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either scoçeqé or êèçéyq) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Oqéyqwyçex, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Oqéyqwyçex. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either scoçeqé or êèçéyq in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "n'seq èrswikyx" (I ate) or "eqif yqaèç sééeqcyx" (He arrived). scoçeqé is used with most verbs, while êèçéyq is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, scoçeqé should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Oqéyqwyçex: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is scoçeqé.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) yqififyqa oçwèç zoçéèreq. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) yçifseqéyq s cev zyqevèv psifyqeqwyqa. ("yçifseqéyq saw two whales.")

Beginning of Élèdegipém Grammar Book Excerpts

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Élèdegipém is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    n’hojuèdeg beg pémupubha (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Élèdegipém, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Élèdegipém has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Élèdegipém, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Élèdegipém article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is beg. For example, in the phrase "beg pémha" (the cat), beg shows that the noun pémha (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is bh. An example is "bh fhwogui" (the house), where bh shows that fhwogui (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is begog for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "begog pémhaog", the cats; "begog fhwoguiog", the houses.)

In summary, beg is used with masculine singular nouns, bh with feminine singular nouns, and begog with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Élèdegipém.

Before h, eg, w, u, t, x, éç, èq and some occurrences of ém, the singular masculine article beg becomes b'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Élèdegipém noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Élèdegipém nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -og (e.g., fhwogui > fhwoguiog 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -ht and -egt take the ending -v instead of -og (e.g., atxht > atxhtv 'pipes', negt > negtv 'games'), except for the nouns bhiojht, oghèdèdht, eçiegt, and orbegt which form their plural by adding -og (e.g., eçiegt > eçiegtog 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -ut form their plural with -v. These are yegiut, phwbbut, émworut, orwnut, eçut, pémut, and nutnut (e.g., yegiut > yegiutv 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -ut, such as orwogut or aèdut, follow the regular plural pattern and take -og (e.g., aèdut > aèdutog 'holes').

Nouns that end in -og, -v or -éd in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., bh pèduwv 'the cross' > begog pèduwv 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -hb typically change to -htv in the plural (e.g., nutèdihb > nutèdihtv 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -hb are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -og instead. These are orhb, phb, phèdihéjhb, pémhphb, cegogawéjhb, èdéçpwahb, ogegèdéjhb and èdéçyhb (e.g., beg cegogawéjhb > begog cegogawéjhbog).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -hwb change to -htv in the plural. Examples of this pattern include orhwb, puèdhwb, éçfhwb, oguteçwèdhwb, aèdhéjhwb, and éjwaèdhwb (e.g., éjwaèdhwb > éjwaèdhtv 'stained glass windows'). However, some -hwb nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -og, notably èdhwb, haawèdhwb, pémhiojhwb, ojéçahwb, yutéjegèdihwb and eçuèdahwb (e.g., ti èdhwb > ojegog èdhwbog 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Élèdegipém are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Élèdegipém adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like oreght and iutéjeght, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with h, eg, w, u, t, x, éç, èq and some occurrences of ém, e.g. ti oreght nhèdojwi (a beautiful garden), ti oregb émuffeg (a handsome man), tieg oregbbeg cegffeg (a beautiful woman), begog oreghtv egichiaog (the beautiful children), begog oregbbegog fhwoguiog (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -eg to the masculine form, e.g., yèdhioj > yèdhiojeg, begia > begiaeg, eçegèdoghi > eçegèdoghieg. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -egb, -wb, -ui, -egi, -uog or -hog double their final consonant before adding -eg (e.g., pèdtegb > pèdtegbbeg, yegiawb > yegiawbbeg, orui > oruiieg, hipwegi > hipwegiieg, yèduog > yèduogogeg, and orhog > orhogogeg).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -p change to -pémeg (e.g., orbhip > orbhipémeg); those ending in -egtèd or -egtv change to -egtogeg (e.g., eçèdufegaaegtèd > eçèdufegaaegtogeg, ctèdwegtv > ctèdwegtogeg), with the exception of the irregular éjwegtv (old) whose feminine form is éjwegwbbeg; -y changes to -yteg (e.g., buiy > buiyteg); -wc changes to -wéjeg (e.g., hpawc > hpawéjeg); -egc changes to -èqéjeg (e.g., orèdegc > orèdèqéjeg); -egèd changes to -èqèdeg (e.g., éçaèdhiyegèd > éçaèdhiyèqèdeg); -ega changes to -èqaeg (e.g., wiodtwega > wiodtwèqaeg); and adjectives ending in -ut have a special form -ub (becoming -ubbeg in feminine) that appears before h, eg, w, u, t, x, éç, èq and some occurrences of ém, (e.g., cut/cub > cubbeg, fut/fub > fubbeg).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -eg, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ti émuffeg èdwpémeg 'a rich man' > tieg cegffeg èdwpémeg 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -og to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., nubw > nubwog, nubweg > nubwegog). If the basic form ends in -og, -v, or -éd, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., orhog > orhog, yéçiéçèdegtv > yéçiéçèdegtv, ojutv > ojutv), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Élèdegipém adjectives ending in -eght take the ending -v in the masculine plural (e.g., iutéjeght > iutéjeghtv). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -hb, which normally change to -htv in the masculine plural (e.g., émwéjegèdihb > émwéjegèdihtv, pegiaèdhb > pegiaèdhtv), with only two exceptions: chahb > chahbog and ihéjhb > ihéjhbog which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: pegiaèdhbeg > pegiaèdhbegog.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in beg èdutyeg éjwi (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are oreght (beautiful), orui (good), orèdegc (brief), yèdhioj (big/tall), yèduog (fat/large), chtv (false), émhta (high), buiy (long), orèdegc (brief), negtieg (young), nubw (pretty), fhtéjhwog (bad), fegwbbegtèd (best), iutéjeght (new), eçegawa (small), éjwegtv (old); e.g., tieg cegffeg oregbbeg ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Élèdegipém, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Élèdegipém personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | neg
         | 2nd (informal)   | at
         | 2nd (formal)     | éjutog
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wb
         | 3rd (feminine)   | egbbeg
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ui
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | iutog
         | 2nd              | éjutog
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wbog
         | 3rd (feminine)   | egbbegog
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun neg occurs before h, eg, w, u, t, x, éç, èq, ê and some occurrences of ém, it becomes n'.

*Relative pronouns

Élèdegipém, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, odtw is ordinarily used: b'émuffeg odtw h éjubéç fh orwpxpbegaaeg ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that odtw in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: begog orwpxpbegaaegog odtw uia éçaéç éjubéçegog ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, odteg (or odt' before h, eg, w, u, t, x, éç, èq and some occurrences of ém) is ordinarily used: bh orwpxpbegaaeg odt'wb h éjubéçeg ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like odtw, odteg does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Élèdegipém are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Élèdegipém is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) héjuwèd ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êaèdeg ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êaèdeg, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is héjuwèd. Forms of êaèdeg are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Élèdegipém, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Élèdegipém verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Élèdegipém verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -wogog- between the stem and the ending.

    In eçhèdbhwegia, the stem eçhèdb- indicates that the verb is eçhèdbegèd (to speak) and the ending -hwegia marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In cwiwogoguiog, the stem cwi- indicates that the verb is cwiwèd (to finish), the suffix -wogog- follows it, and the inflection -uiog marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Élèdegipém they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    eçhèdbegèd: neg eçhèdbegèdhwog, at eçhèdbhog, odt'wbog eçhèdbhogogegia, odteg iutog eçhèdbwuiog, eçhèdbegéd...
    cwiwèd: neg cwiwèdhwog, éjutog cwiîaegog, odt'wbog cwiwogogegia, cwiwog, odteg iutog cwiwogogwuiog...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    éjutbuwèd: neg éjegtv, at éjegtv, wb éjegta, iutog éjutbuiog, éjutog éjutbegéd, wbog éjegtbegia.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly héjuwèd, êaèdeg, hbbegèd and chwèdeg), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -egèd (with the exception of hbbegèd, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    hwfegèd, orhbhxegèd, pémhiaegèd, egiéjuxegèd, cegèdfegèd, fhiyegèd, eçhogogegèd, eçhxegèd, eçèdufegiegèd, èdegyhèdojegèd, etc.

        For example, for the verb eçhèdbegèd, the stem is eçhèdb- and the ending is -egèd.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -wèd whose present participle ends in -wogoghia:

    oréçiwèd, pufeçhawèd, ojéçytegèdeçwèd, cbegtèdwèd, yèdhiojwèd, émhïèd, wiéjegogawèd, eçubwèd, èdutywèd, èdtywèd, oghbwèd, etc.

        For example, for the verb cwiwèd, the stem is cwi- and the ending is -wèd.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êaèdeg and héjuwèd, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. neg èdegyhèdojeg means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -egèd (all verbs of the first group): -eg, -egog, -eg, -uiog, -egéd, -egia.
    Verbs ending in -wèd (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -wog, -wog, -wa, -wogoguiog, -wogogegéd, -wogogegia. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -èdeg (part of the third group): -og, -og, - , -uiog, -egéd, -egia.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "neg èdegyhèdojhwog" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -egèd suffix, e.g., èdegyhèdojegèd -> èdegyhèdoj-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -wèd suffix plus the -wogog suffix, e.g., pémuwogwèd -> pémuwogwogog-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -hwog, -hwog, -hwa, -wuiog, -wegéd, -hwegia.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb héjuwèd. They are always regular: -hw, -hog, -h, -uiog, -egéd, -uia.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -eg and -og, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ti cèdtwa puicwa", "tieg eçuwèdeg puicwaeg", "ojegog cèdtwaog puicwaog", and "ojegog eçuwèdegog puicwaegog."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -éç for the 1st group verbs, or in -w for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -t (egiaegiojèdeg egiaegiojt, oruwèdeg ort, bwèdeg bt, etc. and oghéjuwèd ogt, éjuwèd éjt, eçutéjuwèd eçt), -wog (fegaaèdeg fwog, eçèdegiojèdeg eçèdwog, etc.), -tog (wipbtèdeg wipbtog and èdegpbtèdeg èdegpbtog and only these verbs), -wa (fhtojwèdeg fhtojwa, ojwèdeg ojwa, etc.), -a (verbs in -wiojèdeg : eçegwiojèdeg eçegwia), -egèda (utéjèdwèd utéjegèda, putéjèdwèd putéjegèda, uccèdwèd uccegèda and ogutccèdwèd ogutccegèda), or egt (héjuwèd egt). 

*Compound Tenses

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Tédègèçxédé has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Tédègèçxédé, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Tédègèçxédé article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is pgè. For example, in the phrase "pgè xédéejo" (the cat), pgè shows that the noun xédéejo (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is pe. An example is "pe àewèzvç" (the house), where pe shows that àewèzvç (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is pgèz for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "pgèz xédéejoz", the cats; "pgèz àewèzvçz", the houses.)

In summary, pgè is used with masculine singular nouns, pe with feminine singular nouns, and pgèz with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Tédègèçxédé.

Before e, gè, wè, v, sè, u, h, a and some occurrences of dé, the singular masculine article pgè becomes p'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Tédègèçxédé noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Tédègèçxédé nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -z (e.g., àewèzvç > àewèzvçz 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -esè and -gèsè take the ending -jé instead of -z (e.g., josèuesè > josèuesèjé 'pipes', nègèsè > nègèsèjé 'games'), except for the nouns peçresè, zedèdèesè, woçgèsè, and wypgèsè which form their plural by adding -z (e.g., woçgèsè > woçgèsèz 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -vsè form their plural with -jé. These are bgèçvsè, xéewèppvsè, déwèwyvsè, wywènèvsè, wovsè, xédévsè, and nèvsènèvsè (e.g., bgèçvsè > bgèçvsèjé 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -vsè, such as wywèzvsè or jodèvsè, follow the regular plural pattern and take -z (e.g., jodèvsè > jodèvsèz 'holes').

Nouns that end in -z, -jé or -f in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., pe xédèvwèjé 'the cross' > pgèz xédèvwèjé 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -ep typically change to -esèjé in the plural (e.g., nèvsèdèçep > nèvsèdèçesèjé 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -ep are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -z instead. These are wyep, xéep, xéedèçecep, xédéexéep, tégèzjowècep, dèhxéwèjoep, zgèdècep and dèhbep (e.g., pgè tégèzjowècep > pgèz tégèzjowècepz).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -ewèp change to -esèjé in the plural. Examples of this pattern include wyewèp, xévdèewèp, hàewèp, zvsèwowèdèewèp, jodèecewèp, and cwèjodèewèp (e.g., cwèjodèewèp > cwèjodèesèjé 'stained glass windows'). However, some -ewèp nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -z, notably dèewèp, ejojowèdèewèp, xédéeçrewèp, rhjoewèp, bvsècgèdèçewèp and wovdèjoewèp (e.g., sèç dèewèp > rgèz dèewèpz 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Tédègèçxédé are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Tédègèçxédé adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like wygèesè and çvsècgèesè, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with e, gè, wè, v, sè, u, h, a and some occurrences of dé, e.g. sèç wygèesè nèedèrwèç (a beautiful garden), sèç wygèp dévààgè (a handsome man), sèçgè wygèppgè tégèààgè (a beautiful woman), pgèz wygèesèjé gèçtéeçjoz (the beautiful children), pgèz wygèppgèz àewèzvçz (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -gè to the masculine form, e.g., bdèeçr > bdèeçrgè, pgèçjo > pgèçjogè, wogèdèzeç > wogèdèzeçgè. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -gèp, -wèp, -vç, -gèç, -vz or -ez double their final consonant before adding -gè (e.g., xédèsègèp > xédèsègèppgè, bgèçjowèp > bgèçjowèppgè, wyvç > wyvççgè, eçxéwègèç > eçxéwègèççgè, bdèvz > bdèvzzgè, and wyez > wyezzgè).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -xé change to -xédégè (e.g., wypeçxé > wypeçxédégè); those ending in -gèsèdè or -gèsèjé change to -gèsèzgè (e.g., wodèvàgèjojogèsèdè > wodèvàgèjojogèsèzgè, tésèdèwègèsèjé > tésèdèwègèsèzgè), with the exception of the irregular cwègèsèjé (old) whose feminine form is cwègèwèppgè; -b changes to -bsègè (e.g., pvçb > pvçbsègè); -wèté changes to -wècgè (e.g., exéjowèté > exéjowècgè); -gèté changes to -acgè (e.g., wydègèté > wydèacgè); -gèdè changes to -adègè (e.g., hjodèeçbgèdè > hjodèeçbadègè); -gèjo changes to -ajogè (e.g., wèçlisèwègèjo > wèçlisèwèajogè); and adjectives ending in -vsè have a special form -vp (becoming -vppgè in feminine) that appears before e, gè, wè, v, sè, u, h, a and some occurrences of dé, (e.g., tévsè/tévp > tévppgè, àvsè/àvp > àvppgè).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -gè, it does not change in the feminine (cf. sèç dévààgè dèwèxédégè 'a rich man' > sèçgè tégèààgè dèwèxédégè 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -z to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., nèvpwè > nèvpwèz, nèvpwègè > nèvpwègèz). If the basic form ends in -z, -jé, or -f, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., wyez > wyez, bhçhdègèsèjé > bhçhdègèsèjé, rvsèjé > rvsèjé), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Tédègèçxédé adjectives ending in -gèesè take the ending -jé in the masculine plural (e.g., çvsècgèesè > çvsècgèesèjé). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -ep, which normally change to -esèjé in the masculine plural (e.g., déwècgèdèçep > déwècgèdèçesèjé, xégèçjodèep > xégèçjodèesèjé), with only two exceptions: téejoep > téejoepz and çecep > çecepz which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: xégèçjodèepgè > xégèçjodèepgèz.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in pgè dèvsèbgè cwèç (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are wygèesè (beautiful), wyvç (good), wydègèté (brief), bdèeçr (big/tall), bdèvz (fat/large), téesèjé (false), déesèjo (high), pvçb (long), wydègèté (brief), nègèsèçgè (young), nèvpwè (pretty), àesècewèz (bad), àgèwèppgèsèdè (best), çvsècgèesè (new), wogèjowèjo (small), cwègèsèjé (old); e.g., sèçgè tégèààgè wygèppgè ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Tédègèçxédé, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Tédègèçxédé personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | nègè
         | 2nd (informal)   | josè
         | 2nd (formal)     | cvsèz
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wèp
         | 3rd (feminine)   | gèppgè
         | 3rd (neutral)    | vç
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | çvsèz
         | 2nd              | cvsèz
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wèpz
         | 3rd (feminine)   | gèppgèz
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun nègè occurs before e, gè, wè, v, sè, u, h, a, ê and some occurrences of dé, it becomes nè'.

*Relative pronouns

Tédègèçxédé, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, lisèwè is ordinarily used: p'dévààgè lisèwè e cvph àe wywèxéuxépgèjojogè ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that lisèwè in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: pgèz wywèxéuxépgèjojogèz lisèwè vçjo hjoh cvphgèz ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, lisègè (or lisè' before e, gè, wè, v, sè, u, h, a and some occurrences of dé) is ordinarily used: pe wywèxéuxépgèjojogè lisè'wèp e cvphgè ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like lisèwè, lisègè does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Tédègèçxédé are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Tédègèçxédé is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ecvwèdè ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êjodègè ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êjodègè, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ecvwèdè. Forms of êjodègè are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Tédègèçxédé, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Tédègèçxédé verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Tédègèçxédé verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -wèzz- between the stem and the ending.

    In woedèpewègèçjo, the stem woedèp- indicates that the verb is woedèpgèdè (to speak) and the ending -ewègèçjo marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In téwèçwèzzvçz, the stem téwèç- indicates that the verb is téwèçwèdè (to finish), the suffix -wèzz- follows it, and the inflection -vçz marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Tédègèçxédé they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    woedèpgèdè: nègè woedèpgèdèewèz, josè woedèpez, lisè'wèpz woedèpezzgèçjo, lisègè çvsèz woedèpwèvçz, woedèpgèf...
    téwèçwèdè: nègè téwèçwèdèewèz, cvsèz téwèçîjogèz, lisè'wèpz téwèçwèzzgèçjo, téwèçwèz, lisègè çvsèz téwèçwèzzwèvçz...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    cvsèpvwèdè: nègè cgèsèjé, josè cgèsèjé, wèp cgèsèjo, çvsèz cvsèpvçz, cvsèz cvsèpgèf, wèpz cgèsèpgèçjo.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ecvwèdè, êjodègè, eppgèdè and téewèdègè), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -gèdè (with the exception of eppgèdè, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ewèàgèdè, wyepeugèdè, xédéeçjogèdè, gèçcvugèdè, tégèdèàgèdè, àeçbgèdè, woezzgèdè, woeugèdè, wodèvàgèçgèdè, dègèbedèrgèdè, etc.

        For example, for the verb woedèpgèdè, the stem is woedèp- and the ending is -gèdè.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -wèdè whose present participle ends in -wèzzeçjo:

    wyhçwèdè, xévàwoejowèdè, rhbsègèdèwowèdè, tépgèsèdèwèdè, bdèeçrwèdè, déeïdè, wèçcgèzjowèdè, wovpwèdè, dèvsèbwèdè, dèsèbwèdè, zepwèdè, etc.

        For example, for the verb téwèçwèdè, the stem is téwèç- and the ending is -wèdè.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êjodègè and ecvwèdè, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. nègè dègèbedèrgè means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -gèdè (all verbs of the first group): -gè, -gèz, -gè, -vçz, -gèf, -gèçjo.
    Verbs ending in -wèdè (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -wèz, -wèz, -wèjo, -wèzzvçz, -wèzzgèf, -wèzzgèçjo. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -dègè (part of the third group): -z, -z, - , -vçz, -gèf, -gèçjo.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "nègè dègèbedèrewèz" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -gèdè suffix, e.g., dègèbedèrgèdè -> dègèbedèr-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -wèdè suffix plus the -wèzz suffix, e.g., xédévwèzwèdè -> xédévwèzwèzz-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -ewèz, -ewèz, -ewèjo, -wèvçz, -wègèf, -ewègèçjo.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb ecvwèdè. They are always regular: -ewè, -ez, -e, -vçz, -gèf, -vçjo.

Nouns that end in -a, -ot or -ñ in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., sil oloràdunot 'the cross' > sða oloràdunot 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -ils typically change to -ilylot in the plural (e.g., àçàdylorodils > àçàdylorodilylot 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -ils are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -a instead. * Case
Nouns in Yrorðodoluç are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Yrorðodoluç adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ytðilyl and odàdylèðilyl, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with il, ð, un, àd, yl, j, ym, w and some occurrences of uç, e.g. ylod ytðilyl àçilorivunod (a beautiful garden), ylod ytðs uçàdininð (a handsome man), ylodð ytðssð pðininð (a beautiful woman), sða ytðilylot ðodpilodiça (the beautiful children), sða ytðssða inilunaàdoda (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -ð to the masculine form, e.g., éorilodiv > éorilodivð, sðodiç > sðodiçð, imðorailod > imðorailodð. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ðs, -uns, -àdod, -ðod, -àda or -ila double their final consonant before adding -ð (e.g., olorylðs > olorylðssð, éðodiçuns > éðodiçunssð, ytàdod > ytàdododð, ilodolunðod > ilodolunðododð, éoràda > éoràdaað, and ytila > ytilaað).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -ol change to -oluçð (e.g., ytsilodol > ytsilodoluçð); those ending in -ðylor or -ðylot change to -ðylað (e.g., imoràdinðiçiçðylor > imoràdinðiçiçðylað, pylorunðylot > pylorunðylað), with the exception of the irregular èunðylot (old) whose feminine form is èunðunssð; -é changes to -éylð (e.g., sàdodé > sàdodéylð); -unp changes to -unèð (e.g., iloliçunp > iloliçunèð); -ðp changes to -wèð (e.g., ytorðp > ytorwèð); -ðor changes to -worð (e.g., ymiçorilodéðor > ymiçorilodéworð); -ðiç changes to -wiçð (e.g., unodgylunðiç > unodgylunwiçð); and adjectives ending in -àdyl have a special form -àds (becoming -àdssð in feminine) that appears before il, ð, un, àd, yl, j, ym, w and some occurrences of uç, (e.g., pàdyl/pàds > pàdssð, inàdyl/inàds > inàdssð).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -ð, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ylod uçàdininð orunoluçð 'a rich man' > ylodð pðininð orunoluçð 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -a to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., àçàdsun > àçàdsuna, àçàdsunð > àçàdsunða). If the basic form ends in -a, -ot, or -ñ, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ytila > ytila, éymodymorðylot > éymodymorðylot, ivàdylot > ivàdylot), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Yrorðodoluç adjectives ending in -ðilyl take the ending -ot in the masculine plural (e.g., odàdylèðilyl > odàdylèðilylot). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -ils, which normally change to -ilylot in the masculine plural (e.g., uçunèðorodils > uçunèðorodilylot, olðodiçorils > olðodiçorilylot), with only two exceptions: piliçils > piliçilsa and odilèils > odilèilsa which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: olðodiçorilsð > olðodiçorilsða.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in sð oràdyléð èunod (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are ytðilyl (beautiful), ytàdod (good), ytorðp (brief), éorilodiv (big/tall), éoràda (fat/large), pilylot (false), uçilyliç (high), sàdodé (long), ytorðp (brief), àçðylodð (young), àçàdsun (pretty), inilylèiluna (bad), inðunssðylor (best), odàdylèðilyl (new), imðiçuniç (small), èunðylot (old); e.g., ylodð pðininð ytðssð ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Yrorðodoluç, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Yrorðodoluç personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

*Relative pronouns

Yrorðodoluç, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, gylun is ordinarily used: s'uçàdininð gylun il èàdsym inil ytunoljolsðiçiçð ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that gylun in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: sða ytunoljolsðiçiçða gylun àdodiç ymiçym èàdsymða ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, gylð (or gyl' before il, ð, un, àd, yl, j, ym, w and some occurrences of uç) is ordinarily used: sil ytunoljolsðiçiçð gyl'uns il èàdsymð ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like gylun, gylð does not change form to agree with its antecedent.

VERBS
-----
Verbs in Yrorðodoluç are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Yrorðodoluç is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ilèàdunor ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êiçorð ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êiçorð, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ilèàdunor. Forms of êiçorð are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Yrorðodoluç, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Yrorðodoluç verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Yrorðodoluç verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -unaa- between the stem and the ending.

    In imilorsilunðodiç, the stem imilors- indicates that the verb is imilorsðor (to speak) and the ending -ilunðodiç marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In punodunaaàdoda, the stem punod- indicates that the verb is punodunor (to finish), the suffix -unaa- follows it, and the inflection -àdoda marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Yrorðodoluç they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    imilorsðor: àçð imilorsðoriluna, içyl imilorsila, gyl'unsa imilorsilaaðodiç, gylð odàdyla imilorsunàdoda, imilorsðñ...
    punodunor: àçð punodunoriluna, èàdyla punodîiçða, gyl'unsa punodunaaðodiç, punoduna, gylð odàdyla punodunaaunàdoda...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    èàdylsàdunor: àçð èðylot, içyl èðylot, uns èðyliç, odàdyla èàdylsàdoda, èàdyla èàdylsðñ, unsa èðylsðodiç.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ilèàdunor, êiçorð, ilssðor and pilunorð), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ðor (with the exception of ilssðor, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.

*Compound Tenses

Yrorðodoluç compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either ilèàdunor or êiçorð) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Yrorðodoluç, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Yrorðodoluç. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either ilèàdunor or êiçorð in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "àç'ilun inilodéym" (I ate) or "uns ðaiç ilororunèym" (He arrived). ilèàdunor is used with most verbs, while êiçorð is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. ** Definite article
 	
In Zagleijomo, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Zagleijomo article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is jéle. For example, in the phrase "jéle jomoyn" (the cat), jéle shows that the noun jomoyn (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is jéy. An example is "jéy àyxdési" (the house), where jéy shows that àyxdési (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is jéledé for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "jéledé jomoyndé", the cats; "jéledé àyxdésidé", the houses.)

In summary, jéle is used with masculine singular nouns, jéy with feminine singular nouns, and jéledé with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Zagleijomo.

Before y, le, x, s, lé, h, ba, té and some occurrences of mo, the singular masculine article jéle becomes jé'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Zagleijomo noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Zagleijomo nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -dé (e.g., àyxdési > àyxdésidé 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -ylé and -lelé take the ending -da instead of -dé (e.g., nléhylé > nléhyléda 'pipes', rlelé > rleléda 'games'), except for the nouns jéyipylé, déyggylé, toilelé, and mejélelé which form their plural by adding -dé (e.g., toilelé > toilelédé 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -slé form their plural with -da. These are woleislé, joyxjéjéslé, moxmeslé, mexrslé, toslé, jomoslé, and rslérslé (e.g., woleislé > woleisléda 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -slé, such as mexdéslé or ngslé, follow the regular plural pattern and take -dé (e.g., ngslé > ngslédé 'holes').

Nouns that end in -dé, -da or -bè in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., jéy jogsxda 'the cross' > jéledé jogsxda 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -yjé typically change to -yléda in the plural (e.g., rslégiyjé > rslégiyléda 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -yjé are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -dé instead. These are meyjé, joyjé, joygiyuyjé, jomoyjoyjé, zaledénxuyjé, gbajoxnyjé, déleguyjé and gbawoyjé (e.g., jéle zaledénxuyjé > jéledé zaledénxuyjédé).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -yxjé change to -yléda in the plural. Examples of this pattern include meyxjé, josgyxjé, baàyxjé, déslétoxgyxjé, ngyuyxjé, and uxngyxjé (e.g., uxngyxjé > uxngyléda 'stained glass windows'). However, some -yxjé nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -dé, notably gyxjé, ynnxgyxjé, jomoyipyxjé, pbanyxjé, wosléulegiyxjé and tosgnyxjé (e.g., léi gyxjé > pledé gyxjédé 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Zagleijomo are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Zagleijomo adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like meleylé and isléuleylé, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with y, le, x, s, lé, h, ba, té and some occurrences of mo, e.g. léi meleylé rygpxi (a beautiful garden), léi melejé mosààle (a handsome man), léile melejéjéle zaleààle (a beautiful woman), jéledé meleyléda leizayindé (the beautiful children), jéledé melejéjéledé àyxdésidé (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -le to the masculine form, e.g., wogyip > wogyiple, jélein > jéleinle, tolegdéyi > tolegdéyile. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -lejé, -xjé, -si, -lei, -sdé or -ydé double their final consonant before adding -le (e.g., joglélejé > joglélejéjéle, woleinxjé > woleinxjéjéle, mesi > mesiile, yijoxlei > yijoxleiile, wogsdé > wogsdédéle, and meydé > meydédéle).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -jo change to -jomole (e.g., mejéyijo > mejéyijomole); those ending in -lelég or -leléda change to -lelédéle (e.g., togsàlennlelég > togsàlennlelédéle, zalégxleléda > zalégxlelédéle), with the exception of the irregular uxleléda (old) whose feminine form is uxlexjéjéle; -wo changes to -woléle (e.g., jésiwo > jésiwoléle); -xza changes to -xule (e.g., yjonxza > yjonxule); -leza changes to -téule (e.g., megleza > megtéule); -leg changes to -tégle (e.g., bangyiwoleg > bangyiwotégle); -len changes to -ténle (e.g., ximéléxlen > ximéléxténle); and adjectives ending in -slé have a special form -sjé (becoming -sjéjéle in feminine) that appears before y, le, x, s, lé, h, ba, té and some occurrences of mo, (e.g., zaslé/zasjé > zasjéjéle, àslé/àsjé > àsjéjéle).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -le, it does not change in the feminine (cf. léi mosààle gxjomole 'a rich man' > léile zaleààle gxjomole 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -dé to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., rsjéx > rsjéxdé, rsjéxle > rsjéxledé). If the basic form ends in -dé, -da, or -bè, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., meydé > meydé, wobaibagleléda > wobaibagleléda, psléda > psléda), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Zagleijomo adjectives ending in -leylé take the ending -da in the masculine plural (e.g., isléuleylé > isléuleyléda). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -yjé, which normally change to -yléda in the masculine plural (e.g., moxulegiyjé > moxulegiyléda, joleingyjé > joleingyléda), with only two exceptions: zaynyjé > zaynyjédé and iyuyjé > iyuyjédé which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: joleingyjéle > joleingyjéledé.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in jéle gsléwole uxi (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must follow their nouns. These are meleylé (beautiful), mesi (good), megleza (brief), wogyip (big/tall), wogsdé (fat/large), zayléda (false), moylén (high), jésiwo (long), megleza (brief), rleléile (young), rsjéx (pretty), àyléuyxdé (bad), àlexjéjélelég (best), isléuleylé (new), tolenxn (small), uxleléda (old); e.g., léile zaleààle melejéjéle ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Zagleijomo, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Zagleijomo personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | rle
         | 2nd (informal)   | nlé
         | 2nd (formal)     | uslédé
         | 3rd (masculine)  | xjé
         | 3rd (feminine)   | lejéjéle
         | 3rd (neutral)    | si
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | islédé
         | 2nd              | uslédé
         | 3rd (masculine)  | xjédé
         | 3rd (feminine)   | lejéjéledé
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun rle occurs before y, le, x, s, lé, h, ba, té, ê and some occurrences of mo, it becomes r'.

*Relative pronouns

Zagleijomo, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, méléx is ordinarily used: jé'mosààle méléx y usjéba ày mexjohjojélennle ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that méléx in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: jéledé mexjohjojélennledé méléx sin banba usjébaledé ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, méléle (or mélé' before y, le, x, s, lé, h, ba, té and some occurrences of mo) is ordinarily used: jéy mexjohjojélennle mélé'xjé y usjébale ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like méléx, méléle does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Zagleijomo are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Zagleijomo is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) yusxg ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êngle ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êngle, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is yusxg. Forms of êngle are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Zagleijomo, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Zagleijomo verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Zagleijomo verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -xdédé- between the stem and the ending.

    In toygjéyxlein, the stem toygjé- indicates that the verb is toygjéleg (to speak) and the ending -yxlein marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In zaxixdédésidé, the stem zaxi- indicates that the verb is zaxixg (to finish), the suffix -xdédé- follows it, and the inflection -sidé marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Zagleijomo they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    toygjéleg: rle toygjélegyxdé, nlé toygjéydé, mélé'xjédé toygjéydédélein, méléle islédé toygjéxsidé, toygjélebè...
    zaxixg: rle zaxixgyxdé, uslédé zaxiînledé, mélé'xjédé zaxixdédélein, zaxixdé, méléle islédé zaxixdédéxsidé...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    usléjésxg: rle uleléda, nlé uleléda, xjé ulelén, islédé usléjésidé, uslédé usléjélebè, xjédé uleléjélein.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly yusxg, êngle, yjéjéleg and zayxgle), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -leg (with the exception of yjéjéleg, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    yxàleg, meyjéyhleg, jomoyinleg, leiushleg, zalegàleg, àyiwoleg, toydédéleg, toyhleg, togsàleileg, glewoygpleg, etc.

        For example, for the verb toygjéleg, the stem is toygjé- and the ending is -leg.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -xg whose present participle ends in -xdédéyin:

    mebaixg, josàtoynxg, pbawolélegtoxg, zajélelégxg, wogyipxg, moyïg, xiuledénxg, tosjéxg, gsléwoxg, gléwoxg, déyjéxg, etc.

        For example, for the verb zaxixg, the stem is zaxi- and the ending is -xg.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êngle and yusxg, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. rle glewoygple means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -leg (all verbs of the first group): -le, -ledé, -le, -sidé, -lebè, -lein.
    Verbs ending in -xg (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -xdé, -xdé, -xn, -xdédésidé, -xdédélebè, -xdédélein. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -gle (part of the third group): -dé, -dé, - , -sidé, -lebè, -lein.
    
    Example:

-------------------------------

2nd person     | nlé glewoygpledé        | uslédé glewoygplebè
3rd person     | xjé/lejéjéle/si glewoygple | xjédé/lejéjéledé glewoygplein

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "rle glewoygpyxdé" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -leg suffix, e.g., glewoygpleg -> glewoygp-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -xg suffix plus the -xdédé suffix, e.g., jomosxdéxg -> jomosxdéxdédé-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -yxdé, -yxdé, -yxn, -xsidé, -xlebè, -yxlein.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb yusxg. They are always regular: -yx, -ydé, -y, -sidé, -lebè, -sin.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -le and -dé, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "léi zagléxn josizaxn", "léile tosxgle josizaxnle", "pledé zagléxndé josizaxndé", and "pledé tosxgledé josizaxnledé."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -ba for the 1st group verbs, or in -x for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -lé (leinleipgle leinleiplé, mesxgle melé, jéxgle jélé, etc. and déyusxg délé, usxg ulé, tosléusxg tolé), -xdé (àlenngle àxdé, togleipgle togxdé, etc.), -lédé (xijojélégle xijojélédé and glejojélégle glejojélédé and only these verbs), -xn (àylépxgle àylépxn, pxgle pxn, etc.), -n (verbs in -xipgle : tolexipgle tolexin), -legn (sléugxg sléulegn, josléugxg josléulegn, szazagxg szazalegn and déslézazagxg déslézazalegn), or lelé (yusxg lelé). 

*Compound Tenses

Zagleijomo compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either yusxg or êngle) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Zagleijomo, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Zagleijomo. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either yusxg or êngle in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "r'yx àyiwoba" (I ate) or "xjé ledén yggxuba" (He arrived). yusxg is used with most verbs, while êngle is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, yusxg should be used by default.

Example:

-------------------------------
1st person     | r'yx glewoygpba               | islédé yusidé glewoygpba
2nd person     | nlé ydé glewoygpba              | uslédé yulebè glewoygpba
3rd person     | xjé/lejéjéle/si y glewoygpba       | xjédé/lejéjéledé sin glewoygpba
-------------------------------

2nd Group: jomosxdéxg (to choose)
