As in English, Uèhzàgalà nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme y- (e.g., hzoyfgono > yhzoyfgono 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with qgo- and qzà- take the prefix ze- instead of y- (e.g., qgosàqk > zeqgosàqk 'pipes', qzàni > zeqzàni 'games'), except for the nouns qgophgoé, qgogagagoy, qzàhtà, and qzàézi which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme y- (e.g., qzàhtà > yqzàhtà 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with qzo- form their plural with ze-. These are qzohzàm, qzoééfgoè, qzozifu, qzonifzi, qzotà, qzouè, and qzoniqzoni (e.g., qzohzàm > zeqzohzàm 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with qzo-, such as qzoyfzi or qzogak, follow the regular plural pattern and take y- (e.g., qzogak > yqzogak 'holes').

Nouns that begin with y-, ze- or r- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., zefzogaè goé 'the cross' > zefzogaè yzàé 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with égo- typically change to zeqgo- in the plural (e.g., égohgaqzoni > zeqgohgaqzoni 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with égo- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding y- instead. These are égozi, égoè, égodegohgagoè, égoègouè, égodefkyzàlà, égokfèjoga, égodegazày and égomjoga (e.g., égodefkyzàlà zàé > yégodefkyzàlà yzàé).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with éfgo- change to zeqgo- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include éfgozi, éfgogazoè, éfgonojo, éfgogaftàqzoy, éfgodegogak, and éfgogakfde (e.g., éfgogakfde hq > zeqgogakfde yzàp 'stained-glass windows'). However, some éfgo- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with y-, notably éfgoga, éfgogafkkgo, éfgophgouè, éfgokjop, éfgohgazàdeqzom and éfgokgazotà (e.g., éfgoga zàé > yéfgoga yzàé 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Uèhzàgalà are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Uèhzàgalà adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like qgozàzi and qgozàdeqzoh, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in go, zà, f, zo, q, sà, jo, v and some occurrences of u, e.g. hfpgagoni qgozàzi hq (a beautiful garden), zànonozou ézàzi hq (a handsome man), zànonozàlà zàéézàzi zàhq (a beautiful woman), ykhgolàhzà zeqgozàzi yzàé (the beautiful children), yhzoyfgono yzàéézàzi yzàé (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix zà- to the masculine form, e.g., phgogam > zàphgogam, khzàé > zàkhzàé, hgoygazàtà > zàhgoygazàtà. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with ézà-, éf-, hzo-, hzà-, yzo- or ygo- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix zà- (e.g., ézàqgaè > zàéézàqgaè, éfkhzàm > zàééfkhzàm, hzozi > zàhhzozi, hzàfèhgo > zàhhzàfèhgo, yzogam > zàyyzogam, and ygozi > zàyygozi).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with è- change to zàuè- (e.g., èhgoézi > zàuèhgoézi); those beginning with gaqzà- or zeqzà- change to zàyqzà- (e.g., gaqzàkkzànozogatà > zàyqzàkkzànozogatà, zeqzàfgaqlà > zàyqzàfgaqlà), with the exception of the irregular zeqzàfde (old) whose feminine form is zàééfzàfde; m- changes to zàqm- (e.g., mhzoé > zàqmhzoé); làf- changes to zàdef- (e.g., làfkègo > zàdefkègo); làzà- changes to zàdev- (e.g., làzàgazi > zàdevgazi); gazà- changes to zàgav- (e.g., gazàmhgogakjo > zàgavmhgogakjo); kzà- changes to zàkv- (e.g., kzàfqxhf > zàkvfqxhf); and adjectives beginning with qzo- have a special form ézo- (becoming zàéézo- in feminine) that appears after go, zà, f, zo, q, sà, jo, v and some occurrences of u, (e.g., qzolà/ézolà > zàéézolà, qzono/ézono > zàéézono).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with zà-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. zàuèfga zànonozou hq 'a rich man' > zàuèfga zànonozàlà zàhq 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix y- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., fézoni > yfézoni, zàfézoni > yzàfézoni). If the basic form beginning with y-, ze-, or r-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ygozi > ygozi, zeqzàgajohjom > zeqzàgajohjom, zeqzop > zeqzop), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Uèhzàgalà adjectives beginning with qgozà- take the prefix ze- in the masculine plural (e.g., qgozàdeqzoh > zeqgozàdeqzoh). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with égo-, which normally change to zeqgo- in the masculine plural (e.g., égohgazàdefu > zeqgohgazàdefu, égogakhzàè > zeqgogakhzàè), with only two exceptions: égokgolà > yégokgolà and égodegoh > yégodegoh which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: zàégogakhzàè > yzàégogakhzàè.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in zàmqzoga zàé hfde (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are qgozàzi (beautiful), hzozi (good), làzàgazi (brief), phgogam (big/tall), yzogam (fat/large), zeqgolà (false), kqgou (high), mhzoé (long), làzàgazi (brief), zàhqzàni (young), fézoni (pretty), yfgodeqgono (bad), gaqzàééfzàno (better), qgozàdeqzoh (new), kfkzàtà (small), zeqzàfde (old); e.g., zànonozàlà zàhq zàéézàzi ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Uèhzàgalà, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
uèhzàgalà personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | zàni
         | 2nd (informal)   | qk
         | 2nd (formal)     | yqzode
         | 3rd (masculine)  | éf
         | 3rd (feminine)   | zàéézà
         | 3rd (neutral)    | hzo
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | yqzoh
         | 2nd              | yqzode
         | 3rd (masculine)  | yéf
         | 3rd (feminine)   | yzàéézà
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun zàni occurs after go, zà, f, zo, q, sà, jo, v, ê and some occurrences of u, it becomes 'ni.

*Relative pronouns

uèhzàgalà, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Uèhzàgalà, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, fqx is ordinarily used: zàkkzàéèsàèfzi gono joézode go fqx zànonozou'é ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that fqx in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: yzàjoézode jokjo khzo fqx yzàkkzàéèsàèfzi yzàé ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, zàqx (or 'qx after go, zà, f, zo, q, sà, jo, v, ê and some occurrences of u) is ordinarily used: zàjoézode go éf'qx zàkkzàéèsàèfzi goé ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like fqx, zàqx does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Uèhzàgalà are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Uèhzàgalà is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) gafzodego ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of zàgakê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is zàgakê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is gafzodego. Forms of zàgakê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Uèhzàgalà, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

uèhzàgalà verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -yyf- between the stem and the ending.

    In khzàfgoégagotà, the stem -égagotà indicates that the verb is gazàégagotà (to speak) and the prefix khzàfgo- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In yhzoyyfhflà, the stem -hflà indicates that the verb is gafhflà (to finish), the prefix -yyf- precedes it, and the inflection yhzo- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Uèhzàgalà they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    gazàégagotà: yfgogazàégagotà zàni, ygoégagotà qk, khzàyygoégagotà yéf'qx, yhzofégagotà yqzoh zàqx, rzàégagotà...
    gafhflà: yfgogafhflà zàni, yzàkîhflà yqzode, khzàyyfhflà yéf'qx, yfhflà, yhzofyyfhflà yqzoh zàqx...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    gafzoéqzode: zeqzàde zàni, zeqzàde qk, kqzàde éf, yhzoéqzode yqzoh, rzàéqzode yqzode, khzàéqzàde yéf.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly gafzodego, zàgakê, gazàéégo and zàgafgolà), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with gazà- (with the exception of gazàéégo, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    gazànofgo, gazàsàgoégozi, gazàkhgouè, gazàsàzodehzà, gazànogazàlà, gazàmhgono, gazàyygotà, gazàsàgotà, gazàhzànozogatà, gazàpgagomzàga, etc.

        For example, for the verb gazàégagotà, the stem is -égagotà and the infinitive prefix is gazà-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with gaf- whose present participle begins with khgoyyf-:

    gafhjozi, gafkgotànozoè, gaftàgazàqmjop, gafgaqzàélà, gafphgogam, gaïgou, gafkyzàdehf, gafézotà, gafmqzoga, gafmqga, gafégoy, etc.

        For example, for the verb gafhflà, the stem is -hflà and the infinitive prefix is gaf-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries zàgakê and gafzodego, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. zàpgagomzàga zàni means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with gazà- (all verbs of the first group): zà-, yzà-, zà-, yhzo-, rzà-, khzà-.
    Verbs beginning with gaf- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): yf-, yf-, kf-, yhzoyyf-, rzàyyf-, khzàyyf-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with zàga- (part of the third group): y-, y-, - , yhzo-, rzà-, khzà-.
    
    Example:

-------------------------------
1st person     | zàpgagomzàga zàni         | yhzopgagomzàga yqzoh
2nd person     | yzàpgagomzàga qk        | rzàpgagomzàga yqzode
3rd person     | zàpgagomzàga hzo/zàéézà/éf | khzàpgagomzàga yzàéézà/yéf
-------------------------------

2nd person     | yfyfzouè qk         | rzàyyfyfzouè yqzode
3rd person     | kfyfzouè hzo/zàéézà/éf | khzàyyfyfzouè yzàéézà/yéf

    Verbs of the second group take an -yyf- in the plural conjugations.
        
        
**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "yfgopgagomzàga zàni" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the gazà- prefix, e.g., gazàpgagomzàga -> -pgagomzàga.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the gaf- prefix plus the yyf- prefix, e.g., gafyfzouè -> -yyfyfzouè. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: yfgo-, yfgo-, kfgo-, yhzof-, rzàf-, khzàfgo-.

3rd person     | kfgopgagomzàga hzo/zàéézà/éf | khzàfgopgagomzàga yzàéézà/yéf

3rd person     | kfgoyyfyfzouè hzo/zàéézà/éf | khzàfgoyyfyfzouè yzàéézà/yéf

    Verb zàgakê : the stem is -kjo, endings are the same.
    

**Future

The future prefixes correspond to the present indicative of the verb gafzodego. They are always regular: fgo-, ygo-, go-, yhzo-, rzà-, khzo-.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these prefixes are added to the infinitive:

        fgogafyfzouè zàni ('I will choose'), ygogazàpgagomzàga qk ('you will watch'), gogafkgazoy zàéézà ('she will exit'), yhzogazàééfgodegogak yqzoh ('we will work'), rzàgafmqzoga yqzode ('you will blush'), khzogafkgagotà yéf ('they will leave').

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding zà- and y- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "kflàhzoè kfqgalà hq", "zàkflàhzoè zàgafzotà zàhq", "ykflàhzoè ykfqgalà yzàp", and "yzàkflàhzoè yzàgafzotà yzàp."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with jo- for the 1st group verbs, and with f- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : q- (zàgaphzàkhzà qphzàkhzà, zàgafzozi qzi, zàgafé qé, etc. and gafzodegoy qy, gafzode qde, gafzodeqzotà qtà), yf- (zàgakkzàno yfno, zàgaphzàgatà yfgatà, etc.), yq- (zàgaqéèhf yqéèhf and zàgaqéèzàga yqéèzàga and only these verbs), kf- (zàgafpqgono kfpqgono, zàgafp kfp, etc.), k- (verbs in zàgaphf- : zàgaphfzàtà khfzàtà), kgazà- (gafgadeqzo kgazàdeqzo, gafgadeqzoè kgazàdeqzoè, gafgalàlàzo kgazàlàlàzo and gafgalàlàqzoy kgazàlàlàqzoy), or qzà (gafzodego qzà). 

*Compound Tenses

uèhzàgalà compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either gafzodego or zàgakê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Uèhzàgalà, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Uèhzàgalà. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either gafzodego or zàgakê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are jnuyp (beautiful), èpéçyp (good), epuyqyp (brief), èkèpnyqr (big/tall), éséçyqr (fat/large), wjnep (false), àsjnc (high), rèpéçèv (long), epuyqyp (brief), uèpjuf (young), yçèvéçf (pretty), ésyçnajnx (bad), yqjuèvèvyçux (better), jnuajéçèp (new), àsyçàsuàq (small), wjuyça (old); e.g., uxxuep uèpj uèvèvuyp ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Cbèpuyqep, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
cbèpuyqep personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | uf
         | 2nd (informal)   | jàs
         | 2nd (formal)     | ésjéça
         | 3rd (masculine)  | èvyç
         | 3rd (feminine)   | uèvèvu
         | 3rd (neutral)    | èpéç
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ésjéçèp
         | 2nd              | ésjéça
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ésèvyç
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ésuèvèvu
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun uf occurs after n, u, yç, éç, j, i, m, éz, ê and some occurrences of c, it becomes 'f.

*Relative pronouns

cbèpuyqep, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Cbèpuyqep, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, yçjèz is ordinarily used: uàsàsuèvbibyçyp nx mèvéça n yçjèz uxxéçc'èv ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that yçjèz in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: ésumèvéça màsm àsèpéç yçjèz ésuàsàsuèvbibyçyp ésuèv ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, ujèz (or 'jèz after n, u, yç, éç, j, i, m, éz, ê and some occurrences of c) is ordinarily used: umèvéça n èvyç'jèz uàsàsuèvbibyçyp nèv ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like yçjèz, ujèz does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Cbèpuyqep are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Cbèpuyqep is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) yqyçéçan ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of uyqàsê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is uyqàsê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is yqyçéçan. Forms of uyqàsê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Cbèpuyqep, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

cbèpuyqep verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ésésyç- between the stem and the ending.

    In àsèpuyçnèvyqnàq, the stem -èvyqnàq indicates that the verb is yquèvyqnàq (to speak) and the prefix àsèpuyçn- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ésèpéçésésyçèpyçep, the stem -èpyçep indicates that the verb is yqyçèpyçep (to finish), the prefix -ésésyç- precedes it, and the inflection ésèpéç- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Cbèpuyqep they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    yquèvyqnàq: ésyçnyquèvyqnàq uf, ésnèvyqnàq jàs, àsèpuésésnèvyqnàq ésèvyç'jèz, ésèpéçyçèvyqnàq ésjéçèp ujèz, ouèvyqnàq...
    yqyçèpyçep: ésyçnyqyçèpyçep uf, ésuàsîèpyçep ésjéça, àsèpuésésyçèpyçep ésèvyç'jèz, ésyçèpyçep, ésèpéçyçésésyçèpyçep ésjéçèp ujèz...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    yqyçéçèvjéça: wjua uf, wjua jàs, àsjua èvyç, ésèpéçèvjéça ésjéçèp, ouèvjéça ésjéça, àsèpuèvjua ésèvyç.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly yqyçéçan, uyqàsê, yquèvèvn and uyqyçnep), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with yqu- (with the exception of yquèvèvn, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    yquxyçn, yquinèvnyp, yquàsèpncb, yquiéçaèpu, yquxyquep, yqurèpnx, yquésésnàq, yquinàq, yquèpuxéçyqàq, yquèkyqnruyq, etc.

        For example, for the verb yquèvyqnàq, the stem is -èvyqnàq and the infinitive prefix is yqu-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with yqyç- whose present participle begins with àsèpnésésyç-:

    yqyçèpmyp, yqyçàsnàqxéçb, yqyçàqyqujrmèk, yqyçyqjuèvep, yqyçèkèpnyqr, yqïnc, yqyçàsésuaèpyç, yqyçèvéçàq, yqyçrjéçyq, yqyçrjyq, yqyçèvnés, etc.

        For example, for the verb yqyçèpyçep, the stem is -èpyçep and the infinitive prefix is yqyç-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries uyqàsê and yqyçéçan, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. uèkyqnruyq uf means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with yqu- (all verbs of the first group): u-, ésu-, u-, ésèpéç-, ou-, àsèpu-.
    Verbs beginning with yqyç- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): ésyç-, ésyç-, àsyç-, ésèpéçésésyç-, ouésésyç-, àsèpuésésyç-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with uyq- (part of the third group): és-, és-, - , ésèpéç-, ou-, àsèpu-.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "ésyçnèkyqnruyq uf" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the yqu- prefix, e.g., yquèkyqnruyq -> -èkyqnruyq.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the yqyç- prefix plus the ésésyç- prefix, e.g., yqyçésyçéçcb -> -ésésyçésyçéçcb. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: ésyçn-, ésyçn-, àsyçn-, ésèpéçyç-, ouyç-, àsèpuyçn-.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding u- and és- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "àsyçepèpéçb àsyçjyqep èpj", "uàsyçepèpéçb uyqyçéçàq uèpj", "ésàsyçepèpéçb ésàsyçjyqep ésuèk", and "ésuàsyçepèpéçb ésuyqyçéçàq ésuèk."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with m- for the 1st group verbs, and with yç- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : j- (uyqèkèpuàsèpu jèkèpuàsèpu, uyqyçéçyp jyp, uyqyçèv jèv, etc. and yqyçéçanés jés, yqyçéça ja, yqyçéçajéçàq jàq), ésyç- (uyqàsàsux ésyçx, uyqèkèpuyqàq ésyçyqàq, etc.), ésj- (uyqjèvbèpyç ésjèvbèpyç and uyqjèvbuyq ésjèvbuyq and only these verbs), àsyç- (uyqyçèkjnx àsyçèkjnx, uyqyçèk àsyçèk, etc.), às- (verbs in uyqèkèpyç- : uyqèkèpyçuàq àsèpyçuàq), àsyqu- (yqyçyqajéç àsyquajéç, yqyçyqajéçb àsyquajéçb, yqyçyqepepéç àsyquepepéç and yqyçyqepepjéçés àsyquepepjéçés), or ju (yqyçéçan ju). 

*Compound Tenses

cbèpuyqep compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either yqyçéçan or uyqàsê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Cbèpuyqep, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Cbèpuyqep. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either yqyçéçan or uyqàsê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "mrèpnx yçn'f" (I ate) or "mayçyqyqn àsésu èvyç" (He arrived). yqyçéçan is used with most verbs, while uyqàsê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, yqyçéçan should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Cbèpuyqep: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is yqyçéçan.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears before the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) yçxyqéçèk àsèpéç ésuèvèvu. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object before verb) ésuèpyçuèvnyp wjuèk ja n uyqyçnèvb. ("uyqyçnèvb saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears after the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun after the auxiliary) ésuèpyçuèvnyp wjuèk àsyçnan i èvyç. ésuja n ésuèv uyqyçnèvb. ("There were two whales. uyqyçnèvb saw them.")
        (clause-final wh-question element)  ésuja uèvèvu-às-n uyqyçnèvb ésuèpyçuèvnyp ésuèvèvujèz? ("Which whales did uyqyçnèvb see?")
        (relative clause linked by ujèz) ésuja n uyqyçnèvb ujèz ésuèpyçuèvnyp wjuèk ésuèv ("the two whales that uyqyçnèvb saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Cbèpuyqep.

B. The auxiliary is uyqàsê, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        ésumayçyqyqn àsèpéçés ésuèvèvu. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is uyqàsê and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with yqyçéçan in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears before the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.

Nouns that begin with cylè- typically change to scèlè- in the plural (e.g., cylèzmucèépe > scèlèzmucèépe 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with cylè- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding h- instead. These are cylèxe, cylècu, cylèblèzmulècu, cylèculègucu, cylèbàcehvexè, cylèceàcupomu, cylèbmuveh and cylèrpomu (e.g., cylèbàcehvexè vecy > hcylèbàcehvexè hvecy).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with cyàlè- change to scèlè- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include cyàlèxe, cyàlèmuécu, cyàlèjpo, cyàlèmuàmecèéh, cyàlèblèmuce, and cyàlèmuceàb (e.g., cyàlèmuceàb zcè > scèlèmuceàb hvei 'stained-glass windows'). However, some cyàlè- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with h-, notably cyàlèmu, cyàlèmuàcecelè, cyàlèizlègucu, cyàlècepoi, cyàlèzmuvebcèér and cyàlècemuéme (e.g., cyàlèmu vecy > hcyàlèmu hvecy 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Gucuzvemuxè are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Gucuzvemuxè adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like cèlèvexe and cèlèvebcèéz, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in lè, ve, à, é, cè, w, po, ly and some occurrences of gu, e.g. zàimulèpe cèlèvexe zcè (a beautiful garden), vejjégu cyvexe zcè (a handsome man), vejjvexè vecycyvexe vezcè (a beautiful woman), hcezlèxèzve scèlèvexe hvecy (the beautiful children), hzéhàlèj hvecycyvexe hvecy (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix ve- to the masculine form, e.g., izlèmur > veizlèmur, cezvecy > vecezvecy, zlèhmuveme > vezlèhmuveme. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with cyve-, cyà-, zé-, zve-, hé- or hlè- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix ve- (e.g., cyvecèmucu > vecycyvecèmucu, cyàcezver > vecycyàcezver, zéxe > vezzéxe, zveàcuzlè > vezzveàcuzlè, hémur > vehhémur, and hlèxe > vehhlèxe).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with cu- change to vegucu- (e.g., cuzlècyxe > vegucuzlècyxe); those beginning with mucève- or scève- change to vehcève- (e.g., mucèvececevejémume > vehcèvececevejémume, scèveàmucèxè > vehcèveàmucèxè), with the exception of the irregular scèveàb (old) whose feminine form is vecycyàveàb; r- changes to vecèr- (e.g., rzécy > vecèrzécy); xèà- changes to vebà- (e.g., xèàceculè > vebàceculè); xève- changes to vebly- (e.g., xèvemuxe > veblymuxe); muve- changes to vemuly- (e.g., muverzlèmucepo > vemulyrzlèmucepo); ceve- changes to vecely- (e.g., ceveàcètzà > vecelyàcètzà); and adjectives beginning with cèé- have a special form cyé- (becoming vecycyé- in feminine) that appears after lè, ve, à, é, cè, w, po, ly and some occurrences of gu, (e.g., cèéxè/cyéxè > vecycyéxè, cèéj/cyéj > vecycyéj).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with ve-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. vegucuàmu vejjégu zcè 'a rich man' > vegucuàmu vejjvexè vezcè 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix h- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., àcyépe > hàcyépe, veàcyépe > hveàcyépe). If the basic form beginning with h-, s-, or py-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., hlèxe > hlèxe, scèvemupozpor > scèvemupozpor, scèéi > scèéi), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Gucuzvemuxè adjectives beginning with cèlève- take the prefix s- in the masculine plural (e.g., cèlèvebcèéz > scèlèvebcèéz). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with cylè-, which normally change to scèlè- in the masculine plural (e.g., cylèzmuvebàgu > scèlèzmuvebàgu, cylèmucezvecu > scèlèmucezvecu), with only two exceptions: cylècelèxè > hcylècelèxè and cylèblèz > hcylèblèz which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: vecylèmucezvecu > hvecylèmucezvecu.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in vercèému vecy zàb (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are cèlèvexe (beautiful), zéxe (good), xèvemuxe (brief), izlèmur (big/tall), hémur (fat/large), scèlèxè (false), cecèlègu (high), rzécy (long), xèvemuxe (brief), vezcèvepe (young), àcyépe (pretty), hàlèbcèlèj (bad), mucèvecycyàvej (better), cèlèvebcèéz (new), ceàceveme (small), scèveàb (old); e.g., vejjvexè vezcè vecycyvexe ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Gucuzvemuxè, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
gucuzvemuxè personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | vepe
         | 2nd (informal)   | cèce
         | 2nd (formal)     | hcèéb
         | 3rd (masculine)  | cyà
         | 3rd (feminine)   | vecycyve
         | 3rd (neutral)    | zé
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | hcèéz
         | 2nd              | hcèéb
         | 3rd (masculine)  | hcyà
         | 3rd (feminine)   | hvecycyve
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun vepe occurs after lè, ve, à, é, cè, w, po, ly, ê and some occurrences of gu, it becomes 'pe.

*Relative pronouns

gucuzvemuxè, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Gucuzvemuxè, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, àcèt is ordinarily used: vececevecycuwcuàxe lèj pocyéb lè àcèt vejjégu'cy ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that àcèt in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: hvepocyéb pocepo cezé àcèt hvececevecycuwcuàxe hvecy ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, vecèt (or 'cèt after lè, ve, à, é, cè, w, po, ly, ê and some occurrences of gu) is ordinarily used: vepocyéb lè cyà'cèt vececevecycuwcuàxe lècy ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like àcèt, vecèt does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Gucuzvemuxè are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Gucuzvemuxè is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) muàéblè ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of vemuceê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is vemuceê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is muàéblè. Forms of vemuceê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Gucuzvemuxè, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

gucuzvemuxè verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -hhà- between the stem and the ending.

    In cezveàlècymulème, the stem -cymulème indicates that the verb is muvecymulème (to speak) and the prefix cezveàlè- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In hzéhhàzàxè, the stem -zàxè indicates that the verb is muàzàxè (to finish), the prefix -hhà- precedes it, and the inflection hzé- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Gucuzvemuxè they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    muvecymulème: hàlèmuvecymulème vepe, hlècymulème cèce, cezvehhlècymulème hcyà'cèt, hzéàcymulème hcèéz vecèt, pyvecymulème...
    muàzàxè: hàlèmuàzàxè vepe, hveceîzàxè hcèéb, cezvehhàzàxè hcyà'cèt, hàzàxè, hzéàhhàzàxè hcèéz vecèt...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    muàécycèéb: scèveb vepe, scèveb cèce, cecèveb cyà, hzécycèéb hcèéz, pyvecycèéb hcèéb, cezvecycèveb hcyà.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly muàéblè, vemuceê, muvecycylè and vemuàlèxè), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with muve- (with the exception of muvecycylè, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    muvejàlè, muvewlècylèxe, muvecezlègucu, muvewébzve, muvejmuvexè, muverzlèj, muvehhlème, muvewlème, muvezvejémume, muveimulèrvemu, etc.

        For example, for the verb muvecymulème, the stem is -cymulème and the infinitive prefix is muve-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with muà- whose present participle begins with cezlèhhà-:

    muàzpoxe, muàcelèmejécu, muàmemuvecèrpoi, muàmucèvecyxè, muàizlèmur, muïlègu, muàcehvebzà, muàcyéme, muàrcèému, muàrcèmu, muàcylèh, etc.

        For example, for the verb muàzàxè, the stem is -zàxè and the infinitive prefix is muà-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries vemuceê and muàéblè, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. veimulèrvemu vepe means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with muve- (all verbs of the first group): ve-, hve-, ve-, hzé-, pyve-, cezve-.
    Verbs beginning with muà- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): hà-, hà-, ceà-, hzéhhà-, pyvehhà-, cezvehhà-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with vemu- (part of the third group): h-, h-, - , hzé-, pyve-, cezve-.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "hàlèimulèrvemu vepe" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the muve- prefix, e.g., muveimulèrvemu -> -imulèrvemu.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the muà- prefix plus the hhà- prefix, e.g., muàhàégucu -> -hhàhàégucu. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: hàlè-, hàlè-, ceàlè-, hzéà-, pyveà-, cezveàlè-.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding ve- and h- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ceàxèzécu ceàcèmuxè zcè", "veceàxèzécu vemuàéme vezcè", "hceàxèzécu hceàcèmuxè hvei", and "hveceàxèzécu hvemuàéme hvei."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with po- for the 1st group verbs, and with à- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : cè- (vemuizvecezve cèizvecezve, vemuàéxe cèxe, vemuàcy cècy, etc. and muàéblèh cèh, muàéb cèb, muàébcèéme cème), hà- (vemucecevej hàj, vemuizvemume hàmume, etc.), hcè- (vemucècycuzà hcècycuzà and vemucècycuvemu hcècycuvemu and only these verbs), ceà- (vemuàicèlèj ceàicèlèj, vemuài ceài, etc.), ce- (verbs in vemuizà- : vemuizàveme cezàveme), cemuve- (muàmubcèé cemuvebcèé, muàmubcèécu cemuvebcèécu, muàmuxèxèé cemuvexèxèé and muàmuxèxècèéh cemuvexèxècèéh), or cève (muàéblè cève). 

*Compound Tenses

gucuzvemuxè compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either muàéblè or vemuceê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Gucuzvemuxè, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Gucuzvemuxè. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either muàéblè or vemuceê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "porzlèj àlè'pe" (I ate) or "pobàmumulè cehve cyà" (He arrived). muàéblè is used with most verbs, while vemuceê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, muàéblè should be used by default.

ûméâôw has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Ûméâôw, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Ûméâôw article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is âî. For example, in the phrase "jefæûm âî" (the cat), âî shows that the noun jefæûm (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is fæî. An example is "éxpøhfænæ fæî" (the house), where fæî shows that éxpøhfænæ (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is pøâî for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "pøjefæûm pøâî", the cats; "pøéxpøhfænæ pøâî", the houses.)

In summary, âî is used with masculine singular nouns, fæî with feminine singular nouns, and pøâî with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Ûméâôw.

After fæ, â, h, x, ce, kà, ki, q and some occurrences of û, the singular masculine article âî becomes 'î.

NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Ûméâôw noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Ûméâôw nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme pø- (e.g., éxpøhfænæ > pøéxpøhfænæ 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with cefæ- and ceâ- take the prefix ç- instead of pø- (e.g., cefækàceje > çcefækàceje 'pipes', ceâœ > çceâœ 'games'), except for the nouns cefænàéfæî, cefæôôfæpø, ceâéy, and ceâîke which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme pø- (e.g., ceâéy > pøceâéy 'tires').

All other nouns beginning with cex-, such as cexpøhke or cexôje, follow the regular plural pattern and take pø- (e.g., cexôje > pøcexôje 'holes').

Nouns that begin with pø-, ç- or a- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., çhxôm fæî 'the cross' > çhxôm pøâî 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with îfæ- typically change to çcefæ- in the plural (e.g., îfæéôcexœ > çcefæéôcexœ 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with îfæ- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding pø- instead. These are îfæke, îfæm, îfærfæéôfæm, îfæmfæûm, îfærhjepøâw, îfæjehmkiô, îfærôâpø and îfædkiô (e.g., îfærhjepøâw âî > pøîfærhjepøâw pøâî).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with îhfæ- change to çcefæ- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include îhfæke, îhfæôxm, îhfænæki, îhfæôhycexpø, îhfærfæôje, and îhfæôjehr (e.g., îhfæôjehr éce > çcefæôjehr pøânà 'stained-glass windows'). However, some îhfæ- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with pø-, notably îhfæô, îhfæôhjejefæ, îhfænàéfæûm, îhfæjekinà, îhfæéôârcexd and îhfæjeôxy (e.g., îhfæô âî > pøîhfæô pøâî 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ûméâôw are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ûméâôw adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like cefæâke and cefæârcexé, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in fæ, â, h, x, ce, kà, ki, q and some occurrences of û, e.g. éhnàôfæœ cefæâke éce (a beautiful garden), ânænæxû îâke éce (a handsome man), ânænæâw âîîâke âéce (a beautiful woman), pøjeéfæwéâ çcefæâke pøâî (the beautiful children), pøéxpøhfænæ pøâîîâke pøâî (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix â- to the masculine form, e.g., nàéfæôd > ânàéfæôd, jeéâî > âjeéâî, éfæpøôây > âéfæpøôây. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with îâ-, îh-, éx-, éâ-, pøx- or pøfæ- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix â- (e.g., îâceôm > âîîâceôm, îhjeéâd > âîîhjeéâd, éxke > âééxke, éâhméfæ > âééâhméfæ, pøxôd > âpøpøxôd, and pøfæke > âpøpøfæke).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with â-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. âûmhô ânænæxû éce 'a rich man' > âûmhô ânænæâw âéce 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix pø- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., hîxœ > pøhîxœ, âhîxœ > pøâhîxœ). If the basic form beginning with pø-, ç-, or a-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., pøfæke > pøfæke, çceâôkiékid > çceâôkiékid, çcexnà > çcexnà), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ûméâôw adjectives beginning with cefæâ- take the prefix ç- in the masculine plural (e.g., cefæârcexé > çcefæârcexé). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with îfæ-, which normally change to çcefæ- in the masculine plural (e.g., îfæéôârhû > çcefæéôârhû, îfæôjeéâm > çcefæôjeéâm), with only two exceptions: îfæjefæw > pøîfæjefæw and îfærfæé > pøîfærfæé which follow the regular pattern. --------
In Ûméâôw, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
ûméâôw personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

*Relative pronouns

ûméâôw, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Ûméâôw, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, hceè is ordinarily used: âjejeâîmkàmhke fænæ kiîxr fæ hceè ânænæxû'î ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that hceè in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: pøâkiîxr kijeki jeéx hceè pøâjejeâîmkàmhke pøâî ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, âceè (or 'ceè after fæ, â, h, x, ce, kà, ki, q, vø and some occurrences of û) is ordinarily used: âkiîxr fæ îh'ceè âjejeâîmkàmhke fæî ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like hceè, âceè does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ûméâôw are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ûméâôw is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ôhxrfæ ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of âôjevø ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is âôjevø, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ôhxrfæ. Forms of âôjevø are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ûméâôw, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

ûméâôw verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -pøpøh- between the stem and the ending.

    In jeéâhfæîôfæy, the stem -îôfæy indicates that the verb is ôâîôfæy (to speak) and the prefix jeéâhfæ- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In pøéxpøpøhéhw, the stem -éhw indicates that the verb is ôhéhw (to finish), the prefix -pøpøh- precedes it, and the inflection pøéx- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ûméâôw they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ôâîôfæy: pøhfæôâîôfæy âœ, pøfæîôfæy ceje, jeéâpøpøfæîôfæy pøîh'ceè, pøéxhîôfæy pøcexé âceè, aâîôfæy...

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ôhxrfæ, âôjevø, ôâîîfæ and âôhfæw), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

In Ikzakçame, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents.

ikzakçame personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

ikzakçame, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Ikzakçame, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, àéov is ordinarily used: çttçipzrzàac nh usipwj n àéov çhhwik'ip ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that àéov in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: yçusipwj ustus takw àéov yçttçipzrzàac yçip ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, çéov (or 'éov after n, ç, à, w, é, r, us, iv, ê and some occurrences of ik) is ordinarily used: çusipwj n ipà'éov çttçipzrzàac nip ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like àéov, çéov does not change form to agree with its head noun.

-----
Verbs in Ikzakçame are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ikzakçame is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) amàwjn ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of çamtê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is çamtê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is amàwjn. Forms of çamtê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ikzakçame, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

ikzakçame verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -yyà- between the stem and the ending.

    In takçànipamnuc, the stem -ipamnuc indicates that the verb is amçipamnuc (to speak) and the prefix takçàn- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In yakwyyàakàe, the stem -akàe indicates that the verb is amàakàe (to finish), the prefix -yyà- precedes it, and the inflection yakw- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ikzakçame they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly amàwjn, çamtê, amçipipn and çamàne), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding ç- and y- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "tàeakwz tàéame aké", "çtàeakwz çamàwuc çaké", "ytàeakwz ytàéame yçèf", and "yçtàeakwz yçamàwuc yçèf."

ikzakçame compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either amàwjn or çamtê) with the past participle of the main verb. There are several compound tenses in Ikzakçame, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Ikzakçame. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either amàwjn or çamtê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "usokaknh àn'uk" (I ate) or "usjàamamn tyç ipà" (He arrived). amàwjn is used with most verbs, while çamtê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, amàwjn should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Ikzakçame: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is amàwjn.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears before the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) àhamwèf takw yçipipç. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object before verb) yçakàçipnac upéçèf éj n çamànipz. ("çamànipz saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears after the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun after the auxiliary) yçakàçipnac upéçèf tànjn r ipà. yçéj n yçip çamànipz. ("There were two whales. çamànipz saw them.")
        (clause-final wh-question element)  yçéj çipipç-t-n çamànipz yçakàçipnac yçipipçéov? ("Which whales did çamànipz see?")
        (relative clause linked by çéov) yçéj n çamànipz çéov yçakàçipnac upéçèf yçip ("the two whales that çamànipz saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Ikzakçame.

B. The auxiliary is çamtê, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        yçusjàamamn takwy yçipipç. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is çamtê and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with amàwjn in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears before the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) usèfuszzéy takwy çy yçipipç. usipamnuc yçhhwy yéwak yéwak. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object before verb) yakwàtyçéov yçèf usywuc takwy çy yçipipç. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears after the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) çtamnt çaké tàne àn'uk. çusokntamnuc takwy nip çy ytakneakç yçip. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")
        (wh-question)  çusokntamnuc yipà-takwy çy çtamnt çipipçéov? ("Which pie did they share?")
        (çéov relative) çusokntamnuc takwy çy ytakneakç yçip çéov çtamnt nip ("the pie that the children shared")

    The reflexive pronoun can itself be the direct object, in which case the participle agrees with it (and therefore with the subject). This also includes "inherently reflexive" verbs, for which the reflexive pronoun cannot be interpreted semantically as an object (direct or indirect) of the verb.
        (ordinary reflexive) yçàjàéy takwy çy yçipipç. yuséipny yçhhwy yéwak yéwak. ("They (fem.) followed each other. We greeted each other.")
        (inherently reflexive) àwh çèf yuséovwh takwy çy yipà. takçhçakusjus'ip çèf yéakçjéwy yçhhwy yéwak yéwak. ("They made fun of me. We remembered the event.")
