Nouns that begin with dég- typically change to byjg- in the plural (e.g., dégkcéjpf > byjgkcéjpf 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with dég- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding bé- instead. These are dégda, dégbe, dégsgkcégbe, dégbegèbe, dégswaxébéàdy, dégxéwabecocé, dégscéàbé and dégçococé (e.g., dégswaxébéàdy àdé > bédégswaxébéàdy béàdé).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with déwag- change to byjg- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include déwagda, déwagcépbe, déwagico, déwagcéwahjpbé, déwagsgcéxé, and déwagcéxéwas (e.g., déwagcéxéwas kj > byjgcéxéwas béàxa 'stained-glass windows'). However, some déwag- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with bé-, notably déwagcé, déwagcéwaxéxég, déwagxakgèbe, déwagxécoxa, déwagkcéàsjpço and déwagxécéph (e.g., déwagcé àdé > bédéwagcé béàdé 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Èbekàcédy are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Èbekàcédy adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like jgàda and jgàsjpk, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in g, à, wa, p, j, n, co, vo and some occurrences of è, e.g. kwaxacégf jgàda kj (a beautiful garden), àiipè déàda kj (a handsome man), àiiàdy àdédéàda àkj (a beautiful woman), béxékgdykà byjgàda béàdé (the beautiful children), békpbéwagi béàdédéàda béàdé (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix à- to the masculine form, e.g., xakgcéço > àxakgcéço, xékàdé > àxékàdé, kgbécéàh > àkgbécéàh. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with déà-, déwa-, kp-, kà-, bép- or bég- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix à- (e.g., déàjcébe > àdédéàjcébe, déwaxékàço > àdédéwaxékàço, kpda > àkkpda, kàwabekg > àkkàwabekg, bépcéço > àbébépcéço, and bégda > àbébégda).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with be- change to àèbe- (e.g., bekgdéda > àèbekgdéda); those beginning with céjà- or byjà- change to àbéjà- (e.g., céjàxéxéàipcéh > àbéjàxéxéàipcéh, byjàwacéjdy > àbéjàwacéjdy), with the exception of the irregular byjàwas (old) whose feminine form is àdédéwaàwas; ço- changes to àjço- (e.g., çokpdé > àjçokpdé); dywa- changes to àswa- (e.g., dywaxébeg > àswaxébeg); dyà- changes to àsvo- (e.g., dyàcéda > àsvocéda); céà- changes to àcévo- (e.g., céàçokgcéxéco > àcévoçokgcéxéco); xéà- changes to àxévo- (e.g., xéàwajlkwa > àxévowajlkwa); and adjectives beginning with jp- have a special form dép- (becoming àdédép- in feminine) that appears after g, à, wa, p, j, n, co, vo and some occurrences of è, (e.g., jpdy/dépdy > àdédépdy, jpi/dépi > àdédépi).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with à-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. àèbewacé àiipè kj 'a rich man' > àèbewacé àiiàdy àkj 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix bé- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., wadépf > béwadépf, àwadépf > béàwadépf). If the basic form beginning with bé-, by-, or u-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., bégda > bégda, byjàcécokcoço > byjàcécokcoço, byjpxa > byjpxa), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Èbekàcédy adjectives beginning with jgà- take the prefix by- in the masculine plural (e.g., jgàsjpk > byjgàsjpk). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with dég-, which normally change to byjg- in the masculine plural (e.g., dégkcéàswaè > byjgkcéàswaè, dégcéxékàbe > byjgcéxékàbe), with only two exceptions: dégxégdy > bédégxégdy and dégsgk > bédégsgk which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: àdégcéxékàbe > béàdégcéxékàbe.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in àçojpcé àdé kwas (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are jgàda (beautiful), kpda (good), dyàcéda (brief), xakgcéço (big/tall), bépcéço (fat/large), byjgdy (false), xéjgè (high), çokpdé (long), dyàcéda (brief), àkjàf (young), wadépf (pretty), béwagsjgi (bad), céjàdédéwaài (better), jgàsjpk (new), xéwaxéàh (small), byjàwas (old); e.g., àiiàdy àkj àdédéàda ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Èbekàcédy, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
èbekàcédy personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | àf
         | 2nd (informal)   | jxé
         | 2nd (formal)     | béjps
         | 3rd (masculine)  | déwa
         | 3rd (feminine)   | àdédéà
         | 3rd (neutral)    | kp
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | béjpk
         | 2nd              | béjps
         | 3rd (masculine)  | bédéwa
         | 3rd (feminine)   | béàdédéà
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun àf occurs after g, à, wa, p, j, n, co, vo, ê and some occurrences of è, it becomes 'f.

*Relative pronouns

èbekàcédy, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Èbekàcédy, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, wajl is ordinarily used: àxéxéàdébenbewada gi codéps g wajl àiipè'dé ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that wajl in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: béàcodéps coxéco xékp wajl béàxéxéàdébenbewada béàdé ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, àjl (or 'jl after g, à, wa, p, j, n, co, vo, ê and some occurrences of è) is ordinarily used: àcodéps g déwa'jl àxéxéàdébenbewada gdé ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like wajl, àjl does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Èbekàcédy are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Èbekàcédy is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) céwapsg ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of àcéxéê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is àcéxéê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is céwapsg. Forms of àcéxéê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Èbekàcédy, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

èbekàcédy verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -bébéwa- between the stem and the ending.

    In xékàwagdécégh, the stem -décégh indicates that the verb is céàdécégh (to speak) and the prefix xékàwag- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In békpbébéwakwady, the stem -kwady indicates that the verb is céwakwady (to finish), the prefix -bébéwa- precedes it, and the inflection békp- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Èbekàcédy they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    céàdécégh: béwagcéàdécégh àf, bégdécégh jxé, xékàbébégdécégh bédéwa'jl, békpwadécégh béjpk àjl, uàdécégh...
    céwakwady: béwagcéwakwady àf, béàxéîkwady béjps, xékàbébéwakwady bédéwa'jl, béwakwady, békpwabébéwakwady béjpk àjl...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    céwapdéjps: byjàs àf, byjàs jxé, xéjàs déwa, békpdéjps béjpk, uàdéjps béjps, xékàdéjàs bédéwa.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly céwapsg, àcéxéê, céàdédég and àcéwagdy), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with céà- (with the exception of céàdédég, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    céàiwag, céàngdégda, céàxékgèbe, céànpskà, céàicéàdy, céàçokgi, céàbébégh, céàngh, céàkàipcéh, céàxacégçoàcé, etc.

        For example, for the verb céàdécégh, the stem is -décégh and the infinitive prefix is céà-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with céwa- whose present participle begins with xékgbébéwa-:

    céwakcoda, céwaxéghipbe, céwahcéàjçocoxa, céwacéjàdédy, céwaxakgcéço, céïgè, céwaxébéàskwa, céwadéph, céwaçojpcé, céwaçojcé, céwadégbé, etc.

        For example, for the verb céwakwady, the stem is -kwady and the infinitive prefix is céwa-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries àcéxéê and céwapsg, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. àxacégçoàcé àf means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with céà- (all verbs of the first group): à-, béà-, à-, békp-, uà-, xékà-.
    Verbs beginning with céwa- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): béwa-, béwa-, xéwa-, békpbébéwa-, uàbébéwa-, xékàbébéwa-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with àcé- (part of the third group): bé-, bé-, - , békp-, uà-, xékà-.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "béwagxacégçoàcé àf" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: béwag-, béwag-, xéwag-, békpwa-, uàwa-, xékàwag-.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding à- and bé- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "xéwadykpbe xéwajcédy kj", "àxéwadykpbe àcéwaph àkj", "béxéwadykpbe béxéwajcédy béàxa", and "béàxéwadykpbe béàcéwaph béàxa."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with co- for the 1st group verbs, and with wa- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : j- (àcéxakàxékà jxakàxékà, àcéwapda jda, àcéwadé jdé, etc. and céwapsgbé jbé, céwaps js, céwapsjph jh), béwa- (àcéxéxéài béwai, àcéxakàcéh béwacéh, etc.), béj- (àcéjdébekwa béjdébekwa and àcéjdébeàcé béjdébeàcé and only these verbs), xéwa- (àcéwaxajgi xéwaxajgi, àcéwaxa xéwaxa, etc.), xé- (verbs in àcéxakwa- : àcéxakwaàh xékwaàh), xécéà- (céwacésjp xécéàsjp, céwacésjpbe xécéàsjpbe, céwacédydyp xécéàdydyp and céwacédydyjpbé xécéàdydyjpbé), or jà (céwapsg jà). 

*Compound Tenses

èbekàcédy compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either céwapsg or àcéxéê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Èbekàcédy, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Èbekàcédy. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either céwapsg or àcéxéê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "coçokgi wag'f" (I ate) or "coswacécég xébéà déwa" (He arrived). céwapsg is used with most verbs, while àcéxéê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, céwapsg should be used by default.

-------------------------------

2nd person     | coxacégçoàcé bég jxé              | coxacégçoàcé uàsg béjps

Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with owq-, which normally change to uèjq- in the masculine plural (e.g., owqçxotydodèg > uèjqçxotydodèg, owqxizçotèf > uèjqxizçotèf), with only two exceptions: owqizqil > ytowqizqil and owqydqç > ytowqydqç which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: otowqxizçotèf > ytotowqxizçotèf.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in otyfèjojx otow çodyd (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are èjqots (beautiful), çojs (good), ilotxs (brief), eçqxyf (big/tall), ytojxyf (fat/large), uèjqil (false), izèjqèg (high), yfçojow (long), ilotxs (brief), otçèjotyl (young), odowojyl (pretty), ytodqydèjqn (bad), xèjotowowodotn (better), èjqotydèjojç (new), izodizotiw (small), uèjotodyd (old); e.g., otnnotil otçèj otowowots ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ègèfçotxil, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
ègèfçotxil personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | otyl
         | 2nd (informal)   | èjiz
         | 2nd (formal)     | ytèjojyd
         | 3rd (masculine)  | owod
         | 3rd (feminine)   | otowowot
         | 3rd (neutral)    | çoj
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ytèjojç
         | 2nd              | ytèjojyd
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ytowod
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ytotowowot
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun otyl occurs after q, ot, od, oj, èj, it, ag, m, ê and some occurrences of èg, it becomes 'yl.

*Relative pronouns

ègèfçotxil, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Ègèfçotxil, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, odèjé is ordinarily used: otizizotowèfitèfods qn agowojyd q odèjé otnnojèg'ow ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that odèjé in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: ytotagowojyd agizag izçoj odèjé ytotizizotowèfitèfods ytotow ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, otèjé (or 'èjé after q, ot, od, oj, èj, it, ag, m, ê and some occurrences of èg) is ordinarily used: otagowojyd q owod'èjé otizizotowèfitèfods qow ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like odèjé, otèjé does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ègèfçotxil are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ègèfçotxil is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) xodojydq ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of otxizê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is otxizê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is xodojydq. Forms of otxizê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ègèfçotxil, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

ègèfçotxil verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ytytod- between the stem and the ending.

    In izçotodqowxqiw, the stem -owxqiw indicates that the verb is xotowxqiw (to speak) and the prefix izçotodq- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ytçojytytodçodil, the stem -çodil indicates that the verb is xodçodil (to finish), the prefix -ytytod- precedes it, and the inflection ytçoj- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ègèfçotxil they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    xotowxqiw: ytodqxotowxqiw otyl, ytqowxqiw èjiz, izçotytytqowxqiw ytowod'èjé, ytçojodowxqiw ytèjojç otèjé, ikotowxqiw...
    xodçodil: ytodqxodçodil otyl, ytotizîçodil ytèjojyd, izçotytytodçodil ytowod'èjé, ytodçodil, ytçojodytytodçodil ytèjojç otèjé...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    xodojowèjojyd: uèjotyd otyl, uèjotyd èjiz, izèjotyd owod, ytçojowèjojyd ytèjojç, ikotowèjojyd ytèjojyd, izçotowèjotyd ytowod.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly xodojydq, otxizê, xotowowq and otxodqil), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with xot- (with the exception of xotowowq, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    xotnodq, xotitqowqs, xotizçqègèf, xotitojydçot, xotnxotil, xotyfçqn, xotytytqiw, xotitqiw, xotçotnojxiw, xotexqyfotx, etc.

        For example, for the verb xotowxqiw, the stem is -owxqiw and the infinitive prefix is xot-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with xod- whose present participle begins with izçqytytod-:

    xodçags, xodizqiwnojèf, xodiwxotèjyfage, xodxèjotowil, xodeçqxyf, xïqèg, xodizytotydçod, xodowojiw, xodyfèjojx, xodyfèjx, xodowqyt, etc.

        For example, for the verb xodçodil, the stem is -çodil and the infinitive prefix is xod-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries otxizê and xodojydq, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. otexqyfotx otyl means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with xot- (all verbs of the first group): ot-, ytot-, ot-, ytçoj-, ikot-, izçot-.
    Verbs beginning with xod- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): ytod-, ytod-, izod-, ytçojytytod-, ikotytytod-, izçotytytod-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with otx- (part of the third group): yt-, yt-, - , ytçoj-, ikot-, izçot-.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "ytodqexqyfotx otyl" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the xot- prefix, e.g., xotexqyfotx -> -exqyfotx.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the xod- prefix plus the ytytod- prefix, e.g., xodytodojègèf -> -ytytodytodojègèf. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: ytodq-, ytodq-, izodq-, ytçojod-, ikotod-, izçotodq-.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding ot- and yt- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "izodilçojèf izodèjxil çèj", "otizodilçojèf otxodojiw otçèj", "ytizodilçojèf ytizodèjxil ytote", and "ytotizodilçojèf ytotxodojiw ytote."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with ag- for the 1st group verbs, and with od- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : èj- (otxeçotizçot èjeçotizçot, otxodojs èjs, otxodow èjow, etc. and xodojydqyt èjyt, xodojyd èjyd, xodojydèjojiw èjiw), ytod- (otxizizotn ytodn, otxeçotxiw ytodxiw, etc.), ytèj- (otxèjowèfçod ytèjowèfçod and otxèjowèfotx ytèjowèfotx and only these verbs), izod- (otxodeèjqn izodeèjqn, otxode izode, etc.), iz- (verbs in otxeçod- : otxeçodotiw izçodotiw), izxot- (xodxydèjoj izxotydèjoj, xodxydèjojèf izxotydèjojèf, xodxililoj izxotililoj and xodxililèjojyt izxotililèjojyt), or èjot (xodojydq èjot). 

*Compound Tenses

ègèfçotxil compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either xodojydq or otxizê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Ègèfçotxil, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Ègèfçotxil. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either xodojydq or otxizê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "agyfçqn odq'yl" (I ate) or "agydodxxq izytot owod" (He arrived). xodojydq is used with most verbs, while otxizê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, xodojydq should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Ègèfçotxil: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is xodojydq.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears before the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) odnxoje izçoj ytotowowot. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object before verb) ytotçodotowqs uèjote èjyd q otxodqowèf. ("otxodqowèf saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears after the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun after the auxiliary) ytotçodotowqs uèjote izodqydq it owod. ytotèjyd q ytotow otxodqowèf. ("There were two whales. otxodqowèf saw them.")
        (clause-final wh-question element)  ytotèjyd otowowot-iz-q otxodqowèf ytotçodotowqs ytotowowotèjé? ("Which whales did otxodqowèf see?")
        (relative clause linked by otèjé) ytotèjyd q otxodqowèf otèjé ytotçodotowqs uèjote ytotow ("the two whales that otxodqowèf saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Ègèfçotxil.

B. The auxiliary is otxizê, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        ytotagydodxxq izçojyt ytotowowot. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is otxizê and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with xodojydq in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears before the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) ageagèfèfèjyt izçojyt otyt ytotowowot. agowxqiw ytotnnojyt ytèjojç ytèjojç. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object before verb) ytçojodizytotèjé ytote agytojiw izçojyt otyt ytotowowot. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears after the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

- The article is odaçl for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "odsuçeriw odaçl", the cats; "odqvodmuçn odaçl", the houses.)

In summary, açl is used with masculine singular nouns, uçl with feminine singular nouns, and odaçl with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Eriwqaçuweb.

After uç, aç, m, v, è, ez, y, ef and some occurrences of er, the singular masculine article açl becomes 'l.


-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Eriwqaçuweb noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Eriwqaçuweb nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme od- (e.g., qvodmuçn > odqvodmuçn 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with èuç- and èaç- take the prefix g- instead of od- (e.g., èuçezès > gèuçezès 'pipes', èaçà > gèaçà 'games'), except for the nouns èuçéquçl, èuçuwuwuçod, èaçqp, and èaçlj which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme od- (e.g., èaçqp > odèaçqp 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with èv- form their plural with g-. These are èvqaçuh, èvllmuçiw, èvjmer, èvàmj, èvp, èveriw, and èvàèvà (e.g., èvqaçuh > gèvqaçuh 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with èv-, such as èvodmj or èvuws, follow the regular plural pattern and take od- (e.g., èvuws > odèvuws 'holes').

Nouns that begin with od-, g- or t- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., gmvuwiw uçl 'the cross' > gmvuwiw odaçl 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with luç- typically change to gèuç- in the plural (e.g., luçquwèvà > gèuçquwèvà 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with luç- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding od- instead. These are luçj, luçiw, luçxuçquwuçiw, luçiwuçeriw, luçxmsodaçeb, luçsmiwyuw, luçxuwaçod and luçuhyuw (e.g., luçxmsodaçeb açl > odluçxmsodaçeb odaçl).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with lmuç- change to gèuç- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include lmuçj, lmuçuwviw, lmuçny, lmuçuwmpèvod, lmuçxuçuws, and lmuçuwsmx (e.g., lmuçuwsmx qè > gèuçuwsmx odaçé 'stained-glass windows'). However, some lmuç- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with od-, notably lmuçuw, lmuçuwmssuç, lmuçéquçeriw, lmuçsyé, lmuçquwaçxèvuh and lmuçsuwvp (e.g., lmuçuw açl > odlmuçuw odaçl 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Eriwqaçuweb are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Eriwqaçuweb adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like èuçaçj and èuçaçxèvq, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in uç, aç, m, v, è, ez, y, ef and some occurrences of er, e.g. qméuwuçà èuçaçj qè (a beautiful garden), açnnver laçj qè (a handsome man), açnnaçeb açllaçj açqè (a beautiful woman), odsquçebqaç gèuçaçj odaçl (the beautiful children), odqvodmuçn odaçllaçj odaçl (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix aç- to the masculine form, e.g., équçuwuh > açéquçuwuh, sqaçl > açsqaçl, quçoduwaçp > açquçoduwaçp. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with laç-, lm-, qv-, qaç-, odv- or oduç- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix aç- (e.g., laçèuwiw > açllaçèuwiw, lmsqaçuh > açllmsqaçuh, qvj > açqqvj, qaçmiwquç > açqqaçmiwquç, odvuwuh > açododvuwuh, and oduçj > açododuçj).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with iw- change to açeriw- (e.g., iwquçlj > açeriwquçlj); those beginning with uwèaç- or gèaç- change to açodèaç- (e.g., uwèaçssaçnvuwp > açodèaçssaçnvuwp, gèaçmuwèeb > açodèaçmuwèeb), with the exception of the irregular gèaçmx (old) whose feminine form is açllmaçmx; uh- changes to açèuh- (e.g., uhqvl > açèuhqvl); ebm- changes to açxm- (e.g., ebmsiwuç > açxmsiwuç); ebaç- changes to açxef- (e.g., ebaçuwj > açxefuwj); uwaç- changes to açuwef- (e.g., uwaçuhquçuwsy > açuwefuhquçuwsy); saç- changes to açsef- (e.g., saçmèoçqm > açsefmèoçqm); and adjectives beginning with èv- have a special form lv- (becoming açllv- in feminine) that appears after uç, aç, m, v, è, ez, y, ef and some occurrences of er, (e.g., èveb/lveb > açllveb, èvn/lvn > açllvn).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with aç-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. açeriwmuw açnnver qè 'a rich man' > açeriwmuw açnnaçeb açqè 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix od- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., mlvà > odmlvà, açmlvà > odaçmlvà). If the basic form beginning with od-, g-, or t-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., oduçj > oduçj, gèaçuwyqyuh > gèaçuwyqyuh, gèvé > gèvé), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Eriwqaçuweb adjectives beginning with èuçaç- take the prefix g- in the masculine plural (e.g., èuçaçxèvq > gèuçaçxèvq). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with luç-, which normally change to gèuç- in the masculine plural (e.g., luçquwaçxmer > gèuçquwaçxmer, luçuwsqaçiw > gèuçuwsqaçiw), with only two exceptions: luçsuçeb > odluçsuçeb and luçxuçq > odluçxuçq which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: açluçuwsqaçiw > odaçluçuwsqaçiw.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in açuhèvuw açl qmx (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are èuçaçj (beautiful), qvj (good), ebaçuwj (brief), équçuwuh (big/tall), odvuwuh (fat/large), gèuçeb (false), sèuçer (high), uhqvl (long), ebaçuwj (brief), açqèaçà (young), mlvà (pretty), odmuçxèuçn (bad), uwèaçllmaçn (better), èuçaçxèvq (new), smsaçp (small), gèaçmx (old); e.g., açnnaçeb açqè açllaçj ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Eriwqaçuweb, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
eriwqaçuweb personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | açà
         | 2nd (informal)   | ès
         | 2nd (formal)     | odèvx
         | 3rd (masculine)  | lm
         | 3rd (feminine)   | açllaç
         | 3rd (neutral)    | qv
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | odèvq
         | 2nd              | odèvx
         | 3rd (masculine)  | odlm
         | 3rd (feminine)   | odaçllaç
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun açà occurs after uç, aç, m, v, è, ez, y, ef, ê and some occurrences of er, it becomes 'à.

*Relative pronouns

eriwqaçuweb, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Eriwqaçuweb, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, mèoç is ordinarily used: açssaçliweziwmj uçn ylvx uç mèoç açnnver'l ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that mèoç in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: odaçylvx ysy sqv mèoç odaçssaçliweziwmj odaçl ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, açèoç (or 'èoç after uç, aç, m, v, è, ez, y, ef, ê and some occurrences of er) is ordinarily used: açylvx uç lm'èoç açssaçliweziwmj uçl ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like mèoç, açèoç does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Eriwqaçuweb are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Eriwqaçuweb is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) uwmvxuç ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of açuwsê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is açuwsê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is uwmvxuç. Forms of açuwsê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Eriwqaçuweb, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

eriwqaçuweb verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ododm- between the stem and the ending.

    In sqaçmuçluwuçp, the stem -luwuçp indicates that the verb is uwaçluwuçp (to speak) and the prefix sqaçmuç- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In odqvododmqmeb, the stem -qmeb indicates that the verb is uwmqmeb (to finish), the prefix -ododm- precedes it, and the inflection odqv- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Eriwqaçuweb they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    uwaçluwuçp: odmuçuwaçluwuçp açà, oduçluwuçp ès, sqaçododuçluwuçp odlm'èoç, odqvmluwuçp odèvq açèoç, taçluwuçp...
    uwmqmeb: odmuçuwmqmeb açà, odaçsîqmeb odèvx, sqaçododmqmeb odlm'èoç, odmqmeb, odqvmododmqmeb odèvq açèoç...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    uwmvlèvx: gèaçx açà, gèaçx ès, sèaçx lm, odqvlèvx odèvq, taçlèvx odèvx, sqaçlèaçx odlm.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly uwmvxuç, açuwsê, uwaçlluç and açuwmuçeb), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with uwaç- (with the exception of uwaçlluç, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    uwaçnmuç, uwaçezuçluçj, uwaçsquçeriw, uwaçezvxqaç, uwaçnuwaçeb, uwaçuhquçn, uwaçododuçp, uwaçezuçp, uwaçqaçnvuwp, uwaçéuwuçuhaçuw, etc.

        For example, for the verb uwaçluwuçp, the stem is -luwuçp and the infinitive prefix is uwaç-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with uwm- whose present participle begins with squçododm-:

    uwmqyj, uwmsuçpnviw, uwmpuwaçèuhyé, uwmuwèaçleb, uwméquçuwuh, uwïuçer, uwmsodaçxqm, uwmlvp, uwmuhèvuw, uwmuhèuw, uwmluçod, etc.

        For example, for the verb uwmqmeb, the stem is -qmeb and the infinitive prefix is uwm-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries açuwsê and uwmvxuç, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. açéuwuçuhaçuw açà means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with uwaç- (all verbs of the first group): aç-, odaç-, aç-, odqv-, taç-, sqaç-.
    Verbs beginning with uwm- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): odm-, odm-, sm-, odqvododm-, taçododm-, sqaçododm-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with açuw- (part of the third group): od-, od-, - , odqv-, taç-, sqaç-.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "odmuçéuwuçuhaçuw açà" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the uwaç- prefix, e.g., uwaçéuwuçuhaçuw -> -éuwuçuhaçuw.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the uwm- prefix plus the ododm- prefix, e.g., uwmodmveriw -> -ododmodmveriw. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: odmuç-, odmuç-, smuç-, odqvm-, taçm-, sqaçmuç-.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding aç- and od- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "smebqviw smèuweb qè", "açsmebqviw açuwmvp açqè", "odsmebqviw odsmèuweb odaçé", and "odaçsmebqviw odaçuwmvp odaçé."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with y- for the 1st group verbs, and with m- for the 2nd group verbs. If the basic form beginning with ê-, e-, or èp-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., êôrôl > êôrôl, eæqîcæñôñæñd > eæqîcæñôñæñd, eæqàbç > eæqàbç), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Âèbôñîcz adjectives beginning with æqôrî- take the prefix e- in the masculine plural (e.g., æqôrîàwæqàbôñ > eæqôrîàwæqàbôñ). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with àñôr-, which normally change to eæqôr- in the masculine plural (e.g., àñôrôñcîàwægâ > eæqôrôñcîàwægâ, àñôrcþôñîèb > eæqôrcþôñîèb), with only two exceptions: àñôrþôrz > êàñôrþôrz and àñôràwôrôñ > êàñôràwôrôñ which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: îàñôrcþôñîèb > êîàñôrcþôñîèb.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in îdæqàbc îàñ ôñægàw (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are æqôrîôl (beautiful), ôñàbôl (good), zîcôl (brief), çôñôrcd (big/tall), êàbcd (fat/large), eæqôrz (false), þæqôrâ (high), dôñàbàñ (long), zîcôl (brief), îôñæqîèl (young), ægàñàbèl (pretty), êægôràwæqôri (bad), cæqîàñàñægîi (better), æqôrîàwæqàbôñ (new), þægþîx (small), eæqîægàw (old); e.g., îiiîz îôñæq îàñàñîôl ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Âèbôñîcz, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
âèbôñîcz personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | îèl
         | 2nd (informal)   | æqþ
         | 2nd (formal)     | êæqàbàw
         | 3rd (masculine)  | àñæg
         | 3rd (feminine)   | îàñàñî
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ôñàb
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | êæqàbôñ
         | 2nd              | êæqàbàw
         | 3rd (masculine)  | êàñæg
         | 3rd (feminine)   | êîàñàñî
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun îèl occurs after ôr, î, æg, àb, æq, û, æñ, ék, v and some occurrences of â, it becomes 'èl.

*Relative pronouns

âèbôñîcz, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Âèbôñîcz, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, ægæqôp is ordinarily used: îþþîàñèbûèbægôl ôri æñàñàbàw ôr ægæqôp îiiàbâ'àñ ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ægæqôp in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: êîæñàñàbàw æñþæñ þôñàb ægæqôp êîþþîàñèbûèbægôl êîàñ ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, îæqôp (or 'æqôp after ôr, î, æg, àb, æq, û, æñ, ék, v and some occurrences of â) is ordinarily used: îæñàñàbàw ôr àñæg'æqôp îþþîàñèbûèbægôl ôràñ ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ægæqôp, îæqôp does not change form to agree with its head noun.

VERBS
-----
Verbs in Âèbôñîcz are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Âèbôñîcz is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) cægàbàwôr ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of îcþv ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is îcþv, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is cægàbàwôr. Forms of îcþv are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Âèbôñîcz, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

âèbôñîcz verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -êêæg- between the stem and the ending.

    In þôñîægôràñcôrx, the stem -àñcôrx indicates that the verb is cîàñcôrx (to speak) and the prefix þôñîægôr- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In êôñàbêêægôñægz, the stem -ôñægz indicates that the verb is cægôñægz (to finish), the prefix -êêæg- precedes it, and the inflection êôñàb- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Âèbôñîcz they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    cîàñcôrx: êægôrcîàñcôrx îèl, êôràñcôrx æqþ, þôñîêêôràñcôrx êàñæg'æqôp, êôñàbægàñcôrx êæqàbôñ îæqôp, èpîàñcôrx...
    cægôñægz: êægôrcægôñægz îèl, êîþéñôñægz êæqàbàw, þôñîêêægôñægz êàñæg'æqôp, êægôñægz, êôñàbægêêægôñægz êæqàbôñ îæqôp...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    cægàbàñæqàbàw: eæqîàw îèl, eæqîàw æqþ, þæqîàw àñæg, êôñàbàñæqàbàw êæqàbôñ, èpîàñæqàbàw êæqàbàw, þôñîàñæqîàw êàñæg.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly cægàbàwôr, îcþv, cîàñàñôr and îcægôrz), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with cî- (with the exception of cîàñàñôr, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    cîiægôr, cîûôràñôrôl, cîþôñôrâèb, cîûàbàwôñî, cîicîz, cîdôñôri, cîêêôrx, cîûôrx, cîôñîiàbcx, cîçcôrdîc, etc.

        For example, for the verb cîàñcôrx, the stem is -àñcôrx and the infinitive prefix is cî-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with cæg- whose present participle begins with þôñôrêêæg-:

    cægôñæñôl, cægþôrxiàbèb, cægxcîæqdæñç, cægcæqîàñz, cægçôñôrcd, cïôrâ, cægþêîàwôñæg, cægàñàbx, cægdæqàbc, cægdæqc, cægàñôrê, etc.

        For example, for the verb cægôñægz, the stem is -ôñægz and the infinitive prefix is cæg-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries îcþv and cægàbàwôr, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding î- and ê- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "þægzôñàbèb þægæqcz ôñæq", "îþægzôñàbèb îcægàbx îôñæq", "êþægzôñàbèb êþægæqcz êîç", and "êîþægzôñàbèb êîcægàbx êîç."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with æñ- for the 1st group verbs, and with æg- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : æq- (îcçôñîþôñî æqçôñîþôñî, îcægàbôl æqôl, îcægàñ æqàñ, etc. and cægàbàwôrê æqê, cægàbàw æqàw, cægàbàwæqàbx æqx), êæg- (îcþþîi êægi, îcçôñîcx êægcx, etc.), êæq- (îcæqàñèbôñæg êæqàñèbôñæg and îcæqàñèbîc êæqàñèbîc and only these verbs), þæg- (îcægçæqôri þægçæqôri, îcægç þægç, etc.), þ- (verbs in îcçôñæg- : îcçôñægîx þôñægîx), þcî- (cægcàwæqàb þcîàwæqàb, cægcàwæqàbèb þcîàwæqàbèb, cægczzàb þcîzzàb and cægczzæqàbê þcîzzæqàbê), or æqî (cægàbàwôr æqî). 

*Compound Tenses

âèbôñîcz compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either cægàbàwôr or îcþv) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Âèbôñîcz, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Âèbôñîcz. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either cægàbàwôr or îcþv in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "æñdôñôri ægôr'èl" (I ate) or "æñàwægccôr þêî àñæg" (He arrived). cægàbàwôr is used with most verbs, while îcþv is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, cægàbàwôr should be used by default.

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Çørkœcig, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
çørkœcig has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Çørkœcig, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Çørkœcig article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is kœf. For example, in the phrase "xæçø kœf" (the cat), kœf shows that the noun xæçø (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is æœf. An example is "rôpnæyw æœf" (the house), where æœf shows that rôpnæyw (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is pkœf for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "pxæçø pkœf", the cats; "prôpnæyw pkœf", the houses.)

In summary, kœf is used with masculine singular nouns, æœf with feminine singular nouns, and pkœf with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Çørkœcig.

After æ, k, n, ô, îh, è, îc, l and some occurrences of ç, the singular masculine article kœf becomes 'œf.

NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Çørkœcig noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Çørkœcig nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme p- (e.g., rôpnæyw > prôpnæyw 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with îhæ- and îhk- take the prefix þ- instead of p- (e.g., îhæèîhx > þîhæèîhx 'pipes', îhkð > þîhkð 'games'), except for the nouns îhævræœf, îhæœcœcæp, îhkrœd, and îhkœfyg which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme p- (e.g., îhkrœd > pîhkrœd 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with îhô- form their plural with þ-. These are îhôrké, îhôœfœfnæø, îhôygnç, îhôðnyg, îhôœd, îhôçø, and îhôðîhôð (e.g., îhôrké > þîhôrké 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with îhô-, such as îhôpnyg or îhôœcx, follow the regular plural pattern and take p- (e.g., îhôœcx > pîhôœcx 'holes').

Nouns that begin with p-, þ- or û- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., þnôœcø æœf 'the cross' > þnôœcø pkœf 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with œfæ- typically change to þîhæ- in the plural (e.g., œfærœcîhôð > þîhærœcîhôð 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with œfæ- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding p- instead. These are œfæyg, œfæø, œfæœtærœcæø, œfæøæçø, œfæœtnxpkig, œfæxnøîcœc, œfæœtœckp and œfæéîcœc (e.g., œfæœtnxpkig kœf > pœfæœtnxpkig pkœf).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with œfnæ- change to þîhæ- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include œfnæyg, œfnæœcôø, œfnæywîc, œfnæœcnœdîhôp, œfnæœtæœcx, and œfnæœcxnœt (e.g., œfnæœcxnœt rîh > þîhæœcxnœt pkv 'stained-glass windows'). However, some œfnæ- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with p-, notably œfnæœc, œfnæœcnxxæ, œfnævræçø, œfnæxîcv, œfnærœckœtîhôé and œfnæxœcôœd (e.g., œfnæœc kœf > pœfnæœc pkœf 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Çørkœcig are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Çørkœcig adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like îhækyg and îhækœtîhôr, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in æ, k, n, ô, îh, è, îc, l and some occurrences of ç, e.g. rnvœcæð îhækyg rîh (a beautiful garden), kywywôç œfkyg rîh (a handsome man), kywywkig kœfœfkyg krîh (a beautiful woman), pxræigrk þîhækyg pkœf (the beautiful children), prôpnæyw pkœfœfkyg pkœf (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix k- to the masculine form, e.g., vræœcé > kvræœcé, xrkœf > kxrkœf, ræpœckœd > kræpœckœd. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with œfk-, œfn-, rô-, rk-, pô- or pæ- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix k- (e.g., œfkîhœcø > kœfœfkîhœcø, œfnxrké > kœfœfnxrké, rôyg > krrôyg, rknøræ > krrknøræ, pôœcé > kppôœcé, and pæyg > kppæyg).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with ø- change to kçø- (e.g., øræœfyg > kçøræœfyg); those beginning with œcîhk- or þîhk- change to kpîhk- (e.g., œcîhkxxkywôœcœd > kpîhkxxkywôœcœd, þîhknœcîhig > kpîhknœcîhig), with the exception of the irregular þîhknœt (old) whose feminine form is kœfœfnknœt; é- changes to kîhé- (e.g., érôœf > kîhérôœf); ign- changes to kœtn- (e.g., ignxøæ > kœtnxøæ); igk- changes to kœtl- (e.g., igkœcyg > kœtlœcyg); œck- changes to kœcl- (e.g., œckéræœcxîc > kœcléræœcxîc); xk- changes to kxl- (e.g., xknîhjrn > kxlnîhjrn); and adjectives beginning with îhô- have a special form œfô- (becoming kœfœfô- in feminine) that appears after æ, k, n, ô, îh, è, îc, l and some occurrences of ç, (e.g., îhôig/œfôig > kœfœfôig, îhôyw/œfôyw > kœfœfôyw).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with k-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. kçønœc kywywôç rîh 'a rich man' > kçønœc kywywkig krîh 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix p- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., nœfôð > pnœfôð, knœfôð > pknœfôð). If the basic form beginning with p-, þ-, or û-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., pæyg > pæyg, þîhkœcîcrîcé > þîhkœcîcrîcé, þîhôv > þîhôv), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Çørkœcig adjectives beginning with îhæk- take the prefix þ- in the masculine plural (e.g., îhækœtîhôr > þîhækœtîhôr). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with œfæ-, which normally change to þîhæ- in the masculine plural (e.g., œfærœckœtnç > þîhærœckœtnç, œfæœcxrkø > þîhæœcxrkø), with only two exceptions: œfæxæig > pœfæxæig and œfæœtær > pœfæœtær which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: kœfæœcxrkø > pkœfæœcxrkø.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in kéîhôœc kœf rnœt (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are îhækyg (beautiful), rôyg (good), igkœcyg (brief), vræœcé (big/tall), pôœcé (fat/large), þîhæig (false), xîhæç (high), érôœf (long), igkœcyg (brief), krîhkð (young), nœfôð (pretty), pnæœtîhæyw (bad), œcîhkœfœfnkyw (better), îhækœtîhôr (new), xnxkœd (small), þîhknœt (old); e.g., kywywkig krîh kœfœfkyg ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Çørkœcig, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
çørkœcig personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

------------------------

------------------------

         | 2nd (informal)   | îhx
         | 2nd (formal)     | pîhôœt
         | 3rd (masculine)  | œfn
         | 3rd (feminine)   | kœfœfk
         | 3rd (neutral)    | rô
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | pîhôr
         | 2nd              | pîhôœt
         | 3rd (masculine)  | pœfn
         | 3rd (feminine)   | pkœfœfk
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun kð occurs after æ, k, n, ô, îh, è, îc, l, a and some occurrences of ç, it becomes 'ð.

*Relative pronouns

çørkœcig, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Çørkœcig, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, nîhj is ordinarily used: kxxkœføèønyg æyw îcœfôœt æ nîhj kywywôç'œf ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that nîhj in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: pkîcœfôœt îcxîc xrô nîhj pkxxkœføèønyg pkœf ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, kîhj (or 'îhj after æ, k, n, ô, îh, è, îc, l, a and some occurrences of ç) is ordinarily used: kîcœfôœt æ œfn'îhj kxxkœføèønyg æœf ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like nîhj, kîhj does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Çørkœcig are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Çørkœcig is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) œcnôœtæ ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of kœcxa ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is kœcxa, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is œcnôœtæ. Forms of kœcxa are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Çørkœcig, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

çørkœcig verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ppn- between the stem and the ending.

    In xrknæœfœcæœd, the stem -œfœcæœd indicates that the verb is œckœfœcæœd (to speak) and the prefix xrknæ- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In prôppnrnig, the stem -rnig indicates that the verb is œcnrnig (to finish), the prefix -ppn- precedes it, and the inflection prô- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Çørkœcig they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    œckœfœcæœd: pnæœckœfœcæœd kð, pæœfœcæœd îhx, xrkppæœfœcæœd pœfn'îhj, prônœfœcæœd pîhôr kîhj, ûkœfœcæœd...
    œcnrnig: pnæœcnrnig kð, pkxornig pîhôœt, xrkppnrnig pœfn'îhj, pnrnig, prônppnrnig pîhôr kîhj...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    œcnôœfîhôœt: þîhkœt kð, þîhkœt îhx, xîhkœt œfn, prôœfîhôœt pîhôr, ûkœfîhôœt pîhôœt, xrkœfîhkœt pœfn.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly œcnôœtæ, kœcxa, œckœfœfæ and kœcnæig), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with œck- (with the exception of œckœfœfæ, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    œckywnæ, œckèæœfæyg, œckxræçø, œckèôœtrk, œckywœckig, œckéræyw, œckppæœd, œckèæœd, œckrkywôœcœd, œckvœcæékœc, etc.

        For example, for the verb œckœfœcæœd, the stem is -œfœcæœd and the infinitive prefix is œck-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with œcn- whose present participle begins with xræppn-:

    œcnrîcyg, œcnxæœdywôø, œcnœdœckîhéîcv, œcnœcîhkœfig, œcnvræœcé, œcïæç, œcnxpkœtrn, œcnœfôœd, œcnéîhôœc, œcnéîhœc, œcnœfæp, etc.

        For example, for the verb œcnrnig, the stem is -rnig and the infinitive prefix is œcn-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries kœcxa and œcnôœtæ, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "pnævœcæékœc kð" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the œck- prefix, e.g., œckvœcæékœc -> -vœcæékœc.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the œcn- prefix plus the ppn- prefix, e.g., œcnpnôçø -> -ppnpnôçø. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: pnæ-, pnæ-, xnæ-, prôn-, ûkn-, xrknæ-.
