**Future

The future prefixes correspond to the present indicative of the verb faqotoèþy. They are always regular: qoþy-, þoþy-, þy-, þohto-, nog-, fuhto-.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these prefixes are added to the infinitive:

        qoþyfaqoþoqotonyna gqa ('I will choose'), þoþyfagçifaþyfigfa þufu ('you will watch'), þyfaqofufatoþo gxxg ('she will exit'), þohtofagxxqoþyèþyfafu þoþutoh ('we will work'), nogfaqofiþutofa þoþutoè ('you will blush'), fuhtofaqofufaþyþa þoxqo ('they will leave').

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

Seven nouns beginning with pwê- form their plural with œ-. These are pwêfîv, pwêççæyq, pwêjèæxè, pwêâæjè, pwêsô, pwêxèq, and pwêâpwêâ (e.g., pwêfîv > œpwêfîv 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with pwê-, such as pwêgæjè or pwêkeb, follow the regular plural pattern and take g- (e.g., pwêkeb > gpwêkeb 'holes').

Nouns that begin with g-, œ- or wû- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., œæwêkeq yç 'the cross' > œæwêkeq gîç 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with çy- typically change to œpy- in the plural (e.g., çyfkepwêâ > œpyfkepwêâ 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with çy- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding g- instead. These are çyjè, çyq, çytyfkeyq, çyqyxèq, çytæbgîkû, çybæqoke, çytkeîg and çyvoke (e.g., çytæbgîkû îç > gçytæbgîkû gîç).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with çæy- change to œpy- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include çæyjè, çæykewêq, çæyweo, çæykeæsôpwêg, çæytykeb, and çæykebæt (e.g., çæykebæt fp > œpykebæt gîhê 'stained-glass windows'). However, some çæy- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with g-, notably çæyke, çæykeæbby, çæyhêfyxèq, çæybohê, çæyfkeîtpwêv and çæybkewêsô (e.g., çæyke îç > gçæyke gîç 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Xèqfîkekû are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Xèqfîkekû adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like pyîjè and pyîtpwêf, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in y, î, æ, wê, p, c, o, z and some occurrences of xè, e.g. fæhêkeyâ pyîjè fp (a beautiful garden), îwewewêxè çîjè fp (a handsome man), îweweîkû îççîjè îfp (a beautiful woman), gbfykûfî œpyîjè gîç (the beautiful children), gfwêgæywe gîççîjè gîç (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix î- to the masculine form, e.g., hêfykev > îhêfykev, bfîç > îbfîç, fygkeîsô > îfygkeîsô. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with çî-, çæ-, fwê-, fî-, gwê- or gy- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix î- (e.g., çîpkeq > îççîpkeq, çæbfîv > îççæbfîv, fwêjè > îffwêjè, fîæqfy > îffîæqfy, gwêkev > îggwêkev, and gyjè > îggyjè).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with q- change to îxèq- (e.g., qfyçjè > îxèqfyçjè); those beginning with kepî- or œpî- change to îgpî- (e.g., kepîbbîwewêkesô > îgpîbbîwewêkesô, œpîækepkû > îgpîækepkû), with the exception of the irregular œpîæt (old) whose feminine form is îççæîæt; v- changes to îpv- (e.g., vfwêç > îpvfwêç); kûæ- changes to îtæ- (e.g., kûæbqy > îtæbqy); kûî- changes to îtz- (e.g., kûîkejè > îtzkejè); keî- changes to îkez- (e.g., keîvfykebo > îkezvfykebo); bî- changes to îbz- (e.g., bîæpafæ > îbzæpafæ); and adjectives beginning with pwê- have a special form çwê- (becoming îççwê- in feminine) that appears after y, î, æ, wê, p, c, o, z and some occurrences of xè, (e.g., pwêkû/çwêkû > îççwêkû, pwêwe/çwêwe > îççwêwe).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with î-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. îxèqæke îwewewêxè fp 'a rich man' > îxèqæke îweweîkû îfp 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix g- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., æçwêâ > gæçwêâ, îæçwêâ > gîæçwêâ). If the basic form beginning with g-, œ-, or wû-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., gyjè > gyjè, œpîkeofov > œpîkeofov, œpwêhê > œpwêhê), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Xèqfîkekû adjectives beginning with pyî- take the prefix œ- in the masculine plural (e.g., pyîtpwêf > œpyîtpwêf). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with çy-, which normally change to œpy- in the masculine plural (e.g., çyfkeîtæxè > œpyfkeîtæxè, çykebfîq > œpykebfîq), with only two exceptions: çybykû > gçybykû and çytyf > gçytyf which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: îçykebfîq > gîçykebfîq.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in îvpwêke îç fæt (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are pyîjè (beautiful), fwêjè (good), kûîkejè (brief), hêfykev (big/tall), gwêkev (fat/large), œpykû (false), bpyxè (high), vfwêç (long), kûîkejè (brief), îfpîâ (young), æçwêâ (pretty), gæytpywe (bad), kepîççæîwe (better), pyîtpwêf (new), bæbîsô (small), œpîæt (old); e.g., îweweîkû îfp îççîjè ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Xèqfîkekû, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
xèqfîkekû personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | îâ
         | 2nd (informal)   | pb
         | 2nd (formal)     | gpwêt
         | 3rd (masculine)  | çæ
         | 3rd (feminine)   | îççî
         | 3rd (neutral)    | fwê
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | gpwêf
         | 2nd              | gpwêt
         | 3rd (masculine)  | gçæ
         | 3rd (feminine)   | gîççî
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun îâ occurs after y, î, æ, wê, p, c, o, z, d and some occurrences of xè, it becomes 'â.

*Relative pronouns

xèqfîkekû, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Xèqfîkekû, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, æpa is ordinarily used: îbbîçqcqæjè ywe oçwêt y æpa îwewewêxè'ç ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that æpa in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: gîoçwêt obo bfwê æpa gîbbîçqcqæjè gîç ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, îpa (or 'pa after y, î, æ, wê, p, c, o, z, d and some occurrences of xè) is ordinarily used: îoçwêt y çæ'pa îbbîçqcqæjè yç ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like æpa, îpa does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Xèqfîkekû are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Xèqfîkekû is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) keæwêty ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of îkebd ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is îkebd, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is keæwêty. Forms of îkebd are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Xèqfîkekû, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

xèqfîkekû verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ggæ- between the stem and the ending.

    In bfîæyçkeysô, the stem -çkeysô indicates that the verb is keîçkeysô (to speak) and the prefix bfîæy- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In gfwêggæfækû, the stem -fækû indicates that the verb is keæfækû (to finish), the prefix -ggæ- precedes it, and the inflection gfwê- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Xèqfîkekû they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    keîçkeysô: gæykeîçkeysô îâ, gyçkeysô pb, bfîggyçkeysô gçæ'pa, gfwêæçkeysô gpwêf îpa, wûîçkeysô...
    keæfækû: gæykeæfækû îâ, gîbnefækû gpwêt, bfîggæfækû gçæ'pa, gæfækû, gfwêæggæfækû gpwêf îpa...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    keæwêçpwêt: œpît îâ, œpît pb, bpît çæ, gfwêçpwêt gpwêf, wûîçpwêt gpwêt, bfîçpît gçæ.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly keæwêty, îkebd, keîççy and îkeæykû), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with keî- (with the exception of keîççy, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    keîweæy, keîcyçyjè, keîbfyxèq, keîcwêtfî, keîwekeîkû, keîvfywe, keîggysô, keîcysô, keîfîwewêkesô, keîhêkeyvîke, etc.

        For example, for the verb keîçkeysô, the stem is -çkeysô and the infinitive prefix is keî-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with keæ- whose present participle begins with bfyggæ-:

    keæfojè, keæbysôwewêq, keæsôkeîpvohê, keækepîçkû, keæhêfykev, keïyxè, keæbgîtfæ, keæçwêsô, keævpwêke, keævpke, keæçyg, etc.

        For example, for the verb keæfækû, the stem is -fækû and the infinitive prefix is keæ-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries îkebd and keæwêty, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. îhêkeyvîke îâ means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with keî- (all verbs of the first group): î-, gî-, î-, gfwê-, wûî-, bfî-.
    Verbs beginning with keæ- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): gæ-, gæ-, bæ-, gfwêggæ-, wûîggæ-, bfîggæ-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with îke- (part of the third group): g-, g-, - , gfwê-, wûî-, bfî-.
    
    Example:

-------------------------------
1st person     | îhêkeyvîke îâ         | gfwêhêkeyvîke gpwêf
2nd person     | gîhêkeyvîke pb        | wûîhêkeyvîke gpwêt
3rd person     | îhêkeyvîke fwê/îççî/çæ | bfîhêkeyvîke gîççî/gçæ

2nd person     | gægæwêxèq pb         | wûîggægæwêxèq gpwêt

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "gæyhêkeyvîke îâ" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the keî- prefix, e.g., keîhêkeyvîke -> -hêkeyvîke.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the keæ- prefix plus the ggæ- prefix, e.g., keægæwêxèq -> -ggægæwêxèq. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: gæy-, gæy-, bæy-, gfwêæ-, wûîæ-, bfîæy-.

2nd person     | gæyhêkeyvîke pb         | wûîæhêkeyvîke gpwêt
3rd person     | bæyhêkeyvîke fwê/îççî/çæ | bfîæyhêkeyvîke gîççî/gçæ

    Verb îkebd : the stem is -bo, endings are the same.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding î- and g- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "bækûfwêq bæpkekû fp", "îbækûfwêq îkeæwêsô îfp", "gbækûfwêq gbæpkekû gîhê", and "gîbækûfwêq gîkeæwêsô gîhê."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with o- for the 1st group verbs, and with æ- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : p- (îkehêfîbfî phêfîbfî, îkeæwêjè pjè, îkeæç pç, etc. and keæwêtyg pg, keæwêt pt, keæwêtpwêsô psô), gæ- (îkebbîwe gæwe, îkehêfîkesô gækesô, etc.), gp- (îkepçqfæ gpçqfæ and îkepçqîke gpçqîke and only these verbs), bæ- (îkeæhêpywe bæhêpywe, îkeæhê bæhê, etc.), b- (verbs in îkehêfæ- : îkehêfæîsô bfæîsô), bkeî- (keæketpwê bkeîtpwê, keæketpwêq bkeîtpwêq, keækekûkûwê bkeîkûkûwê and keækekûkûpwêg bkeîkûkûpwêg), or pî (keæwêty pî). 

*Compound Tenses

xèqfîkekû compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either keæwêty or îkebd) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Xèqfîkekû, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Xèqfîkekû. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either keæwêty or îkebd in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "ovfywe æy'â" (I ate) or "otækekey bgî çæ" (He arrived). keæwêty is used with most verbs, while îkebd is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, keæwêty should be used by default.

Example:

Person         | Singular                     | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | ohêkeyvîke æy'â               | ohêkeyvîke gfwêty gpwêf
2nd person     | ohêkeyvîke gy pb              | ohêkeyvîke wûîty gpwêt
3rd person     | ohêkeyvîke y fwê/îççî/çæ       | ohêkeyvîke bfwê gîççî/gçæ
-------------------------------

2nd Group: keægæwêxèq (to choose)
-------------------------------

* Case
Nouns in Fçþèpor are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Fçþèpor adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like hèðpv and hèðpbhèqþè, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in ð, p, cè, q, hè, þe, w, gy and some occurrences of f, e.g. þècèkoðxi hèðpv þèhè (a beautiful garden), pééqf tpv þèhè (a handsome man), péépr pttpv pþèhè (a beautiful woman), cenyþèðrþèp zhèðpv cept (the beautiful children), ceþèqcecèðé cepttpv cept (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix p- to the masculine form, e.g., kþèðole > pkþèðole, nyþèpt > pnyþèpt, þèðceophy > pþèðceophy. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with tp-, tcè-, þèq-, þèp-, ceq- or ceð- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix p- (e.g., tphèoç > pttphèoç, tcènyþèple > pttcènyþèple, þèqv > pþèþèqv, þèpcèçþèð > pþèþèpcèçþèð, ceqole > pceceqole, and ceðv > pceceðv).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with ç- change to pfç- (e.g., çþèðtv > pfçþèðtv); those beginning with ohèp- or zhèp- change to pcehèp- (e.g., ohèpnynypéqohy > pcehèpnynypéqohy, zhèpcèohèr > pcehèpcèohèr), with the exception of the irregular zhèpcèb (old) whose feminine form is pttcèpcèb; le- changes to phèle- (e.g., leþèqt > phèleþèqt); rcè- changes to pbcè- (e.g., rcènyçð > pbcènyçð); rp- changes to pbgy- (e.g., rpov > pbgyov); op- changes to pogy- (e.g., opleþèðonyw > pogyleþèðonyw); nyp- changes to pnygy- (e.g., nypcèhèuþècè > pnygycèhèuþècè); and adjectives beginning with hèq- have a special form tq- (becoming pttq- in feminine) that appears after ð, p, cè, q, hè, þe, w, gy and some occurrences of f, (e.g., hèqr/tqr > pttqr, hèqé/tqé > pttqé).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with p-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. pfçcèo pééqf þèhè 'a rich man' > pfçcèo péépr pþèhè 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix ce- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., cètqxi > cecètqxi, pcètqxi > cepcètqxi). If the basic form beginning with ce-, z-, or hà-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ceðv > ceðv, zhèpowþèwle > zhèpowþèwle, zhèqk > zhèqk), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Fçþèpor adjectives beginning with hèðp- take the prefix z- in the masculine plural (e.g., hèðpbhèqþè > zhèðpbhèqþè). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with tð-, which normally change to zhèð- in the masculine plural (e.g., tðþèopbcèf > zhèðþèopbcèf, tðonyþèpç > zhèðonyþèpç), with only two exceptions: tðnyðr > cetðnyðr and tðbðþè > cetðbðþè which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ptðonyþèpç > ceptðonyþèpç.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in plehèqo pt þècèb (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are hèðpv (beautiful), þèqv (good), rpov (brief), kþèðole (big/tall), ceqole (fat/large), zhèðr (false), nyhèðf (high), leþèqt (long), rpov (brief), pþèhèpxi (young), cètqxi (pretty), cecèðbhèðé (bad), ohèpttcèpé (better), hèðpbhèqþè (new), nycènyphy (small), zhèpcèb (old); e.g., péépr pþèhè pttpv ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Fçþèpor, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
fçþèpor personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

         | 2nd (formal)     | cehèqb
         | 3rd (masculine)  | tcè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | pttp
         | 3rd (neutral)    | þèq
------------------------

         | 2nd              | cehèqb

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun pxi occurs after ð, p, cè, q, hè, þe, w, gy, ê and some occurrences of f, it becomes 'xi.

*Relative pronouns

fçþèpor, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Fçþèpor, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, cèhèu is ordinarily used: pnynyptçþeçcèv ðé wtqb ð cèhèu pééqf't ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that cèhèu in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: cepwtqb wnyw nyþèq cèhèu cepnynyptçþeçcèv cept ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, phèu (or 'hèu after ð, p, cè, q, hè, þe, w, gy, ê and some occurrences of f) is ordinarily used: pwtqb ð tcè'hèu pnynyptçþeçcèv ðt ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like cèhèu, phèu does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Fçþèpor are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Fçþèpor is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ocèqbð ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of ponyê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is ponyê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ocèqbð. Forms of ponyê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Fçþèpor, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

fçþèpor verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -cececè- between the stem and the ending.

    In nyþèpcèðtoðhy, the stem -toðhy indicates that the verb is optoðhy (to speak) and the prefix nyþèpcèð- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ceþèqcececèþècèr, the stem -þècèr indicates that the verb is ocèþècèr (to finish), the prefix -cececè- precedes it, and the inflection ceþèq- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Fçþèpor they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    optoðhy: cecèðoptoðhy pxi, ceðtoðhy hèny, nyþèpceceðtoðhy cetcè'hèu, ceþèqcètoðhy cehèqþè phèu, hàptoðhy...
    ocèþècèr: cecèðocèþècèr pxi, cepnyîþècèr cehèqb, nyþèpcececèþècèr cetcè'hèu, cecèþècèr, ceþèqcècececèþècèr cehèqþè phèu...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ocèqthèqb: zhèpb pxi, zhèpb hèny, nyhèpb tcè, ceþèqthèqb cehèqþè, hàpthèqb cehèqb, nyþèpthèpb cetcè.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ocèqbð, ponyê, opttð and pocèðr), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with op- (with the exception of opttð, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    opécèð, opþeðtðv, opnyþèðfç, opþeqbþèp, opéopr, opleþèðé, opceceðhy, opþeðhy, opþèpéqohy, opkoðlepo, etc.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with ocè- whose present participle begins with nyþèðcececè-:

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries ponyê and ocèqbð, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

*Compound Tenses

fçþèpor compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either ocèqbð or ponyê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Fçþèpor, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

Verbs in Kérébgufi are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Kérébgufi: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

A. The auxiliary verb is ufyrymiç.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears before the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).

        (direct object before verb) dgbfygjçv ràqga qmi ç gufyçjré. ("gufyçjré saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears after the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun after the auxiliary) dgbfygjçv ràqga hfyçmiç xo jfy. dgqmi ç dgj gufyçjré. ("There were two whales. gufyçjré saw them.")
        (clause-final wh-question element)  dgqmi gjjg-h-ç gufyçjré dgbfygjçv dgjjgqcé? ("Which whales did gufyçjré see?")
        (relative clause linked by gqcé) dgqmi ç gufyçjré gqcé dgbfygjçv ràqga dgj ("the two whales that gufyçjré saw")

B. The auxiliary is guhê, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

C. The auxiliary is guhê and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with ufyrymiç in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

        (direct object before verb) dbryfyhdgqcé dga wdrye hbryd gd dgjjg. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears after the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is éreþ. For example, in the phrase "bvqñ éreþ" (the cat), éreþ shows that the noun bvqñ (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is veþ. An example is "kehcèvyt veþ" (the house), where veþ shows that kehcèvyt (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is céreþ for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "cbvqñ céreþ", the cats; "ckehcèvyt céreþ", the houses.)

In summary, éreþ is used with masculine singular nouns, veþ with feminine singular nouns, and céreþ with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Qñkérzyr.

After v, ér, è, eh, j, ét, ég, el and some occurrences of q, the singular masculine article éreþ becomes 'eþ.


-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Qñkérzyr noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Qñkérzyr nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme c- (e.g., kehcèvyt > ckehcèvyt 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with jv- and jér- take the prefix à- instead of c- (e.g., jvétjb > àjvétjb 'pipes', jérç > àjérç 'games'), except for the nouns jvskveþ, jvzzvc, jérkah, and jéreþén which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme c- (e.g., jérkah > cjérkah 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with jeh- form their plural with à-. These are jehkéréþ, jeheþeþèvñ, jehénèq, jehçèén, jehah, jehqñ, and jehçjehç (e.g., jehkéréþ > àjehkéréþ 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with jeh-, such as jehcèén or jehzb, follow the regular plural pattern and take c- (e.g., jehzb > cjehzb 'holes').

Nouns that begin with c-, à- or f- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., àèehzñ veþ 'the cross' > àèehzñ céreþ 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with eþv- typically change to àjv- in the plural (e.g., eþvkzjehç > àjvkzjehç 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with eþv- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding c- instead. These are eþvén, eþvñ, eþvðvkzvñ, eþvñvqñ, eþvðèbcéryr, eþvbèñégz, eþvðzérc and eþvéþégz (e.g., eþvðèbcéryr éreþ > ceþvðèbcéryr céreþ).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with eþèv- change to àjv- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include eþèvén, eþèvzehñ, eþèvytég, eþèvzèahjehc, eþèvðvzb, and eþèvzbèð (e.g., eþèvzbèð kj > àjvzbèð cérs 'stained-glass windows'). However, some eþèv- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with c-, notably eþèvz, eþèvzèbbv, eþèvskvqñ, eþèvbégs, eþèvkzérðjehéþ and eþèvbzehah (e.g., eþèvz éreþ > ceþèvz céreþ 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Qñkérzyr are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Qñkérzyr adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like jvérén and jvérðjehk, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in v, ér, è, eh, j, ét, ég, el and some occurrences of q, e.g. kèszvç jvérén kj (a beautiful garden), érytytehq eþérén kj (a handsome man), érytytéryr éreþeþérén érkj (a beautiful woman), cbkvyrkér àjvérén céreþ (the beautiful children), ckehcèvyt céreþeþérén céreþ (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix ér- to the masculine form, e.g., skvzéþ > érskvzéþ, bkéreþ > érbkéreþ, kvczérah > érkvczérah. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with eþér-, eþè-, keh-, kér-, ceh- or cv- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix ér- (e.g., eþérjzñ > éreþeþérjzñ, eþèbkéréþ > éreþeþèbkéréþ, kehén > érkkehén, kérèñkv > érkkérèñkv, cehzéþ > érccehzéþ, and cvén > érccvén).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with ñ- change to érqñ- (e.g., ñkveþén > érqñkveþén); those beginning with zjér- or àjér- change to ércjér- (e.g., zjérbbérytehzah > ércjérbbérytehzah, àjérèzjyr > ércjérèzjyr), with the exception of the irregular àjérèð (old) whose feminine form is éreþeþèérèð; éþ- changes to érjéþ- (e.g., éþkeheþ > érjéþkeheþ); yrè- changes to érðè- (e.g., yrèbñv > érðèbñv); yrér- changes to érðel- (e.g., yrérzén > érðelzén); zér- changes to érzel- (e.g., zéréþkvzbég > érzeléþkvzbég); bér- changes to érbel- (e.g., bérèjokè > érbelèjokè); and adjectives beginning with jeh- have a special form eþeh- (becoming éreþeþeh- in feminine) that appears after v, ér, è, eh, j, ét, ég, el and some occurrences of q, (e.g., jehyr/eþehyr > éreþeþehyr, jehyt/eþehyt > éreþeþehyt).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with ér-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. érqñèz érytytehq kj 'a rich man' > érqñèz érytytéryr érkj 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix c- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., èeþehç > cèeþehç, érèeþehç > cérèeþehç). If the basic form beginning with c-, à-, or f-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., cvén > cvén, àjérzégkégéþ > àjérzégkégéþ, àjehs > àjehs), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Qñkérzyr adjectives beginning with jvér- take the prefix à- in the masculine plural (e.g., jvérðjehk > àjvérðjehk). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with eþv-, which normally change to àjv- in the masculine plural (e.g., eþvkzérðèq > àjvkzérðèq, eþvzbkérñ > àjvzbkérñ), with only two exceptions: eþvbvyr > ceþvbvyr and eþvðvk > ceþvðvk which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: éreþvzbkérñ > céreþvzbkérñ.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in éréþjehz éreþ kèð (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are jvérén (beautiful), kehén (good), yrérzén (brief), skvzéþ (big/tall), cehzéþ (fat/large), àjvyr (false), bjvq (high), éþkeheþ (long), yrérzén (brief), érkjérç (young), èeþehç (pretty), cèvðjvyt (bad), zjéreþeþèéryt (better), jvérðjehk (new), bèbérah (small), àjérèð (old); e.g., érytytéryr érkj éreþeþérén ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Qñkérzyr, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
qñkérzyr personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | érç
         | 2nd (informal)   | jb
         | 2nd (formal)     | cjehð
         | 3rd (masculine)  | eþè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | éreþeþér
         | 3rd (neutral)    | keh
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | cjehk
         | 2nd              | cjehð
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ceþè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | céreþeþér
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun érç occurs after v, ér, è, eh, j, ét, ég, el, ê and some occurrences of q, it becomes 'ç.

*Relative pronouns

qñkérzyr, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Qñkérzyr, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, èjo is ordinarily used: érbbéreþñétñèén vyt égeþehð v èjo érytytehq'eþ ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that èjo in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: cérégeþehð égbég bkeh èjo cérbbéreþñétñèén céreþ ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, érjo (or 'jo after v, ér, è, eh, j, ét, ég, el, ê and some occurrences of q) is ordinarily used: érégeþehð v eþè'jo érbbéreþñétñèén veþ ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like èjo, érjo does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Qñkérzyr are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Qñkérzyr is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) zèehðv ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of érzbê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is érzbê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is zèehðv. Forms of érzbê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Qñkérzyr, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

qñkérzyr verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ccè- between the stem and the ending.

    In bkérèveþzvah, the stem -eþzvah indicates that the verb is zéreþzvah (to speak) and the prefix bkérèv- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ckehccèkèyr, the stem -kèyr indicates that the verb is zèkèyr (to finish), the prefix -ccè- precedes it, and the inflection ckeh- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Qñkérzyr they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    zéreþzvah: cèvzéreþzvah érç, cveþzvah jb, bkérccveþzvah ceþè'jo, ckehèeþzvah cjehk érjo, féreþzvah...
    zèkèyr: cèvzèkèyr érç, cérbîkèyr cjehð, bkérccèkèyr ceþè'jo, cèkèyr, ckehèccèkèyr cjehk érjo...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    zèeheþjehð: àjérð érç, àjérð jb, bjérð eþè, ckeheþjehð cjehk, féreþjehð cjehð, bkéreþjérð ceþè.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly zèehðv, érzbê, zéreþeþv and érzèvyr), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with zér- (with the exception of zéreþeþv, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    zérytèv, zérétveþvén, zérbkvqñ, zérétehðkér, zérytzéryr, zéréþkvyt, zérccvah, zérétvah, zérkérytehzah, zérszvéþérz, etc.

        For example, for the verb zéreþzvah, the stem is -eþzvah and the infinitive prefix is zér-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with zè- whose present participle begins with bkvccè-:

    zèkégén, zèbvahytehñ, zèahzérjéþégs, zèzjéreþyr, zèskvzéþ, zïvq, zèbcérðkè, zèeþehah, zèéþjehz, zèéþjz, zèeþvc, etc.

        For example, for the verb zèkèyr, the stem is -kèyr and the infinitive prefix is zè-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries érzbê and zèehðv, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. érszvéþérz érç means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with érz- (part of the third group): c-, c-, - , ckeh-, fér-, bkér-.

**Past participle

In Bemyçdpu, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. ** Definite article
 	
In Bemyçdpu, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Bemyçdpu article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is çsu. For example, in the phrase "wèlybe çsu" (the cat), çsu shows that the noun wèlybe (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is lysu. An example is "myxéqxylyt lysu" (the house), where lysu shows that myxéqxylyt (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

In summary, çsu is used with masculine singular nouns, lysu with feminine singular nouns, and qçsu with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Bemyçdpu.

* Gender
Every Bemyçdpu noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Bemyçdpu nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme q- (e.g., myxéqxylyt > qmyxéqxylyt 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with rly- and rç- take the prefix v- instead of q- (e.g., rlyxèrwè > vrlyxèrwè 'pipes', rçh > vrçh 'games'), except for the nouns rlypémylysu, rlyddlyq, rçmyc, and rçsufy which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme q- (e.g., rçmyc > qrçmyc 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with rxé- form their plural with v-. These are rxémyçg, rxésusuxylye, rxéfyxyb, rxéhxyfy, rxéc, rxébe, and rxéhrxéh (e.g., rxémyçg > vrxémyçg 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with rxé-, such as rxéqxyfy or rxédwè, follow the regular plural pattern and take q- (e.g., rxédwè > qrxédwè 'holes').

Nouns that begin with q-, v- or jo- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., vxyxéde lysu 'the cross' > vxyxéde qçsu 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with suly- typically change to vrly- in the plural (e.g., sulymydrxéh > vrlymydrxéh 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with suly- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding q- instead. These are sulyfy, sulye, sulyzlymydlye, sulyelybe, sulyzxywèqçpu, sulywèxyead, sulyzdçq and sulygad (e.g., sulyzxywèqçpu çsu > qsulyzxywèqçpu qçsu).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with suxyly- change to vrly- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include suxylyfy, suxylydxée, suxylyta, suxylydxycrxéq, suxylyzlydwè, and suxylydwèxyz (e.g., suxylydwèxyz myr > vrlydwèxyz qçpé 'stained-glass windows'). However, some suxyly- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with q-, notably suxylyd, suxylydxywèwèly, suxylypémylybe, suxylywèapé, suxylymydçzrxég and suxylywèdxéc (e.g., suxylyd çsu > qsuxylyd qçsu 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Bemyçdpu are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Bemyçdpu adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like rlyçfy and rlyçzrxémy, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in ly, ç, xy, xé, r, xè, a, mè and some occurrences of b, e.g. myxypédlyh rlyçfy myr (a beautiful garden), çttxéb suçfy myr (a handsome man), çttçpu çsusuçfy çmyr (a beautiful woman), qwèmylypumyç vrlyçfy qçsu (the beautiful children), qmyxéqxylyt qçsusuçfy qçsu (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix ç- to the masculine form, e.g., pémylydg > çpémylydg, wèmyçsu > çwèmyçsu, mylyqdçc > çmylyqdçc. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with suç-, suxy-, myxé-, myç-, qxé- or qly- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix ç- (e.g., suçrde > çsusuçrde, suxywèmyçg > çsusuxywèmyçg, myxéfy > çmymyxéfy, myçxyemyly > çmymyçxyemyly, qxédg > çqqxédg, and qlyfy > çqqlyfy).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with e- change to çbe- (e.g., emylysufy > çbemylysufy); those beginning with drç- or vrç- change to çqrç- (e.g., drçwèwèçtxédc > çqrçwèwèçtxédc, vrçxydrpu > çqrçxydrpu), with the exception of the irregular vrçxyz (old) whose feminine form is çsusuxyçxyz; g- changes to çrg- (e.g., gmyxésu > çrgmyxésu); puxy- changes to çzxy- (e.g., puxywèely > çzxywèely); puç- changes to çzmè- (e.g., puçdfy > çzmèdfy); dç- changes to çdmè- (e.g., dçgmylydwèa > çdmègmylydwèa); wèç- changes to çwèmè- (e.g., wèçxyrnmyxy > çwèmèxyrnmyxy); and adjectives beginning with rxé- have a special form suxé- (becoming çsusuxé- in feminine) that appears after ly, ç, xy, xé, r, xè, a, mè and some occurrences of b, (e.g., rxépu/suxépu > çsusuxépu, rxét/suxét > çsusuxét).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with ç-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. çbexyd çttxéb myr 'a rich man' > çbexyd çttçpu çmyr 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix q- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., xysuxéh > qxysuxéh, çxysuxéh > qçxysuxéh). If the basic form beginning with q-, v-, or jo-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., qlyfy > qlyfy, vrçdamyag > vrçdamyag, vrxépé > vrxépé), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Bemyçdpu adjectives beginning with rlyç- take the prefix v- in the masculine plural (e.g., rlyçzrxémy > vrlyçzrxémy). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with suly-, which normally change to vrly- in the masculine plural (e.g., sulymydçzxyb > vrlymydçzxyb, sulydwèmyçe > vrlydwèmyçe), with only two exceptions: sulywèlypu > qsulywèlypu and sulyzlymy > qsulyzlymy which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: çsulydwèmyçe > qçsulydwèmyçe.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in çgrxéd çsu myxyz (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are rlyçfy (beautiful), myxéfy (good), puçdfy (brief), pémylydg (big/tall), qxédg (fat/large), vrlypu (false), wèrlyb (high), gmyxésu (long), puçdfy (brief), çmyrçh (young), xysuxéh (pretty), qxylyzrlyt (bad), drçsusuxyçt (better), rlyçzrxémy (new), wèxywèçc (small), vrçxyz (old); e.g., çttçpu çmyr çsusuçfy ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Bemyçdpu, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
bemyçdpu personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | çh
         | 2nd (informal)   | rwè
         | 2nd (formal)     | qrxéz
         | 3rd (masculine)  | suxy
         | 3rd (feminine)   | çsusuç
         | 3rd (neutral)    | myxé
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | qrxémy
         | 2nd              | qrxéz
         | 3rd (masculine)  | qsuxy
         | 3rd (feminine)   | qçsusuç
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun çh occurs after ly, ç, xy, xé, r, xè, a, mè, ê and some occurrences of b, it becomes 'h.

*Relative pronouns

bemyçdpu, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Bemyçdpu, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, xyrn is ordinarily used: çwèwèçsuexèexyfy lyt asuxéz ly xyrn çttxéb'su ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that xyrn in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: qçasuxéz awèa wèmyxé xyrn qçwèwèçsuexèexyfy qçsu ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, çrn (or 'rn after ly, ç, xy, xé, r, xè, a, mè, ê and some occurrences of b) is ordinarily used: çasuxéz ly suxy'rn çwèwèçsuexèexyfy lysu ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like xyrn, çrn does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Bemyçdpu are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Bemyçdpu is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) dxyxézly ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of çdwèê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is çdwèê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is dxyxézly. Forms of çdwèê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Bemyçdpu, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

bemyçdpu verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -qqxy- between the stem and the ending.

    In wèmyçxylysudlyc, the stem -sudlyc indicates that the verb is dçsudlyc (to speak) and the prefix wèmyçxyly- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In qmyxéqqxymyxypu, the stem -myxypu indicates that the verb is dxymyxypu (to finish), the prefix -qqxy- precedes it, and the inflection qmyxé- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Bemyçdpu they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    dçsudlyc: qxylydçsudlyc çh, qlysudlyc rwè, wèmyçqqlysudlyc qsuxy'rn, qmyxéxysudlyc qrxémy çrn, joçsudlyc...
    dxymyxypu: qxylydxymyxypu çh, qçwèîmyxypu qrxéz, wèmyçqqxymyxypu qsuxy'rn, qxymyxypu, qmyxéxyqqxymyxypu qrxémy çrn...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    dxyxésurxéz: vrçz çh, vrçz rwè, wèrçz suxy, qmyxésurxéz qrxémy, joçsurxéz qrxéz, wèmyçsurçz qsuxy.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly dxyxézly, çdwèê, dçsusuly and çdxylypu), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with dç- (with the exception of dçsusuly, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    dçtxyly, dçxèlysulyfy, dçwèmylybe, dçxèxézmyç, dçtdçpu, dçgmylyt, dçqqlyc, dçxèlyc, dçmyçtxédc, dçpédlygçd, etc.

        For example, for the verb dçsudlyc, the stem is -sudlyc and the infinitive prefix is dç-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with dxy- whose present participle begins with wèmylyqqxy-:

    dxymyafy, dxywèlyctxée, dxycdçrgapé, dxydrçsupu, dxypémylydg, dïlyb, dxywèqçzmyxy, dxysuxéc, dxygrxéd, dxygrd, dxysulyq, etc.

        For example, for the verb dxymyxypu, the stem is -myxypu and the infinitive prefix is dxy-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries çdwèê and dxyxézly, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. çpédlygçd çh means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with dxy- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): qxy-, qxy-, wèxy-, qmyxéqqxy-, joçqqxy-, wèmyçqqxy-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with çd- (part of the third group): q-, q-, - , qmyxé-, joç-, wèmyç-.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "qxylypédlygçd çh" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the dç- prefix, e.g., dçpédlygçd -> -pédlygçd.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the dxy- prefix plus the qqxy- prefix, e.g., dxyqxyxébe -> -qqxyqxyxébe. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: qxyly-, qxyly-, wèxyly-, qmyxéxy-, joçxy-, wèmyçxyly-.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding ç- and q- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "wèxypumyxée wèxyrdpu myr", "çwèxypumyxée çdxyxéc çmyr", "qwèxypumyxée qwèxyrdpu qçpé", and "qçwèxypumyxée qçdxyxéc qçpé."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with a- for the 1st group verbs, and with xy- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : r- (çdpémyçwèmyç rpémyçwèmyç, çdxyxéfy rfy, çdxysu rsu, etc. and dxyxézlyq rq, dxyxéz rz, dxyxézrxéc rc), qxy- (çdwèwèçt qxyt, çdpémyçdc qxydc, etc.), qr- (çdrsuemyxy qrsuemyxy and çdrsueçd qrsueçd and only these verbs), wèxy- (çdxypérlyt wèxypérlyt, çdxypé wèxypé, etc.), wè- (verbs in çdpémyxy- : çdpémyxyçc wèmyxyçc), wèdç- (dxydzrxé wèdçzrxé, dxydzrxée wèdçzrxée, dxydpupuxé wèdçpupuxé and dxydpupurxéq wèdçpupurxéq), or rç (dxyxézly rç). 

*Compound Tenses

bemyçdpu compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either dxyxézly or çdwèê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Bemyçdpu, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Bemyçdpu. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either dxyxézly or çdwèê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "agmylyt xyly'h" (I ate) or "azxyddly wèqç suxy" (He arrived). dxyxézly is used with most verbs, while çdwèê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, dxyxézly should be used by default.

Example:

Verbs in Mewigwejz are conjugated to reflect the following information:

In Mewigwejz, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

véféñeñiq has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Véféñeñiq, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Véféñeñiq article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is eñy. For example, in the phrase "nezvéf eñy" (the cat), eñy shows that the noun nezvéf (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is ezy. An example is "éñgktezép ezy" (the house), where ezy shows that éñgktezép (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is keñy for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "knezvéf keñy", the cats; "kéñgktezép keñy", the houses.)

In summary, eñy is used with masculine singular nouns, ezy with feminine singular nouns, and keñy with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Véféñeñiq.

After ez, eñ, t, g, ac, u, ém, x and some occurrences of v, the singular masculine article eñy becomes 'y.


-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Véféñeñiq noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Véféñeñiq nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme k- (e.g., éñgktezép > kéñgktezép 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with acez- and aceñ- take the prefix ab- instead of k- (e.g., acezuacn > abacezuacn 'pipes', aceñéc > abaceñéc 'games'), except for the nouns acezoñéñezy, aceziiezk, aceñéñéj, and aceñyoz which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme k- (e.g., aceñéñéj > kaceñéñéj 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with acg- form their plural with ab-. These are acgéñeñw, acgyytezéf, acgoztv, acgéctoz, acgéj, acgvéf, and acgécacgéc (e.g., acgéñeñw > abacgéñeñw 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with acg-, such as acgktoz or acgin, follow the regular plural pattern and take k- (e.g., acgin > kacgin 'holes').

Nouns that begin with k-, ab- or ef- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., abtgiéf ezy 'the cross' > abtgiéf keñy 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with yez- typically change to abacez- in the plural (e.g., yezéñiacgéc > abacezéñiacgéc 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with yez- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding k- instead. These are yezoz, yezéf, yezdezéñiezéf, yezéfezvéf, yezdtnkeñq, yezntéfémi, yezdieñk and yezwémi (e.g., yezdtnkeñq eñy > kyezdtnkeñq keñy).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with ytez- change to abacez- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include ytezoz, ytezigéf, ytezépém, ytezitéjacgk, ytezdezin, and ytezintd (e.g., ytezintd éñac > abacezintd keñoñ 'stained-glass windows'). However, some ytez- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with k-, notably ytezi, ytezitnnez, ytezoñéñezvéf, yteznémoñ, ytezéñieñdacgw and yteznigéj (e.g., ytezi eñy > kytezi keñy 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Véféñeñiq are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Véféñeñiq adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like acezeñoz and acezeñdacgéñ, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in ez, eñ, t, g, ac, u, ém, x and some occurrences of v, e.g. éñtoñiezéc acezeñoz éñac (a beautiful garden), eñépépgv yeñoz éñac (a handsome man), eñépépeñq eñyyeñoz eñéñac (a beautiful woman), knéñezqéñeñ abacezeñoz keñy (the beautiful children), kéñgktezép keñyyeñoz keñy (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix eñ- to the masculine form, e.g., oñéñeziw > eñoñéñeziw, néñeñy > eñnéñeñy, éñezkieñéj > eñéñezkieñéj. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with yeñ-, yt-, éñg-, éñeñ-, kg- or kez- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix eñ- (e.g., yeñaciéf > eñyyeñaciéf, ytnéñeñw > eñyytnéñeñw, éñgoz > eñéñéñgoz, éñeñtéféñez > eñéñéñeñtéféñez, kgiw > eñkkgiw, and kezoz > eñkkezoz).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with éf- change to eñvéf- (e.g., éféñezyoz > eñvéféñezyoz); those beginning with iaceñ- or abaceñ- change to eñkaceñ- (e.g., iaceñnneñépgiéj > eñkaceñnneñépgiéj, abaceñtiacq > eñkaceñtiacq), with the exception of the irregular abaceñtd (old) whose feminine form is eñyyteñtd; w- changes to eñacw- (e.g., wéñgy > eñacwéñgy); qt- changes to eñdt- (e.g., qtnéfez > eñdtnéfez); qeñ- changes to eñdx- (e.g., qeñioz > eñdxioz); ieñ- changes to eñix- (e.g., ieñwéñeziném > eñixwéñeziném); neñ- changes to eñnx- (e.g., neñtacðéñt > eñnxtacðéñt); and adjectives beginning with acg- have a special form yg- (becoming eñyyg- in feminine) that appears after ez, eñ, t, g, ac, u, ém, x and some occurrences of v, (e.g., acgq/ygq > eñyygq, acgép/ygép > eñyygép).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with eñ-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. eñvéfti eñépépgv éñac 'a rich man' > eñvéfti eñépépeñq eñéñac 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix k- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., tygéc > ktygéc, eñtygéc > keñtygéc). If the basic form beginning with k-, ab-, or ef-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., kezoz > kezoz, abaceñiéméñémw > abaceñiéméñémw, abacgoñ > abacgoñ), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Véféñeñiq adjectives beginning with acezeñ- take the prefix ab- in the masculine plural (e.g., acezeñdacgéñ > abacezeñdacgéñ). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with yez-, which normally change to abacez- in the masculine plural (e.g., yezéñieñdtv > abacezéñieñdtv, yezinéñeñéf > abacezinéñeñéf), with only two exceptions: yeznezq > kyeznezq and yezdezéñ > kyezdezéñ which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: eñyezinéñeñéf > keñyezinéñeñéf.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in eñwacgi eñy éñtd (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are acezeñoz (beautiful), éñgoz (good), qeñioz (brief), oñéñeziw (big/tall), kgiw (fat/large), abacezq (false), nacezv (high), wéñgy (long), qeñioz (brief), eñéñaceñéc (young), tygéc (pretty), ktezdacezép (bad), iaceñyyteñép (better), acezeñdacgéñ (new), ntneñéj (small), abaceñtd (old); e.g., eñépépeñq eñéñac eñyyeñoz ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Véféñeñiq, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
véféñeñiq personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | eñéc
         | 2nd (informal)   | acn
         | 2nd (formal)     | kacgd
         | 3rd (masculine)  | yt
         | 3rd (feminine)   | eñyyeñ
         | 3rd (neutral)    | éñg
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | kacgéñ
         | 2nd              | kacgd
         | 3rd (masculine)  | kyt
         | 3rd (feminine)   | keñyyeñ
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun eñéc occurs after ez, eñ, t, g, ac, u, ém, x, ê and some occurrences of v, it becomes 'éc.

*Relative pronouns

véféñeñiq, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Véféñeñiq, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, tacð is ordinarily used: eñnneñyéfuéftoz ezép émygd ez tacð eñépépgv'y ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that tacð in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: keñémygd émném néñg tacð keñnneñyéfuéftoz keñy ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, eñacð (or 'acð after ez, eñ, t, g, ac, u, ém, x, ê and some occurrences of v) is ordinarily used: eñémygd ez yt'acð eñnneñyéfuéftoz ezy ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like tacð, eñacð does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Véféñeñiq are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Véféñeñiq is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) itgdez ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of eñinê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is eñinê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is itgdez. Forms of eñinê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Véféñeñiq, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

véféñeñiq verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -kkt- between the stem and the ending.

    In néñeñtezyiezéj, the stem -yiezéj indicates that the verb is ieñyiezéj (to speak) and the prefix néñeñtez- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In kéñgkktéñtq, the stem -éñtq indicates that the verb is itéñtq (to finish), the prefix -kkt- precedes it, and the inflection kéñg- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Véféñeñiq they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ieñyiezéj: ktezieñyiezéj eñéc, kezyiezéj acn, néñeñkkezyiezéj kyt'acð, kéñgtyiezéj kacgéñ eñacð, efeñyiezéj...
    itéñtq: ktezitéñtq eñéc, keñnîéñtq kacgd, néñeñkktéñtq kyt'acð, ktéñtq, kéñgtkktéñtq kacgéñ eñacð...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    itgyacgd: abaceñd eñéc, abaceñd acn, naceñd yt, kéñgyacgd kacgéñ, efeñyacgd kacgd, néñeñyaceñd kyt.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly itgdez, eñinê, ieñyyez and eñitezq), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with ieñ- (with the exception of ieñyyez, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ieñéptez, ieñuezyezoz, ieñnéñezvéf, ieñugdéñeñ, ieñépieñq, ieñwéñezép, ieñkkezéj, ieñuezéj, ieñéñeñépgiéj, ieñoñiezweñi, etc.

        For example, for the verb ieñyiezéj, the stem is -yiezéj and the infinitive prefix is ieñ-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with it- whose present participle begins with néñezkkt-:

    itéñémoz, itnezéjépgéf, itéjieñacwémoñ, itiaceñyq, itoñéñeziw, iïezv, itnkeñdéñt, itygéj, itwacgi, itwaci, ityezk, etc.

        For example, for the verb itéñtq, the stem is -éñtq and the infinitive prefix is it-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries eñinê and itgdez, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. eñoñiezweñi eñéc means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with ieñ- (all verbs of the first group): eñ-, keñ-, eñ-, kéñg-, efeñ-, néñeñ-.
    Verbs beginning with it- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): kt-, kt-, nt-, kéñgkkt-, efeñkkt-, néñeñkkt-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with eñi- (part of the third group): k-, k-, - , kéñg-, efeñ-, néñeñ-.
    
    Example:
