**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding f- and g- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "mizukedépéb mizquçuk edq", "fmizukedépéb fuçizépoç fedq", "gmizukedépéb gmizquçuk gfa", and "gfmizukedépéb gfuçizépoç gfa."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with uh- for the 1st group verbs, and with iz- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : q- (fuçaedfmedf qaedfmedf, fuçizépj qj, fuçizéw qéw, etc. and uçizépikédg qg, uçizépik qik, uçizépikqépoç qoç), giz- (fuçmmfeh gizeh, fuçaedfuçoç gizuçoç, etc.), gq- (fuçqéwébediz gqéwébediz and fuçqéwébfuç gqéwébfuç and only these verbs), miz- (fuçizaqédeh mizaqédeh, fuçiza miza, etc.), m- (verbs in fuçaediz- : fuçaedizfoç medizfoç), muçf- (uçizuçikqép muçfikqép, uçizuçikqépéb muçfikqépéb, uçizuçukukép muçfukukép and uçizuçukukqépg muçfukukqépg), or qf (uçizépikéd qf). 

*Compound Tenses

èébedfuçuk compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either uçizépikéd or fuçmê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Èébedfuçuk, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Èébedfuçuk. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either uçizépikéd or fuçmê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "uhudedédeh izéd'y" (I ate) or "uhikizuçuçéd mgf éwiz" (He arrived). uçizépikéd is used with most verbs, while fuçmê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, uçizépikéd should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Èébedfuçuk: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is uçizépikéd.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears before the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) izehuçépa medép gféwéwf. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object before verb) gfedizféwédj ñqfa qik éd fuçizédéwéb. ("fuçizédéwéb saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears after the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun after the auxiliary) gfedizféwédj ñqfa mizédikéd eç éwiz. gfqik éd gféw fuçizédéwéb. ("There were two whales. fuçizédéwéb saw them.")
        (clause-final wh-question element)  gfqik féwéwf-m-éd fuçizédéwéb gfedizféwédj gféwéwfqob? ("Which whales did fuçizédéwéb see?")
        (relative clause linked by fqob) gfqik éd fuçizédéwéb fqob gfedizféwédj ñqfa gféw ("the two whales that fuçizédéwéb saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Èébedfuçuk.

B. The auxiliary is fuçmê, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        gfuhikizuçuçéd medépg gféwéwf. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is fuçmê and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with uçizépikéd in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears before the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) uhauhébébqg medépg fg gféwéwf. uhéwuçédoç gfehehépg gqéped gqéped. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object before verb) gedépizmgfqob gfa uhgépoç medépg fg gféwéwf. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears after the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Mèrezdnc adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like çfdmé and çfdlçwz, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in f, d, o, w, ç, té, bà, rè and some occurrences of mè, e.g. zosnfu çfdmé zç (a beautiful garden), diiwmè jydmé zç (a handsome man), diidc djyjydmé dzç (a beautiful woman), vypyzfczd vàçfdmé vydjy (the beautiful children), vyzwvyofi vydjyjydmé vydjy (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix d- to the masculine form, e.g., szfng > dszfng, pyzdjy > dpyzdjy, zfvyndmà > dzfvyndmà. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with jyd-, jyo-, zw-, zd-, vyw- or vyf- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix d- (e.g., jydçnre > djyjydçnre, jyopyzdg > djyjyopyzdg, zwmé > dzzwmé, zdorezf > dzzdorezf, vywng > dvyvywng, and vyfmé > dvyvyfmé).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with re- change to dmère- (e.g., rezfjymé > dmèrezfjymé); those beginning with nçd- or vàçd- change to dvyçd- (e.g., nçdpypydiwnmà > dvyçdpypydiwnmà, vàçdonçc > dvyçdonçc), with the exception of the irregular vàçdol (old) whose feminine form is djyjyodol; g- changes to dçg- (e.g., gzwjy > dçgzwjy); co- changes to dlo- (e.g., copyref > dlopyref); cd- changes to dlrè- (e.g., cdnmé > dlrènmé); nd- changes to dnrè- (e.g., ndgzfnpybà > dnrègzfnpybà); pyd- changes to dpyrè- (e.g., pydoçkèzo > dpyrèoçkèzo); and adjectives beginning with çw- have a special form jyw- (becoming djyjyw- in feminine) that appears after f, d, o, w, ç, té, bà, rè and some occurrences of mè, (e.g., çwc/jywc > djyjywc, çwi/jywi > djyjywi).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with d-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. dmèreon diiwmè zç 'a rich man' > dmèreon diidc dzç 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix vy- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., ojywu > vyojywu, dojywu > vydojywu). If the basic form beginning with vy-, và-, or a-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., vyfmé > vyfmé, vàçdnbàzbàg > vàçdnbàzbàg, vàçws > vàçws), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Mèrezdnc adjectives beginning with çfd- take the prefix và- in the masculine plural (e.g., çfdlçwz > vàçfdlçwz). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with jyf-, which normally change to vàçf- in the masculine plural (e.g., jyfzndlomè > vàçfzndlomè, jyfnpyzdre > vàçfnpyzdre), with only two exceptions: jyfpyfc > vyjyfpyfc and jyflfz > vyjyflfz which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: djyfnpyzdre > vydjyfnpyzdre.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in dgçwn djy zol (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are çfdmé (beautiful), zwmé (good), cdnmé (brief), szfng (big/tall), vywng (fat/large), vàçfc (false), pyçfmè (high), gzwjy (long), cdnmé (brief), dzçdu (young), ojywu (pretty), vyoflçfi (bad), nçdjyjyodi (better), çfdlçwz (new), pyopydmà (small), vàçdol (old); e.g., diidc dzç djyjydmé ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Mèrezdnc, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
mèrezdnc personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | du
         | 2nd (informal)   | çpy
         | 2nd (formal)     | vyçwl
         | 3rd (masculine)  | jyo
         | 3rd (feminine)   | djyjyd
         | 3rd (neutral)    | zw
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | vyçwz
         | 2nd              | vyçwl
         | 3rd (masculine)  | vyjyo
         | 3rd (feminine)   | vydjyjyd
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun du occurs after f, d, o, w, ç, té, bà, rè, ê and some occurrences of mè, it becomes 'u.

*Relative pronouns

mèrezdnc, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Mèrezdnc, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, oçkè is ordinarily used: dpypydjyretéreomé fi bàjywl f oçkè diiwmè'jy ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that oçkè in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: vydbàjywl bàpybà pyzw oçkè vydpypydjyretéreomé vydjy ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, dçkè (or 'çkè after f, d, o, w, ç, té, bà, rè, ê and some occurrences of mè) is ordinarily used: dbàjywl f jyo'çkè dpypydjyretéreomé fjy ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like oçkè, dçkè does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Mèrezdnc are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Mèrezdnc is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) nowlf ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of dnpyê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is dnpyê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is nowlf. Forms of dnpyê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Mèrezdnc, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

mèrezdnc verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -vyvyo- between the stem and the ending.

    In pyzdofjynfmà, the stem -jynfmà indicates that the verb is ndjynfmà (to speak) and the prefix pyzdof- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In vyzwvyvyozoc, the stem -zoc indicates that the verb is nozoc (to finish), the prefix -vyvyo- precedes it, and the inflection vyzw- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Mèrezdnc they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ndjynfmà: vyofndjynfmà du, vyfjynfmà çpy, pyzdvyvyfjynfmà vyjyo'çkè, vyzwojynfmà vyçwz dçkè, adjynfmà...
    nozoc: vyofnozoc du, vydpyîzoc vyçwl, pyzdvyvyozoc vyjyo'çkè, vyozoc, vyzwovyvyozoc vyçwz dçkè...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    nowjyçwl: vàçdl du, vàçdl çpy, pyçdl jyo, vyzwjyçwl vyçwz, adjyçwl vyçwl, pyzdjyçdl vyjyo.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly nowlf, dnpyê, ndjyjyf and dnofc), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with nd- (with the exception of ndjyjyf, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ndiof, ndtéfjyfmé, ndpyzfmère, ndtéwlzd, ndindc, ndgzfi, ndvyvyfmà, ndtéfmà, ndzdiwnmà, ndsnfgdn, etc.

        For example, for the verb ndjynfmà, the stem is -jynfmà and the infinitive prefix is nd-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with no- whose present participle begins with pyzfvyvyo-:

    nozbàmé, nopyfmàiwre, nomàndçgbàs, nonçdjyc, noszfng, nïfmè, nopyvydlzo, nojywmà, nogçwn, nogçn, nojyfvy, etc.

        For example, for the verb nozoc, the stem is -zoc and the infinitive prefix is no-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries dnpyê and nowlf, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. dsnfgdn du means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with nd- (all verbs of the first group): d-, vyd-, d-, vyzw-, ad-, pyzd-.
    Verbs beginning with no- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): vyo-, vyo-, pyo-, vyzwvyvyo-, advyvyo-, pyzdvyvyo-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with dn- (part of the third group): vy-, vy-, - , vyzw-, ad-, pyzd-.

2nd person     | vydsnfgdn çpy        | adsnfgdn vyçwl

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "vyofsnfgdn du" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the nd- prefix, e.g., ndsnfgdn -> -snfgdn.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the no- prefix plus the vyvyo- prefix, e.g., novyowmère -> -vyvyovyowmère. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: vyof-, vyof-, pyof-, vyzwo-, ado-, pyzdof-.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding d- and vy- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "pyoczwre pyoçnc zç", "dpyoczwre dnowmà dzç", "vypyoczwre vypyoçnc vyds", and "vydpyoczwre vydnowmà vyds."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with bà- for the 1st group verbs, and with o- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : ç- (dnszdpyzd çszdpyzd, dnowmé çmé, dnojy çjy, etc. and nowlfvy çvy, nowl çl, nowlçwmà çmà), vyo- (dnpypydi vyoi, dnszdnmà vyonmà, etc.), vyç- (dnçjyrezo vyçjyrezo and dnçjyredn vyçjyredn and only these verbs), pyo- (dnosçfi pyosçfi, dnos pyos, etc.), py- (verbs in dnszo- : dnszodmà pyzodmà), pynd- (nonlçw pyndlçw, nonlçwre pyndlçwre, nonccw pyndccw and nonccçwvy pyndccçwvy), or çd (nowlf çd). 

*Compound Tenses

mèrezdnc compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either nowlf or dnpyê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Mèrezdnc, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Mèrezdnc. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either nowlf or dnpyê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "bàgzfi of'u" (I ate) or "bàlonnf pyvyd jyo" (He arrived). nowlf is used with most verbs, while dnpyê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, nowlf should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Mèrezdnc: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is nowlf.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears before the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) oinws pyzw vydjyjyd. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object before verb) vydzodjyfmé vàçds çl f dnofjyre. ("dnofjyre saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears after the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun after the auxiliary) vydzodjyfmé vàçds pyoflf té jyo. vydçl f vydjy dnofjyre. ("There were two whales. dnofjyre saw them.")
        (clause-final wh-question element)  vydçl djyjyd-py-f dnofjyre vydzodjyfmé vydjyjydçkè? ("Which whales did dnofjyre see?")
        (relative clause linked by dçkè) vydçl f dnofjyre dçkè vydzodjyfmé vàçds vydjy ("the two whales that dnofjyre saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Mèrezdnc.

B. The auxiliary is dnpyê, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        vydbàlonnf pyzwvy vydjyjyd. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is dnpyê and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with nowlf in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears before the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) bàsbàrereçvy pyzwvy dvy vydjyjyd. bàjynfmà vydiiwvy vyçwz vyçwz. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object before verb) vyzwopyvydçkè vyds bàvywmà pyzwvy dvy vydjyjyd. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears after the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) dpynfpy dzç pyofc of'u. dbàgfpynfmà pyzwvy fjy dvy vypyzfczd vydjy. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")
        (wh-question)  dbàgfpynfmà vyjyo-pyzwvy dvy dpynfpy djyjydçkè? ("Which pie did they share?")
        (dçkè relative) dbàgfpynfmà pyzwvy dvy vypyzfczd vydjy dçkè dpynfpy fjy ("the pie that the children shared")

    The reflexive pronoun can itself be the direct object, in which case the participle agrees with it (and therefore with the subject). This also includes "inherently reflexive" verbs, for which the reflexive pronoun cannot be interpreted semantically as an object (direct or indirect) of the verb.
        (ordinary reflexive) vydoloçvy pyzwvy dvy vydjyjyd. vybàçjyfvy vydiiwvy vyçwz vyçwz. ("They (fem.) followed each other. We greeted each other.")

All other nouns beginning with zg-, such as zgshud or zglemà, follow the regular plural pattern and take s- (e.g., zglemà > szglemà 'holes').

Nouns that begin with s-, i- or là- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., ihugleç mubà 'the cross' > ihugleç slobà 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with bàmu- typically change to izmu- in the plural (e.g., bàmuholezgv > izmuholezgv 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with bàmu- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding s- instead. These are bàmud, bàmuç, bàmuamuholemuç, bàmuçmuneç, bàmuahumàslop, bàmumàhuçlyle, bàmualelos and bàmuhàlyle (e.g., bàmuahumàslop lobà > sbàmuahumàslop slobà).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with bàhumu- change to izmu- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include bàhumud, bàhumulegç, bàhumumely, bàhumulehujezgs, bàhumuamulemà, and bàhumulemàhua (e.g., bàhumulemàhua hoz > izmulemàhua slot 'stained-glass windows'). However, some bàhumu- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with s-, notably bàhumule, bàhumulehumàmàmu, bàhumuthomuneç, bàhumumàlyt, bàhumuholeloazghà and bàhumumàlegje (e.g., bàhumule lobà > sbàhumule slobà 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Neçhololep are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Neçhololep adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like zmulod and zmuloazgho, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in mu, lo, hu, g, z, re, ly, x and some occurrences of ne, e.g. hohutlemuv zmulod hoz (a beautiful garden), lomemegne bàlod hoz (a handsome man), lomemelop lobàbàlod lohoz (a beautiful woman), smàhomupholo izmulod slobà (the beautiful children), shogshumume slobàbàlod slobà (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix lo- to the masculine form, e.g., thomulehà > lothomulehà, màholobà > lomàholobà, homusleloje > lohomusleloje. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with bàlo-, bàhu-, hog-, holo-, sg- or smu- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix lo- (e.g., bàlozleç > lobàbàlozleç, bàhumàholohà > lobàbàhumàholohà, hogd > lohohogd, holohuçhomu > lohoholohuçhomu, sglehà > lossglehà, and smud > lossmud).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with ç- change to loneç- (e.g., çhomubàd > loneçhomubàd); those beginning with lezlo- or izlo- change to loszlo- (e.g., lezlomàmàlomegleje > loszlomàmàlomegleje, izlohulezp > loszlohulezp), with the exception of the irregular izlohua (old) whose feminine form is lobàbàhulohua; hà- changes to lozhà- (e.g., hàhogbà > lozhàhogbà); phu- changes to loahu- (e.g., phumàçmu > loahumàçmu); plo- changes to loax- (e.g., ploled > loaxled); lelo- changes to lolex- (e.g., lelohàhomulemàly > lolexhàhomulemàly); màlo- changes to lomàx- (e.g., màlohuzkhohu > lomàxhuzkhohu); and adjectives beginning with zg- have a special form bàg- (becoming lobàbàg- in feminine) that appears after mu, lo, hu, g, z, re, ly, x and some occurrences of ne, (e.g., zgp/bàgp > lobàbàgp, zgme/bàgme > lobàbàgme).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with lo-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. loneçhule lomemegne hoz 'a rich man' > loneçhule lomemelop lohoz 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix s- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., hubàgv > shubàgv, lohubàgv > slohubàgv). If the basic form beginning with s-, i-, or là-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., smud > smud, izlolelyholyhà > izlolelyholyhà, izgt > izgt), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Neçhololep adjectives beginning with zmulo- take the prefix i- in the masculine plural (e.g., zmuloazgho > izmuloazgho). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with bàmu-, which normally change to izmu- in the masculine plural (e.g., bàmuholeloahune > izmuholeloahune, bàmulemàholoç > izmulemàholoç), with only two exceptions: bàmumàmup > sbàmumàmup and bàmuamuho > sbàmuamuho which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: lobàmulemàholoç > slobàmulemàholoç.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in lohàzgle lobà hohua (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically precede their nouns. These are zmulod (beautiful), hogd (good), ploled (brief), thomulehà (big/tall), sglehà (fat/large), izmup (false), màzmune (high), hàhogbà (long), ploled (brief), lohozlov (young), hubàgv (pretty), shumuazmume (bad), lezlobàbàhulome (better), zmuloazgho (new), màhumàloje (small), izlohua (old); e.g., lomemelop lohoz lobàbàlod ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Neçhololep, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
neçhololep personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | lov
         | 2nd (informal)   | zmà
         | 2nd (formal)     | szga
         | 3rd (masculine)  | bàhu
         | 3rd (feminine)   | lobàbàlo
         | 3rd (neutral)    | hog
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | szgho
         | 2nd              | szga
         | 3rd (masculine)  | sbàhu
         | 3rd (feminine)   | slobàbàlo
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun lov occurs after mu, lo, hu, g, z, re, ly, x, ê and some occurrences of ne, it becomes 'v.

*Relative pronouns

neçhololep, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Neçhololep, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, huzk is ordinarily used: lomàmàlobàçreçhud mume lybàga mu huzk lomemegne'bà ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that huzk in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: slolybàga lymàly màhog huzk slomàmàlobàçreçhud slobà ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, lozk (or 'zk after mu, lo, hu, g, z, re, ly, x, ê and some occurrences of ne) is ordinarily used: lolybàga mu bàhu'zk lomàmàlobàçreçhud mubà ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like huzk, lozk does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Neçhololep are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Neçhololep is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) lehugamu ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of lolemàê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is lolemàê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is lehugamu. Forms of lolemàê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Neçhololep, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

neçhololep verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -sshu- between the stem and the ending.

    In màholohumubàlemuje, the stem -bàlemuje indicates that the verb is lelobàlemuje (to speak) and the prefix màholohumu- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In shogsshuhohup, the stem -hohup indicates that the verb is lehuhohup (to finish), the prefix -sshu- precedes it, and the inflection shog- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Neçhololep they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    lelobàlemuje: shumulelobàlemuje lov, smubàlemuje zmà, màholossmubàlemuje sbàhu'zk, shoghubàlemuje szgho lozk, làlobàlemuje...
    lehuhohup: shumulehuhohup lov, slomàîhohup szga, màholosshuhohup sbàhu'zk, shuhohup, shoghusshuhohup szgho lozk...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    lehugbàzga: izloa lov, izloa zmà, màzloa bàhu, shogbàzga szgho, làlobàzga szga, màholobàzloa sbàhu.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly lehugamu, lolemàê, lelobàbàmu and lolehumup), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with lelo- (with the exception of lelobàbàmu, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    lelomehumu, leloremubàmud, lelomàhomuneç, leloregaholo, lelomelelop, lelohàhomume, lelossmuje, leloremuje, leloholomegleje, lelotlemuhàlole, etc.

        For example, for the verb lelobàlemuje, the stem is -bàlemuje and the infinitive prefix is lelo-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with lehu- whose present participle begins with màhomusshu-:

    lehuholyd, lehumàmujemegç, lehujelelozhàlyt, lehulezlobàp, lehuthomulehà, leïmune, lehumàsloahohu, lehubàgje, lehuhàzgle, lehuhàzle, lehubàmus, etc.

        For example, for the verb lehuhohup, the stem is -hohup and the infinitive prefix is lehu-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries lolemàê and lehugamu, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. lotlemuhàlole lov means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with lelo- (all verbs of the first group): lo-, slo-, lo-, shog-, làlo-, màholo-.
    Verbs beginning with lehu- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): shu-, shu-, màhu-, shogsshu-, làlosshu-, màholosshu-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with lole- (part of the third group): s-, s-, - , shog-, làlo-, màholo-.
    
    Example:

-------------------------------

2nd person     | slotlemuhàlole zmà        | làlotlemuhàlole szga
3rd person     | lotlemuhàlole hog/lobàbàlo/bàhu | màholotlemuhàlole slobàbàlo/sbàhu
-------------------------------

-------------------------------

2nd person     | shushugneç zmà         | làlosshushugneç szga
3rd person     | màhushugneç hog/lobàbàlo/bàhu | màholosshushugneç slobàbàlo/sbàhu

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "shumutlemuhàlole lov" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the lelo- prefix, e.g., lelotlemuhàlole -> -tlemuhàlole.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the lehu- prefix plus the sshu- prefix, e.g., lehushugneç -> -sshushugneç. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: shumu-, shumu-, màhumu-, shoghu-, làlohu-, màholohumu-.

**Future

The future prefixes correspond to the present indicative of the verb lehugamu. They are always regular: humu-, smu-, mu-, shog-, làlo-, màhog-.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding lo- and s- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "màhuphogç màhuzlep hoz", "lomàhuphogç lolehugje lohoz", "smàhuphogç smàhuzlep slot", and "slomàhuphogç slolehugje slot."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with ly- for the 1st group verbs, and with hu- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : z- (loletholomàholo ztholomàholo, lolehugd zd, lolehubà zbà, etc. and lehugamus zs, lehuga za, lehugazgje zje), shu- (lolemàmàlome shume, lolethololeje shuleje, etc.), sz- (lolezbàçhohu szbàçhohu and lolezbàçlole szbàçlole and only these verbs), màhu- (lolehutzmume màhutzmume, lolehut màhut, etc.), mà- (verbs in lolethohu- : lolethohuloje màhohuloje), màlelo- (lehuleazg màleloazg, lehuleazgç màleloazgç, lehuleppg màleloppg and lehuleppzgs màleloppzgs), or zlo (lehugamu zlo). 

*Compound Tenses

neçhololep compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either lehugamu or lolemàê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Neçhololep, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Neçhololep. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either lehugamu or lolemàê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "lyhàhomume humu'v" (I ate) or "lyahulelemu màslo bàhu" (He arrived). lehugamu is used with most verbs, while lolemàê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, lehugamu should be used by default.

3rd person     | lytlemuhàlole mu hog/lobàbàlo/bàhu       | lytlemuhàlole màhog slobàbàlo/sbàhu

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Neçhololep: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is lehugamu.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears before the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
